text:
The four levels
This handbook explains machine-learning concepts at four levels of depth. Each lesson begins with an accessible explanation and then progressively adds mechanism, mathematics, code, and modern systems context.

title: Machine Learning Concepts
text:
How to use this book
You can read every level in sequence, or stop when the explanation reaches the depth you need. The code examples are intentionally small: their purpose is to make the underlying mechanism visible before introducing framework abstractions.
This prototype follows a dependency chain:

Gradient descent explains how parameters are updated.
Backpropagation explains how gradients are computed.
The artificial neuron provides the model whose parameters are trained.

text: Chapter orientation

title: What Is Machine Learning?
text:
Why this chapter matters
Machine learning is often described as a system that “learns from data”. That phrase is useful, but incomplete. A machine-learning system does not learn in the human sense. It is given examples, a representation of those examples, an objective, and a procedure for changing its parameters. The result is a function that can produce outputs for new inputs.
This chapter establishes the vocabulary needed for the rest of the book. It also introduces a discipline that will recur throughout: a model’s quality depends not only on its algorithm, but on the question, data, target, evaluation procedure, and setting in which its predictions will be used.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish explicit rules from patterns estimated from data;
identify observations, features, labels, predictions, parameters, and hyperparameters;
describe training, validation, testing, and inference;
distinguish supervised, unsupervised, and generative learning settings;
calculate simple regression and classification metrics;
explain overfitting and generalisation;
identify data leakage and distribution shift;
distinguish a predictive question from a causal question.



Running example: programme uptake
Suppose an organisation wants to estimate whether a household will take up a programme if it is offered. For each household, we might observe:










Household
Age of respondent
Distance to service point
Prior participation
Took up programme?




A
24
2.1 km
0
1


B
58
18.4 km
1
0


C
37
5.8 km
1
1



The first three columns are features: inputs used to make a prediction. The final column is a label: the outcome we want to predict. A model may learn that distance, age, and previous participation are associated with uptake. It does not follow a rule written by an analyst; it estimates parameters from examples.
This example is deliberately limited. A prediction of uptake is not an estimate of whether offering the programme causes uptake. That distinction becomes important when we discuss causal inference and responsible deployment.


The prediction problem comes before the algorithm
A prediction is defined by more than its label. We also need to specify when the prediction is made, for whom it is made, what information is available at that point, and what action may follow from it. “Will this household take up the programme?” is incomplete unless we say whether the prediction is made before contact, after an information session, or after an application has been submitted.
This timing determines which features are legitimate. An application outcome may be highly predictive after an application has been processed, but it cannot be used to decide whom to contact before the application exists. A variable can therefore be statistically useful and operationally invalid at the same time.
The target also needs a precise definition. “Take-up” might mean attending once, completing a programme, receiving a transfer, or remaining enrolled after six months. These outcomes are related but not interchangeable. Changing the label changes the problem the model is solving.


A model is a conditional statement
In the running example, a prediction model estimates a relationship of the form:
\[
P(Y=1\mid X=x),
\]
the probability of observing uptake for cases with observed characteristics \(x\). This is a conditional prediction, not a statement that changing one feature will change the outcome. The distinction is easy to lose because the same variables can appear in both predictive and causal analyses.
For prediction, a feature is valuable when it improves out-of-sample forecasts. For causal analysis, a variable must be connected to a design and assumptions that identify a counterfactual comparison. A model can predict well while offering no credible estimate of what would happen if a programme were offered to a different household.

Machine learning. A procedure that fits a parameterised mapping from inputs to outputs using examples and a stated objective. Training changes the fitted parameters; inference applies the resulting model to new inputs. A prediction can be useful without establishing that its inputs cause the outcome.

title: What Is Machine Learning?
text:
Level 1 - Intuition




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue, teal, orange = "#24527a", "#3a9188", "#d97745"
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.2))
positive = rng.multivariate_normal([6.5, 6], [[1.2, 0.3], [0.3, 1.0]], 45)
negative = rng.multivariate_normal([3.5, 3.4], [[1.0, 0.1], [0.1, 1.1]], 45)
new_case = np.array([5.8, 5.2])
ax.scatter(negative[:, 0], negative[:, 1], color=blue, alpha=0.65, label="examples: no uptake")
ax.scatter(positive[:, 0], positive[:, 1], color=orange, alpha=0.65, label="examples: uptake")
ax.scatter(*new_case, color=teal, edgecolor="white", linewidth=1.5, s=120, marker="*", label="new case")
ax.set(xlabel="Feature 1", ylabel="Feature 2", title="Examples provide a pattern for a new prediction")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 2.1



The model does not memorise a label for the new case. It uses the relationship estimated from the examples to assign a prediction.
The figure shows the basic inferential move made by a prediction model. The coloured points are cases for which the outcome is known. The star is a case for which the outcome is not yet known. The model uses the position of the star relative to the observed pattern to produce an output. The output may be a class, a number, or a probability. It is not a statement that the features caused the outcome.
The model can be wrong in at least two ways. It can miss a pattern that is present in the data, or it can treat a pattern in the development data as if it would continue in new data when it will not. The first problem concerns fitting; the second concerns generalisation. Both are part of the learning problem.

Rules written by people
Traditional software is usually specified as a sequence of instructions. For example:
if distance < 5 km and prior participation = 1:
    predict high uptake
else:
    predict low uptake
The analyst writes the rule, and the computer applies it. If the rule is wrong, the analyst must change it.


Patterns estimated from examples
In machine learning, we provide examples and ask the system to estimate a useful mapping. The model might represent the mapping as a weighted combination of features, a tree of decisions, or a neural network. The computer does not receive a complete list of rules. It receives an objective—make predictions that agree with observed outcomes—and adjusts internal parameters to improve that objective.
The distinction is not absolute. People still choose the data, define the target, choose the model family, and decide how predictions will be used. Machine learning automates part of the pattern-finding process; it does not remove human judgement from the system.




Code
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

rng_rule = np.random.default_rng(17)
n_households = 180
age_rule = rng_rule.uniform(18, 70, n_households)
distance_rule = rng_rule.uniform(0, 20, n_households)
uptake_probability = 1 / (
    1 + np.exp(-(1.5 - 0.18 * distance_rule + 0.035 * (age_rule - 40)))
)
uptake_rule = rng_rule.binomial(1, uptake_probability)

rule_features = np.column_stack([age_rule, distance_rule])
learned_boundary = LogisticRegression().fit(rule_features, uptake_rule)

age_grid = np.linspace(18, 70, 220)
distance_grid = np.linspace(0, 20, 220)
age_mesh, distance_mesh = np.meshgrid(age_grid, distance_grid)
grid_features = np.column_stack([age_mesh.ravel(), distance_mesh.ravel()])

written_predictions = (distance_mesh < 8).astype(int)
learned_predictions = learned_boundary.predict(grid_features).reshape(age_mesh.shape)

region_colours = ["#dce8f2", "#f8e1d5"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.3), sharex=True, sharey=True)

for ax, regions, panel_title in [
    (axes[0], written_predictions, "Hand-written rule: distance < 8 km"),
    (axes[1], learned_predictions, "Pattern estimated from examples"),
]:
    ax.contourf(
        age_mesh,
        distance_mesh,
        regions,
        levels=[-0.5, 0.5, 1.5],
        colors=region_colours,
        alpha=0.85,
    )
    ax.contour(
        age_mesh,
        distance_mesh,
        regions,
        levels=[0.5],
        colors=[teal],
        linewidths=2.2,
    )
    ax.scatter(
        age_rule[uptake_rule == 0],
        distance_rule[uptake_rule == 0],
        color=blue,
        marker="o",
        s=24,
        alpha=0.68,
        edgecolor="white",
        linewidth=0.4,
    )
    ax.scatter(
        age_rule[uptake_rule == 1],
        distance_rule[uptake_rule == 1],
        color=orange,
        marker="^",
        s=30,
        alpha=0.72,
        edgecolor="white",
        linewidth=0.4,
    )
    ax.set_title(panel_title)
    ax.set_xlabel("Age of respondent")

axes[0].set_ylabel("Distance to service point (km)")
legend_handles = [
    Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", color="none", markerfacecolor=blue,
           markeredgecolor="white", markersize=7, label="Observed: no uptake"),
    Line2D([0], [0], marker="^", color="none", markerfacecolor=orange,
           markeredgecolor="white", markersize=8, label="Observed: uptake"),
    Line2D([0], [0], color=teal, linewidth=2.2, label="Prediction boundary"),
]
fig.legend(handles=legend_handles, loc="lower center", ncol=3, frameon=False,
           bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.03))
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.08, 1, 1])
plt.show()



Figure 2.2



Both panels use the same illustrative observations. In the left panel, the analyst decides in advance that distance alone determines the prediction. The boundary is therefore horizontal: age cannot alter the decision. In the right panel, a logistic model estimates how both age and distance separate the observed classes. Its angled boundary reflects the fitted association in these examples. Neither boundary is a causal claim, and the fitted boundary is not automatically preferable; it must still be evaluated on cases that were not used to estimate it.


Prediction is not understanding
A model can produce useful predictions without possessing a human-like explanation of the world. It may exploit regularities that are stable enough in the data but accidental, unfair, or fragile outside that setting. This is why evaluation must ask more than “does the model fit the examples?” It must ask whether the predictions remain useful for the intended population and decision.

title: What Is Machine Learning?
text:
Level 2 - Mechanics




Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 2.2))
ax.text(0.12, 0.5, "features\n(age, distance, prior participation)", ha="center", va="center", color="white", weight="bold",
        bbox={"boxstyle": "round,pad=0.6", "facecolor": blue})
ax.text(0.50, 0.5, "fitted\nmodel", ha="center", va="center", color="white", weight="bold",
        bbox={"boxstyle": "round,pad=0.6", "facecolor": teal})
ax.text(0.86, 0.5, "prediction\nP(uptake)", ha="center", va="center", color="white", weight="bold",
        bbox={"boxstyle": "round,pad=0.6", "facecolor": orange})
ax.annotate("", xy=(0.39, 0.5), xytext=(0.27, 0.5), arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "lw": 2, "color": "#666666"})
ax.annotate("", xy=(0.76, 0.5), xytext=(0.62, 0.5), arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "lw": 2, "color": "#666666"})
ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 2.3



The diagram separates three operations that are often compressed into the word “model”. The features are the information available at prediction time. The fitted model is the function whose parameters were estimated using training data. The prediction is the output for this particular case. The arrows indicate computation, not causation: they show how information is transformed into an output.

The basic objects
An ML dataset can be represented as a table with \(n\) observations and \(p\) features. Let:

\(x_i\) be the feature vector for observation \(i\);
\(y_i\) be its observed label or target;
\(f_\theta\) be a model with parameters \(\theta\);
\(\hat{y}_i=f_\theta(x_i)\) be the model’s prediction.

The model is trained by comparing predictions with labels and changing \(\theta\) so that the discrepancy becomes smaller. A parameter is learned from the training data. A hyperparameter is chosen by the analyst or training procedure, such as a learning rate, tree depth, or regularisation strength.
The notation records the same sequence as the diagram. \(x_i\) is the information entering the model for case \(i\). The function \(f_\theta\) is the fitted rule. Applying that function to \(x_i\) produces \(\hat y_i\), the prediction. The observed \(y_i\) is then used to assess the prediction during training or evaluation. The notation does not imply that \(x_i\) causes \(y_i\); it specifies how the prediction problem is represented.


What the model can and cannot learn
The model only has access to the information encoded in the training data and representation. If distance to a service point is measured poorly, the model receives a noisy version of that feature. If prior participation is missing for households who moved between administrative systems, the missingness may become a more informative signal than the recorded value. If the label is systematically absent for a subgroup, the training objective does not correct the problem by itself.
This is why data preparation is part of model design. Decisions about coding, missing values, exclusions, time windows, and aggregation alter the statistical problem. They can change which population is represented and which patterns are available to the model.


Baselines are part of the evidence
A model should be compared with a simple baseline. For a binary outcome, the baseline may always predict the majority class or use the overall uptake rate as the probability prediction. For a continuous outcome, it may predict the training mean for every case. A complex model that does not improve on a baseline has not demonstrated useful predictive structure.
Baselines also reveal whether a metric is being interpreted correctly. If 90 per cent of cases are negative, a classifier that always predicts “negative” achieves 90 per cent accuracy while detecting no positive cases. Accuracy alone therefore hides the distribution of errors.


Evaluation follows the decision
Evaluation metrics should reflect how predictions will be used. If missing a potential beneficiary is costly, recall may matter more than precision. If follow-up is expensive, precision may matter more. If a model supplies risk scores to different teams, calibration may be more useful than a ranking metric: among cases assigned a probability of 0.7, roughly 70 per cent should experience the outcome if the probabilities are well calibrated.




Code
probability_bins = np.arange(0.1, 1.0, 0.1)
observed_calibrated = np.array([0.09, 0.21, 0.31, 0.39, 0.51, 0.61, 0.68, 0.79, 0.91])
observed_overconfident = np.array([0.24, 0.31, 0.39, 0.46, 0.50, 0.55, 0.62, 0.69, 0.76])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 5.2))
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="#777777", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5,
        label="Perfect calibration")
ax.plot(probability_bins, observed_calibrated, color=teal, marker="o",
        linewidth=2.4, markersize=6, label="Well calibrated")
ax.plot(probability_bins, observed_overconfident, color=orange, marker="s",
        linewidth=2.4, markersize=5.5, label="Overconfident")
ax.fill_between(
    probability_bins,
    probability_bins,
    observed_overconfident,
    color=orange,
    alpha=0.10,
)
ax.annotate(
    "Predicted 0.80;\nobserved rate 0.69",
    xy=(0.8, 0.69),
    xytext=(0.55, 0.84),
    arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "color": orange},
    color="#4a4a4a",
)
ax.set(
    xlim=(0, 1),
    ylim=(0, 1),
    xlabel="Mean predicted probability",
    ylabel="Observed outcome frequency",
    title="A reliability diagram reveals probability error",
)
ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 2.4



The diagonal represents agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies. The teal series stays close to that reference. The orange series is overconfident: its probabilities are more extreme than the observed outcome rates. For example, cases assigned a mean probability of 0.80 have an observed rate of 0.69 in this illustration. Calibration is estimated on held-out observations and is uncertain when few cases fall in a probability range. Guo and colleagues use reliability diagrams and related summaries to assess calibration in neural-network classifiers (Guo et al. 2017).
No metric resolves these choices automatically. The metric makes a particular error structure visible and leaves other aspects unmeasured.


The ML workflow

Define the task. Specify the population, prediction moment, target, and decision that may use the prediction.
Construct the data. Identify observations, features, labels, missing values, and measurement limits.
Choose a representation. Convert raw inputs into numerical or categorical features the model can process.
Choose a model family. A linear model, tree, neural network, or another family imposes different assumptions and trade-offs.
Fit parameters. Use training data to choose parameter values that reduce a loss.
Tune hyperparameters. Use validation data or cross-validation to compare configurations.
Evaluate once on held-out data. The test set estimates performance on new cases.
Deploy and monitor. Check whether data, performance, and consequences change over time.



Training, validation, testing, and inference
The training set is used to fit parameters. The validation set is used to make choices about the model. The test set is held back until the choices are complete. Once the model is deployed, inference means applying the fixed model to new inputs.
If the test set is repeatedly inspected and used to guide decisions, it is no longer a clean test set. This is a subtle but common form of leakage: information from the evaluation data has influenced the model-development process.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue, teal, orange = "#24527a", "#3a9188", "#d97745"
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 2.2))
blocks = [(0.02, 0.55, 0.48, "Training\nfit parameters", blue),
          (0.52, 0.55, 0.22, "Validation\nchoose model", teal),
          (0.76, 0.55, 0.22, "Test\nfinal estimate", orange)]
for x, y, width, label, color in blocks:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, y), width, 0.28, facecolor=color, alpha=0.85))
    ax.text(x + width / 2, y + 0.14, label, ha="center", va="center", color="white", weight="bold")
ax.annotate("development decisions", xy=(0.62, 0.48), xytext=(0.25, 0.18),
            arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "color": "#5c6670"}, ha="center")
ax.annotate("used once", xy=(0.87, 0.48), xytext=(0.87, 0.18),
            arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "color": "#5c6670"}, ha="center")
ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 2.5





Three common learning settings
Supervised learning uses labelled examples. Regression predicts a continuous quantity such as income; classification predicts a category or probability such as uptake.
Unsupervised learning has no observed target for each example. The task may be to identify clusters, compress representations, or detect unusual observations.
Generative learning models how data are produced or represented so that it can generate, complete, or transform examples. Large language models are trained as generative models by predicting tokens, but they also use supervised and preference-based stages later in development.
These categories describe the information available to the training procedure, not the full behaviour of a deployed system. A single language model may be pretrained with a self-supervised next-token objective, fine-tuned with labelled demonstrations, and evaluated with a verifier or human preference signal. The stages use different forms of supervision even when the model architecture remains similar.

title: What Is Machine Learning?
text:
Level 3 - Mathematics & Code
At this level, the earlier vocabulary is translated into a small mathematical model. The equations state exactly what enters the model, what it produces, and how its errors are summarised. The code then implements the same objects so that the relationship between the notation and the computation remains visible.

A linear prediction model
The simplest useful model is a linear function:
\[
\hat{y}_i=w^\top x_i+b.
\]
The equation can be read from left to right. \(x_i\) is the vector of features for one observation. \(w\) contains one weight for each feature. The dot product \(w^\top x_i\) multiplies each feature by its weight and adds the results. The intercept \(b\) shifts the total. The output \(\hat y_i\) is therefore a prediction generated by the current parameter values; it is not yet a measure of whether the prediction is accurate.
Here, \(w\) is a vector of feature weights and \(b\) is an intercept. The model is not necessarily “true” because it is linear. It is a baseline: simple enough to understand, fast to fit, and useful for diagnosing whether the features contain predictive signal.
For regression, a common loss is mean squared error:
\[
\operatorname{MSE}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(\hat{y}_i-y_i)^2.
\]


Code
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, r2_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 120
distance = rng.uniform(1, 25, n)
prior_participation = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
age = rng.uniform(18, 75, n)
uptake_score = 0.75 - 0.025 * distance + 0.18 * prior_participation + rng.normal(0, 0.08, n)

data = pd.DataFrame({
    "distance": distance,
    "prior_participation": prior_participation,
    "age": age,
    "uptake_score": uptake_score,
})

X = data[["distance", "prior_participation", "age"]]
y = data["uptake_score"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=7)

model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
predictions = model.predict(X_test)
print(f"test MSE: {mean_squared_error(y_test, predictions):.3f}")
print(f"test R²:   {r2_score(y_test, predictions):.3f}")


The \(R^2\) statistic measures improvement over a constant-mean baseline in this setting. It is not a universal measure of usefulness. A model can have a respectable \(R^2\) and still be poorly calibrated or too inaccurate for the decision it supports.


Residuals are information
For a regression model, the residual is:
\[
e_i=y_i-\hat y_i.
\]
The mean squared error reduces these residuals to one number. A residual plot preserves more information. A funnel shape can indicate non-constant variance; a curve can indicate that a linear model is missing a systematic relationship; clusters can reveal groups with different measurement processes.




Code
residuals = y_test.to_numpy() - predictions

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.8))
axes[0].scatter(y_test, predictions, color=blue, alpha=0.7)
limits = [min(y_test.min(), predictions.min()), max(y_test.max(), predictions.max())]
axes[0].plot(limits, limits, color=orange, linestyle="--")
axes[0].set(xlabel="Observed score", ylabel="Predicted score", title="Observed and predicted")
axes[1].scatter(predictions, residuals, color=teal, alpha=0.7)
axes[1].axhline(0, color=orange, linestyle="--")
axes[1].set(xlabel="Predicted score", ylabel="Residual", title="Residual diagnostic")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 2.6



The code is deliberately simple, but the principle extends to neural networks and language models. Aggregate performance can hide structured failures. Evaluation should therefore examine examples, subgroups, ranges of predicted risk, and the conditions under which the model is expected to operate.


A confusion matrix
For binary classification, four counts describe the relationship between predictions and outcomes:




Observed positive
Observed negative




Predicted positive
True positive
False positive


Predicted negative
False negative
True negative



From these counts:
\[
\text{precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\qquad
\text{recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}.
\]
Precision asks: among predicted positives, how many were positive? Recall asks: among observed positives, how many did the model identify? They answer different questions and can move in opposite directions as the threshold changes.


Classification and probabilities
For binary classification, a model may output a score that is converted into a probability \(p_i\) between 0 and 1. A threshold turns that probability into a decision:
\[
\hat{y}_i=
\begin{cases}
1 & p_i\geq t\\
0 & p_i<t.
\end{cases}
\]
Changing \(t\) changes the balance between false positives and false negatives. There is no threshold that is best in the abstract; the choice depends on the consequences of each error.




Code
positive = rng.beta(7, 3, 70)
negative = rng.beta(2, 6, 70)
threshold = 0.5

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
ax.hist(negative, bins=12, alpha=0.65, color=blue, label="Observed negative")
ax.hist(positive, bins=12, alpha=0.65, color=orange, label="Observed positive")
ax.axvline(threshold, color=teal, linewidth=2.5, linestyle="--", label="threshold = 0.5")
ax.set(xlabel="Predicted probability", ylabel="Number of observations", title="A threshold converts probabilities into decisions")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 2.7

title: What Is Machine Learning?
text:
Level 4 - Research & Systems
The final level changes the question. It asks what assumptions are required for the preceding workflow to work outside the development data, and what additional problems arise when predictions are used by an institution. The focus is therefore on generalisation, measurement, deployment, and consequences.

The training objective is not the deployment objective
Most formal ML training minimises an average loss over observed examples. A deployed system may be judged by a different quantity: service access, safety, cost, equity, response time, or downstream decisions. The training loss is a proxy for the real objective. This gap between the fitted model and the surrounding production system is a documented source of technical debt (Sculley et al. 2015).
This gap is one reason that data and evaluation design matter so much. If the label is measured with error, the model may learn the measurement process. If the data exclude a population, test performance may not describe that population. If the deployment environment changes, yesterday’s test set may no longer be informative.


Generalization and overfitting
A model that memorises its training examples can achieve low training loss and poor performance on new cases. This is overfitting. Generalisation is the ability to perform well on observations drawn from the relevant target population.
Model complexity is not automatically bad. A complex model can represent useful structure that a simple model cannot. The practical question is whether the additional flexibility captures stable signal or accidental features of the development data.
Overfitting is not limited to models with many visible parameters. It can result from repeated choices by the analyst: trying many feature definitions, thresholds, samples, or model configurations and reporting the most favourable test result. The effective complexity of the workflow includes these decisions, even when the final model is small.




Code
complexity = np.linspace(0.1, 10, 100)
train_error = 0.9 / (complexity + 0.3) + 0.04
test_error = 0.7 / (complexity + 0.4) + 0.012 * (complexity - 3.5) ** 2 + 0.12

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.4))
ax.plot(complexity, train_error, color=blue, linewidth=2.5, label="training error")
ax.plot(complexity, test_error, color=orange, linewidth=2.5, label="test error")
ax.axvline(complexity[np.argmin(test_error)], color=teal, linestyle="--", label="best held-out performance")
ax.set(xlabel="Model flexibility", ylabel="Error", title="Generalization is the target")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 2.8





Leakage, shift, and subgroup performance
Data leakage occurs when information unavailable at prediction time, or information derived from the outcome, enters the features. Leakage can produce impressive validation scores and disappointing deployment performance.
Distribution shift occurs when the relationship between inputs and outcomes changes, or when the deployment population differs from the training population. Monitoring should therefore include input distributions, missingness, calibration, subgroup performance, and decision consequences—not only an overall accuracy score.




Code
distance_shift = np.linspace(0, 25, 300)

def normal_density(values, mean, sd):
    return np.exp(-0.5 * ((values - mean) / sd) ** 2) / (sd * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))

training_density = normal_density(distance_shift, mean=6.5, sd=3.0)
deployment_density = normal_density(distance_shift, mean=12.0, sd=4.0)
training_relationship = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(1.8 - 0.20 * distance_shift)))
deployment_relationship = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(1.0 - 0.20 * distance_shift)))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.1))

axes[0].fill_between(distance_shift, training_density, color=blue, alpha=0.22)
axes[0].plot(distance_shift, training_density, color=blue, linewidth=2.4,
             label="Training population")
axes[0].fill_between(distance_shift, deployment_density, color=orange, alpha=0.20)
axes[0].plot(distance_shift, deployment_density, color=orange, linewidth=2.4,
             label="Deployment population")
axes[0].set(
    xlabel="Distance to service point (km)",
    ylabel="Relative density",
    title="The input population changes",
)
axes[0].set_yticks([])
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)

axes[1].plot(distance_shift, training_relationship, color=blue, linewidth=2.5,
             label="Relationship learned in training")
axes[1].plot(distance_shift, deployment_relationship, color=orange,
             linewidth=2.5, linestyle="--", label="Relationship at deployment")
axes[1].axvline(8, color=teal, linewidth=1.2, alpha=0.7)
axes[1].text(8.35, 0.96, "same distance", color="#4a4a4a", va="top")
axes[1].scatter(
    [8, 8],
    [
        1 / (1 + np.exp(-(1.8 - 0.20 * 8))),
        1 / (1 + np.exp(-(1.0 - 0.20 * 8))),
    ],
    color=[blue, orange],
    s=55,
    zorder=3,
)
axes[1].set(
    xlabel="Distance to service point (km)",
    ylabel="Probability of uptake",
    title="The outcome relationship changes",
    ylim=(0, 1),
)
axes[1].legend(frameon=False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 2.9



The left panel shows an input-distribution change: households in deployment are located farther away than households in the training data. Such a shift does not by itself prove that the model is wrong, but it means that the model is being used more often in a region with less training support. The right panel shows a change in the conditional relationship: at the same distance, uptake is lower in deployment than the relationship estimated during training. In that case, retaining the original mapping produces systematically high probabilities. Empirical studies of dataset shift show that predictive accuracy and calibration can deteriorate together, and that calibration measured on the original test distribution need not survive the shift (Ovadia et al. 2019).
Fairness is not a single metric. Different groups may differ in base rates, error costs, calibration, or access to measurement. A model should be assessed in relation to the decision and institutional context in which it is used.
The distinction between missingness and absence is often material. If a feature is missing because a household was never reached, missingness may encode prior access to the programme. Imputing a single average value does not remove that institutional pattern; it may conceal it. A useful data audit therefore asks who is measured, who is missing, and why.
Evaluation should also be aligned with the unit of deployment. Randomly splitting rows can overstate performance when several rows belong to the same person, household, institution, or time period. A model that predicts a future month should generally be evaluated with a time-respecting split. A model intended for new institutions should be tested on institutions not represented in training. The appropriate split follows the claim about generalisation.


Prediction is not causal inference
The model in this chapter predicts uptake from observed characteristics. It does not estimate the causal effect of offering the programme. To estimate that effect, we would need a causal design, such as a randomized experiment or a credible quasi-experimental strategy, together with assumptions about identification.
This distinction matters in policy work. A model may be good at predicting who would take up a service while being poor at identifying who would benefit from being offered the service. The first is a prediction problem; the second is closer to treatment-effect estimation.

title: What Is Machine Learning?
text:
Common misconceptions

Machine learning removes human judgement. Humans still define the task, data, target, evaluation, and use.
A high training score means the model is useful. Generalization and deployment performance matter.
A feature with predictive power is necessarily causal. Prediction and causal explanation are different goals.
The test set is a second training set. Repeatedly using it to make development decisions contaminates the estimate.
More complex models are always better. Complexity helps only when it captures stable, relevant structure.

title: What Is Machine Learning?
text:
Exercises

Identify the features, label, prediction, parameters, and hyperparameters in the programme-uptake example.
Give one example each of supervised, unsupervised, and generative learning.
Calculate the prediction from \(\hat y=2x+1\) when \(x=4\).
Calculate the MSE for predictions \((2,4,5)\) and targets \((3,3,6)\).
Explain what changes when a classification threshold moves from 0.5 to 0.8.
Give an example of data leakage in a programme-uptake model.
Why might a model have lower accuracy for one subgroup?
Explain why predicting uptake is not the same as predicting who benefits from treatment.
Design a train-validation-test split for data collected over time.
Describe one reason a model can perform well in testing but poorly after deployment.
Write two operational definitions of “programme uptake” that would create different labels. State when each label would be observed.
A feature records whether a household completed the programme. Explain why it is invalid for a model used to decide whom to contact before enrolment.
A classifier makes 80 correct predictions from 100 cases, but all 20 errors occur in one subgroup. State what accuracy does and does not establish about this result.
A model predicts a high probability of uptake for households near a service point. State one causal claim that the model cannot support and what additional design would be needed to assess it.
Name the data, target definition, decision point, and outcome measure that should appear in a short deployment record for the running example.
A programme changes its eligibility rule after the model is trained. Explain how this could change both the observed features and the meaning of the label.

title: What Is Machine Learning?
text:
Summary
Machine learning estimates a mapping from inputs to outputs using examples, a model family, a loss function, and an optimisation procedure. The basic workflow separates fitting, model selection, final evaluation, and inference. Useful ML practice requires attention to generalisation, leakage, distribution shift, subgroup performance, and the difference between prediction and causation.

title: What Is Machine Learning?
text:
Looking ahead
Once a model produces predictions, the model’s output must be distinguished from the observed target and the discrepancy between them must be measured. Chapter 2 develops models, predictions, targets, and loss functions. Chapter 3 then explains how model parameters can be changed systematically to reduce loss.

title: What Is Machine Learning?
text:
Further reading

title: Models, Predictions, and Loss Functions
text: Chapter orientation
crumbs: 3  Models, Predictions, and Loss Functions

title: Models, Predictions, and Loss Functions
text:
Why this chapter matters: models and losses define the learning problem
A model maps inputs to outputs. Its parameters determine the particular function used for prediction, while a loss function measures the discrepancy between predictions and observed targets. Together, the model and the loss define the learning problem: what the system can represent and what it is rewarded for getting right.
These distinctions are easy to blur. A prediction is not an explanation, a loss is not a complete measure of real-world value, and a training score is not evidence that a fitted relationship will generalise. This chapter develops the distinctions before turning to the procedure used to change model parameters.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

describe a model as a parameterised function;
distinguish parameters, hyperparameters, predictions, targets, and losses;
calculate predictions from linear and logistic models;
explain mean squared error and cross-entropy;
compare a model with simple baselines;
understand why the choice of loss affects what the model learns;
explain why a differentiable loss is useful for gradient-based training.



Running example: the four objects in a prediction problem
For observation \(i\), let \(x_i\) denote the input features and \(y_i\) the observed target. A model \(f_\theta\) with parameters \(\theta\) produces:
\[
\hat{y}_i=f_\theta(x_i).
\]
The target is the quantity recorded in the data. The prediction is the model’s output. The loss compares the two. The parameters are the values that specify the model. These are different objects even when they appear in the same line of code.
For a programme-uptake example, \(x_i\) could contain distance, prior participation, and age; \(y_i\) could be an indicator for observed uptake; and \(\hat y_i\) could be a predicted probability. The probability is not the observed outcome and does not become a causal effect because it is expressed on a familiar scale.

Model, parameters, prediction, target, and loss. A model maps an input to a prediction through fitted parameters. The target is the observed outcome against which that prediction is assessed. A loss turns their discrepancy into a number that the training procedure can reduce; it does not by itself decide whether the resulting prediction serves the intended use.


Loss, metric, and objective. A loss scores one prediction against a target. A metric reports a property relevant to evaluation or use. An objective is the quantity that the training procedure is instructed to optimise, which may combine a loss with penalties or constraints. The same formula can appear in more than one role, but the roles are not interchangeable.

title: Models, Predictions, and Loss Functions
text:
Level 1 - Intuition


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue, teal, orange, purple = "#24527a", "#3a9188", "#d97745", "#7655a6"
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 40)
y = 1.5 + 2.2 * x + rng.normal(0, 2.0, len(x))
w, b = 2.0, 1.0
predictions = w * x + b

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.2))
ax.scatter(x, y, color=blue, alpha=0.55, label="observed examples")
ax.plot(x, predictions, color=orange, linewidth=2.5, label="fitted model")
new_x, new_y = 8.4, w * 8.4 + b
ax.scatter([new_x], [new_y], color=teal, s=100, marker="*", label="prediction for new input")
ax.vlines(new_x, 0, new_y, color=teal, linestyle="--", alpha=0.7)
ax.set(xlabel="Input feature", ylabel="Target", title="A model maps inputs to predicted outputs")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 3.1: A fitted line is a model: it maps an input value to a prediction.





The line is the model’s rule for converting an input into an output. The observed points show that the rule is not a perfect description of every case; the vertical distance between a point and the line is the prediction error. The model is therefore useful only if its errors are acceptable for the purpose for which the prediction will be used.

A model is a rule with adjustable parts
A model takes information about a case and returns an output. A linear model combines features using weights. A decision tree applies a sequence of splits. A neural network applies many parameterised transformations. The model family determines the form of the rule; the parameters determine the particular rule fitted to the data.
The distinction between family and parameters is useful. Two linear models can use the same features but produce different predictions because their weights differ. Two neural networks can have the same architecture but different parameters because they were trained on different data or with different optimisation choices.


A loss is a measurement of discrepancy
The model produces an output, but training requires a way to assess that output. A loss function performs this measurement. If the programme model predicts an uptake score of 0.60 and the recorded score is 0.75, the loss assigns a numerical penalty to the discrepancy. The loss does not explain why the prediction was wrong. It supplies a criterion for comparing parameter values.
Different losses express different priorities. Squared error penalises large numerical mistakes strongly. Absolute error treats the same deviations more proportionally. Cross-entropy penalises confident probability assignments that contradict the observed class. Choosing a loss therefore changes the behaviour the model is trained to produce.


A baseline is a claim about added value
Before trusting a model, compare it with a simple rule. A regression baseline might predict the mean target for every case. A classification baseline might predict the most common class or the overall event rate as a probability. The learned model earns its complexity by improving predictions on data that were not used to fit it.


A probability is not yet an action
For a binary model, the probability is an output of the model and the threshold is a later rule for turning that output into a decision. A system can retain the same predicted probabilities while changing the threshold from 0.5 to 0.2, thereby classifying more cases as positive. The model has not changed; the decision policy has.
This separation matters when false positives and false negatives have different consequences. A loss function trains a probability model under a specified objective. A threshold, capacity rule, or human review procedure determines what happens next. Treating all three as the same object makes it difficult to identify whether an error came from the fitted model, the chosen threshold, or the wider decision process.


Code
probability_examples=np.array([.06,.18,.27,.41,.52,.66,.79,.93])
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8.2,3.6))
ax.scatter(probability_examples,np.ones_like(probability_examples),s=85,color=blue,zorder=3)
for threshold,colour,label,ypos in [(0.5,orange,"threshold = 0.5",1.33),(0.2,teal,"threshold = 0.2",.68)]:
    ax.axvline(threshold,color=colour,linewidth=2); ax.text(threshold+.015,ypos,label,color=colour)
ax.text(.73,1.08,"positive at 0.5",color=orange,ha="center")
ax.text(.58,.9,"additional positives at 0.2",color=teal,ha="center")
ax.set(xlim=(0,1),ylim=(.5,1.55),xlabel="Predicted probability of class 1",yticks=[],title="Probability model and decision threshold are separate")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Figure 3.2: A classification threshold converts unchanged predicted probabilities into different decisions; moving the threshold changes the decision rule, not the fitted probability model.





The figure does not identify the appropriate threshold. That choice requires a stated objective, evidence about error consequences, and sometimes constraints outside prediction quality. Chapter 1 introduced that deployment boundary; later chapters return to calibration and generalisation evidence.

title: Models, Predictions, and Loss Functions
text:
Level 2 - Mechanics


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.2))
small_x = np.array([1, 3, 5])
small_y = np.array([2.0, 5.0, 6.5])
small_pred = np.array([2.8, 4.2, 5.5])
ax.scatter(small_x, small_y, color=blue, s=65, label="target")
ax.scatter(small_x, small_pred, color=orange, s=65, label="prediction")
for xi, yi, pi in zip(small_x, small_y, small_pred):
    ax.plot([xi, xi], [yi, pi], color=teal, linewidth=2)
ax.text(5.55, 4.2, "loss aggregates\nthese errors", color="#4a4a4a")
ax.set(xlabel="Observation", ylabel="Outcome", title="From individual errors to a training loss")
ax.set_xticks(small_x)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 3.3: A loss assigns a penalty to each prediction error and aggregates those penalties.





The vertical segments represent individual residuals. The loss function converts each residual into a penalty and then combines the penalties into one number. The model cannot improve a parameter until the training procedure can compare the total error produced by different parameter values.

One batch creates a vector of errors before one scalar loss
Models normally make many predictions in one batch. The loss is not a mysterious scalar emitted by a framework: it begins with one comparison per observation, then applies a reduction such as a mean or sum. A mean makes the reported scale less sensitive to batch size; a sum gives larger batches more total influence unless another part of the update rule compensates.


Code
batch_target=np.array([1.0,3.0,2.0,5.0])
batch_prediction=np.array([.5,3.5,1.0,4.0])
residuals=batch_prediction-batch_target
per_example_squared=residuals**2
print("residuals:",residuals)
print("per-example squared losses:",per_example_squared)
print("mean squared loss:",per_example_squared.mean())
print("summed squared loss:",per_example_squared.sum())


residuals: [-0.5  0.5 -1.  -1. ]
per-example squared losses: [0.25 0.25 1.   1.  ]
mean squared loss: 0.625
summed squared loss: 2.5


The calculation makes the reduction convention explicit. In standard mini-batch training, changing mean to sum without changing the learning-rate convention changes the scale of the gradient passed to the optimiser. Chapter 3 develops that update step; this chapter establishes the quantity being reduced.


Regression
Regression predicts a quantity on a numerical scale. The simplest model is:
\[
\hat y=w_1x_1+w_2x_2+\cdots+w_px_p+b.
\]
The weight \(w_j\) controls the contribution of feature \(x_j\) within the model. The intercept \(b\) is the prediction when all features equal zero, although that interpretation may not be substantively meaningful if zero is outside the observed data range.
For \(n\) observations, mean squared error is:
\[
\operatorname{MSE}(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat y_i-y_i)^2.
\]
The square makes the loss non-negative and gives larger residuals greater influence. This is useful when large errors are particularly undesirable, but it also makes MSE sensitive to outliers.


Classification
Binary classification predicts one of two classes. A linear score can be converted to a probability with the logistic function:
\[
p_i=\sigma(z_i)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z_i}},
\qquad z_i=w^\top x_i+b.
\]
The probability is then converted into a decision using a threshold. The threshold is a decision rule, not usually a learned parameter of the basic model. Altering it changes the confusion matrix even when the model and probabilities remain unchanged.


Cross-entropy
For a binary target \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) and predicted probability \(p_i\), binary cross-entropy is:
\[
\ell_i=-\left[y_i\log(p_i)+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right].
\]
If \(y_i=1\), the loss is \(-\log(p_i)\): confident predictions near one receive low loss, while confident predictions near zero receive a large penalty. If \(y_i=0\), the second term plays the same role. Cross-entropy therefore evaluates probability assignments, not only the final class decision.


Training loss and evaluation loss
The training objective is calculated on the data used to fit parameters. Evaluation metrics are calculated on held-out data or in a deployment setting. The same loss can be reported in both places, but the interpretation differs. A low training loss shows that the model fitted the training examples. A low held-out loss provides evidence that the fitted relationship extends to new cases drawn from the evaluation population.
Loss and metric can therefore coincide without being interchangeable. A binary classifier may train with cross-entropy, monitor held-out cross-entropy to assess probability quality, and also report recall at an operational threshold. Each quantity answers a different question. Replacing one with another because it produces a more favourable number changes the claim being made.

title: Models, Predictions, and Loss Functions
text:
Level 3 - Mathematics & Code
The purpose of this level is to connect the verbal distinction between model, prediction, target, and loss to calculations that can be checked. We begin with a small regression example, then compare different loss functions and use a baseline to assess whether the fitted model adds predictive information.

A small regression problem


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue, teal, orange = "#24527a", "#3a9188", "#d97745"

rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 40)
y = 1.5 + 2.2 * x + rng.normal(0, 2.0, len(x))

w, b = 2.0, 1.0
predictions = w * x + b
mse = np.mean((predictions - y) ** 2)
print(f"MSE: {mse:.2f}")


MSE: 7.31


The model’s predictions can be written as a vector operation:
\[
\hat{\mathbf y}=Xw+b,
\]
where \(X\) is the matrix of features, \(w\) is the vector of weights, and \(b\) is broadcast across observations. This notation becomes essential when the same operations are applied to a batch of examples on a GPU.
The vector notation is the batch version of the scalar equation introduced in Chapter 1. Each row of \(X\) represents one observation. Multiplying \(X\) by \(w\) produces one model score for each row, and adding \(b\) shifts every score by the same amount. The code above performs these operations directly with the chosen values of \(w\) and \(b\); the plot below makes the resulting predictions and residuals visible.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.4))
ax.scatter(x, y, color=blue, alpha=0.75, label="observations")
ax.plot(x, predictions, color=orange, linewidth=2.5, label="model prediction")
for xi, yi, pi in zip(x[::4], y[::4], predictions[::4]):
    ax.plot([xi, xi], [yi, pi], color=teal, alpha=0.7, linewidth=1.2)
ax.set(xlabel="Feature value", ylabel="Target", title="Predictions and residuals")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 3.4: A linear model summarises a relationship while leaving residual variation unexplained.







Loss as a function of the parameter
For a fixed dataset, changing \(w\) changes the predictions and therefore the loss. In a one-parameter example, we can plot that relationship directly. With many parameters, the same object becomes a high-dimensional surface. Chapter 3 explains how gradient descent uses local derivatives of this surface.


Code
residual = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.4))
ax.plot(residual, residual ** 2, color=blue, linewidth=2.5, label="squared error")
ax.plot(residual, np.abs(residual), color=orange, linewidth=2.5, label="absolute error")
ax.axhline(0, color="#777777", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set(xlabel="Residual: target - prediction", ylabel="Loss", title="The loss function determines how errors are weighted")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 3.5: Squared error and absolute error penalise residuals differently.







Numerical cross-entropy


Code
probabilities = np.linspace(0.001, 0.999, 400)
loss_if_positive = -np.log(probabilities)
loss_if_negative = -np.log(1 - probabilities)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.4))
ax.plot(probabilities, loss_if_positive, color=teal, linewidth=2.5, label="observed class = 1")
ax.plot(probabilities, loss_if_negative, color=orange, linewidth=2.5, label="observed class = 0")
ax.set(xlabel="Predicted probability of class 1", ylabel="Cross-entropy loss", title="Confident wrong probabilities receive large penalties")
ax.set_ylim(0, 7)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The graph also explains why numerical implementations use a small positive constant or stable log-sum-exp operations. Evaluating \(\log(0)\) is undefined, and extreme logits can create overflow if the expression is implemented naively.
The important point is that cross-entropy distinguishes a correct prediction from a well-calibrated probability. Assigning probability 0.51 to the observed class and assigning probability 0.99 both lead to the same class decision, but they receive different losses. The second prediction is rewarded more when it is correct and penalised more severely when it is wrong.
Frameworks commonly accept logits rather than already rounded probabilities because a combined loss implementation can calculate the required transformation more stably. Rounding a probability before cross-entropy removes the information needed to distinguish a tentative prediction from a confident one and usually breaks useful gradients. The output representation, loss implementation, and reporting scale must be kept aligned.


Code
logits=np.array([-6.,-1.,0.,1.,6.])
stable_probability=1/(1+np.exp(-logits))
labels=np.array([0.,0.,1.,1.,1.])
stable_bce=np.maximum(logits,0)-logits*labels+np.log1p(np.exp(-np.abs(logits)))
print("probabilities:",stable_probability.round(4))
print("per-example stable cross-entropy:",stable_bce.round(4))


probabilities: [0.0025 0.2689 0.5    0.7311 0.9975]
per-example stable cross-entropy: [0.0025 0.3133 0.6931 0.3133 0.0025]


The stable expression returns finite losses for the displayed extreme logits without first evaluating the logarithm of a rounded probability. It illustrates a numerical contract, not a substitute for a framework’s tested loss function.


A baseline comparison


Code
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

X = x.reshape(-1, 1)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=21)

baseline = DummyRegressor(strategy="mean").fit(X_train, y_train)
linear = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)

baseline_mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, baseline.predict(X_test))
linear_mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, linear.predict(X_test))
print(f"baseline test MSE: {baseline_mse:.2f}")
print(f"linear model MSE:  {linear_mse:.2f}")


baseline test MSE: 28.61
linear model MSE:  4.01


The comparison is more informative than the linear model’s coefficient alone. A coefficient describes the fitted model; the baseline comparison asks whether the fitted relationship improves predictive performance.

title: Models, Predictions, and Loss Functions
text:
Level 4 - Research & Systems
The equations above describe performance on a finite set of observations. This level considers the gap between that calculation and the quantity an organisation cares about after deployment: performance on future cases, under a particular data-generating process, with particular costs attached to errors.
The distinction between these quantities changes how a model should be assessed. A low empirical risk can result from a flexible model fitting accidental features of the training data. A low held-out risk can still be misleading if the held-out cases do not represent the deployment population. A low predictive loss can also coexist with poor decisions when the loss gives little weight to the errors that matter to the organisation using the model.

Empirical risk minimisation
Statistical learning commonly formulates model fitting as empirical risk minimisation (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009).
The average loss over observed examples is the empirical risk:
\[
\hat R(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(f_\theta(x_i),y_i).
\]
Training chooses parameters that reduce this quantity, subject to the model family, optimisation method, regularisation, and data representation. The quantity we actually care about is usually a population or deployment risk:
\[
R(\theta)=\mathbb E_{(X,Y)\sim P}[\ell(f_\theta(X),Y)].
\]
The distribution \(P\) is not known directly. The training data provide an estimate. Generalisation concerns the relationship between empirical risk and performance on future observations from the relevant population. This is why a large training dataset does not automatically solve problems caused by selection, measurement error, or distribution shift.


The loss encodes a decision problem imperfectly
Squared error, cross-entropy, ranking losses, and preference objectives each make particular errors visible and others less visible. The loss is therefore part of the model’s substantive specification. If a deployment decision has asymmetric costs, minimising an unweighted average loss may produce a model that is statistically well behaved but operationally unsuitable.
The issue becomes more complex when predictions feed into subsequent decisions. A probability model may be evaluated with log loss, while the institution using it cares about service capacity, missed cases, waiting time, or unequal error rates. A single training loss cannot represent all of these outcomes. Evaluation must examine the pathway from prediction to decision.
The choice is also a source of distributional assumptions. Average loss weights observations according to the sampling and weighting scheme used in training. If a deployment population, protected subgroup, or rare but costly outcome requires different emphasis, that requirement must be expressed through data collection, loss weighting, threshold policy, evaluation slices, or another stated mechanism. A generic claim that a model minimises error leaves these choices hidden.


Differentiability and optimisation
Gradient-based training requires derivatives of the loss with respect to model parameters. A differentiable loss permits local information to be used for parameter updates. This does not mean that every useful objective must be smooth: some systems use discrete rewards, ranking objectives, or reinforcement-learning signals. In those cases, gradients may be estimated indirectly or applied to a surrogate objective.
For standard neural-network training, the practical combination is a differentiable model, a differentiable loss, automatic differentiation, and an optimiser. Chapter 3 begins with the optimiser: how gradient descent uses the local slope of the loss to change parameters.

title: Models, Predictions, and Loss Functions
text:
Common misconceptions

The model is the prediction. The model is the parameterised function; the prediction is its output for a particular input.
The lowest training loss is always the best model. Held-out performance and deployment conditions determine whether the fitted relationship generalises.
Cross-entropy measures whether the final class is right. It evaluates the quality of the predicted probability, including confidence.
A loss function is an objective measure of usefulness. It is a chosen proxy whose relevance depends on the decision context.
A coefficient is a causal effect. A fitted parameter describes the model’s predictive mapping unless additional causal assumptions and design justify another interpretation.

text:
Summary
A model is a parameterised function that maps inputs to predictions. A loss function measures the discrepancy between predictions and observed targets. Regression and classification use different output representations and losses, and the choice of loss changes which errors receive emphasis. Baselines, held-out evaluation, and decision-specific metrics are needed to interpret model performance.
