title: Neural Network Layers
text: Chapter orientation

title: Neural Network Layers
text:
Why this chapter matters
An artificial neuron produces one scalar. Neural networks become useful by arranging many neuron-equivalent operations into layers, so that one input vector produces another vector that can be passed to the next stage. The shift from a neuron to a layer changes the notation, the tensor shapes, the parameter count, and the way the computation is executed on hardware.
This chapter develops that shift directly. It treats a layer as an affine matrix transformation followed, when appropriate, by an activation. It then shows how layers compose, how batches move through them, how gradients inherit the shapes of parameters, and why wide layers become systems problems. Activation functions appear here only as operations between layers; Chapter 7 examines their behaviour in depth.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

explain why a layer produces a vector rather than one scalar;
distinguish input, hidden, and output layers;
calculate every output of a small dense layer;
interpret the rows of a weight matrix and the entries of a bias vector;
track tensor shapes through one layer, a batch, and a short network;
implement the same forward pass with NumPy and PyTorch;
calculate layer and network parameter counts;
explain how backpropagation produces matrix-shaped gradients;
distinguish depth from width; and
explain why large layers require accelerator kernels and, in some cases, tensor parallelism.



Running example
The input is the three-feature vector used in Chapter 5:
\[
x=(2,4,1).
\]
Instead of producing one value, the layer has three output units. Its weights and biases are:
\[
W=
\begin{bmatrix}
0.5 & -1 & 2\\
-0.25 & 0.5 & 1\\
1 & 0.25 & -0.5
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
b=
\begin{bmatrix}
3\\
-1\\
-4
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The numbers are illustrative parameters, not estimated effects. They allow every operation to be checked by hand. The layer will produce the pre-activation vector
\[
z=(2,\ 1.5,\ -1.5),
\]
and ReLU will transform it into
\[
h=(2,\ 1.5,\ 0).
\]

Neural-network layer. A shared transformation applied across a batch or sequence of representations. Its weight matrix and bias vector define how input coordinates are combined into output coordinates; broadcasting applies the same bias to each relevant observation. Layer shape determines both the representation interface and the number of trainable parameters.

title: Neural Network Layers
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

A layer asks several questions of the same input
A neuron combines all available inputs into one output. A layer repeats that structure with different weights and biases. Every unit receives the same input vector, but each unit calculates a different weighted combination. The outputs are collected into a new vector.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, FancyArrowPatch

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue, teal, orange = "#24527a", "#3a9188", "#d97745"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
input_y = np.array([0.78, 0.50, 0.22])
output_y = np.array([0.78, 0.50, 0.22])

for i, ypos in enumerate(input_y, start=1):
    ax.add_patch(Circle((0.18, ypos), 0.055, facecolor=blue, edgecolor="white", linewidth=1.2))
    ax.text(0.18, ypos, f"x{i}", ha="center", va="center", color="white", weight="bold")

for j, ypos in enumerate(output_y, start=1):
    ax.add_patch(Circle((0.70, ypos), 0.065, facecolor=orange, edgecolor="white", linewidth=1.2))
    ax.text(0.70, ypos, f"h{j}", ha="center", va="center", color="white", weight="bold")

for y_in in input_y:
    for y_out in output_y:
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(
            (0.24, y_in),
            (0.63, y_out),
            arrowstyle="->",
            mutation_scale=10,
            linewidth=1.2,
            color=teal,
            alpha=0.58,
        ))

ax.text(0.18, 0.93, "Input vector", ha="center", color="#4a4a4a", weight="bold")
ax.text(0.70, 0.93, "Layer output", ha="center", color="#4a4a4a", weight="bold")
ax.text(0.44, 0.08, "Each output uses its own weights and bias", ha="center", color="#4a4a4a")
ax.set_xlim(0, 0.9)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 7.1: A dense layer applies several different weighted combinations to the same input vector.





The diagram is fully connected because each output unit uses all three inputs. The three orange nodes do not vote on one decision. Together they form a three-dimensional output vector. The next layer receives that vector as its input.


A layer changes the representation
The original coordinates have substantive meanings such as distance, prior participation, and access to information. A hidden layer produces new coordinates defined by its learned parameters. One output may respond strongly to short distance and previous participation; another may respond to a different combination. These outputs are often called a representation because they describe the same observation in a new coordinate system.
The individual coordinates should not automatically be assigned human-readable concepts. A layer is trained as part of a larger objective, and useful information can be distributed across many units. The relevant claim is computational: the layer has transformed one vector into another.


Width and depth describe different choices
The width of a layer is its number of output units. A layer with 128 outputs is wider than one with 32. The depth of a network counts successive parameterised layers along the computation path. Adding units changes how much a layer can represent at one stage. Adding layers changes how many transformations are composed.
The distinction is structural, not evaluative. A wider or deeper network is not automatically better. It has a different parameter count, computational cost, and set of functions it can represent. Whether that additional capacity improves performance depends on the data, training procedure, and evaluation setting.


Input, hidden, and output layers
The phrase input layer usually refers to the values supplied to the network rather than a learned calculation. A hidden layer produces an internal representation that is passed onwards. An output layer maps the final hidden representation to the form required by the task, such as one regression score or a set of class logits.
These names describe position in the network. The matrix operation can be the same in a hidden layer and an output layer even though their outputs have different interpretations.

title: Neural Network Layers
text:
Level 2 - Mechanics
The layer diagram can now be read as a sequence of concrete operations. The important change from Chapter 5 is that the calculation is repeated for several units and organised as one matrix operation.

Six operations in a dense layer
For one observation, a dense layer:

receives an input vector;
gives each output unit its own row of weights;
multiplies every input by the corresponding weight in that row;
sums each row’s contributions;
adds one bias per output unit; and
applies an activation to each pre-activation when the architecture specifies one.

For the running example, the three unit calculations are:



Unit
Weighted sum
Bias
Pre-activation
ReLU output




1
\(0.5(2)-1(4)+2(1)=-1\)
\(3\)
\(2\)
\(2\)


2
\(-0.25(2)+0.5(4)+1(1)=2.5\)
\(-1\)
\(1.5\)
\(1.5\)


3
\(1(2)+0.25(4)-0.5(1)=2.5\)
\(-4\)
\(-1.5\)
\(0\)



The third pre-activation is negative, so ReLU replaces it with zero. The layer output is therefore \((2,1.5,0)\).


Code
x_mech = np.array([2.0, 4.0, 1.0])
W_mech = np.array([
    [0.5, -1.0, 2.0],
    [-0.25, 0.5, 1.0],
    [1.0, 0.25, -0.5],
])
b_mech = np.array([3.0, -1.0, -4.0])
contribution_matrix = W_mech * x_mech[np.newaxis, :]
z_mech = contribution_matrix.sum(axis=1) + b_mech
h_mech = np.maximum(0, z_mech)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.3), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.15, 1]})
image = axes[0].imshow(contribution_matrix, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-4, vmax=4, aspect="auto")
for row in range(contribution_matrix.shape[0]):
    for col in range(contribution_matrix.shape[1]):
        value = contribution_matrix[row, col]
        axes[0].text(col, row, f"{value:.1f}", ha="center", va="center",
                     color="white" if abs(value) > 2.2 else "#303030", weight="bold")
axes[0].set_xticks(range(3), [r"$x_1$", r"$x_2$", r"$x_3$"])
axes[0].set_yticks(range(3), ["Unit 1", "Unit 2", "Unit 3"])
axes[0].set_title("Weighted input contributions")
fig.colorbar(image, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.046, pad=0.04, label="Contribution")

positions = np.arange(3)
bar_width = 0.34
axes[1].bar(positions - bar_width / 2, z_mech, bar_width, color=blue, label="Pre-activation")
axes[1].bar(positions + bar_width / 2, h_mech, bar_width, color=orange, label="After ReLU")
axes[1].axhline(0, color="#666666", linewidth=0.9)
axes[1].set_xticks(positions, ["Unit 1", "Unit 2", "Unit 3"])
axes[1].set_ylabel("Value")
axes[1].set_title("Bias and activation complete the layer")
axes[1].legend(frameon=False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 7.2: Rows of the weight matrix define output units; row sums and biases produce the pre-activation vector.





The heatmap preserves information hidden by the final sum. The first row contains a contribution of \(-4\) from the second input, which is offset by the first and third contributions and the bias. The bar chart then separates the affine result from the activation. This distinction matters because the weight matrix and bias define the affine layer, while ReLU is a separate operation.


Rows are units and columns are inputs
The orientation of the weight matrix is a common source of confusion. In this book, and in PyTorch’s linear layer:

each row contains the weights for one output unit;
each column corresponds to one input feature;
the number of rows is the output width; and
the number of columns is the input width.

A \(3\times3\) matrix is ambiguous by inspection because the input and output widths happen to match. For a layer with three inputs and five outputs, the weight matrix has five rows and three columns. Writing the dimensions before calculating prevents many shape errors.


One layer processes a batch
Training normally processes several observations together. If a batch contains four households and each has three features, the input has shape \((4,3)\). The same weight matrix is applied to every row, producing four output vectors.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.6))
blocks = [
    (0.11, r"Input $X$" + "\n" + r"$B \times 3$", blue),
    (0.36, r"Multiply by $W^\top$" + "\n" + r"$3 \times 3$", teal),
    (0.61, r"Add bias $b$" + "\n" + r"$3$", orange),
    (0.86, r"Output $Z$" + "\n" + r"$B \times 3$", blue),
]
for xpos, label, colour in blocks:
    ax.text(xpos, 0.56, label, ha="center", va="center", color="white", weight="bold",
            bbox={"boxstyle": "round,pad=0.55", "facecolor": colour})
for left, right in zip(blocks[:-1], blocks[1:]):
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(
        (left[0] + 0.095, 0.56),
        (right[0] - 0.095, 0.56),
        arrowstyle="->",
        mutation_scale=14,
        color="#666666",
    ))
ax.text(0.5, 0.12, "The batch dimension B is preserved", ha="center", color="#4a4a4a")
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 7.3: A batch changes the number of observations, while the layer determines the output width.





The layer changes the last dimension from input width to output width. It does not mix observations across the batch. Every row uses the same \(W\) and \(b\). This parameter sharing is what allows one fitted layer to process new observations after training.


Layers compose by matching dimensions
Suppose the first layer maps three inputs to four hidden values. A second layer can consume those values only if its input width is four. If it produces two outputs, the shape sequence for one observation is:
\[
(3)\rightarrow(4)\rightarrow(2).
\]
For a batch of size \(B\), the same sequence is:
\[
(B,3)\rightarrow(B,4)\rightarrow(B,2).
\]
The adjacent dimensions must match. A network architecture is therefore partly a contract between layers: the output width of one layer becomes the input width of the next.


Training changes the matrix, not the layer rule
During the forward pass, the layer uses its current \(W\) and \(b\). Backpropagation calculates a gradient for every matrix and bias entry. The optimiser changes those entries, and the next forward pass uses the updated values. The rule \(Z=XW^\top+b\) remains fixed; training changes the parameters inside that rule.

title: Neural Network Layers
text:
Level 3 - Mathematics & Code
The mechanics can now be expressed with dimensions that remain valid when the input width, output width, and batch size differ. The code will implement the same calculation three ways and verify that the results agree.

One observation
Let:

\(x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}\) be one input vector;
\(W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}}\) be the weight matrix;
\(b\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}\) be the bias vector;
\(z\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}\) be the pre-activation; and
\(h\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}\) be the activated output.

The layer computes:
\[
z=Wx+b,
\qquad
h=g(z).
\]
The \(j\)th output is:
\[
z_j=\sum_{k=1}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}W_{jk}x_k+b_j.
\]
The index \(j\) selects one row of \(W\), so it selects one output unit. The index \(k\) runs across the inputs. The formula is the neuron equation from Chapter 5 repeated for every row.


A batch
Let \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times d_{\mathrm{in}}}\) store \(B\) observations as rows. PyTorch stores the weight matrix in output-by-input orientation, so the batch calculation is:
\[
Z=XW^\top+b,
\]
with:
\[
Z\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times d_{\mathrm{out}}}.
\]
The bias vector is broadcast across the batch: the same \(b_j\) is added to output \(j\) for every observation. Broadcasting does not create separate learned biases for each observation.








Object
Shape
Meaning




\(X\)
\(B\times d_{\mathrm{in}}\)
batch of input vectors


\(W\)
\(d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}\)
one row per output unit


\(b\)
\(d_{\mathrm{out}}\)
one bias per output unit


\(Z\)
\(B\times d_{\mathrm{out}}\)
batch of pre-activation vectors





NumPy calculation
The following code calculates the running example without a neural-network library. Its purpose is to expose the matrix multiplication, bias addition, and activation separately.


Code
import numpy as np

x = np.array([2.0, 4.0, 1.0])
W = np.array([
    [0.5, -1.0, 2.0],
    [-0.25, 0.5, 1.0],
    [1.0, 0.25, -0.5],
])
b = np.array([3.0, -1.0, -4.0])

z_numpy = W @ x + b
h_numpy = np.maximum(0, z_numpy)

print("pre-activation:", z_numpy)
print("after ReLU:    ", h_numpy)


pre-activation: [ 2.   1.5 -1.5]
after ReLU:     [2.  1.5 0. ]


The matrix product returns \((2,1.5,-1.5)\). ReLU changes only the negative component, producing \((2,1.5,0)\). The code uses one matrix multiplication, but it is numerically identical to the three row-by-row calculations in Level 2.


The same layer in PyTorch
PyTorch’s nn.Linear stores \(W\) with shape (out_features, in_features). The activation remains a separate operation.


Code
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch_layer = nn.Linear(in_features=3, out_features=3)
with torch.no_grad():
    torch_layer.weight.copy_(torch.tensor(W, dtype=torch.float32))
    torch_layer.bias.copy_(torch.tensor(b, dtype=torch.float32))

x_torch = torch.tensor(x, dtype=torch.float32)
z_torch = torch_layer(x_torch)
h_torch = torch.relu(z_torch)

print("weight shape:  ", tuple(torch_layer.weight.shape))
print("bias shape:    ", tuple(torch_layer.bias.shape))
print("pre-activation:", z_torch.detach().numpy())
print("after ReLU:    ", h_torch.detach().numpy())
print("matches NumPy: ", np.allclose(h_numpy, h_torch.detach().numpy()))


weight shape:   (3, 3)
bias shape:     (3,)
pre-activation: [ 2.   1.5 -1.5]
after ReLU:     [2.  1.5 0. ]
matches NumPy:  True


The final line verifies that the NumPy and PyTorch outputs agree. This check is useful when translating an equation into a framework: matching values are stronger evidence than matching tensor shapes alone.


Composing two layers
A two-layer forward computation can be written:
\[
h=g(W_1x+b_1),
\]
\[
s=W_2h+b_2.
\]
The first layer produces a hidden representation \(h\). The second produces an output score \(s\). For the running example, use:
\[
W_2=
\begin{bmatrix}
0.6 & -0.4 & 1.2
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad b_2=-0.2.
\]
Then:
\[
s=0.6(2)-0.4(1.5)+1.2(0)-0.2=0.4.
\]


Code
second_layer = nn.Linear(3, 1)
with torch.no_grad():
    second_layer.weight.copy_(torch.tensor([[0.6, -0.4, 1.2]]))
    second_layer.bias.copy_(torch.tensor([-0.2]))

network = nn.Sequential(torch_layer, nn.ReLU(), second_layer)
score = network(x_torch)
print(f"network score: {score.item():.1f}")


network score: 0.4


The score is \(0.4\), matching the manual calculation. It is not yet a probability. An output interpretation requires an appropriate final transformation and loss, which depend on the task.


Parameter counts
A dense layer has:
\[
d_{\mathrm{out}}d_{\mathrm{in}}
\]
weights and:
\[
d_{\mathrm{out}}
\]
biases. Its total parameter count is:
\[
d_{\mathrm{out}}d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}}
=d_{\mathrm{out}}(d_{\mathrm{in}}+1).
\]
The first \(3\rightarrow3\) layer has \(3(3+1)=12\) parameters. The \(3\rightarrow1\) output layer has \(1(3+1)=4\). The two-layer network therefore has 16 parameters.


Code
parameter_table = []
total_parameters = 0
for name, parameter in network.named_parameters():
    count = parameter.numel()
    total_parameters += count
    parameter_table.append((name, tuple(parameter.shape), count))

for name, shape, count in parameter_table:
    print(f"{name:10s} shape={str(shape):8s} parameters={count}")
print("total parameters:", total_parameters)


0.weight   shape=(3, 3)   parameters=9
0.bias     shape=(3,)     parameters=3
2.weight   shape=(1, 3)   parameters=3
2.bias     shape=(1,)     parameters=1
total parameters: 16


The framework count agrees with the formula. Parameter counting should be done layer by layer because biases, embeddings, normalisation parameters, and tied weights can make a network total less obvious than a single dense-layer calculation.


Gradient shapes
Let \(G=\partial L/\partial Z\) contain the gradient arriving from the next operation, with shape \(B\times d_{\mathrm{out}}\). For \(Z=XW^\top+b\), the layer gradients are:
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}=G^\top X,
\]
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=\sum_{i=1}^{B}G_{i,:}.
\]
The matrix product \(G^\top X\) has shape \(d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}\), exactly matching \(W\). The bias gradient sums over observations because the same bias was broadcast to every row during the forward pass.


Code
x_batch = torch.tensor([
    [2.0, 4.0, 1.0],
    [1.0, 0.0, 2.0],
], dtype=torch.float32)

network.zero_grad()
batch_scores = network(x_batch)
loss = (batch_scores ** 2).mean()
loss.backward()

for name, parameter in network.named_parameters():
    print(f"{name:10s} parameter={tuple(parameter.shape)} gradient={tuple(parameter.grad.shape)}")


0.weight   parameter=(3, 3) gradient=(3, 3)
0.bias     parameter=(3,) gradient=(3,)
2.weight   parameter=(1, 3) gradient=(1, 3)
2.bias     parameter=(1,) gradient=(1,)


Every gradient has the same shape as its parameter. Backpropagation does not produce one generic learning signal for a layer; it produces one derivative for every stored weight and bias.

title: Neural Network Layers
text:
Level 4 - Research & Systems
The small layer fits comfortably in a table. Large models use the same algebra with dimensions that change memory use, arithmetic cost, and communication requirements. The relevant systems object is no longer an individual neuron but a matrix multiplication.

Dense layers are matrix-multiplication kernels
For a batch matrix \(X\) and weight matrix \(W\), computing \(XW^\top\) requires approximately:
\[
2B\,d_{\mathrm{in}}d_{\mathrm{out}}
\]
floating-point operations when a multiply and an addition are counted separately. The layer stores \(d_{\mathrm{in}}d_{\mathrm{out}}\) weights and produces \(B\,d_{\mathrm{out}}\) output activations.
These quantities scale differently. For a square layer with width \(d\), parameter count grows as \(d^2\), while output activations for a fixed batch grow as \(Bd\). Doubling width therefore approximately quadruples the weights but only doubles the output activation count.


Code
widths = np.array([128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192])
batch_size = 128
square_parameters = widths ** 2 + widths
output_activations = batch_size * widths

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.1))
axes[0].plot(widths, square_parameters, marker="o", color=blue, linewidth=2.5)
axes[0].set_xscale("log", base=2)
axes[0].set_yscale("log")
axes[0].set(
    xlabel="Layer width d",
    ylabel="Parameters",
    title=r"Square layer: $d^2+d$ parameters",
)
axes[0].annotate(
    f"{square_parameters[-1] / 1e6:.1f} million",
    xy=(widths[-1], square_parameters[-1]),
    xytext=(2100, 1.6e7),
    arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "color": blue},
    color="#4a4a4a",
)

axes[1].plot(widths, output_activations, marker="s", color=orange, linewidth=2.5)
axes[1].set_xscale("log", base=2)
axes[1].set_yscale("log")
axes[1].set(
    xlabel="Layer width d",
    ylabel="Output values",
    title=rf"Output activations: $B d$, with $B={batch_size}$",
)
axes[1].annotate(
    f"{output_activations[-1] / 1e6:.2f} million",
    xy=(widths[-1], output_activations[-1]),
    xytext=(2100, 2.7e5),
    arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "color": orange},
    color="#4a4a4a",
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 7.4: For a square dense layer, parameter count grows quadratically with width while output activations grow linearly for a fixed batch.





At width 8,192, one square layer contains about 67 million parameters before optimiser state or gradients are counted. The plotted activation count covers only the layer output for a batch of 128, not every intermediate value retained for backpropagation. Parameter memory and activation memory must therefore be estimated separately.


Layer shape determines memory traffic
A matrix multiplication needs the input activations and weights to be available to the accelerator, and it writes an output tensor. If a matrix is reused across many observations or token positions, the arithmetic performed per weight load can be high. Small or irregular operations may spend proportionally more time moving data than multiplying it.
This is why implementations combine compatible operations when possible. Bias addition and activation can be fused with, or scheduled close to, the matrix multiplication so that intermediate values do not make unnecessary trips through device memory. The mathematical layer is unchanged, but the execution plan affects latency and throughput.


When one device cannot hold the matrix
If a weight matrix is too large for one accelerator, it can be partitioned. Tensor parallelism splits the matrix operation itself across devices. One approach assigns different groups of output rows to different accelerators. Each device computes part of the output vector, and the parts are then concatenated or combined.


Code
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.2))
gpu_colours = [blue, teal, orange, "#6f7f93"]
block_y = [0.72, 0.54, 0.36, 0.18]

ax.text(0.09, 0.52, r"Input $x$", ha="center", va="center", color="white", weight="bold",
        bbox={"boxstyle": "round,pad=0.5", "facecolor": blue})
ax.annotate("", xy=(0.25, 0.52), xytext=(0.15, 0.52),
            arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "color": "#666666", "lw": 1.6})

for idx, (ypos, colour) in enumerate(zip(block_y, gpu_colours), start=1):
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0.27, ypos), 0.28, 0.13, facecolor=colour, alpha=0.88))
    ax.text(0.41, ypos + 0.065, f"Rows on GPU {idx}", ha="center", va="center",
            color="white", weight="bold")
    ax.annotate("", xy=(0.69, ypos + 0.065), xytext=(0.56, ypos + 0.065),
                arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "color": colour, "lw": 1.5})

ax.text(0.77, 0.52, "Partial\noutputs", ha="center", va="center", color="#4a4a4a", weight="bold")
ax.annotate("", xy=(0.91, 0.52), xytext=(0.83, 0.52),
            arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "color": "#666666", "lw": 1.6})
ax.text(0.95, 0.52, r"Full $z$", ha="center", va="center", color="white", weight="bold",
        bbox={"boxstyle": "round,pad=0.45", "facecolor": orange})
ax.text(0.41, 0.92, r"Partitioned weight matrix $W$", ha="center", color="#4a4a4a", weight="bold")
ax.set_xlim(0, 1.05)
ax.set_ylim(0.08, 1)
ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 7.5: Tensor parallelism can divide the rows of a large weight matrix across accelerators.





The figure shows a row-wise partition for explanation; production systems also use column-wise partitions and combine them across successive operations. Megatron-LM demonstrated that intra-layer model parallelism can distribute large Transformer matrix multiplications with a small number of communication operations (Shoeybi et al. 2019). The benefit depends on whether reduced per-device memory and computation compensate for communication between devices.


Depth, width, and expressivity
Successive layers can create functions that would require many more units in a shallower architecture, but such statements depend on the activation, function class, and approximation criterion. Research on neural-network expressivity therefore studies specific architectural families rather than treating depth as a universal measure of intelligence. Raghu and colleagues analyse how trajectory-based measures of functional complexity change with depth (Raghu et al. 2017).
The practical choice of depth and width also involves optimisation and generalisation. A network can have enough representational capacity and still train poorly, overfit, or fail under distribution shift. Parameter count describes architecture; it does not establish that the parameters can be estimated reliably from the available data.


Not every layer is dense
A dense layer gives every output its own weight for every input. Other layer types impose structure:

convolutional layers reuse local filters across spatial positions;
attention layers calculate input-dependent weighted combinations across sequence positions;
embedding layers retrieve learned rows from a table; and
mixture-of-experts layers route an input through a subset of available parameter blocks.

These operations still transform tensors and expose parameters to backpropagation, but their connectivity and parameter sharing differ from a dense matrix. Later chapters will derive them separately. Treating every layer as nn.Linear would hide the architectural assumptions that make those models useful.


What should be measured in a real system
For a layer or block, a systems audit should record:

input and output shapes, including batch and sequence dimensions;
parameter count and numerical precision;
activation sizes needed during training;
forward and backward execution time;
communication introduced by parallelism; and
whether the measured operation is limited by arithmetic, memory movement, or synchronisation.

The matrix dimensions provide a first estimate, but measured performance depends on the accelerator, kernel library, surrounding operations, and degree of parallelism. A parameter count alone cannot predict training time or inference latency.

title: Neural Network Layers
text:
Common misconceptions

A layer is one neuron with more inputs. A dense layer contains several output units and returns a vector.
Each hidden unit must correspond to one interpretable concept. Useful information can be distributed across many coordinates.
The batch size changes the number of learned weights. The same weights are reused for every observation in the batch.
Rows of a PyTorch weight matrix correspond to inputs. Rows correspond to outputs; columns correspond to inputs.
The bias has one value per input. A dense layer normally has one bias per output unit.
A wider layer always improves the model. Width increases capacity and cost, but performance depends on data and training.
Stacking affine layers is enough to obtain a nonlinear network. Without nonlinear operations between them, the composition remains affine.
Parameter count determines memory use. Training also stores gradients, optimiser state, and activations.
A matrix split across GPUs eliminates communication. Partial results must still be combined or passed between partitions.
All neural-network layers are dense. Convolution, attention, embeddings, and expert routing use different connectivity.

title: Neural Network Layers
text:
Exercises

A layer receives four inputs and produces six outputs. Write the shapes of \(W\), \(b\), and \(z\) for one observation.
Write the corresponding shapes for a batch of 32 observations.
Calculate the parameter count of the \(4\rightarrow6\) layer, including biases.
Use the running-example matrix to calculate the second pre-activation by hand.
Explain why the third output becomes zero after ReLU.
Describe the difference between a layer’s width and a network’s depth.
A network has shape sequence \(10\rightarrow20\rightarrow5\rightarrow1\). Calculate the parameter count of each dense layer and the total.
Implement the running example using NumPy without a loop over output units.
Reproduce the same calculation with nn.Linear and verify numerical agreement.
Explain why the bias gradient sums across observations in a batch.
For \(B=64\), \(d_{\mathrm{in}}=1024\), and \(d_{\mathrm{out}}=4096\), calculate the number of output activation values and the layer’s parameter count.
Explain why doubling the width of a square dense layer approximately quadruples its parameter count.
Give one reason tensor parallelism can make a layer feasible and one reason it may reduce efficiency.
Compare a dense layer with one structured layer type named in Level 4. Which weights are shared or omitted?
A model receives a tensor of shape \((32,10)\) but a layer was constructed with in_features=12. Identify the incompatible dimensions and state one legitimate repair.
For a \(512\rightarrow2048\rightarrow512\) block, calculate the parameter count of both layers including biases. Explain why the intermediate width, rather than the input or output width alone, determines most of the parameter cost.

title: Neural Network Layers
text:
Summary
A dense layer applies several neuron-equivalent calculations at once. For one observation it computes \(z=Wx+b\); for a batch it computes \(Z=XW^\top+b\) when weights are stored in output-by-input orientation. Rows of \(W\) define output units, columns correspond to inputs, and the bias has one entry per output.
Layer composition requires adjacent dimensions to match. Parameter counts grow with input and output width, while backpropagation produces gradients with the same shapes as the stored parameters. At scale, dense layers are matrix-multiplication kernels whose feasibility depends on parameter memory, activation memory, numerical precision, and communication. Tensor parallelism can split a matrix across accelerators, but it exchanges local memory constraints for coordination costs.

title: Neural Network Layers
text:
Looking ahead
Layers can be composed without producing a genuinely nonlinear model. Chapter 7 examines the activation functions placed between layers, how they change representation and gradient flow, and why different architectures use different nonlinearities.

Intra-layer tensor parallelism for large language models is presented by Shoeybi et al. (2019).

title: Activation Functions and Non-linearity
text: Chapter orientation

title: Activation Functions and Non-linearity
text:
Why this chapter matters
Chapter 6 showed how a layer maps an input vector to an output vector. Stacking such layers appears to produce a deeper model, but depth alone does not guarantee a richer function. If every layer applies only an affine transformation, the entire stack can be rewritten as one affine transformation. Additional matrices increase the number of operations without changing the class of functions represented by the network.
Activation functions alter this result. They transform each layer’s pre-activations before those values enter the next layer. This chapter explains how that local operation changes the shape of the complete network, how it affects gradients, and why the choice of activation must be assessed together with architecture, initialisation, numerical precision, and hardware.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

show algebraically why a stack of affine layers remains affine;
explain how an activation function creates nonlinear input-output relationships;
calculate ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, and GELU outputs for representative inputs;
distinguish hidden-layer activations from output transformations;
derive the local derivatives used during backpropagation;
implement and compare activations in NumPy and PyTorch;
explain saturation, inactive ReLU units, and gradient-flow trade-offs;
relate activation choice to expressivity, memory traffic, kernel fusion, and modern architectures.



Running examples
The first example continues the layer calculation from Chapter 6. Its pre-activation vector is
\[
z=(2,1.5,-1.5).
\]
Applying ReLU gives \(h=(2,1.5,0)\). This example will be used to connect the forward calculation to the backward gradient.
A second, one-dimensional network will make the geometry visible:
\[
y(x)=\operatorname{ReLU}(2x+1)-\operatorname{ReLU}(2x-1).
\]
The two hidden units introduce changes in slope at \(x=-0.5\) and \(x=0.5\). Those changes cannot be produced by one affine function.

Activation function. A fixed, usually coordinate-wise non-linear transformation applied to a layer’s pre-activations. Activations allow stacked layers to represent relationships that a composition of affine transformations cannot. An activation used inside a hidden layer has a different role from an output transformation interpreted as a probability.

title: Activation Functions and Non-linearity
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

More layers do not help if every layer follows the same straight rule
An affine layer can rotate, rescale, and shift its input. A second affine layer can repeat those operations. Their composition is still one rotation, rescaling, and shift. The intermediate representation may have more coordinates, but the final relationship between input and output has not acquired a bend.
Activation functions are inserted between layers to change that relationship. Each hidden unit first calculates a pre-activation. The activation then decides how that value is passed forward. ReLU, for example, keeps positive values and replaces negative values with zero. Different units cross zero at different input values, so the network can follow different affine rules in different regions of the input space.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue, teal, orange, grey = "#24527a", "#3a9188", "#d97745", "#5f6b76"

x_grid = np.linspace(-2, 2, 401)
affine_y = 1.2 * x_grid + 0.4
relu_network_y = np.maximum(0, 2 * x_grid + 1) - np.maximum(0, 2 * x_grid - 1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.2), sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(x_grid, affine_y, color=blue, linewidth=3)
axes[0].set_title("Affine layers without activation")
axes[0].text(-1.7, 2.1, "one slope everywhere", color=blue)

axes[1].plot(x_grid, relu_network_y, color=orange, linewidth=3)
axes[1].axvline(-0.5, color=grey, linestyle="--", alpha=0.7)
axes[1].axvline(0.5, color=grey, linestyle="--", alpha=0.7)
axes[1].text(-1.75, 1.05, "flat", color=grey)
axes[1].text(-0.35, 1.05, "rising", color=orange)
axes[1].text(1.15, 1.05, "flat", color=grey)
axes[1].set_title("Two ReLU units between layers")

for ax in axes:
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("Input x")
    ax.set_ylabel("Network output")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 8.1



The left panel has one slope across the full input range. The right panel uses three regions. For inputs below \(-0.5\), both ReLU units are inactive and the output is zero. Between \(-0.5\) and \(0.5\), the first unit is active and the output rises. Above \(0.5\), both are active and their slopes cancel, leaving an output of two. The activation has not made the network arbitrary; it has allowed the network to join several simple rules.


An activation acts on values, not on substantive meaning
In a dense hidden layer, the same activation function is normally applied to every coordinate. If \(z=(2,1.5,-1.5)\), ReLU processes the three numbers independently and returns \((2,1.5,0)\). It does not know that one coordinate may describe distance or that another may represent prior participation. The weights create the pre-activations; the activation applies a fixed numerical rule.


Nonlinearity and probability are different jobs
An activation between hidden layers expands what the network can represent. A transformation at the output often serves another purpose: sigmoid maps one score to a value between zero and one, while softmax converts several scores into values that sum to one. Those outputs may be used as probabilities when the model, loss, data, and calibration support that interpretation. Bounded output alone does not establish calibration.
The main conclusion at this level is therefore specific: hidden activations prevent a deep network from collapsing into one affine map. The next level examines what several common activation rules do to individual values.

title: Activation Functions and Non-linearity
text:
Level 2 - Mechanics

The activation step has three parts
For a hidden layer, the forward calculation can be separated into three operations:

calculate the pre-activation \(z=Wx+b\);
apply an activation independently to each coordinate, \(h_j=\phi(z_j)\);
pass the resulting vector \(h\) to the next layer.

For the Chapter 6 vector, ReLU gives
\[
\operatorname{ReLU}(2)=2,\qquad
\operatorname{ReLU}(1.5)=1.5,\qquad
\operatorname{ReLU}(-1.5)=0.
\]
The third unit is not removed from the network. Its output is zero for this observation. The same unit may be active for another observation whose pre-activation is positive.


Common activations transform the same input differently
Four functions will be compared throughout this chapter:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{ReLU}(z) &= \max(0,z),\\
\sigma(z) &= \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}},\\
\tanh(z) &= \frac{e^z-e^{-z}}{e^z+e^{-z}},\\
\operatorname{GELU}(z) &= z\Phi(z),
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\Phi(z)\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. ReLU discards negative values. Sigmoid compresses all values into \((0,1)\). Tanh compresses them into \((-1,1)\). GELU attenuates negative inputs smoothly and approaches the identity for sufficiently positive inputs (Hendrycks and Gimpel 2016).




Code
from math import erf

def sigmoid_np(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

def gelu_np(z):
    erf_values = np.vectorize(erf)(z / np.sqrt(2))
    return 0.5 * z * (1 + erf_values)

z_plot = np.linspace(-4, 4, 500)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.plot(z_plot, np.maximum(0, z_plot), label="ReLU", color=blue, linewidth=2.7)
ax.plot(z_plot, sigmoid_np(z_plot), label="sigmoid", color=teal, linewidth=2.4)
ax.plot(z_plot, np.tanh(z_plot), label="tanh", color=orange, linewidth=2.4)
ax.plot(z_plot, gelu_np(z_plot), label="GELU", color="#7a5195", linewidth=2.4)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Pre-activation z")
ax.set_ylabel("Activation phi(z)")
ax.set_title("Four activation rules")
ax.legend(ncol=2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 8.2



The graph shows why the name of an activation is not enough to describe its effect. ReLU and GELU are unbounded above, whereas sigmoid and tanh approach fixed limits. Tanh is centred around zero; sigmoid is not. ReLU has a sharp corner at zero; sigmoid, tanh, and GELU are smooth. These differences affect both the values sent forward and the gradients sent backward.
For a few representative inputs:



\(z\)
ReLU
sigmoid
tanh
GELU




-2.0
0.000
0.119
-0.964
-0.046


-0.5
0.000
0.378
-0.462
-0.154


0.0
0.000
0.500
0.000
0.000


0.5
0.500

0.346


2.0
2.000
0.881

The table should be read row by row. At \(z=-2\), ReLU transmits no value, while GELU transmits a small negative value and sigmoid returns a positive value because its output range starts at zero. At \(z=2\), ReLU is exactly linear, GELU is close to linear, and the bounded functions are already flattening.


The backward pass uses the local slope
Backpropagation multiplies the gradient arriving from the next operation by the activation’s derivative. ReLU therefore behaves as a gate away from zero: positive pre-activations pass the gradient; negative pre-activations return zero. With upstream gradient
\[
g_h=(0.6,-0.4,1.2),
\]
the running example gives
\[
g_z=g_h\odot(1,1,0)=(0.6,-0.4,0).
\]
The third unit receives no gradient through ReLU for this observation. This is an observation-specific statement. A batch containing positive pre-activations for that unit can still update its incoming weights.




Code
z_run = np.array([2.0, 1.5, -1.5])
upstream = np.array([0.6, -0.4, 1.2])
h_run = np.maximum(0, z_run)
grad_z = upstream * (z_run > 0)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2))
positions = np.arange(3)
width = 0.35
axes[0].bar(positions - width/2, z_run, width, label="pre-activation", color=blue)
axes[0].bar(positions + width/2, h_run, width, label="after ReLU", color=orange)
axes[0].set_title("Forward pass")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Value")
axes[0].legend()
axes[1].bar(positions - width/2, upstream, width, label="arriving gradient", color=teal)
axes[1].bar(positions + width/2, grad_z, width, label="through ReLU", color="#7a5195")
axes[1].set_title("Backward pass")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Gradient")
axes[1].legend()
for ax in axes:
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_xticks(positions, ["Unit 1", "Unit 2", "Unit 3"])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 8.3



The two panels describe the same mask. Unit 3 is inactive in the forward pass and blocks this observation’s gradient in the backward pass. Units 1 and 2 preserve their values and pass the arriving gradients unchanged.


Activation choice depends on where the function is used
ReLU and GELU are common hidden activations because their positive side does not approach a fixed upper bound. Sigmoid is useful when a scalar output must lie between zero and one, and it also appears inside gates. Tanh remains useful where a bounded, zero-centred state is wanted. Softmax is usually applied across a vector of output scores, rather than independently to each coordinate. No single activation has the same role in every location.
Mechanically, an activation changes values and local slopes. Level 3 makes these claims algebraic and verifies them in code.

title: Activation Functions and Non-linearity
text:
Level 3 - Mathematics & Code

Two affine layers collapse into one
Let the first layer be
\[
z_1=W_1x+b_1
\]
and the second
\[
y=W_2z_1+b_2.
\]
Substitution gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
y &= W_2(W_1x+b_1)+b_2\\
  &= (W_2W_1)x+(W_2b_1+b_2).
\end{aligned}
\]
Define \(W_*=W_2W_1\) and \(b_*=W_2b_1+b_2\). Then \(y=W_*x+b_*\). The dimensions of the intermediate layer may be large, but the represented function remains affine.
With an activation,
\[
y=W_2\phi(W_1x+b_1)+b_2,
\]
the same simplification is generally unavailable because \(\phi(W_1x+b_1)\) cannot be replaced by a fixed matrix multiplying \(x\). For ReLU, the active units depend on the input. Within a region where the active set stays fixed, the network is affine; crossing a ReLU threshold changes the effective affine map.


The one-dimensional network is piecewise affine
The running scalar network can be written in three regions:
\[
y(x)=
\begin{cases}
0, & x<-0.5,\\
2x+1, & -0.5\leq x<0.5,\\
2, & x\geq0.5.
\end{cases}
\]
At \(x=-1\), both hidden pre-activations are non-positive and \(y=0\). At \(x=0\), the first is active, the second inactive, and \(y=1\). At \(x=1\), both are active and \(y=3-1=2\). This calculation explains the three regions shown in the Level 1 figure.


Code
# Verify the piecewise calculation directly.
def small_relu_network(x):
    hidden = np.maximum(0, np.array([2*x + 1, 2*x - 1]))
    return hidden[0] - hidden[1]

for value in [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0]:
    print(f"x={value:>4.1f}, y={small_relu_network(value):.1f}")


The outputs are 0, 1, and 2. They agree with the region-specific formula. The code contains no special cases because ReLU creates the regions through its elementwise rule.


Derivatives determine gradient transmission
Away from points where a derivative is undefined, the common derivatives are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{ReLU}'(z) &= \begin{cases}0&z<0\\1&z>0,\end{cases}\\
\sigma'(z) &= \sigma(z)[1-\sigma(z)],\\
\tanh'(z) &= 1-\tanh^2(z),\\
\operatorname{GELU}'(z) &= \Phi(z)+z\varphi(z),
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\varphi(z)\) is the standard normal density. ReLU is not differentiable at zero; software libraries assign a conventional subgradient there, commonly zero. This single-point convention is different from ReLU’s zero derivative over the entire negative half-line.




Code
normal_pdf = np.exp(-0.5 * z_plot**2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)
normal_cdf = 0.5 * (1 + np.vectorize(erf)(z_plot / np.sqrt(2)))

derivatives = {
    "ReLU": (z_plot > 0).astype(float),
    "sigmoid": sigmoid_np(z_plot) * (1 - sigmoid_np(z_plot)),
    "tanh": 1 - np.tanh(z_plot)**2,
    "GELU": normal_cdf + z_plot * normal_pdf,
}
colours = [blue, teal, orange, "#7a5195"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
for (name, derivative), colour in zip(derivatives.items(), colours):
    ax.plot(z_plot, derivative, label=name, color=colour, linewidth=2.4)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Pre-activation z")
ax.set_ylabel("Local derivative")
ax.set_title("Local gradient multipliers")
ax.legend(ncol=2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 8.4



Sigmoid’s derivative never exceeds \(0.25\) and approaches zero for large positive or negative inputs. Tanh has derivative one at zero but also flattens at both extremes. Repeated multiplication by small derivatives can shrink gradients across many layers. ReLU avoids positive-side saturation, but its negative-side derivative is exactly zero. GELU has a smooth derivative and can transmit a small gradient for moderately negative inputs.


NumPy and PyTorch implement the same elementwise rule


Code
# NumPy forward and backward calculations for the running vector.
z = np.array([2.0, 1.5, -1.5])
upstream_gradient = np.array([0.6, -0.4, 1.2])

h = np.maximum(0, z)
local_derivative = (z > 0).astype(float)
gradient_to_layer = upstream_gradient * local_derivative

print("activation:", h)
print("local derivative:", local_derivative)
print("gradient to preceding layer:", gradient_to_layer)


The multiplication is elementwise. No matrix multiplication occurs inside ReLU. The activation returns \((2,1.5,0)\) and its local derivative returns \((1,1,0)\), so the gradient passed to the preceding layer is \((0.6,-0.4,0)\).


Code
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

z_torch = torch.tensor([2.0, 1.5, -1.5], requires_grad=True)
h_torch = F.relu(z_torch)
h_torch.backward(torch.tensor([0.6, -0.4, 1.2]))

print("PyTorch activation:", h_torch.detach())
print("PyTorch gradient:", z_torch.grad)


PyTorch records the activation in the computation graph and applies the same local derivative during backpropagation. The result should match the manual NumPy calculation exactly.


Code
# Compare library implementations over the same inputs.
values = torch.tensor([-2.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 2.0])
comparison = torch.stack([
    F.relu(values),
    torch.sigmoid(values),
    torch.tanh(values),
    F.gelu(values),
], dim=1)
print(comparison)


The columns correspond to ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, and GELU. Small numerical differences from the table can arise from rounding, not from a different definition.


Finite differences require care at a kink
A centred finite-difference approximation estimates
\[
f'(z)\approx\frac{f(z+\epsilon)-f(z-\epsilon)}{2\epsilon}.
\]
For ReLU at zero, this calculation returns approximately \(0.5\) because it averages slopes from opposite sides. PyTorch returns zero at zero by convention. Neither value makes ReLU differentiable there; they answer different operational questions. Gradient checks should therefore avoid placing non-smooth activations exactly at a kink.


Code
epsilon = 1e-5
finite_difference_at_zero = (
    np.maximum(0, epsilon) - np.maximum(0, -epsilon)
) / (2 * epsilon)
print(f"Centred finite difference at zero: {finite_difference_at_zero:.1f}")


The distinction matters when diagnosing a failed gradient check. A discrepancy at a non-differentiable point need not imply that automatic differentiation is incorrect.
Level 3 has treated an activation as a mathematical function with a local derivative. At research and production scale, the same function also changes optimisation, activation distributions, memory movement, and kernel design.

title: Activation Functions and Non-linearity
text:
Level 4 - Research & Systems

Expressivity depends on activation and architecture together
ReLU networks represent piecewise-affine functions. Increasing depth can increase the number and arrangement of linear regions that a network can represent, although counts of regions are architecture-dependent and do not by themselves measure useful learning. The expressivity results discussed by Raghu et al. (2017) concern specified network families and complexity measures; they do not establish that adding depth will improve accuracy on a particular dataset.
Smooth activations generate different function classes and optimisation surfaces. Classical universal-approximation results show that networks with suitable nonlinear activations can approximate broad classes of functions under stated conditions (Cybenko 1989). They do not specify the amount of data, computation, network width, or optimisation effort needed to find a useful approximation. Expressive capacity and trainability remain separate questions.


Saturation changes gradient flow
Sigmoid and tanh approach horizontal asymptotes. When pre-activations enter those regions, their derivatives approach zero and the gradient passed to earlier layers shrinks. Glorot and Bengio (2010) connect this saturation behaviour to difficulties in training deep feed-forward networks and analyse how activation and initialisation interact. An activation cannot be assessed independently of the distribution of values entering it.
ReLU avoids saturation on its positive side and produced sparse activations in early deep-network experiments (Nair and Hinton 2010; Glorot, Bordes, and Bengio 2011). It introduces another failure mode: a unit whose pre-activation is negative for every relevant observation receives zero gradient through ReLU. A sufficiently large parameter update can therefore leave a unit inactive across the training distribution. Leaky ReLU assigns a small non-zero slope to the negative side, but that change is not a guarantee against poor optimisation.


Smooth alternatives make different empirical trade-offs
GELU multiplies an input by the Gaussian cumulative probability associated with that input (Hendrycks and Gimpel 2016). Swish uses \(z\sigma(\beta z)\) and emerged from a search over candidate functions (Ramachandran, Zoph, and Le 2017). Both retain smooth transitions around zero and allow some negative output. Their reported improvements are empirical results for tested architectures and datasets, not a ranking that transfers automatically to every model.
The original Transformer used ReLU in its feed-forward sublayers (Vaswani et al. 2017). Later Transformer families use GELU or gated variants such as those evaluated by Shazeer (2020). This change also alters parameterisation and kernel structure; attributing a model-level result to the scalar activation alone is usually not possible without a controlled comparison.


Elementwise does not mean free
A dense layer performs roughly \(2Bd_{\mathrm{in}}d_{\mathrm{out}}\) floating-point operations for a batch, while an elementwise activation performs work proportional to the number of output values, \(Bd_{\mathrm{out}}\). Matrix multiplication normally dominates arithmetic. The activation still reads and writes the full activation tensor. On accelerators, this can make an unfused activation limited by memory movement rather than arithmetic.




Code
widths = np.array([128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192])
batch = 128
dense_ops = 2 * batch * widths**2
activation_evals = batch * widths

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.plot(widths, dense_ops, marker="o", color=blue, linewidth=2.5,
        label=r"dense layer: $2Bd^2$ operations")
ax.plot(widths, activation_evals, marker="s", color=orange, linewidth=2.5,
        label=r"activation: $Bd$ values")
ax.set_xscale("log", base=2)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("Square-layer width d")
ax.set_ylabel("Approximate operation or value count")
ax.set_title("Arithmetic scaling for B = 128")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



Figure 8.5



The separation in operation counts should not be read as an equivalent separation in elapsed time. A matrix-multiplication kernel can achieve high device utilisation through data reuse, whereas a separate activation kernel may spend much of its time moving values. Compilers and specialised kernels therefore fuse bias addition, activation, dropout, or related operations when the architecture permits it. Fusion reduces intermediate memory traffic and kernel-launch overhead without changing the mathematical function.


Backward passes need activation information
ReLU’s backward pass needs to know which pre-activations were positive. Smooth functions may need either the input or output to calculate their derivatives efficiently. Training frameworks save such tensors during the forward pass, increasing activation memory. Activation checkpointing saves memory by retaining fewer intermediate values and recomputing them during backpropagation. The trade-off is additional computation.
Lower numerical precision introduces further considerations. Stable sigmoid implementations avoid directly evaluating expressions that overflow for large magnitudes. Approximate GELU formulas replace the Gaussian cumulative distribution function with cheaper expressions. An approximation that is adequate in one precision and hardware stack should still be tested in the intended training and inference configuration.


A defensible activation choice is an empirical design decision
A systems review should record:

the activation and its exact parameterisation;
where it appears, including hidden, gated, and output locations;
the distribution of pre-activations and the fraction of inactive or saturated units;
gradient norms across depth;
compatibility with initialisation, normalisation, and residual connections;
available fused kernels in the target precision and hardware;
task quality, training stability, memory use, throughput, and latency under a controlled comparison.

Changing an activation while also changing width, initialisation, normalisation, or optimiser settings does not isolate the activation’s effect. The appropriate choice is the one supported by measurements for the complete architecture and deployment setting.

title: Activation Functions and Non-linearity
text:
Common misconceptions

A deeper stack is nonlinear by definition. A stack of affine layers remains affine unless a nonlinear operation intervenes.
ReLU removes a neuron permanently whenever its input is negative. It sets that unit’s output to zero for the current observation; other observations may activate it.
A zero ReLU output means the corresponding weight is zero. The weighted sum and bias may simply produce a negative pre-activation.
Sigmoid outputs are automatically calibrated probabilities. Calibration depends on training, data, loss, and evaluation, not only the output range.
Tanh never has vanishing gradients because its derivative is one at zero. Its derivative approaches zero for large positive and negative inputs.
ReLU has no saturation problem. It does not saturate for positive inputs, but its negative side has zero slope.
GELU is a smooth ReLU with the same derivative everywhere. GELU is a distinct function and can have a small negative derivative in part of its domain.
Non-differentiability at zero prevents ReLU training. Automatic-differentiation libraries use a conventional subgradient at that point.
The activation with the best benchmark result is best for every network. Reported comparisons depend on architecture, training procedure, data, and implementation.
Elementwise activations have negligible systems cost. Their arithmetic is small relative to a matrix multiplication, but tensor reads, writes, and kernel launches can remain material.
Changing the activation changes only the forward pass. It also changes local derivatives, saved tensors, gradient flow, and potentially fused kernels.

title: Activation Functions and Non-linearity
text:
Exercises

Show that three affine layers can be rewritten as one affine layer. Identify the combined weight and bias.
Evaluate ReLU, sigmoid, and tanh at \(z=-1\), \(0\), and \(1\).
Apply ReLU to \(z=(2,1.5,-1.5)\) and explain each coordinate.
With upstream gradient \((0.6,-0.4,1.2)\), calculate the gradient through ReLU for the running example.
Derive the three-region formula for \(\operatorname{ReLU}(2x+1)-\operatorname{ReLU}(2x-1)\).
Identify the active hidden units at \(x=-1\), \(x=0\), and \(x=1\) in the scalar network.
Explain why sigmoid’s derivative cannot exceed \(0.25\).
Calculate tanh’s derivative at zero and describe what happens as \(|z|\) grows.
Implement ReLU and its backward pass in NumPy without using np.maximum.
Compare torch.relu, torch.sigmoid, torch.tanh, and torch.nn.functional.gelu over inputs from \(-5\) to \(5\).
Use finite differences to estimate the ReLU derivative at \(z=-1\), \(z=1\), and \(z=0\). Explain the result at zero.
Construct a ReLU unit that is inactive for every observation in a small dataset, then change its bias so that at least one observation activates it.
Explain why a separate activation kernel can be limited by memory traffic even when its arithmetic cost is small.
For \(B=128\) and \(d=4096\), compare \(Bd\) activation values with approximately \(2Bd^2\) dense-layer operations.
Design a controlled experiment comparing ReLU and GELU. State which settings must remain fixed and which outcomes should be measured.
A binary classifier uses a sigmoid output and binary cross-entropy. Explain why replacing the output sigmoid with ReLU changes the output contract, even if ReLU remains appropriate for hidden layers.

title: Activation Functions and Non-linearity
text:
Summary
Affine layers can change dimension, rotate, rescale, and shift values, but any stack containing only affine operations reduces to one affine map. An activation function prevents that collapse by changing each pre-activation before the next layer. ReLU creates input-dependent affine regions; sigmoid and tanh produce bounded smooth transformations; GELU smoothly attenuates inputs according to a Gaussian weighting.
The activation’s derivative determines local gradient transmission. Saturating functions can repeatedly shrink gradients, while ReLU passes positive-side gradients and blocks negative-side gradients. These properties interact with initialisation, data, normalisation, depth, and the training procedure.
At system scale, elementwise activations require less arithmetic than dense matrix multiplication but still move full tensors and store information for backpropagation. Kernel fusion, recomputation, numerical approximation, and hardware support therefore form part of activation choice. Architecture-level evidence is more informative than a context-free ranking of scalar functions.

title: Activation Functions and Non-linearity
text:
Looking ahead
Chapters 2–7 have introduced the components of a trainable neural network separately: predictions, loss, parameter updates, backpropagation, neurons, layers, and activations. Chapter 8 assembles them into one small network and follows a complete training loop from data to updated predictions.

title: Activation Functions and Non-linearity
text:
Further reading
The approximation result for sigmoidal networks is established by Cybenko (1989). Training difficulties associated with sigmoid and tanh saturation are analysed by Glorot and Bengio (2010). Rectified activations are examined by Nair and Hinton (2010) and Glorot, Bordes, and Bengio (2011). GELU is introduced by Hendrycks and Gimpel (2016), the activation search that produced Swish is reported by Ramachandran, Zoph, and Le (2017), and gated Transformer variants are evaluated by Shazeer (2020). The relation between depth and measures of functional complexity is studied by Raghu et al. (2017).

text: Chapter orientation
