title: Sequence Modelling Before Transformers
text: Chapter orientation

title: Sequence Modelling Before Transformers
text:
Why this chapter matters
Embeddings represent items at individual positions. A sequence model must also represent order and decide which earlier information remains available when a later item is processed. A bag of embeddings cannot distinguish red then blue from blue then red if it reduces them by an order-insensitive sum or mean.
Recurrent neural networks address this problem by carrying a state from one position to the next. Their limitations explain several later design choices: gates were introduced to preserve useful information over longer spans, bidirectional encoders use future context when a task permits it, and attention avoids forcing an entire source sequence through one fixed-size vector. This chapter establishes those problems before Chapter 19 introduces the attention mechanism itself.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

explain why order-sensitive tasks require more than pooled embeddings;
describe a recurrent state as a learned summary of an ordered prefix;
unroll a recurrent network through time and identify the shared parameters;
calculate simple recurrent updates and distinguish state from output;
derive backpropagation through time as repeated use of the chain rule;
explain vanishing and exploding gradients as products of temporal Jacobians;
describe the update, reset, forget, input, and output gates at the level needed to diagnose their role;
distinguish causal, bidirectional, encoder, and decoder sequence processing;
explain why fixed-length sequence summaries become a bottleneck;
state which sequence metadata, masks, states, and truncation rules must be recorded;
explain why recurrence limits parallel execution across positions.



Running task
The running task is a constructed delayed-copy problem. The first position contains either \(+1\) or \(-1\). The remaining positions contain zeros. At the final position, the model must return the first signal. The task is deliberately simple: success requires retaining one early value across a growing number of steps, so failures of state and gradient propagation become visible.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue, teal, orange, purple, grey = "#24527a", "#3a9188", "#d97745", "#5f6b76"

fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(11,4.2)); axes[0].axis("off"); axes[1].axis("off")
for row,sequence in enumerate([["red","blue"],["blue","red"]]):
    y=3.0-row*1.5
    for col,item in enumerate(sequence):
        colour=orange if item=="red" else blue
        axes[0].add_patch(Rectangle((.4+col*1.35,y),1.05,.65,facecolor=colour,edgecolor="white"))
        axes[0].text(.925+col*1.35,y+.325,item,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
    axes[0].add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((3.25,y+.325),(4.25,y+.325),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=13,color=grey))
    axes[0].text(4.5,y+.325,"same mean",va="center")
axes[0].set_xlim(0,6); axes[0].set_ylim(.4,4.1); axes[0].set_title("Pooling removes order")
for row,sequence in enumerate([["red","blue"],["blue","red"]]):
    y=3.0-row*1.5
    last_x=.35
    for col,item in enumerate(sequence):
        axes[1].add_patch(Rectangle((.45+col*1.55,y),1.05,.65,facecolor=orange if item=="red" else blue,edgecolor="white"))
        axes[1].text(.975+col*1.55,y+.325,item,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
        axes[1].add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((1.55+col*1.55,y+.325),(2.0+col*1.55,y+.325),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=11,color=grey))
    axes[1].add_patch(Rectangle((3.9,y),1.25,.65,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white"))
    axes[1].text(4.525,y+.325,"state differs",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
axes[1].set_xlim(0,5.7); axes[1].set_ylim(.4,4.1); axes[1].set_title("Recurrent processing preserves order")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 19.1



The figure does not claim that every recurrent network succeeds automatically. It identifies a capacity: a recurrent update can make the representation at position two depend on position one and two in order. Whether training finds a useful state depends on parameters, data, objective, and gradient flow.

title: Sequence Modelling Before Transformers
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

A sequence is more than a set of embeddings
An embedding layer maps each identifier to a vector, preserving the sequence axis. A later operation must decide how those vectors interact. Summing them is appropriate when order is irrelevant, for example in some set-like count tasks. It fails when earlier and later positions play different roles.
A recurrent network processes one position at a time. It combines the current input with a state produced at the previous position. The new state becomes a summary of the prefix seen so far. The same update rule is used at every position, so the model can process sequences longer or shorter than those used in one batch.


State is memory with limited capacity
The hidden state is a finite vector. It can retain a useful feature of a long prefix, overwrite it with newer information, or encode several features in different coordinates. It cannot preserve every detail of an arbitrarily long sequence with fixed precision and fixed width.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(11.5,3.6)); ax.axis("off")
positions=range(4)
for t in positions:
    x=1+t*2.55
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,.25),.9,.55,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.45,.525,f"x{t+1}",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.4),.9,.8,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.45,1.8,"cell\nθ",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x+.45,.83),(x+.45,1.35),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=12,color=grey))
    ax.text(x+.45,2.55,f"h{t+1}",ha="center")
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x+.45,2.18),(x+.45,2.45),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=12,color=grey))
    if t>0: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x-1.65,1.8),(x-.05,1.8),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=12,color=grey))
ax.text(.15,1.8,"h0",va="center"); ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((.45,1.8),(.95,1.8),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=12,color=grey))
ax.set_xlim(0,11.5); ax.set_ylim(0,2.95); ax.set_title("One parameterised transition applied through time"); plt.show()



Figure 19.2



The unrolled picture contains several cells for explanation. The implementation stores one set of parameters. Parameter sharing is what turns a fixed update rule into a sequence model.


The task determines when an output is available
A many-to-one model reads a sequence and produces one output, such as a final classification. A many-to-many model produces an output at each position, such as a tag for each item. An encoder reads a source sequence into states; a decoder produces a target sequence step by step. The same recurrent mechanism can appear in each arrangement, but the permitted direction of information differs.
For the delayed-copy task, the final output may use the final state. A causal next-item model at position \(t\) may use only positions up to \(t\). A bidirectional encoder may use both earlier and later positions, which is appropriate for labelling a complete observed sequence but invalid for real-time prediction.


State updates make order explicit
If an early signal is useful, the recurrent update must preserve it. If a newer signal makes it irrelevant, the update should overwrite it. Plain recurrence has no explicit switch between these behaviours. Gated units add learned values between zero and one that regulate what is carried forward and what is replaced.
Level 1 established the operational purpose of state. Level 2 follows a delayed signal through a recurrence and its gates.

title: Sequence Modelling Before Transformers
text:
Level 2 - Mechanics

A plain recurrent cell combines input and prior state
For input \(x_t\) and hidden state \(h_{t-1}\), a basic recurrent update is
\[
h_t=\tanh(W_xx_t+W_hh_{t-1}+b).
\]
The input term introduces current evidence. The recurrent term carries transformed earlier evidence. Tanh bounds each coordinate, which can stabilise values but can also reduce gradients in saturated regions.


Code
x_values=np.array([1.,0.,0.,0.,0.])
W_x,W_h,b=1.0,.72,0.0
states=[]; h=0.0
for x in x_values:
    h=np.tanh(W_x*x+W_h*h+b); states.append(h)
print("inputs:",x_values)
print("states:",np.round(states,3))


The first input enters the state. Later zero inputs do not restore the previous state; the recurrent multiplier and nonlinearity determine how rapidly the signal changes. A trained model has vector states and matrices, but the scalar calculation exposes the same dependence.


Repeated transitions can erase or amplify a signal




Code
steps=30
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,4.8))
for recurrent_weight,colour in [(0.3,orange),(0.72,teal),(1.05,purple)]:
    h=0.; values=[]
    for x in [1.]+[0.]*(steps-1):
        h=np.tanh(x+recurrent_weight*h); values.append(h)
    ax.plot(range(1,steps+1),values,label=f"recurrent weight {recurrent_weight}",color=colour,linewidth=2.3)
ax.set_xlabel("Position"); ax.set_ylabel("Hidden state"); ax.set_title("Retention in a scalar tanh recurrence"); ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 19.3



The values do not follow a pure power because tanh is nonlinear. The comparison nevertheless shows the mechanism: a state that is repeatedly contracted loses early evidence. A larger recurrent weight can retain more signal but may also create unstable dynamics in other regions of state space.


Gates create a direct controlled path
An LSTM maintains a cell state \(c_t\) and uses gates to regulate its update (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997). In a simplified form,
\[
c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot \tilde c_t,
\]
where \(f_t\) is the forget gate, \(i_t\) the input gate, and \(\tilde c_t\) a candidate update. Values near one preserve or write; values near zero block the corresponding contribution. An output gate determines how the cell becomes the visible hidden state.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3.8)); ax.axis("off")
boxes=[(.5,2.2,"prior\ncell c(t-1)",blue),(3.0,2.2,"forget\ngate f(t)",teal),(5.6,2.2,"new\ncell c(t)",purple),(.5,.55,"candidate\nupdate",orange),(3.0,.55,"input\ngate i(t)",teal)]
for x,y,label,colour in boxes:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,y),1.45,.72,facecolor=colour,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.725,y+.36,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
for start,end in [((1.98,2.56),(2.94,2.56)),((4.48,2.56),(5.54,2.56)),((1.98,.91),(2.94,.91)),((4.48,.91),(5.54,2.42))]:
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(start,end,arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=14,color=grey))
ax.text(5.15,1.55,"+",fontsize=22,ha="center"); ax.set_xlim(.1,7.5); ax.set_ylim(.2,3.35); ax.set_title("Gated addition creates a path for retained state"); plt.show()



Figure 19.4



A GRU uses a related update gate to interpolate between a previous hidden state and a candidate state (Cho et al. 2014). Different gated formulations make different parameter and state choices, but each tries to give optimisation a route through time that plain recurrence lacks.


Bidirectionality uses information from both sides




Code
tokens=["the","small","truck","carries","cargo"]
fig,axes=plt.subplots(3,1,figsize=(10,5.4),sharex=True)
for ax,title in zip(axes,["Causal forward states","Backward states","Bidirectional encoder states"]):
    ax.set_title(title,loc="left",fontsize=11); ax.axis("off"); ax.set_xlim(-.3,5.3); ax.set_ylim(-.2,1.2)
    for i,token in enumerate(tokens):
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((i,.25),.82,.48,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(i+.41,.49,token,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for i in range(4): axes[0].add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((i+.82,.97),(i+1,.97),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=11,color=teal))
for i in range(4): axes[1].add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((i+1,.02),(i+.82,.02),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=11,color=orange))
for i in range(4):
    axes[2].add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((i+.82,.97),(i+1,.97),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=11,color=teal))
    axes[2].add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((i+1,.02),(i+.82,.02),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=11,color=orange))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 19.5



The backward pass is available only after the complete sequence is observed. It cannot be used unchanged for a system that must produce a prediction before future events arrive. Masking and sequence boundaries are part of this direction contract.


Encoder-decoder models expose a fixed-vector bottleneck
An early sequence-to-sequence encoder maps a source sequence to a final state. A decoder conditions each target step on that one state and on earlier target outputs. This permits variable source and target lengths, but it asks a fixed-width vector to make source details available across all decoding steps.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(11,3.8)); ax.axis("off")
for i,label in enumerate(["source 1","source 2","source 3","source 4"]):
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.3+i*.85,2.4),.7,.48,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(.65+i*.85,2.64,label,ha="center",va="center",fontsize=8,color="white")
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((2.0,1.15),2.2,.72,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(3.1,1.51,"recurrent encoder",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((5.0,1.15),1.1,.72,facecolor=orange,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(5.55,1.51,"fixed\nstate",ha="center",va="center")
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((6.9,1.15),2.2,.72,facecolor=purple,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(8.0,1.51,"recurrent decoder",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
for i in range(4): ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((.65+i*.85,2.36),(3.1,1.92),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=11,color=grey,alpha=.65))
for start,end in [((4.25,1.51),(4.95,1.51)),((6.15,1.51),(6.85,1.51))]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(start,end,arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=14,color=grey))
for i,label in enumerate(["target 1","target 2","target 3"]):
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((7.0+i*.78,.25),.65,.46,facecolor=purple,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(7.325+i*.78,.48,label,ha="center",va="center",fontsize=8,color="white")
ax.set_xlim(0,10); ax.set_ylim(0,3.2); ax.set_title("Source information reaches the decoder through a fixed-size interface"); plt.show()



Figure 19.6



The bottleneck is not a statement that the final state contains no useful information. It is a constraint on access: every decoder decision must rely on the same compressed source summary. Chapter 19 examines the mechanism that lets a decoder construct a different source-dependent context at each step.
Level 2 described recurrent operation and its practical pressure points. Level 3 derives the temporal gradient and implements recurrent modules.

title: Sequence Modelling Before Transformers
text:
Level 3 - Mathematics & Code

Unrolling turns recurrence into a deep computation graph
For the plain recurrence \(h_t=\phi(W_xx_t+W_hh_{t-1}+b)\), a final loss \(L\) depends on \(h_1\) through every later state. The gradient with respect to an earlier state contains products of Jacobians:
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial h_t}=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial h_T}
\prod_{k=t+1}^{T}\frac{\partial h_k}{\partial h_{k-1}}.
\]
For a scalar linear recurrence with multiplier \(a\), the product is \(a^{T-t}\). If \(|a|<1\), it shrinks exponentially; if \(|a|>1\), it grows exponentially. In nonlinear networks, each factor also contains activation derivatives and matrix directions.




Code
steps=np.arange(1,41)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,4.7))
for derivative,colour in [(0.8,orange),(1.0,teal),(1.2,purple)]:
    ax.plot(steps,derivative**steps,label=f"local multiplier {derivative}",color=colour,linewidth=2.3)
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("Number of recurrent transitions"); ax.set_ylabel("Relative gradient magnitude")
ax.set_title("Products of temporal derivatives"); ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 19.7



Backpropagation through time applies the same chain rule introduced in Chapter 4 to the unrolled graph. Pascanu, Mikolov, and Bengio (2013) analyse the vanishing and exploding gradient problems in recurrent networks and discuss gradient clipping as one response to explosions. Clipping limits update magnitude; it does not restore information lost through sustained contraction.


Gated cell equations expose retention paths
One common LSTM parameterisation is
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_t&=\sigma(W_f[x_t,h_{t-1}]+b_f),\\
i_t&=\sigma(W_i[x_t,h_{t-1}]+b_i),\\
\tilde c_t&=\tanh(W_c[x_t,h_{t-1}]+b_c),\\
c_t&=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot\tilde c_t,\\
o_t&=\sigma(W_o[x_t,h_{t-1}]+b_o),\\
h_t&=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t).
\end{aligned}
\]
The forget gate directly multiplies the prior cell. When \(f_t\) remains near one and the remaining terms are controlled, a component of \(c_{t-1}\) can persist across many steps. This is a learned possibility, not a guarantee that a fitted model will use long-range information.


Code
forget_values=np.array([.15,.55,.92])
initial_cell=1.0
for forget in forget_values:
    retained=initial_cell*forget**20
    print(f"forget gate {forget:.2f}: cell contribution after 20 steps = {retained:.5f}")


The calculation isolates one path by setting new candidate contributions aside. In a real LSTM, input, output, and forget gates depend on inputs and hidden state at every position; the full dynamics can retain, overwrite, or mix information in more complex ways.


Framework modules preserve the sequence axis


Code
import torch
from torch import nn

torch.manual_seed(18)
inputs=torch.randn(3,5,4)  # batch, positions, embedding features
gru=nn.GRU(input_size=4,hidden_size=6,batch_first=True)
outputs,final_state=gru(inputs)
bidirectional=nn.GRU(input_size=4,hidden_size=6,batch_first=True,bidirectional=True)
bi_outputs,bi_final=bidirectional(inputs)
print("forward outputs:",tuple(outputs.shape),"final state:",tuple(final_state.shape))
print("bidirectional outputs:",tuple(bi_outputs.shape),"final state:",tuple(bi_final.shape))


The forward GRU returns one six-dimensional output at each of five positions and one final state per batch item. The bidirectional output concatenates forward and backward features, giving width twelve at each position. Framework shape validity does not establish causal validity: a bidirectional output includes future positions by construction.


Variable lengths require packing or masks


Code
lengths=torch.tensor([5,3,2])
sequence=torch.randn(3,5,4)
packed=nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence(sequence,lengths,batch_first=True,enforce_sorted=False)
packed_output,packed_final=gru(packed)
unpacked,returned_lengths=nn.utils.rnn.pad_packed_sequence(packed_output,batch_first=True)
print("unpacked shape:",tuple(unpacked.shape),"returned lengths:",returned_lengths.tolist())


Packing prevents recurrent updates from treating padded positions as observations. A masking implementation must provide equivalent protection. The final-state convention, padding side, sorted order, and truncation rule should be recorded because they change which state represents each sequence.
Level 3 has connected temporal derivatives and tensor shapes to recurrent computation. Level 4 considers sequence models as training and systems objects, and marks the precise transition to attention.

title: Sequence Modelling Before Transformers
text:
Level 4 - Research & Systems

Recurrent models have sequential depth
A recurrent layer has one transition per position. Within a position, matrix multiplications can use accelerator parallelism across batch items and hidden dimensions. Across positions, the next state depends on the preceding state. This dependency limits training and inference parallelism over sequence length.
Padding creates wasted recurrent steps when sequence lengths vary. Bucketing similar lengths, packing valid positions, and truncating or chunking streams can reduce this waste. Each choice changes batching, memory use, latency, and the span over which gradients and state can propagate.


Truncated backpropagation creates an explicit learning horizon
Long streams are often divided into segments. Hidden state may be carried from one segment to the next while gradients are detached at the boundary. The forward state then contains older information, but parameter updates receive no gradient through the detached history. This is a substantive training assumption, not only a memory optimisation.
An implementation should state segment length, overlap, state-reset conditions, detach points, and whether evaluation uses the same state policy. Leakage can arise if a state carries information across independent sequences or across train, validation, and test boundaries.


Gates improve optimisation but do not remove all sequence limits
LSTM and GRU units address plain recurrent gradient paths by offering additive or interpolating memory updates (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997; Cho et al. 2014). They still have finite state width, may forget information, and process positions sequentially. Gating also adds parameter matrices and elementwise operations, so shorter sequences or smaller states can remain more efficient even when long dependency capacity is desirable.
Gate values are diagnostics, not explanations by themselves. A forget gate near one at one position does not show which information was preserved or whether it affected the output. Useful analysis connects controlled changes in input or state to later predictions under a declared task.


Encoder-decoder bottlenecks motivated attention
Early encoder-decoder systems encoded a variable-length source in one fixed-length vector (Cho et al. 2014). This is workable for short patterns but creates a constrained interface as source length and target requirements grow. Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio (2015) introduced a learned alignment mechanism that lets a decoder form a different weighted context from encoder states at each output step.
The historical motivation should not be read as a claim that attention automatically solves long-context reliability, memory, or computation. It changes the access pattern: source states become separately available to a decoder. Chapter 19 derives that weighted retrieval operation. Chapters 20–22 then develop self-attention, positional information, and the Transformer block.


Sequence direction is a deployment constraint
Bidirectional encoders can use future context and are therefore appropriate for retrospective labelling, document classification, and some offline analysis. Autoregressive generation and streaming alerts require causal processing. A model trained with a bidirectional encoder can report optimistic validation results if its deployment target lacks future observations.
The representation contract must state which positions are visible at prediction time. It should also state clock definitions, ordering rules for tied events, missing-position treatment, padding, resets, and whether a hidden state can cross a user, document, session, or device boundary.


A sequence-model audit connects information flow to evaluation
An audit should record:

the item encoding, sequence order, time unit, and treatment of tied or missing events;
the task arrangement: many-to-one, many-to-many, encoder-decoder, causal, or bidirectional;
hidden-state width, cell type, layers, dropout, initial-state rule, and parameter count;
padding, masks, packing, bucketing, truncation, segment length, and reset policy;
gradient norms by time span, clipping frequency, non-finite values, and gate or state summaries where relevant;
train, validation, and test boundaries for stateful streams;
latency, throughput, sequence-length distribution, and peak activation memory;
accuracy and calibration by dependency length, position, sequence length, and relevant population or domain group.

The final point is often neglected. A model can achieve strong average performance by relying mainly on recent information while failing precisely when the target depends on a long earlier span.

title: Sequence Modelling Before Transformers
text:
Common misconceptions

Embeddings already model order. Lookup preserves position but does not combine positions.
A recurrent state stores the full sequence. It is a fixed-width learned summary.
Unrolling creates separate parameters for each position. The same recurrent weights are reused.
A stable hidden value proves a stable gradient. Forward-state retention and backward derivatives are related but distinct.
A recurrent multiplier below one always causes vanishing gradients at the same rate. Activation derivatives and matrix directions also enter the product.
Gradient clipping solves long-term dependency learning. It limits exploding updates but does not reverse contraction.
LSTMs never forget. Their gates can preserve, overwrite, or block information.
A gate value explains a prediction. It describes one update factor, not causal use of a feature.
Bidirectional models are stronger causal models. They use future observations unavailable in causal deployment.
Padding values are harmless in recurrence. Unmasked recurrence can update state from padding.
Carrying state across batches is always efficient. It can leak information across independent sequences or splits.
The encoder final state is a complete source representation. It is one fixed-width interface with limited access capacity.
Attention removes sequence order automatically. Attention requires an explicit treatment of position, addressed in Chapter 21.
Recurrent networks cannot process long sequences. They can, but optimisation, memory, latency, and dependency quality must be measured.

title: Sequence Modelling Before Transformers
text:
Exercises

Give two sequences with identical sums of embedding vectors but different order-dependent meanings or targets.
Write the shape of a batch of 32 sequences, length 100, embedding width 256 before and after a forward GRU with hidden width 512.
Calculate five scalar recurrent updates for \(h_t=\tanh(x_t+0.6h_{t-1})\) with one initial signal followed by zeros.
Repeat the calculation with a recurrent multiplier of 1.1 and compare the forward states.
Explain why both calculations are insufficient to establish trainability.
Derive the gradient product for a scalar linear recurrence over ten steps.
Plot the products for local derivatives 0.9, 1.0, and 1.1 over 100 steps.
Explain the roles of the forget, input, and output gates in an LSTM.
Calculate the retained contribution of an initial cell value under three constant forget-gate values.
Compare a GRU update gate with the LSTM’s separate forget and input gates.
Implement a causal GRU and verify that permuting future positions leaves an earlier output unchanged.
Implement a bidirectional GRU and show why that test no longer holds.
Use packed sequences with lengths 6, 4, and 1 and verify that padded positions do not create valid outputs.
Define a state-reset policy for independent user sessions and explain the leakage risk of violating it.
Design a delayed-copy dataset with dependency lengths from 1 to 100 and report accuracy by length.
Implement truncated backpropagation through time and state its gradient horizon.
Compare full and truncated gradients on a short sequence where both are feasible.
Draw the information available at position four for causal, backward, and bidirectional processing.
Explain why a fixed encoder vector can constrain a long source-to-target task.
Specify the metadata required to reproduce one sequence-model prediction in a streaming system.
Estimate how doubling sequence length changes the number of recurrent transitions and saved states for one layer.
Design an evaluation that detects whether a model relies on the first, middle, or final portion of a sequence.

title: Sequence Modelling Before Transformers
text:
Summary
Sequence models must make earlier and later positions interact. Recurrent networks do this by carrying a hidden state through an ordered sequence with shared parameters. The state is a learned prefix summary, not a complete record. It can retain, overwrite, or mix information according to the recurrent transition and, in gated models, learned control values.
Unrolling a recurrent network produces a computation graph whose gradient contains products of temporal derivatives. These products can contract or expand sharply with sequence length. LSTMs and GRUs create more direct controlled paths through state, but they retain finite memory, sequential dependence, and optimisation limits.
Bidirectional encoders use both sides of a position and therefore require a complete sequence. Encoder-decoder systems show a further constraint when one final source state must support all target decisions. The next chapter introduces attention as a learned way to construct a different source-dependent context at each output step.

title: Sequence Modelling Before Transformers
text:
Looking ahead
Chapter 19 introduces attention. It replaces the fixed-vector access pattern by comparing a current query with a collection of source representations, converting the resulting scores into weights, and forming a weighted retrieval vector.

title: Sequence Modelling Before Transformers
text:
Further reading
The simple recurrent network is developed by Elman (1990). The original LSTM architecture is described by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997), and the GRU encoder-decoder by Cho et al. (2014). Temporal gradient problems are analysed by Pascanu, Mikolov, and Bengio (2013). The fixed-vector encoder-decoder limitation and its attention-based response are developed by Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio (2015).






Bahdanau, Dzmitry, Kyunghyun Cho, and Yoshua Bengio. 2015. “Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate.” In International Conference on Learning Representations. https://mlanthology.org/iclr/2015/bahdanau2015iclr-neural/.


Cho, Kyunghyun, Bart van Merriënboer, Caglar Gulcehre, Dzmitry Bahdanau, Fethi Bougares, Holger Schwenk, and Yoshua Bengio. 2014. “Learning Phrase Representations Using RNN Encoder–Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation.” In Proceedings of the 2014 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 1724–34. Association for Computational Linguistics. https://doi.org/10.3115/v1/D14-1179.


Elman, Jeffrey L. 1990. “Finding Structure in Time.” Cognitive Science 14 (2): 179–211. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1402_1.


Hochreiter, Sepp, and Jürgen Schmidhuber. 1997. “Long Short-Term Memory.” Neural Computation 9 (8): 1735–80. https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1997.9.8.1735.


Pascanu, Razvan, Tomas Mikolov, and Yoshua Bengio. 2013. “On the Difficulty of Training Recurrent Neural Networks.” In Proceedings of the 30th International Conference on Machine Learning, 28:1310–18. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v28/pascanu13.html.

title: Attention
text: Chapter orientation

title: Attention
Attention
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Attention changes access to stored representations
An encoder produces a sequence of representations. A decoder that receives only the final encoder state must use that one vector for every output decision. Attention retains the encoder states and lets the decoder compare its current state with each one.
The comparison produces a relevance score for every source position. A normalisation turns scores into non-negative weights that sum to one. The context vector is the weighted average of source values. Positions with greater weight contribute more to the returned vector, but every unmasked value can contribute.


Query, key, and value name different jobs
The query describes what the current computation is seeking. The key is the representation used for matching. The value is the representation returned after matching. A system may use the same encoder state for key and value, as in early encoder-decoder attention. It may also learn separate projections, so matching is performed in one space and retrieved content is expressed in another.




Code
source_labels=["source 1","source 2","source 3","source 4","source 5"]
weights=np.array([[.05,.48,.36,.08,.03],[.03,.05,.10,.37,.45]])
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(10,3.8),sharey=True)
for ax,row,title in zip(axes,weights,["Query: retrieve an early detail","Query: retrieve a later detail"]):
    image=ax.imshow(row[None,:],cmap="YlGnBu",vmin=0,vmax=.5,aspect="auto")
    ax.set_xticks(range(5),source_labels,rotation=25,ha="right"); ax.set_yticks([0],["weight"]); ax.set_title(title)
    for i,value in enumerate(row): ax.text(i,0,f"{value:.2f}",ha="center",va="center",fontsize=9,color="black" if value<.28 else "white")
fig.colorbar(image,ax=axes.ravel().tolist(),label="attention weight",shrink=.8); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 20.2



The two rows use the same source sequence. Their difference comes entirely from the query and score function. Attention therefore does not designate one globally important source position; relevance is conditional on the computation asking the question.


Attention is a differentiable retrieval rule
Hard retrieval would choose the single largest score and return one value. Soft attention returns a weighted combination, allowing gradients to flow through every score and every unmasked value. A sharply concentrated distribution approaches selection; a diffuse distribution combines several positions.
This differentiability is useful for training, but it has an interpretive consequence. A large weight identifies a strong route through one particular attention operation. It does not by itself show that changing that source item would change the final prediction, because later layers, residual paths, value vectors, and other attention heads can compensate.


Attention does not supply order by itself
If two source states have identical keys and values, swapping their positions leaves ordinary content attention unchanged. The source encoder may already carry order through recurrence or convolution. Self-attention architectures need an explicit positional treatment, which Chapter 21 develops. Attention determines access to the representations supplied to it; it does not determine what those representations encode.
Level 1 defined attention as query-dependent retrieval. Level 2 follows the computation from scores to a context vector and identifies the operational role of masks.

title: Attention
text:
Level 2 - Mechanics

Scores compare one query with every key
Let \(q\) be a decoder query and \(k_i\) be the key at source position \(i\). A dot-product score is \(e_i=q^\top k_i\). A bilinear score is \(e_i=q^\top Wk_i\). Additive attention uses a learned nonlinear comparison such as
\[
e_i=v_a^\top\tanh(W_q q+W_k k_i+b_a).
\]
The score has no requirement to lie between zero and one. It is a compatibility value whose scale and distribution depend on the parameterisation and inputs. Bahdanau attention used an additive alignment function in an encoder-decoder model (Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio 2015). Luong and colleagues compared dot-product, general bilinear, and related score functions (Luong, Pham, and Manning 2015).


Code
query=np.array([.8,-.3,.5])
keys=np.array([[.2,.7,-.1],[.9,-.2,.4],[.1,.3,.8],[-.6,.2,.5],[.4,-.8,-.2]])
values=np.array([[1.,0.,.2],[.7,.4,.1],[.2,.9,.3],[.1,.3,.8],[.4,.2,1.]])
dot_scores=keys@query
W=np.array([[1.,.1,0.],[0.,.8,.2],[.2,0.,1.]])
bilinear_scores=keys@(W.T@query)
print("dot-product scores:",np.round(dot_scores,3))
print("bilinear scores:   ",np.round(bilinear_scores,3))


The two score patterns differ because the bilinear matrix changes which key directions match the query. Score choice is part of the model’s learned interface.


Softmax makes scores compete
For scores \(e_1,\ldots,e_S\), softmax defines
\[
\alpha_i=\frac{\exp(e_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{S}\exp(e_j)}.
\]
Every \(\alpha_i\) is non-negative and the weights sum to one. Raising one score affects all weights through the denominator. Adding the same constant to every score leaves the distribution unchanged, so stable implementations subtract the maximum score before exponentiation.


Code
def softmax(scores):
    shifted=scores-scores.max()
    exp=np.exp(shifted)
    return exp/exp.sum()

attention_weights=softmax(dot_scores)
context=attention_weights@values
print("weights:",np.round(attention_weights,3),"sum:",attention_weights.sum())
print("context:",np.round(context,3))


The context has the same width as one value vector. It is not a longer concatenation of source states. The attention distribution determines how much each value contributes to each coordinate of the returned context.


Temperature changes concentration
Dividing scores by a positive temperature \(\tau\) before softmax gives
\[
\alpha_i(\tau)=\frac{\exp(e_i/\tau)}{\sum_j\exp(e_j/\tau)}.
\]
A smaller temperature makes score differences more decisive. A larger temperature makes weights more uniform. Dot-product attention in Transformers uses a scale factor related to key dimension; Chapter 20 derives that specific form.




Code
temperatures=[.5,1.,2.]
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(12,3.8),sharey=True)
for ax,temp in zip(axes,temperatures):
    w=softmax(dot_scores/temp)
    ax.bar(range(1,6),w,color=teal)
    ax.set_title(f"temperature {temp}"); ax.set_xlabel("Source position"); ax.set_ylim(0,.8)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Attention weight"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 20.3



Very sharp distributions can make learning sensitive to small score changes. Very diffuse distributions can blur distinctions the decoder needs. The appropriate scale is learned or selected within a full training configuration, not inferred from one visualisation.


Masks define which keys are eligible
Attention often receives rectangular batches containing padding. A padding key must receive zero weight. A causal decoder must not retrieve a future source or target position when the task prohibits it. A mask enforces this by assigning an ineligible score a value that becomes zero after softmax.




Code
valid=np.array([True,True,True,False,False])
masked_scores=dot_scores.copy(); masked_scores[~valid]=-np.inf
masked_weights=softmax(masked_scores)
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(10,3.8),sharey=True)
axes[0].bar(range(1,6),attention_weights,color=orange); axes[0].set_title("Unmasked")
axes[1].bar(range(1,6),masked_weights,color=teal); axes[1].set_title("Positions 4-5 masked")
for ax in axes: ax.set_xlabel("Source position"); ax.set_ylim(0,.8)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Attention weight"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 20.4



Masking after softmax and then failing to renormalise is a different operation: the returned weights no longer sum to one and the context scale changes with padding length. Boolean-mask conventions, fill values, and broadcast dimensions should be tested explicitly.


Global and local access trade coverage for cost
Global attention scores every available source state. Local attention restricts scoring to a window or selected subset. Global access can retrieve any source position but grows with sequence length. Local access reduces work and may suit monotonic or spatially local tasks, but it can miss a relevant position outside the window. Luong et al. compared global and local attention in neural machine translation (Luong, Pham, and Manning 2015).




Code
fig,axes=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(10,4.4),sharex=True)
for ax,title,active in [(axes[0],"Global: all source positions eligible",set(range(10))),(axes[1],"Local: window around predicted centre",set(range(3,7)))]:
    for i in range(10):
        colour=teal if i in active else "#d9dde1"
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((i,.25),.75,.5,facecolor=colour,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(i+.375,.5,str(i+1),ha="center",va="center",fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlim(-.1,10); ax.set_ylim(0,1); ax.axis("off"); ax.set_title(title,loc="left",fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 20.5



The access pattern is an assumption about what a query may retrieve. It should be stated before interpreting observed weights or comparing runtime.
Level 2 described the forward computation and its eligibility rules. Level 3 expresses the batched operation in tensor notation and verifies a masked implementation.

title: Attention
text:
Level 3 - Mathematics & Code

Attention has a compact tensor form
For one query \(q\in\mathbb{R}^{D_k}\), keys \(K\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times D_k}\), and values \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times D_v}\), dot-product attention is
\[
\alpha=\operatorname{softmax}(Kq),
\qquad
c=\alpha^\top V.
\]
Here \(Kq\in\mathbb{R}^{S}\) supplies one score per source position, \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{S}\) supplies one weight per position, and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{D_v}\) is the context vector. The key dimension and value dimension need not be equal.
For a batch of decoder queries \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times D_k}\) and source keys \(K\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times S\times D_k}\), the score tensor has shape \(B\times T\times S\). Each target position has its own distribution over source positions.


Code
import torch

torch.manual_seed(19)
B,T,S,D_k,D_v=2,3,5,4,6
Q=torch.randn(B,T,D_k)
K=torch.randn(B,S,D_k)
V=torch.randn(B,S,D_v)
scores=torch.matmul(Q,K.transpose(-2,-1))
weights=torch.softmax(scores,dim=-1)
contexts=torch.matmul(weights,V)
print("scores:  ",tuple(scores.shape))
print("weights: ",tuple(weights.shape),"row sums:",weights[0,0].sum().item())
print("contexts:",tuple(contexts.shape))


The final dimension of scores indexes source positions and is the dimension over which softmax must operate. Applying softmax across target positions or batch items can produce plausible tensor shapes while implementing a different model.


Masked softmax requires a stable fill value


Code
def masked_attention(query,keys,values,valid_positions):
    scores=query@keys.T
    scores=np.where(valid_positions,scores,-np.inf)
    weights=softmax(scores)
    return weights,weights@values

one_query=np.array([.8,-.3,.5])
one_keys=keys
one_values=values
one_mask=np.array([True,True,True,False,False])
checked_weights,checked_context=masked_attention(one_query,one_keys,one_values,one_mask)
print("masked weights:",np.round(checked_weights,3))
print("masked context:",np.round(checked_context,3))
print("masked mass:",checked_weights[~one_mask].sum())


-np.inf is conceptually exact for this NumPy example. Hardware kernels often use a large finite negative number compatible with the dtype. Under reduced precision, that value, the order of casting, and the all-masked-row policy require tests because softmax([-inf,-inf,...]) is undefined.


Weighted sums are mixtures, not discrete selections
If all attention weights are non-negative and sum to one, the context lies in the convex hull of the value vectors. A context coordinate can be between the corresponding coordinates of the supplied values. Attention cannot return a value outside that hull without later transformations, residual additions, or a value projection.




Code
value_points=np.array([[0.,0.],[2.6,.25],[.55,2.1]])
weight_sets=np.array([[.6,.3,.1],[.15,.25,.6]])
contexts_2d=weight_sets@value_points
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6,5.2))
polygon=np.vstack([value_points,value_points[0]])
ax.plot(polygon[:,0],polygon[:,1],color=grey,linestyle="--")
for i,(x,y) in enumerate(value_points): ax.scatter(x,y,s=90,color=blue); ax.text(x+.06,y+.06,f"value {i+1}")
for i,(x,y) in enumerate(contexts_2d):
    ax.scatter(x,y,s=95,color=orange if i==0 else teal); ax.text(x+.06,y-.18,f"context {i+1}: {weight_sets[i]}",fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("value coordinate 1"); ax.set_ylabel("value coordinate 2"); ax.set_title("Attention contexts remain within the value mixture"); ax.set_aspect("equal"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 20.6



This geometric constraint is useful when debugging. If a purported weighted average lies outside coordinate-wise ranges of unprojected values, a mask, axis, normalisation, or code path differs from the stated operation.


Additive scores learn a comparison space
For query \(q_t\) and encoder state \(h_i\), additive attention uses
\[
e_{ti}=v_a^\top\tanh(W_q q_t+W_h h_i+b_a).
\]
The matrices can map decoder and encoder representations with different widths into a shared alignment width. The learned vector \(v_a\) reduces the nonlinear comparison to one scalar score. This formulation can express interactions beyond a direct dot product, but it adds parameters and elementwise work for every query-key pair.


Code
rng=np.random.default_rng(19)
query_width,source_width,alignment_width=4,6,5
q=rng.normal(size=query_width); source=rng.normal(size=(5,source_width))
W_q=rng.normal(size=(alignment_width,query_width)); W_h=rng.normal(size=(alignment_width,source_width)); v_a=rng.normal(size=alignment_width)
additive_scores=np.array([v_a@np.tanh(W_q@q+W_h@h) for h in source])
print("additive score shape:",additive_scores.shape)
print("additive weights:    ",np.round(softmax(additive_scores),3))


The code computes one source score at a time to expose the equation. Vectorised kernels broadcast the transformed query across source positions and compute all scores together. The mathematical dependency remains one query against each eligible key.
Level 3 established attention as a masked batched tensor operation. Level 4 examines what changes at scale and why weights require careful interpretation.

title: Attention
text:
Level 4 - Research & Systems

Attention alters information access, not the need for representation quality
Attention lets a decoder retrieve from individual encoder states instead of depending solely on one final state (Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio 2015). It does not guarantee that encoder states preserve the required detail, that scores identify the most useful position, or that the output model uses the context in the intended way. Encoder architecture, value projection, decoder state, objective, and data distribution remain part of the system.
Cross-attention uses one sequence or modality to query another. Self-attention uses a sequence to query itself and will be treated separately in Chapter 20. Both use score matrices and weighted value sums, but their masks, source-target relationships, and computational patterns differ.


Attention weights are not sufficient explanations
High attention weight is evidence about one routing distribution within the implemented computation. It does not establish that the associated input is necessary, sufficient, or causally responsible for the final output. Distinct attention distributions can sometimes yield similar outputs because values are redundant or later components compensate.
Jain and Wallace found that attention weights in several NLP models could be uncorrelated with gradient-based importance measures and that alternative attention distributions could produce equivalent predictions (Jain and Wallace 2019). This does not make weights useless for diagnosis. It means explanatory claims require tests: remove or replace source content, intervene on weights or values, compare outputs, and report the model components held fixed.


Score scale, dtype, and masking affect numerical behaviour
Exponentiation magnifies score scale. Subtracting the row maximum before softmax prevents overflow without changing the result. Low-precision score accumulation can alter close rankings, and large negative mask fills must be representable in the selected dtype. All-masked rows need explicit handling rather than allowing NaNs to propagate silently.
The scale of dot products grows with key dimension under common random assumptions. Transformer attention uses a dimension-based scaling factor for this reason; Chapter 20 will derive and test it. The current chapter’s conclusion is narrower: any implementation must state score function, scaling, dtype, mask convention, and normalisation axis.


Cost follows the query-key access pattern
With \(T\) queries, \(S\) keys, key width \(D_k\), and value width \(D_v\), global attention forms or streams through \(T\times S\) scores. The arithmetic for scores and weighted values is on the order of
\[
O(TS(D_k+D_v)).
\]
Storing weights costs \(O(TS)\) elements per batch item and head. Decoder cross-attention often has modest \(T\) per generation step but may cache encoder keys and values. Full self-attention has \(T=S\) and creates a quadratic score matrix; Chapter 20 examines that case directly.
Local windows, sparse patterns, chunking, and monotonic constraints reduce the eligible pair set. They also impose a retrieval restriction that can change outputs. A runtime comparison should report effective source length, valid-token fraction, mask density, dtype, cached state, and whether the implementation materialises the score matrix.


Attention modules need targeted tests
An attention audit should record:

query, key, and value sources, shapes, projections, and parameter sharing;
score function, scale or temperature, normalisation dimension, and dropout placement;
global, local, causal, padding, and cross-source eligibility rules;
mask dtype, broadcast shape, fill value, and all-masked-row behaviour;
source and target position conventions, truncation, and cache policy;
score ranges, entropy of weight distributions, masked mass, non-finite values, and output norms;
latency, peak memory, valid-token throughput, and score-matrix materialisation;
intervention results supporting any claim that selected positions explain an output.

The audit distinguishes a valid weighted retrieval computation from a claim about model reasoning.

title: Attention
text:
Common misconceptions

Attention chooses exactly one source item. Standard soft attention returns a weighted combination of eligible values.
Keys and values must be identical. Early models often reused states, but separate learned projections can give them different roles.
Attention weights are independent probabilities. Softmax makes them compete through a shared denominator.
Scores are probabilities. Scores are unnormalised compatibility values and can be negative or arbitrarily scaled.
A larger score always means a larger final contribution. Masks, softmax competition, value magnitude, later projections, and other paths also matter.
Masking after softmax is equivalent to masking before it. Post-softmax masking changes total mass unless weights are renormalised.
Padding masks and causal masks are interchangeable. They encode different eligibility rules.
A sharp distribution proves the model has found the correct evidence. Concentration is a geometric property of one attention operation.
Attention weights are causal explanations. They need intervention and output tests before supporting that claim.
Attention supplies order. It operates on the representations and positional information it receives.
Global attention is always preferable. It expands access and cost; local restrictions can be appropriate when justified by the task.
Attention removes quadratic cost in self-attention. Full self-attention scores every query-key pair.
All-masked rows have zero attention by default. Naive softmax can return undefined values for them.
Matching output shape proves the correct softmax axis was used. Normalising across the wrong dimension can preserve shape while changing the model.

title: Attention
text:
Exercises

Identify the query, keys, values, scores, weights, and context in the running example.
Compute dot-product scores for one query and three supplied keys.
Calculate softmax weights by hand for three scores and verify that they sum to one.
Show algebraically that adding a constant to every score leaves softmax unchanged.
Compare attention distributions at temperatures 0.5, 1, and 2 for one score vector.
Calculate a context vector from three values and a supplied weight vector.
Verify that the result lies in the convex hull of the values.
Implement a stable softmax and compare it with a naive implementation on large scores.
Construct a padding mask for a batch with source lengths 5, 3, and 1.
Test that masked keys receive exactly zero probability in a masked-attention implementation.
Define and test the intended behaviour for an all-masked row.
Implement dot-product and bilinear attention and compare their score shapes.
Implement additive attention for query and key vectors with different widths.
Explain how using the wrong softmax axis changes a batched cross-attention computation.
Compare global attention with a fixed local window on a task where the relevant source position lies outside the window.
Calculate the score-matrix shape and element count for batch 8, target length 64, source length 512, and four heads.
Derive the arithmetic order for global cross-attention with \(T\) queries and \(S\) keys.
Design a test showing that one decoder query retrieves a different context from another query over the same source states.
Replace a high-weight source value with a control value and measure the change in output; state what this does and does not establish.
Design an audit for a masked cross-attention module used in a clinical or policy-text classifier.
Compare attention-weight entropy across short and long source sequences and interpret the result cautiously.
Specify the data required to reproduce one attention map from a deployed model.

title: Attention
text:
Summary
Attention is a query-dependent weighted retrieval operation. A query scores a set of keys, softmax converts eligible scores into competing weights, and the weights mix the corresponding values into a context vector. Different queries can retrieve different contexts from the same source representations.
Score functions, temperature, masks, and the softmax axis define the computation. Masking is part of the model’s information-access contract: padding, causal restrictions, local windows, and cross-source boundaries each determine which values can affect a context. Weighted sums are differentiable mixtures, not discrete selections.
Attention expands access to source states but does not guarantee faithful representations, correct alignment, causal explanation, or low cost. Numerical stability, mask handling, source length, dtype, and score-matrix storage all affect practical behaviour. The next chapter applies query-key-value attention within one sequence and introduces multiple learned attention subspaces.

title: Attention
text:
Looking ahead
Chapter 20 examines self-attention and multi-head attention. The sequence will supply its own queries, keys, and values, allowing each position to retrieve from other positions under a declared mask; multiple heads will learn several retrieval patterns in parallel.

title: Attention
text:
Further reading
Additive encoder-decoder attention is introduced by Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio (2015). Dot-product, bilinear, global, and local variants are compared by Luong, Pham, and Manning (2015). The limits of treating attention weights as explanations are examined by Jain and Wallace (2019).






Bahdanau, Dzmitry, Kyunghyun Cho, and Yoshua Bengio. 2015. “Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate.” In International Conference on Learning Representations. https://mlanthology.org/iclr/2015/bahdanau2015iclr-neural/.


Jain, Sarthak, and Byron C. Wallace. 2019. “Attention Is Not Explanation.” In Proceedings of the 2019 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, 3543–56. Association for Computational Linguistics. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/N19-1357.


Luong, Thang, Hieu Pham, and Christopher D. Manning. 2015. “Effective Approaches to Attention-Based Neural Machine Translation.” In Proceedings of the 2015 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 1412–21. Association for Computational Linguistics. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/D15-1166.

title: Self-attention and Multi-head Attention
text: Chapter orientation

title: Self-attention and Multi-head Attention
Self-attention and Multi-head Attention
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Every position asks its own retrieval question
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_S\) be the representations supplied to a self-attention layer. Position \(t\) creates a query from \(x_t\) and compares it with keys created from every eligible position. The resulting context at \(t\) can combine information from distant positions in one layer.
This differs from recurrence, where information at position one reaches position five only after four state transitions. It does not remove dependency constraints: a causal mask prevents position four from using position five, and positional information is still needed to distinguish sequences with the same items in different orders.




Code
length=5
mask=np.tril(np.ones((length,length),dtype=bool))
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2,4.4)); ax.imshow(mask,cmap="YlGnBu",vmin=0,vmax=1)
for i in range(length):
    for j in range(length): ax.text(j,i,"eligible" if mask[i,j] else "blocked",ha="center",va="center",fontsize=8,color="white" if mask[i,j] else "black")
ax.set_xticks(range(length),range(1,length+1)); ax.set_yticks(range(length),range(1,length+1)); ax.set_xlabel("Key position"); ax.set_ylabel("Query position"); ax.set_title("Causal eligibility")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 21.2





Projections separate matching from retrieved content
The input representation is not used directly for all three roles. Learned matrices project it into query, key, and value spaces. Queries and keys determine which positions match; values determine what content is returned. Separate projections allow a model to use one feature direction for matching and another for retrieved information.
The names describe a retrieval analogy, not three kinds of token. A query asks what the present position needs; a key says what a position can be matched on; a value is the information offered if that position is selected. Consider a word whose interpretation depends on an earlier qualifier. Its query can favour keys that mark a relevant qualifier, while the retrieved value carries the representation that changes the present context. Which feature plays each role is learned from the training objective. The same input position therefore supplies all three, but through different learned projections.
The distinction also prevents a common error. A high score does not mean that a key vector is copied into the output. Scores determine weights; the output is a weighted mixture of value vectors. A model can match positions on one property and retrieve a different property from them.


Heads provide several retrieval subspaces
One head produces one set of weights and one context vector per position. Multi-head attention uses several independently parameterised projections. A head can learn a local, long-range, syntactic, or domain-specific pattern if that helps the objective, but no such role is guaranteed by the head number.
At fixed model width, multi-head attention is not simply “more attention”. It divides the internal feature width into several smaller projected spaces, runs a retrieval calculation in each one, and lets a later output projection mix the results. The useful claim is modest: several learned comparison spaces can represent different routing patterns at the same layer. Whether they do so is an empirical question.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(11,4.2)); ax.axis("off")
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.4,1.55),1.35,.68,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(1.075,1.89,"input sequence X",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
for i,y in enumerate([3.05,1.8,.55]):
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((1.8,1.89),(3.0,y),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=13,color=grey))
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((3.05,y-.3),1.45,.6,facecolor=[teal,orange,purple][i],edgecolor="white")); ax.text(3.775,y,f"head {i+1}",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((4.55,y),(6.0,1.89),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=13,color=grey))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((6.05,1.55),1.5,.68,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(6.8,1.89,"concatenate",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((7.6,1.89),(8.55,1.89),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=13,color=grey))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((8.6,1.55),1.6,.68,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(9.4,1.89,"output projection",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(0,10.7); ax.set_ylim(0,3.7); plt.show()



Figure 21.3







Code
local=np.array([[1,0,0,0,0],[.35,.65,0,0,0],[.08,.32,.60,0,0],[.03,.10,.31,.56,0],[.02,.06,.13,.30,.49]])
retrieve=np.array([[1,0,0,0,0],[.72,.28,0,0,0],[.63,.10,.27,0,0],[.52,.09,.13,.26,0],[.47,.08,.10,.14,.21]])
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(9,3.8),sharey=True)
for ax,a,title in zip(axes,[local,retrieve],["head A: local pattern","head B: earlier retrieval"]):
    im=ax.imshow(a,cmap="YlGnBu",vmin=0,vmax=1); ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("Key position"); ax.set_xticks(range(5),range(1,6)); ax.set_yticks(range(5),range(1,6))
axes[0].set_ylabel("Query position"); fig.colorbar(im,ax=axes,shrink=.8,label="attention weight"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 21.4



The figure is deliberately synthetic. It shows a possibility, not evidence that a trained head has a stable semantic identity. In particular, the output projection can combine or cancel information from multiple heads, so an attention map is a diagnostic object rather than a complete explanation of a prediction.
Level 1 defined the operation. Level 2 follows the matrix products and mask through one attention head.

title: Self-attention and Multi-head Attention
text:
Level 2 - Mechanics

Scaled dot products create one score row per query
For input \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times D}\), one head projects
\[Q=XW_Q,\quad K=XW_K,\quad V=XW_V.\]
The score matrix is \(QK^\top\). Entry \((t,j)\) compares query position \(t\) with key position \(j\). Scaled dot-product attention uses
\[A=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{D_k}}+M\right),\qquad C=AV,\]
where softmax is applied across keys and \(M\) encodes eligibility. The division by \(\sqrt{D_k}\) controls score scale as key width changes (Vaswani et al. 2017).


Code
X=np.array([[1.,0.,.2,.1],[.8,.2,.1,.3],[.1,.9,.3,.2],[.3,.4,.8,.2],[.2,.1,.6,.9]])
Wq=np.array([[.7,0.],[.1,.6],[.2,.4],[.4,.1]])
Wk=np.array([[.5,.2],[.2,.7],[.6,.1],[.1,.5]])
Wv=np.array([[.4,.1,.2],[.2,.5,.1],[.1,.3,.6],[.5,.2,.2]])
Q,K,V=X@Wq,X@Wk,X@Wv
scores=Q@K.T/np.sqrt(Q.shape[-1])
def row_softmax(z):
    z=z-z.max(axis=-1,keepdims=True); ez=np.exp(z); return ez/ez.sum(axis=-1,keepdims=True)
weights=row_softmax(scores); contexts=weights@V
print("Q, K, V:",Q.shape,K.shape,V.shape)
print("scores, weights, contexts:",scores.shape,weights.shape,contexts.shape)
print("row sums:",weights.sum(axis=-1).round(6))


Each row of weights is a separate distribution. Softmax over columns makes a query’s eligible keys compete. Softmax over rows would create a different and usually unintended model.
The context \(C_t\) is the attention contribution for position \(t\), not yet a complete Transformer-layer output. A full Transformer block also retains the position’s prior representation through a residual path, normalises appropriate axes, and applies a position-wise feed-forward transformation. Those components are intentionally deferred to Chapter 22, so that the retrieval operation remains visible here.


Causal and padding masks combine by exclusion
A causal mask blocks future key positions. A padding mask blocks positions that do not contain source data. Both act on score entries before softmax. For a batch, the padding mask is broadcast over query positions; the causal mask is broadcast over batch items and heads.


Code
causal=np.tril(np.ones((5,5),dtype=bool))
valid_keys=np.array([True,True,True,True,False])
eligible=causal & valid_keys[None,:]
masked_scores=np.where(eligible,scores,-np.inf)
masked_weights=row_softmax(masked_scores)
print("masked weight at query 4:",masked_weights[3].round(3))
print("future mass at query 2:",masked_weights[1,2:].sum())


An all-masked query row requires an explicit policy. It may arise from malformed lengths or empty examples. Letting it become NaN hides an input-contract failure.
Mask orientation matters. In the displayed matrices, rows are queries and columns are keys, so a causal mask is lower triangular: query four may use keys one through four. Some libraries use different argument names or boolean conventions, where True can mean either keep or block. A tiny hand-checked example and a future-perturbation test are safer than copying a mask expression without checking its contract.


Heads split width, not sequence responsibility
With model width \(D\) and \(H\) heads, many implementations use head width \(d_h=D/H\). Each head has its own \(W_Q^{(h)}, W_K^{(h)}, W_V^{(h)}\). Contexts concatenate along features and an output projection maps them back to width \(D\).
Splitting width does not allocate different token positions to each head. Every head usually sees the same eligible positions. It receives different projected coordinates, so its scores and retrieved mixtures can differ.
For example, with \(D=512\) and \(H=8\), a conventional implementation uses \(d_h=64\). Each head still produces a score for every allowed query-key pair; it has fewer coordinates in which to construct that score. The concatenated head outputs recover width 512 before the output projection. Other designs use unequal widths or grouped key/value projections, but the shape contract must be made explicit rather than inferred from the word “head”.

title: Self-attention and Multi-head Attention
text:
Level 3 - Mathematics & Code

Batched multi-head shapes make the contracts explicit
For \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times S\times D}\), reshape projections into \(B\times H\times S\times d_h\). The score tensor then has shape \(B\times H\times S\times S\). Its last axis is keys; its penultimate axis is queries.


Code
import torch
from torch import nn

torch.manual_seed(20)
B,S,D,H=2,5,8,2; d_h=D//H
x=torch.randn(B,S,D)
qkv=nn.Linear(D,3*D,bias=False)(x)
q,k,v=qkv.chunk(3,dim=-1)
def split_heads(t): return t.view(B,S,H,d_h).transpose(1,2)
q,k,v=map(split_heads,(q,k,v))
scores=torch.matmul(q,k.transpose(-2,-1))/np.sqrt(d_h)
causal_mask=torch.tril(torch.ones(S,S,dtype=torch.bool))
scores=scores.masked_fill(~causal_mask,-torch.inf)
attention=torch.softmax(scores,dim=-1)
head_context=torch.matmul(attention,v)
merged=head_context.transpose(1,2).contiguous().view(B,S,D)
print("scores:",tuple(scores.shape),"attention:",tuple(attention.shape))
print("merged output:",tuple(merged.shape),"masked mass:",attention[0,0,1,2:].sum().item())


The transpose changes the logical axis order. contiguous() makes the requested feature merge explicit before view. The output projection, omitted here for visibility, is another learned linear layer and does not change the sequence length.


Scaling controls score variance
If independent query and key coordinates have zero mean and unit variance, an unscaled dot product has variance proportional to \(D_k\). Larger key widths can therefore make softmax excessively concentrated early in training. Dividing by \(\sqrt{D_k}\) keeps the scale closer to constant under those assumptions.




Code
rng=np.random.default_rng(20); widths=np.array([4,8,16,32,64,128,256]); raw=[]; scaled=[]
for width in widths:
    dots=(rng.normal(size=(4000,width))*rng.normal(size=(4000,width))).sum(axis=1)
    raw.append(dots.std()); scaled.append((dots/np.sqrt(width)).std())
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5,4.4)); ax.plot(widths,raw,marker="o",color=orange,label="unscaled"); ax.plot(widths,scaled,marker="o",color=teal,label="divided by sqrt(key width)")
ax.set_xscale("log",base=2); ax.set_xlabel("Key width"); ax.set_ylabel("Score standard deviation"); ax.set_title("Random score scale changes with key width"); ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 21.5



This is a distributional argument about initial scores, not a guarantee about trained representations. Learned norms, normalisation, precision, and masks also affect score scale.


A module test should assert information boundaries


Code
class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self,width,heads):
        super().__init__(); self.width=width; self.heads=heads; self.head_width=width//heads
        self.qkv=nn.Linear(width,3*width); self.out=nn.Linear(width,width)
    def forward(self,x):
        b,s,_=x.shape; q,k,v=self.qkv(x).chunk(3,dim=-1)
        def split(t): return t.view(b,s,self.heads,self.head_width).transpose(1,2)
        q,k,v=map(split,(q,k,v)); score=(q@k.transpose(-2,-1))/np.sqrt(self.head_width)
        mask=torch.tril(torch.ones(s,s,device=x.device,dtype=torch.bool)); score=score.masked_fill(~mask,-torch.inf)
        a=torch.softmax(score,dim=-1); c=(a@v).transpose(1,2).contiguous().view(b,s,self.width)
        return self.out(c),a

layer=CausalSelfAttention(8,2); base=torch.randn(1,5,8); changed=base.clone(); changed[:,4]+=100
out_base,_=layer(base); out_changed,_=layer(changed)
print("earlier outputs unchanged:",torch.allclose(out_base[:,:4],out_changed[:,:4],atol=1e-6))


The perturbation test checks a causal promise: changing a future input cannot alter earlier outputs. It is stronger than inspecting a triangular plot because it tests the complete implemented path.

title: Self-attention and Multi-head Attention
text:
Level 4 - Research & Systems

Self-attention exchanges sequential depth for all-pairs work
All sequence positions can form queries, keys, and values in parallel. Full self-attention then compares every query-key pair. For length \(S\), the score matrix has \(S^2\) entries per head and batch item. This permits direct interaction between distant positions in one layer but produces quadratic memory and arithmetic in sequence length (Vaswani et al. 2017).
For a dense score tensor the element count is \(BHS^2\). At four-byte floating point precision, scores alone require roughly \(4BHS^2\) bytes before accounting for weights, gradients, activations, projections, and framework overhead. This accounting is why a change from length 1,024 to 8,192 is not an eight-fold enlargement of dense attention: the score relation is sixty-four times larger.
Flash-style kernels, blockwise computation, sparse patterns, and approximate methods can reduce materialised memory or restrict pair sets. Their equivalence conditions, mask semantics, numerical tolerances, and hardware dependence must be stated; an implementation that changes eligible pairs changes the model.


Multi-head patterns require tests before interpretation
Head maps can reveal routing patterns or implementation errors, especially masked mass, repeated rows, dead heads, and unexpectedly uniform distributions. They do not assign a semantic role to a head or establish causal explanation. Heads can be redundant, later projections can mix them, and removing one head can trigger compensation elsewhere.
Interventions should vary a source value, a head output, or a selected edge while holding the relevant rest of the model fixed, then measure the output change. Even then, a local intervention does not establish a global natural-language explanation.


Autoregressive inference caches prior keys and values
In causal generation, recomputing keys and values for every earlier position at each new token repeats work. A key-value cache retains projected keys and values from prior positions. Each new query attends to the cache plus its current key and value. The cache lowers repeated projection work but grows linearly with generated length, layers, heads, batch size, and value width.
The cache is not a separate memory of text: it is a collection of projected tensors with a specific model checkpoint, layer, dtype, position convention, and mask history. Chapter 27 examines this inference contract and its memory consequences in more detail.


A self-attention audit records eligibility and cost
An audit should record model width, heads, head width, all projection shapes, scale factor, softmax axis, causal and padding masks, all-masked-row policy, dropout, dtype, score ranges, attention entropy, masked mass, sequence lengths, cache policy, peak memory, and valid-token throughput. It should test causal invariance, padding invariance, shape contracts, and numerical agreement with a small reference implementation.

title: Self-attention and Multi-head Attention
text:
Common misconceptions

Self-attention knows order from token embeddings alone. It needs order encoded in its input or a separate positional mechanism.
Each head attends to a different subset of tokens by design. Heads usually receive the same eligible positions with different learned projections.
Causal masking means all positions receive the same context. Each query row has a different eligible prefix and different scores.
The scale factor makes attention stable in every setting. It addresses one score-variance mechanism under stated assumptions.
Multi-head attention is several independent models. Heads are recombined by an output projection and trained jointly.
A triangular heatmap proves causal implementation. A perturbation test must include all code paths.
Full self-attention has linear memory in sequence length. Its dense score relations are quadratic.
A key-value cache removes attention cost. It avoids repeated projections but each new query still scores cached keys.

text:
Exercises

Reproduce the scaling figure for non-unit coordinate variance.
Implement the omitted output projection in the batched example.

Estimate key-value cache bytes for a specified layer count, head width, and generated length.
Design a test for an all-masked input row.

title: Self-attention and Multi-head Attention
text:
Summary
Self-attention uses every sequence position as a query, key, and value source. Scaled dot products create one score distribution over eligible keys for every query position, and weighted value sums produce new contextual representations. Causal and padding masks define the information boundary.
Multi-head attention repeats this retrieval operation in several learned projection spaces, concatenates the resulting contexts, and projects them back to model width. It permits direct long-range interaction but creates a dense query-key relation whose cost grows quadratically with length.

title: Self-attention and Multi-head Attention
text:
Looking ahead
Chapter 21 supplies positional information, allowing non-recurrent self-attention to distinguish sequence order explicitly. Chapter 22 then places attention inside a complete Transformer block.

Further reading
Scaled dot-product and multi-head attention are introduced by Vaswani et al. (2017). The general attention operation and its alignment-based origins are covered in Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio (2015) and Luong, Pham, and Manning (2015).
