title: Tokens and Tokenisation
text:
Why this chapter matters
Transformer models process tensors, not raw character strings. Before an embedding lookup, a tokenisation procedure converts text into a sequence of discrete token identifiers under a fixed vocabulary and set of text-processing conventions. The procedure affects which distinctions the model can represent directly, the sequence length it receives, the cost of attention, and the compatibility of training, evaluation, and inference inputs.
Tokenisation is therefore part of the model, not a harmless pre-processing detail. This chapter defines the text-to-ID contract, compares word, character, byte, and subword units, and explains how vocabulary and normalisation choices affect coverage and cost. It does not yet define the probability distribution or training loss over the resulting IDs; Chapter 25 does that.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish text, tokens, token strings, token IDs, and embedding vectors;
explain why an identifier has no numerical meaning before embedding lookup;
describe word, character, byte, and subword tokenisation trade-offs;
explain the basic logic of byte-pair encoding and vocabulary-limited segmentation;
identify special tokens, padding, truncation, and normalisation as interface choices;
implement and test a small vocabulary encoder and decoder;
estimate how tokenisation changes sequence length and dense-attention cost; and
specify the tokeniser metadata required to reproduce a trained model’s input interface.



Running text
The running text is replaying replay. The repeated form makes it possible to compare a word-level representation, character sequence, and a subword segmentation without implying that any one segmentation is intrinsically correct.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(11,3.2)); ax.axis("off")
items=[("raw text\nreplaying replay",blue),("tokens\nre play ing | re play",teal),("IDs\n[14, 27, 91, 14, 27]",orange),("embedding rows\n[e14, e27, e91, e14, e27]",purple)]
for i,(label,colour) in enumerate(items):
    x=.25+i*2.68; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.05),2.05,.72,facecolor=colour,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+1.025,1.41,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
    if i<3: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x+2.08,1.41),(x+2.58,1.41),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=13,color=grey))
ax.text(5.45,.48,"The IDs index a fixed vocabulary; their magnitude is not a semantic quantity.",ha="center",color=grey)
ax.set_xlim(0,11); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.25); plt.show()



Figure 25.1

title: Tokens and Tokenisation
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Text must cross a discrete interface
The string replaying replay is a sequence of characters visible to a reader. A model needs a finite set of discrete symbols that can index rows in an embedding table. A tokeniser chooses a segmentation, assigns each chosen token a vocabulary ID, and records conventions for spaces, punctuation, Unicode, and special markers. The embedding layer in Chapter 17 then replaces each ID with a learned vector.
An ID is an address, not an ordered quantity. ID 27 is not twice as meaningful as ID 14, and neighbouring IDs do not imply similar tokens. Permuting the rows of an embedding table and applying the same permutation to token IDs leaves the model function unchanged. Meaning is learned in the embedding vectors and later transformations, not in the integers used to retrieve them.


A token is a modelling unit, not necessarily a word
Word tokenisation gives a readable segmentation but needs a policy for rare or unseen words. Character tokenisation has a small vocabulary and can represent any sequence of known characters, but it creates long sequences. Byte tokenisation can represent arbitrary byte strings under a fixed alphabet, but its pieces may split one human character across several bytes. Subword tokenisation chooses reusable pieces between characters and words.




Code
forms=[("word",["replaying","replay"]),("character",list("replaying replay")),("subword",["re","play","ing","re","play"])]
fig,axes=plt.subplots(3,1,figsize=(10,3.8))
for ax,(name,pieces) in zip(axes,forms):
    ax.axis("off"); ax.text(.01,.5,name,ha="left",va="center",weight="bold",color=grey,transform=ax.transAxes)
    width=min(.74/max(len(pieces),1),.23)
    for i,piece in enumerate(pieces):
        x=.18+i*width*1.05; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,.22),width,.56,facecolor=[blue,orange,teal][["word","character","subword"].index(name)],edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+width/2,.5,piece if len(piece)<5 else piece[:4]+"…",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
    ax.text(.93,.5,f"{len(pieces)} units",ha="right",va="center",color=grey,transform=ax.transAxes)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 25.2



No segmentation removes ambiguity from language. Tokenisation determines the discrete units supplied to the model; contextual layers can later combine their representations. A word split that appears linguistically familiar is not automatically superior for prediction, and a subword split need not correspond to a morphological boundary.
Byte-level methods make a different guarantee. A byte vocabulary can represent any input expressed in the chosen byte encoding without requiring an unknown-word token, but a visible character may become several byte tokens. This can be useful for arbitrary strings, mixed scripts, code, or malformed text, while increasing token counts for some inputs. The guarantee concerns representability of bytes; it does not guarantee that a trained model has useful evidence for every resulting sequence.


Vocabulary coverage has a cost
A larger vocabulary can store more frequent whole units and may shorten sequences. It also enlarges the embedding table and the output interface used in token prediction. A smaller vocabulary reduces those tables but usually makes sequences longer. For a Transformer, longer sequences affect attention relations quadratically, as Chapter 20 showed.
The relevant comparison is not simply “fewer tokens is better”. Coverage, language mix, spelling variation, throughput, memory, the training corpus, and the intended task all matter. A tokenizer is fitted or configured on a particular text distribution, then becomes fixed at the model boundary.




Code
names=["word","subword","character","byte"]
vocab_sizes=np.array([50000,32000,150,256]); average_lengths=np.array([9,12,45,52])
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.8,4.3))
for name,vocab,length,colour in zip(names,vocab_sizes,average_lengths,[blue,teal,orange,purple]):
    ax.scatter(vocab,length,s=115,color=colour); ax.text(vocab*1.08,length+.8,name,color=colour)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("Vocabulary entries (illustrative)"); ax.set_ylabel("Tokens per fixed text (illustrative)"); ax.set_title("Vocabulary size and sequence length are coupled design choices")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 25.3



The coordinates are illustrative rather than a benchmark. Actual token counts depend on language, corpus, normalisation, and the particular vocabulary. The point is architectural: a vocabulary entry consumes embedding and output-interface capacity, while a longer segmentation consumes positions and attention relations.
Level 1 established the interface. Level 2 follows its operational steps and failure modes.

title: Tokens and Tokenisation
text:
Level 2 - Mechanics

The tokenizer contract has several stages
A practical pipeline commonly: reads a Unicode string; applies a specified normalisation or preservation policy; inserts or recognises special markers; segments text into token strings; maps strings to IDs; pads, truncates, or packs sequences; and supplies an attention mask alongside IDs. Each stage can change the sequence supplied to the model.
For example, lowercasing can merge distinctions between May and may. Normalising a Unicode form can make visually similar text share a representation, but it can also erase distinctions relevant to a language or task. A tokenizer must therefore document its transformations rather than treating them as universally neutral cleanup.


Code
vocabulary={"<pad>":0,"<unk>":1,"<bos>":2,"<eos>":3,"re":4,"play":5,"ing":6," ":7}
inverse={idx:token for token,idx in vocabulary.items()}
pieces=["<bos>","re","play","ing"," ","re","play","<eos>"]
ids=[vocabulary.get(piece,vocabulary["<unk>"]) for piece in pieces]
print("pieces:",pieces)
print("ids:",ids)
print("decoded pieces:",[inverse[i] for i in ids])


The special IDs are ordinary vocabulary entries with an agreed role. They are not self-describing to a model. If one checkpoint treats ID 0 as padding and another treats it as a visible token, their input interfaces are incompatible even when their embedding matrices have the same shape.
The interface also needs a decoding rule. A reversible tokenisation can reconstruct the stored text representation from valid token pieces, but it cannot necessarily recover distinctions already removed by normalisation, lowercasing, truncation, or an unknown-token replacement. “Detokenises correctly” should therefore mean correct under a declared text representation and special-token policy.


Unknown items, padding, and truncation are distinct policies
An unknown-token policy replaces an unrecognised unit with an available placeholder ID. Padding adds artificial positions so a batch has a common tensor shape. Truncation drops selected positions to meet a maximum length. These operations have different consequences and require different metadata.
Padding should be paired with a padding mask so attention and losses can ignore artificial positions. Truncation can remove content and change a task’s answer. An unknown token keeps sequence length but collapses different unseen strings onto one identifier. These are modelling choices that must be tested on the intended distribution.


Code
batch_ids=np.array([[2,4,5,6,3,0,0],[2,4,5,7,4,5,3]])
pad_id=0; attention_mask=batch_ids!=pad_id
print("token IDs:\n",batch_ids)
print("valid-token mask:\n",attention_mask.astype(int))
print("valid lengths:",attention_mask.sum(axis=1))


The mask uses True for valid positions in this example. Frameworks vary in whether an argument expects a valid-token mask or a padding mask, so a model interface must state the convention and include a small test that padded content cannot influence valid outputs.


Subword vocabularies reuse frequent pieces
Byte-pair encoding (BPE) begins from small units and repeatedly merges frequent adjacent pairs in a training corpus. The learned merge list defines a vocabulary and a segmentation procedure. Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch used subword units based on BPE to address rare and unknown words in neural machine translation (Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch 2016).
Unigram-style tokenisers begin with a candidate inventory and select segmentations under a probabilistic vocabulary model. SentencePiece provides BPE and unigram approaches trained directly from raw sentences, avoiding a required language-specific pre-tokenisation stage (Kudo and Richardson 2018). The algorithms differ, but both make the vocabulary and segmentation rules part of the trained model interface.




Code
stages=[list("replay"),["re","p","l","a","y"],["re","play"]]
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(10,2.7))
for ax,pieces,title in zip(axes,stages,["initial small units","merge r + e","later merge"]):
    ax.axis("off"); ax.set_title(title,fontsize=10); width=.75/max(len(pieces),1)
    for i,piece in enumerate(pieces):
        x=.1+i*width*1.08; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,.37),width,.38,facecolor=[blue,teal,orange][min(len(pieces)-1,2)],edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+width/2,.56,piece,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 25.4



The figure is a toy procedure, not a tokenizer trainer. Real BPE implementations define initial symbols, pre-tokenisation or raw-text handling, merge order, vocabulary limits, special tokens, and byte or Unicode representation. These choices affect which strings can be represented and how many IDs they consume.
Segmentation can also be ambiguous. With pieces re, play, ing, and replay, the text replaying could be divided as replay plus ing or as re plus play plus ing. A deterministic BPE implementation resolves the choice using its learned merge order; a unigram formulation can score alternatives. The resulting model sees only the selected sequence unless training deliberately samples alternatives. Tokenisation is therefore a learned or configured view of text, not a transparent transcription.

title: Tokens and Tokenisation
text:
Level 3 - Mathematics & Code

IDs select rows; they are not numerical features
Let a vocabulary contain \(V\) entries and let its embedding matrix be \(E\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times D}\). For ID \(i_t\in\{0,\ldots,V-1\}\) at position \(t\), embedding lookup returns
\[x_t=E_{i_t,:}.\]
For a batch of IDs \(I\in\mathbb{N}^{B\times S}\), lookup produces \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times S\times D}\). This is the interface between tokenisation and the embeddings in Chapter 17. Replacing an input token changes the selected row; adding one to an ID does not make a meaningful incremental change.


Code
import torch
from torch import nn

torch.manual_seed(24)
embedding=nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=len(vocabulary),embedding_dim=4,padding_idx=0)
ids_tensor=torch.tensor(batch_ids)
vectors=embedding(ids_tensor)
print("IDs:",tuple(ids_tensor.shape),"embedding output:",tuple(vectors.shape))
print("same ID gives the same row before contextual layers:",torch.allclose(vectors[0,1],vectors[1,1]))
print("padding row is zeroed by this embedding configuration:",vectors[0,5].detach().numpy().round(4))


The equality check uses the same token ID in two positions. Later contextual layers can transform those positions into different representations, but the lookup itself is a row selection. padding_idx=0 is an implementation policy; it does not remove the need for masks in attention and loss calculations.


A simple longest-match encoder makes the vocabulary dependence visible


Code
def longest_match_encode(text,pieces,unk="<unk>"):
    output=[]; cursor=0; choices=sorted(pieces,key=len,reverse=True)
    while cursor<len(text):
        match=next((piece for piece in choices if text.startswith(piece,cursor)),None)
        if match is None: output.append(unk); cursor+=1
        else: output.append(match); cursor+=len(match)
    return output

piece_inventory={"re","play","ing"," ","<bos>","<eos>"}
print(longest_match_encode("replaying replay",piece_inventory))
print(longest_match_encode("replayed",piece_inventory))


The second result contains an unknown item because the toy inventory lacks pieces needed for the final characters. Real systems avoid this particular failure in different ways, including character or byte fallback. The example shows the contract: a segmentation algorithm and an inventory jointly determine what token sequence is available to the model.


Code
text="café"
characters=list(text); utf8_bytes=list(text.encode("utf-8"))
print("characters:",characters,"count:",len(characters))
print("UTF-8 byte values:",utf8_bytes,"count:",len(utf8_bytes))


The displayed text has four Unicode characters but five UTF-8 bytes because the final character uses more than one byte in that encoding. A byte-level tokenizer works with the latter sequence, while a character-level account works with the former. Neither representation is automatically wrong; they expose different units and different length conventions that should not be mixed in reporting.


Token counts affect tensor and attention sizes
If a text becomes \(S\) tokens, one batch of embeddings has shape \(B\times S\times D\). Dense self-attention creates score relations proportional to \(BHS^2\), for batch size \(B\) and heads \(H\). Splitting one linguistic unit into several tokens therefore changes both the number of embedding lookups and the number of possible attention pairs.




Code
lengths=np.array([16,32,64,128,256]); heads=8; batch=2
entries=batch*heads*lengths**2
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4,4.1)); ax.plot(lengths,entries,marker="o",color=orange)
ax.set_xscale("log",base=2); ax.set_yscale("log",base=2); ax.set_xlabel("Token sequence length"); ax.set_ylabel("Score entries: B × H × S²"); ax.set_title("Token length changes dense-attention scale"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 25.5



This accounting does not mean that the tokenizer alone determines inference cost. Width, layers, cache policy, batching, kernel choice, and decoding strategy also matter. It identifies why token-count comparisons are meaningful systems measurements and why character counts are not a reliable substitute across tokenisers.

title: Tokens and Tokenisation
text:
Level 4 - Research & Systems

Tokenisation choices distribute coverage unevenly
A vocabulary trained on one corpus or language mix may encode common forms concisely while splitting other forms into long sequences. Names, dialects, spelling variants, scripts, code, URLs, and rare morphological forms can receive disproportionate fragmentation. The resulting length increase affects context allocation, throughput, truncation risk, and the number of learning events associated with a visible string.
No general statement that one tokeniser is fair, multilingual, or robust follows from its unit type alone. Evaluation should report token counts and unknown or fallback rates by relevant language, script, domain, and input class. It should inspect the text transformations applied before segmentation and test whether important distinctions are preserved at the model boundary.


Training and inference must use the identical interface
A model checkpoint expects the vocabulary ordering, merge rules or unigram model, normalisation policy, added-token map, maximum length, padding side, truncation side, and special-token IDs used during training. Replacing a tokenizer with another that has the same vocabulary size is incompatible: ID 14 may select a different embedding row, and the same text may have different positions and masks.
The tokeniser should therefore be versioned and loaded with the model. An audit should preserve the tokenizer artefact or exact training configuration; vocabulary hash; special-token map; normalisation and pre-tokenisation rules; byte fallback policy; maximum length; truncation and padding policy; source and target tokenisers where relevant; and token-length distributions on train, evaluation, and deployment data.
The audit should also run round-trip and boundary tests. A reversible input should satisfy an explicitly defined encode-decode comparison. Special tokens should not be inserted or removed unexpectedly. Padding should have no effect on valid-token output. Inputs at the maximum length and one position beyond it should expose the truncation or rejection policy. These tests are small, but they prevent tokenisation mismatches from appearing later as unexplained model failures.


Text interfaces create security and evaluation boundaries
Tokenisation occurs before the model’s learned computation, so a pipeline should test malformed Unicode, unusual whitespace, control characters, repeated delimiters, very long inputs, and text that is visually similar but encoded differently. These tests do not establish model safety or factual reliability. They establish that the input interface behaves as specified and that monitoring counts the same units the model actually consumes.
Token-level metrics also need interpretation. A system may have a fixed maximum number of tokens, but the amount of human-readable text that fits varies by language and segmentation. Reporting only character limits can conceal this difference; reporting only token limits can conceal the user-visible burden. Both may be required for a deployment claim.

title: Tokens and Tokenisation
text:
Common misconceptions

A token is always a word. Tokens can be words, characters, bytes, subwords, or special markers.
Token IDs have ordinal meaning. They are vocabulary addresses used for lookup.
A larger vocabulary always improves a model. It changes coverage, table size, sequence length, data sparsity, and output cost.
Subword pieces are guaranteed linguistic morphemes. Their boundaries follow the tokenisation objective and corpus statistics.
Padding is harmless without a mask. Artificial positions can affect attention, loss, and pooled outputs unless excluded.
An unknown token and truncation do the same thing. One replaces a unit; the other removes positions.
A model can use any tokenizer with the same vocabulary size. It needs the exact ID mapping and preprocessing contract used in training.
A context limit in tokens means the same text length for every language. Token counts vary with segmentation and script.

title: Tokens and Tokenisation
text:
Exercises

Distinguish a token string, token ID, and embedding vector in a supplied example.
Explain why permuting a vocabulary and embedding rows together can preserve model behaviour.
Segment replaying replay into words, characters, and the running subword inventory.
Calculate the embedding-table parameter count for vocabulary 50,000 and width 768.
Calculate the relative increase in dense score entries when token length rises from 128 to 256.
Implement an encoder that adds beginning and end special tokens.
Implement a decoder that omits padding and special tokens from displayed text.
Write a test that padded positions receive zero attention mass in a small causal model.
Give an example of a text transformation that can change a token sequence.
Explain why an unknown-token policy can collapse distinct strings.
Compare the systems consequences of word and character tokenisation for a long document.
Explain why BPE merge rules must be saved with a model checkpoint.
Design a tokenisation evaluation across two scripts or language varieties.
State the source and target tokeniser metadata an encoder-decoder model requires.
Test a tokenizer on unusual whitespace and a long repeated input.
State which chapter introduces the next-token probability objective.

title: Tokens and Tokenisation
text:
Summary
Tokenisation converts text into a sequence of vocabulary identifiers, and embedding lookup converts those identifiers into vectors. The vocabulary, segmentation method, special tokens, normalisation, padding, truncation, and maximum length together form a model input contract.
Word, character, byte, and subword units make different coverage, vocabulary-size, and sequence-length trade-offs. These trade-offs affect representation, attention cost, evaluation, and deployment. A tokenizer must be versioned and evaluated with the model rather than substituted at inference.

title: Tokens and Tokenisation
text:
Looking ahead
Chapter 25 uses token IDs to define next-token probability distributions, training loss, and autoregressive generation.

title: Tokens and Tokenisation
text:
Further reading
Subword units based on BPE are developed by Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch (2016). SentencePiece’s language-independent raw-text interface and its support for BPE and unigram segmentation are described by Kudo and Richardson (2018).






Kudo, Taku, and John Richardson. 2018. “SentencePiece: A Simple and Language Independent Subword Tokenizer and Detokenizer for Neural Text Processing.” In Proceedings of the 2018 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations, 66–71. Association for Computational Linguistics. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/D18-2012.


Sennrich, Rico, Barry Haddow, and Alexandra Birch. 2016. “Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units.” In Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 1715–25. Association for Computational Linguistics. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/P16-1162.

title: Next-token Prediction
text: Chapter orientation

title: Next-token Prediction
text:
Why this chapter matters
A tokeniser turns text into IDs. A language model assigns a conditional probability distribution to the next ID, given a permitted prefix. The distribution is the direct output of a decoder language model before a generation rule chooses a continuation. Training changes parameters so that observed next tokens receive higher probability under the prefixes supplied by the training data.
This chapter defines that objective, its cross-entropy loss, and its limits. It distinguishes model probabilities from selected output tokens, and teacher-forced training from sequential inference. Chapter 28 will compare practical decoding rules; Chapter 26 examines the data and scale that determine what a base model can learn.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

write the autoregressive factorisation of a token sequence probability;
distinguish logits, softmax probabilities, targets, and sampled or selected output IDs;
calculate a next-token cross-entropy loss for a small vocabulary;
explain the target shift used in teacher-forced training;
identify padding, masking, and context-boundary errors in a language-model batch;
interpret perplexity as an exponentiated average loss while stating its limitations;
implement stable softmax, negative log likelihood, and masked loss calculations; and
state why next-token prediction alone does not specify useful, safe, or truthful generation.



Running sequence
We use the short token sequence <bos> the cat slept <eos>. At each position, the model may use only the tokens to its left. The target for a position is the subsequent token.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
tokens=["<bos>","the","cat","slept","<eos>"]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,2.8)); ax.axis("off")
for i,t in enumerate(tokens):
    x=.35+i*1.85; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.15),1.45,.55,facecolor=blue if i<4 else purple,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.725,1.425,t,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
    if i<4: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x+.72,1.08),(x+2.02,1.08),arrowstyle="-|>",color=orange,mutation_scale=12)); ax.text(x+1.37,.76,"target",ha="center",color=grey,fontsize=8)
ax.text(4.7,.25,"At position t, the model predicts token t+1 from the allowed prefix through t.",ha="center",color=grey)
ax.set_xlim(0,9.7); ax.set_ylim(0,2.1); plt.show()



Figure 26.1

title: Next-token Prediction
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

The output is a distribution, not a sentence
After a decoder Transformer processes a prefix, its final representation at the latest usable position is transformed into one score for each vocabulary item. Those scores become probabilities through softmax. A high probability means that, under the model and the supplied prefix, that token is assigned more probability mass than alternatives. It does not mean that the token is true, intended by an author, safe to emit, or the only defensible continuation.
For the prefix <bos> the cat, a training example may identify slept as the observed next token. The objective rewards the model for assigning it high probability, while assigning probability across every vocabulary entry. The model is not trained from a sentence-level label saying that the complete continuation is good. It receives many local prediction events derived from sequences.




Code
names=np.array(["slept","ran","ate","other"]); probs=np.array([.62,.19,.11,.08])
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,3.6)); bars=ax.bar(names,probs,color=[teal,blue,blue,grey]); ax.set_ylim(0,.75); ax.set_ylabel("probability"); ax.set_title("Distribution after '<bos> the cat'")
ax.text(0,.66,"observed target",ha="center",color=teal); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 26.2



The target probability is enough to calculate the loss for this example: -log(0.62). It falls as the model assigns more mass to the observed target and rises sharply when the target probability approaches zero. The remaining probabilities still matter because softmax couples them: increasing one logit changes the normalised distribution.


Sequence probability is built from conditional probabilities
For token IDs (x_1,,x_T), an autoregressive model defines
[ p(x_1,,x_T)={t=1}^{T}p(x_tx{<t}). ]
The notation says that the probability of the whole sequence is decomposed into conditional choices. A beginning marker commonly supplies an initial context. A causal mask, introduced in Chapters 20 and 23, prevents a prediction position from reading later tokens when the model computes all training positions in parallel.
This factorisation does not imply that language is generated word by word. It operates over the token units defined in Chapter 24. One visible word can require several decisions, and an end marker is also a prediction event.

title: Next-token Prediction
text:
Level 2 - Mechanics

Logits become probabilities through softmax
Let (z^{|V|}) be the output logits for one position. For vocabulary entry (j),
[ p_j=. ]
Logits are unconstrained real numbers; probabilities are non-negative and sum to one. Adding the same constant to every logit does not alter softmax, which permits a stable implementation that subtracts the largest logit before exponentiating.


Code
def stable_softmax(logits):
    shifted=logits-np.max(logits)
    weights=np.exp(shifted)
    return weights/weights.sum()

logits=np.array([2.0,0.8,0.2,-0.1])
probabilities=stable_softmax(logits)
print(np.round(probabilities,3), probabilities.sum())


The output projection has one column or row per vocabulary item, depending on notation. Vocabulary size therefore affects both the embedding interface and the final prediction interface. A tokenizer mismatch changes what each output index denotes, so an otherwise compatible checkpoint cannot be safely used with a rearranged vocabulary.


Cross-entropy selects the observed target
For a one-hot target ID (y), the negative log likelihood is (-p_y). Over valid sequence positions, the usual language-modelling loss averages those values:
[ =-{n=1}^{N}p(x_nx_{<n}). ]
Here (N) must count valid predicted tokens, not padded tensor cells. Cross-entropy is a name for the same calculation when the target distribution is one-hot. It compares a target distribution with the model distribution; it does not assess factuality, instruction-following, or downstream usefulness.


Code
target_id=0
loss=-np.log(probabilities[target_id])
print("target probability:",round(probabilities[target_id],3),"loss:",round(loss,3))




Training shifts inputs and targets
For a stored sequence [<bos>, the, cat, slept, <eos>], the model input may be the first four IDs and targets the final four IDs. Each input position produces a distribution for the token one place to the right. The full prefix is supplied to compute those positions efficiently, but the causal mask preserves the conditional information boundary.


Code
sequence=np.array([2,11,34,58,3])
inputs,targets=sequence[:-1],sequence[1:]
print("inputs: ",inputs)
print("targets:",targets)


An off-by-one error can make the model predict the current input token, expose the next target as input, or omit the end marker. These errors can produce plausible shapes and falling losses, so exact small examples should be inspected before a large run.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5,2.8)); ax.axis("off")
for row,(label,values,colour) in enumerate([("input",inputs,blue),("target",targets,orange)]):
    ax.text(.05,1.72-row*.8,label,weight="bold",color=grey)
    for i,v in enumerate(values):
        x=1+i*1.6; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.43-row*.8),1.05,.48,facecolor=colour,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.525,1.67-row*.8,str(v),ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.text(4.2,.15,"Target at each column is the next token in the original sequence.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,7.8); ax.set_ylim(0,2.25); plt.show()



Figure 26.3

title: Next-token Prediction
text:
Level 3 - Formal model and implementation

Causal representations and the output head
Let (h_t^{d}) be the decoder representation at position (t), computed with causal access to (x_{t}). An output head produces (z_t=W h_t+b), where (W) has a vocabulary axis. Softmax turns (z_t) into (p_(x_{t})). Depending on the indexing convention, this distribution is trained against (x_{t+1}). Weight tying can use the input embedding matrix in the output projection, but it does not remove the vocabulary distribution or change the target shift.


Code
hidden=np.array([.4,-.2,.6])
W=np.array([[.2,.1,-.3],[-.4,.5,.2],[.1,-.2,.7],[.3,.3,.1]])
b=np.array([.0,.1,-.1,.0])
logits=W@hidden+b
print("logits:",np.round(logits,3))
print("probabilities:",np.round(stable_softmax(logits),3))




Masks determine which losses count
In a padded batch, valid-token masks usually govern both attention eligibility and loss aggregation, but they are not interchangeable with causal masks. The causal mask forbids future access. The valid-token mask removes artificial positions. An implementation must specify whether it predicts an end token, whether packed documents permit cross-document attention, and whether loss includes special markers.


Code
logit_batch=np.array([[[2.,.5],[.1,1.3]],[[.7,.2],[1.1,.4]]])
target_batch=np.array([[0,1],[0,0]])
valid=np.array([[1,1],[1,0]],dtype=bool)
token_losses=np.array([-np.log(stable_softmax(row)[target]) for rows,targets in zip(logit_batch,target_batch) for row,target in zip(rows,targets)]).reshape(2,2)
masked_loss=(token_losses*valid).sum()/valid.sum()
print(np.round(token_losses,3)); print("masked mean:",round(masked_loss,3))


The example has deliberately separate names for the tensor and mask axes. A loss averaged over all four cells would silently reward or penalise a padding placeholder. The equivalent issue arises when an incorrect attention mask lets padding or a later target affect a valid prediction.


Perplexity is a transformed loss, not a general evaluation
Perplexity is commonly (()) when the loss uses natural logarithms. It can be interpreted as an effective branching factor under the particular tokenisation and evaluation corpus. Comparing perplexity across different tokenisers is generally invalid because one model may make more prediction events per visible string. It also does not measure whether continuations are accurate for a user task, calibrated under distribution shift, or appropriate after decoding.


Code
mean_nll=np.array([.69,1.39,2.30])
print("losses:",mean_nll)
print("perplexities:",np.round(np.exp(mean_nll),2))






Code
loss_grid=np.linspace(0,3,100)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.3,3.8)); ax.plot(loss_grid,np.exp(loss_grid),color=purple,lw=2.5); ax.set_xlabel("mean negative log likelihood"); ax.set_ylabel("perplexity"); ax.set_title("Perplexity is exp(mean loss)"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 26.4

title: Next-token Prediction
text:
Level 4 - Auditing the objective

Training and generation have different inputs
Teacher forcing supplies observed previous tokens at every training position. At inference, the model receives its own selected token from the preceding step. This difference is operational rather than a contradiction in the objective: the same conditional distribution is evaluated repeatedly, but the prefix source changes. A single wrong early selection can therefore move a generation into a prefix region poorly represented in training data.


Code
prefix=[2]
chosen=[11,34,58,3]
for token in chosen:
    # In a real model, probabilities depend on the current prefix.
    print("prefix",prefix,"-> choose",token)
    prefix.append(token)


The objective identifies a probability distribution. A decoding rule chooses from it. Greedy decoding selects the highest-probability token; sampling draws according to some transformed distribution; constrained systems may reject choices or stop at defined markers. Treating an argmax token as the model’s only belief discards the distribution that training actually produced.


Code
np.random.seed(4)
print("greedy ID:",int(probabilities.argmax()))
print("sampled IDs:",np.random.choice(len(probabilities),size=8,p=probabilities))




A minimal audit
An objective audit should record the tokenizer and vocabulary version, position convention, input-target shift, output-head shape, causal-mask orientation, padding convention, loss denominator, document-boundary policy, special-token treatment, precision used for softmax and loss, and the metric corpus. A checkpoint cannot be interpreted from its parameter count alone.
Tests should include a hand-calculated one-position loss, invariance of an earlier prediction to a changed future token, invariance to additional padding, and agreement between the batch loss and the mean of valid token losses. They should also check that generation begins from the intended start context and that an end marker stops only under the declared generation policy.


Code
assert np.isclose(stable_softmax(logits).sum(),1.0)
assert inputs.shape==targets.shape
assert valid.sum()==3
assert np.isfinite(masked_loss)
print("basic objective-interface checks passed")




What the likelihood objective estimates
The loss is evaluated on tokens observed in a corpus. It estimates how well the model distribution matches the evaluation distribution under the chosen representation and context rule. A low average loss on a held-out sample is evidence about that predictive task. It is not evidence that the sample is representative of all future use, that the corpus is accurate, or that a continuation selected at inference will satisfy a different quality criterion.
This distinction is practical. The corpus can contain duplicated text, inconsistent claims, private conventions, or sequences that are unsuitable as answers. A model that assigns those sequences probability has learned a regularity of its training distribution. Whether that regularity should be surfaced in an application depends on the training data, adaptation procedure, system instructions, retrieval context, and decoding rule. Later chapters address those additional components; they should not be attributed to the next-token loss alone.
The objective also makes no independent decision about the unit of evaluation. The same visible sentence can have different losses under different tokenisers because it contains different numbers of prediction events. A report should therefore state the tokenizer, maximum context length, preprocessing, split construction, whether document boundaries are preserved, and whether the reported loss includes special markers. Without those details, a perplexity comparison can describe different quantities under the same label.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2,3.8))
ax.bar(["tokeniser A","tokeniser B"],[6,10],color=[teal,orange])
ax.set_ylabel("next-token prediction events")
ax.set_title("Visible text length is not a fixed token-level denominator")
for i,n in enumerate([6,10]): ax.text(i,n+.25,str(n),ha="center",color=grey)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 26.5





Context boundaries are part of the example definition
The conditional notation hides an operational choice: which earlier tokens count as the prefix. In a document-level corpus, a beginning marker or separator may indicate that one text has ended and another has begun. If preprocessing concatenates documents without a boundary policy, the model can be trained to predict the start of one item from the end of an unrelated item. Packing can improve hardware utilisation, but its attention and loss masks must state whether tokens may attend across packed segments.
Finite context windows create a second boundary. A position near the end of a long sequence is conditioned on the retained window, not necessarily the entire preceding document. The objective is still a conditional likelihood, but the condition is truncated. This affects claims about long-range dependence and makes maximum length a property of the trained system rather than a deployment-only setting. Chapter 27 examines the inference and systems consequences of finite context in detail.


Code
document=np.array([2,11,34,58,71,89,3])
window=4
for end in range(1,len(document)):
    start=max(0,end-window)
    print("context",document[start:end],"target",document[end])




Error analysis starts with the conditional event
An average loss can conceal very different patterns. A model may perform well on frequent punctuation and common short tokens while assigning poor probability to dates, names, a language variety, or a rare formatting sequence. Error analysis should therefore retain token-level events and group them by a declared property: position in the document, token frequency, script, source, length, or task-relevant category. Such groups are descriptive only when their construction and sample sizes are reported.
The most probable alternative is often informative, but it should not be treated as a diagnosis by itself. If the target slept receives little probability after a clear prefix, the distribution may prefer a semantically related verb, a frequent generic continuation, or a tokenisation-dependent fragment. Inspecting the prefix, target, alternative tokens, and preprocessing records makes the failure analysable. A generated continuation alone does not reveal whether the error began in the model distribution, a decoding decision, or an input-interface mismatch.


Code
vocab=np.array(["slept","ran","ate","<eos>"])
rank=np.argsort(probabilities)[::-1]
for idx in rank:
    print(vocab[idx],round(probabilities[idx],3))

title: Next-token Prediction
text:
Common misconceptions

The largest logit is already a probability. Logits become probabilities only after normalisation.
A low loss proves a model is truthful. Loss rewards agreement with held-out token sequences under a specified distribution.
Teacher forcing means the model sees future targets. It supplies earlier observed tokens; a causal mask must still block later positions.
Perplexity can compare any two language models. Tokenisation, corpus, preprocessing, and loss conventions must match.
Next-token prediction specifies how a model should answer a person. It defines a base predictive objective; adaptation and decoding remain separate choices.
Padding is harmless without an explicit mask. It can affect attention and loss unless the implementation excludes it.

title: Next-token Prediction
text:
Summary
Next-token prediction trains a causal language model to assign probability to the observed subsequent token under an allowed prefix. Logits are normalised by softmax, and cross-entropy averages the negative log probability of valid targets. The target shift, causal mask, padding policy, vocabulary mapping, and loss denominator are part of the objective definition.
The training objective produces conditional distributions, not directly a finished answer or a factual guarantee. Generation applies a selection rule sequentially to those distributions. Chapter 26 examines the data, objectives, and scale that shape a base model before Chapter 28 treats decoding rules in detail.

title: Next-token Prediction
text:
Looking ahead
Next-token prediction specifies the objective applied to a token sequence. Chapter 26 examines how the training corpus, data-processing rules, token budget, and scale choices determine what that objective is actually fitted to.

title: Pretraining Data, Objectives, and Scale
text:
Why this chapter matters
Next-token prediction defines a loss over token sequences. It does not define which sequences enter training, how they are filtered and sampled, how many are processed, or how model capacity and compute are allocated. Those decisions determine the distribution a base model is fitted to and the evidence available for claims about its behaviour.
Pretraining trains a model on broad corpora using a self-supervised objective. A base model learns conditional regularities in that constructed stream. It does not independently verify text, acquire a stable instruction policy, or guarantee suitable completions. This chapter separates corpus construction, objective choice, scale, and reproducibility. Chapter 29 turns to instruction tuning; Chapter 34 turns to evaluation.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish a corpus, sampled training stream, token budget, and optimisation run;
explain why provenance, filtering, deduplication, and mixture weights affect a base model;
compare causal, masked, and sequence-to-sequence pretraining objectives;
account for parameters, training tokens, batch size, steps, and compute;
interpret scaling-law findings under their measured conditions; and
specify a reproducible pretraining record.



Running example
Suppose a training stream mixes public web text, reference material, code, and curated multilingual material. Source size does not determine exposure: sampling weights and repetitions determine which tokens enter optimiser updates.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3.6)); ax.axis("off")
for i,(label,c) in enumerate([("web",blue),("reference",teal),("code",orange),("multilingual",purple)]):
    y=2.7-i*.55; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.25,y),1.5,.35,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(1,y+.175,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white"); ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((1.78,y+.175),(2.45,1.6),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=10))
for x,label,c in [(2.55,"weighted\nsampler",grey),(4.55,"tokeniser",teal),(6.25,"batches",orange),(7.95,"model, loss,\nupdate",blue)]:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.28),1.35,.65,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.675,1.6,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for x in [3.95,5.85,7.55]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,1.6),(x+.52,1.6),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=10))
ax.text(5.2,.55,"The sampled stream, not a source list alone, defines exposure during training.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,9.7); ax.set_ylim(.3,3.2); plt.show()



Figure 27.1
crumbs: 27  Pretraining Data, Objectives, and Scale

title: Pretraining Data, Objectives, and Scale
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Training data are constructed, not simply collected
Pretraining corpora are assembled through collection, access and licensing choices, parsing, filtering, deduplication, language identification, document segmentation, tokenisation, and sampling. Each operation changes the sequence distribution on which the loss is minimised. Calling this material “internet data” conceals choices that affect coverage and exclusion.
Public web text differs from books, scientific literature, code repositories, private correspondence, and spoken language. Availability determines whose writing enters the source pool. A filter can remove spam and repeated pages while also removing low-resource languages, unusual formatting, or text misclassified by a quality system. These are properties of a pipeline to document and test, not background noise.




Code
names=["web","reference","code","multilingual"]
raw=np.array([65,15,12,8]); sampled=np.array([45,20,20,15]); x=np.arange(4); w=.36
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); ax.bar(x-w/2,raw,w,label="raw source share",color=blue); ax.bar(x+w/2,sampled,w,label="sampled token share",color=teal); ax.set_xticks(x,names); ax.set_ylabel("per cent (illustrative)"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Source size and training exposure can differ"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 27.2



The values are illustrative. The point is that a data card needs both raw source quantities and mixture policy. Oversampling a smaller collection can give it substantial gradient influence. Repeating a source also raises the importance of removing exact and near duplicates.


Self-supervision supplies targets from text
Causal pretraining uses earlier tokens to predict the next token. The stored sequence supplies the target after tokenisation and shifting, without a separate human label for each prediction. This allows large-scale training, but the objective inherits the corpus’s errors, omissions, conventions, and correlations.
Masked-language objectives hide selected units and predict them using left and right context. Sequence-to-sequence objectives predict a target sequence from a corrupted or transformed source. These objectives expose different information boundaries and fit different model architectures. They are not interchangeable descriptions of “learning language”.




Code
fig,axes=plt.subplots(3,1,figsize=(9,4.2))
rows=[("causal",["the","cat","?"],[blue,blue,orange]),("masked",["the","[mask]","slept"],[teal,orange,teal]),("seq2seq",["corrupted","→","target"],[purple,grey,orange])]
for ax,(name,pieces,cols) in zip(axes,rows):
    ax.axis("off"); ax.text(.02,.5,name,weight="bold",color=grey,transform=ax.transAxes)
    for i,(p,c) in enumerate(zip(pieces,cols)):
        x=.2+i*.23; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,.23),.19,.54,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.095,.5,p,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 27.3
crumbs: 27  Pretraining Data, Objectives, and Scale

title: Pretraining Data, Objectives, and Scale
text:
Level 2 - Data mechanics

A corpus record needs more than a headline token count
A reproducible account identifies sources and dates, access conditions, document and token counts, language and domain labels, filtering rules, deduplication method, personally identifiable information policy, and held-out splits. It distinguishes raw collection from retained documents and from the final sampled stream. If sources cannot be fully disclosed because of privacy, licensing, or access restrictions, that limitation should be stated rather than replaced with an imprecise label.
Deduplication is consequential. Exact removal identifies identical records; near-duplicate removal depends on a similarity rule and threshold. It may retain templated copies or remove legitimate repetition. Evaluation contamination occurs when benchmark items or close variants enter training. A contaminated score does not estimate performance on unseen instances alone.


Code
documents=["A short report on water quality.","A short report on water quality.","A short report on water-quality.","Different document."]
unique=list(dict.fromkeys(documents))
print("raw:",len(documents),"exact-unique:",len(unique))
print("near duplicates require a declared similarity rule")




Tokens, batches, steps, and epochs count different things
If a run processes (T) valid tokens with global batch size (B) tokens, it performs about (T/B) optimiser updates, subject to packing and gradient accumulation. An epoch means one pass through a defined finite dataset; it becomes ambiguous when a mixture is resampled or repeated.


Code
training_tokens=300_000_000_000
global_batch_tokens=4_000_000
steps=training_tokens/global_batch_tokens
print(f"optimiser steps: {steps:,.0f}")


The token count depends on the tokenizer. A batch may be reported in sequences, examples, tokens, or tokens per device; these are not equivalent for variable lengths. A run record should give global valid tokens per update, maximum length, packing policy, accumulation steps, and total valid tokens processed.
crumbs: 27  Pretraining Data, Objectives, and Scale

title: Pretraining Data, Objectives, and Scale
text:
Level 3 - Objectives and scale

Objective choice determines the prediction task
A decoder-only causal objective predicts targets from a prefix. An encoder objective can form bidirectional representations for a complete input. An encoder-decoder objective predicts a causal target conditioned on a source. Chapter 23 established these architecture boundaries; pretraining selects the sequence task through which parameters are updated. Parameter count does not identify an objective.
Loss weights can also change the effective data mixture. A run may weight sources, ignore selected targets, or normalise losses per sequence rather than per token. These choices alter gradient contributions and should be reported with the primary cross-entropy.


Code
losses=np.array([1.1,1.8,2.2])
weights=np.array([.5,.3,.2])
print("unweighted mean:",losses.mean())
print("weighted mixture loss:",(losses*weights).sum())




Scaling laws are fitted evidence, not a general capability law
Scaling-law studies report regular relationships between held-out loss, parameter count, data, and training compute under specified training regimes (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022). They inform planning inside those conditions. They do not establish that every capability, safety property, language, or benchmark will improve smoothly with size. Extrapolation depends on architecture, data, tokenisation, optimisation, and the range studied.




Code
compute=np.logspace(1,5,100); loss=1.0+2.2*compute**-.18
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5,4)); ax.plot(compute,loss,color=purple,lw=2.5); ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("training compute (illustrative log scale)"); ax.set_ylabel("held-out loss (illustrative)"); ax.set_title("Diminishing loss reductions in a fitted regime"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 27.4



Compute accounting needs more than parameters times tokens. Actual cost depends on sequence length, attention implementation, precision, communication, activation recomputation, failed runs, and hardware utilisation. Chapter 15 developed these systems distinctions. A pretraining report must connect them to data and objective budgets rather than provide a single uninterpretable compute headline.


Data repetition changes the meaning of a token budget
A headline such as “trained on one trillion tokens” reports processing volume. It does not say how many distinct documents or unique token sequences were available. A smaller, repeatedly sampled corpus and a larger, more diverse corpus can yield the same processed-token count while exposing the model to different evidence. The difference affects both generalisation and memorisation risks. It also affects the interpretation of a scaling comparison: a run can receive more arithmetic without receiving proportionately more independent data.
Repetition is not always an error. Curated code, mathematical text, or low-resource languages may be deliberately oversampled because raw availability would otherwise leave them nearly absent from the gradient stream. The required record is the sampling rule, the number of effective passes or repetitions, and the reason for the weighting. A report that lists source sizes but not exposure cannot establish whether a small source was protected, ignored, or repeatedly replayed.


Code
source_tokens=np.array([800,120,40])
sampling_weights=np.array([.5,.3,.2])
processed=1_000
exposure=processed*sampling_weights/source_tokens
for name,passes in zip(["web","reference","small curated"],exposure):
    print(name,"illustrative expected passes:",round(passes,2))


The calculation uses a simplified fixed mixture. Real pipelines may sample documents, shards, or length-normalised examples; may replace exhausted sources; and may alter weights during a run. Those details belong in the training record because they define which losses contribute to parameter updates.


Validation needs an information boundary of its own
Training and validation must be separated before duplicate handling and mixture construction are finalised. A random split at the document level can still leak closely related pages, translated versions, template variants, or consecutive records from one source. Time-based and source-based boundaries may be more appropriate when a model will be evaluated on later or distinct material. The appropriate rule depends on the claim, but the rule must be specified.
For language-model loss, the validation stream should use the same tokenizer and objective convention as training. It should not silently use a different normalisation policy, maximum context, special-token treatment, or padding denominator. Source-stratified results can identify a mixture average that is dominated by common material and conceals poor fit on a smaller intended population.


Code
validation={"web":(10000,1.55),"reference":(3000,1.32),"multilingual":(2000,2.11)}
weighted=sum(count*loss for count,loss in validation.values())/sum(count for count,_ in validation.values())
print("aggregate loss:",round(weighted,3))
print("source-specific losses:",validation)


The aggregate loss is useful for a declared mixture but cannot replace the rows from which it was calculated. A model intended for a multilingual or technical application requires validation evidence for those conditions. Holding out a generic sample of the same source pool is a narrower claim.


Scale has several bottlenecks
Parameter count measures stored learned values, not the full resource requirement. Training tokens measure prediction events under a tokenizer, not the diversity or quality of documents. FLOP estimates measure arithmetic under assumptions, not the wall-clock cost of moving data and synchronising devices. Context length affects attention and activation memory. Batch size affects the number of updates for a fixed token budget and can interact with optimiser settings. These quantities should be reported together because changing one can change the useful allocation of the others.
The compute-optimal results of Hoffmann and colleagues apply to their measured Transformer family, data, and training setup (Hoffmann et al. 2022). They provide evidence that model and data allocation matters under a compute budget. They do not provide a universal ratio that can be transferred without checking objective, data mixture, architecture, sequence length, and target deployment constraints. Scaling work is most useful when it leads to smaller controlled runs, documented extrapolations, and tests of the assumptions that support a large run.


Code
parameter_counts=np.array([1e8,1e9,1e10])
token_budgets=np.array([2e9,2e10,2e11])
for params,tokens in zip(parameter_counts,token_budgets):
    print(f"parameters={params:.0e}, tokens={tokens:.0e}, tokens/parameter={tokens/params:.1f}")




Base-model claims need proportionate language
Pretraining can produce useful representations and conditional distributions across a wide range of text. It does not show that a system follows instructions, reports sources, abstains appropriately, protects private information, or remains reliable under a changed task distribution. Those behaviours require their own training, interface design, and evaluation. A report should therefore distinguish “the model was pretrained on” from “the deployed system was shown to do”.
This distinction also prevents an opaque model scale claim from standing in for evidence. A model can be larger while having a narrower data mixture, a shorter context, a different objective, or less suitable evaluation. The relevant comparison begins with matched definitions and ends with tests that represent the intended use.
crumbs: 27  Pretraining Data, Objectives, and Scale

title: Pretraining Data, Objectives, and Scale
text:
Level 4 - Audit and interpretation

A pretraining claim requires a data and run record
An audit should record architecture and parameter count; tokenizer version; objective and target mask; source list and dates; filtering and deduplication procedures; mixture weights and resampling; raw, retained, and processed tokens; sequence and packing policy; batch and optimiser configuration; precision and hardware; checkpoints; validation construction; contamination checks; and stopping rule.


Code
run_record={"tokenizer":"versioned vocabulary","objective":"causal next-token","valid_tokens":300_000_000_000,"max_length":2048,"mixture":"documented weights"}
required={"tokenizer","objective","valid_tokens","max_length","mixture"}
assert required <= set(run_record)
print("minimum run-record fields present")


Average validation loss can conceal failure on rare inputs, arithmetic, long contexts, low-resource languages, or tasks requiring external evidence. It is therefore one form of evidence alongside coverage analysis, contamination checks, memorisation testing, and task-specific evaluation. Optimising token-level likelihood does not resolve copyright, privacy, data-governance, or downstream reliability questions.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.4)); ax.axis("off")
items=[("held-out\nloss",teal,3.6,1.45),("coverage",blue,.4,2.45),("contamination",orange,3.6,2.45),("memorisation",purple,6.8,2.45),("task evaluation",blue,3.6,.35)]
for label,c,x,y in items: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,y),1.8,.48,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.9,y+.24,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for dest in [(2.2,2.7),(4.5,2.45),(6.8,2.7),(4.5,.83)]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((4.5,1.93),dest,arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=10))
ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(0,3.2); plt.show()



Figure 27.5
crumbs: 27  Pretraining Data, Objectives, and Scale

title: Pretraining Data, Objectives, and Scale
text:
Common misconceptions

Pretraining data are a random sample of the web. Collection, access, filtering, and sampling construct the training distribution.
More raw documents mean more effective data. Duplicates, mixture weights, tokenisation, and repetitions determine exposure.
Self-supervision removes data-quality concerns. It removes separate labels, not errors or exclusions in sequence data.
A scaling law guarantees broad capability gains. It describes measured loss relations under stated conditions.
A low validation loss rules out contamination. Contamination needs direct checks against the relevant evaluation material.

title: Pretraining Data, Objectives, and Scale
text:
Summary
Pretraining fits a model to a constructed stream of token sequences under a specified objective. Source collection, filtering, deduplication, tokenisation, mixture weights, document boundaries, token budget, model capacity, and compute all affect the resulting base model.
Scaling findings help plan work within their measured regimes, but they do not replace documentation, contamination checks, coverage analysis, or targeted evaluation. Chapter 27 examines finite contexts and cache mechanics at inference; Chapter 29 examines supervised adaptation for instruction-following behaviour.

title: Context Windows and Model Inference
text: Chapter orientation
crumbs: 28  Context Windows and Model Inference

title: Context Windows and Model Inference
text:
Why this chapter matters
A decoder language model predicts the next token from a finite permitted prefix. The maximum number of tokens it can process is the context window. This limit affects what evidence is available to a prediction, the memory required by attention, the latency of generation, and the interpretation of claims that a model has “read” a long document.
Inference is also sequential. A generated token becomes part of the next prefix. Key-value caching avoids recomputing the representations of earlier tokens at every step, but it retains an expanding memory state. This chapter defines these mechanics and the evidence needed to assess long-context use. Chapter 28 treats how tokens are selected from the next-token distribution.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish context length, generated length, and total sequence length;
explain why causal decoding is sequential even when prompt processing is parallel;
calculate the shape and approximate storage of a key-value cache;
compare full-prefix recomputation with cached decoding;
identify the difference between fitting text into a context and using relevant information from it;
state common long-context evaluation failures; and
specify an inference record that makes latency and length claims interpretable.



Running sequence
We use a prompt of five token IDs and generate three new IDs. A maximum context of six means that a later prediction cannot retain every original prompt token if the system uses a sliding window.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
tokens=["p1","p2","p3","p4","p5","g1","g2","g3"]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3)); ax.axis("off")
for i,t in enumerate(tokens):
    x=.35+i*1.15; c=blue if i<5 else orange
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.25),.9,.5,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.45,1.5,t,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((2.55,1.02),6.85,.95,fill=False,edgecolor=teal,lw=2)); ax.text(5.98,.65,"retained six-token context for g3",ha="center",color=teal)
ax.set_xlim(0,9.8); ax.set_ylim(.3,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 28.1

title: Context Windows and Model Inference
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

A context window is an information boundary
The context window is a token limit, not a guarantee that every retained token affects an answer. A token outside the window cannot be attended to by an ordinary finite-context decoder. A token inside it is available in principle, but the model may assign it little attention, fail to retrieve it among distractors, or use it incorrectly. “Supports 32,000 tokens” therefore describes an input capacity, not a measured ability to answer questions about every position in a 32,000-token document.
The boundary is measured after tokenisation. A page, a word count, or a character count has no fixed conversion because language, formatting, code, and tokeniser affect the number of IDs. Prompts also consume the same budget as generated output in most interfaces. A requested answer can fail because the prompt plus reserved output exceeds the configured total length.




Code
limit=100; prompt=62; reserve=25
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,2.7)); ax.barh([0],[prompt],color=blue,label="prompt"); ax.barh([0],[reserve],left=[prompt],color=orange,label="reserved output"); ax.barh([0],[limit-prompt-reserve],left=[prompt+reserve],color=grey,label="unused"); ax.set_xlim(0,limit); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel("tokens"); ax.legend(ncol=3,loc="upper center"); ax.set_title("A configured maximum length is shared"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 28.2





Prompt processing and generation are different phases
During prompt processing, a causal Transformer can compute representations for supplied positions in parallel under its causal mask. This is commonly called prefill. Once generation begins, token (t+1) cannot be selected until the model has processed the selected token (t). Output is therefore sequential even on highly parallel hardware.
The difference helps interpret latency. A long prompt can create a substantial initial wait before the first new token. A long generated answer can be slow because it requires repeated decode steps. Reporting only total tokens per second mixes these phases and obscures the user-facing bottleneck.


Code
prompt=np.array([2,11,34,58,3]); generated=[]
for chosen in [17,29,3]:
    print("prefix length before selection:",len(prompt)+len(generated),"choose:",chosen)
    generated.append(chosen)
crumbs: 28  Context Windows and Model Inference

title: Context Windows and Model Inference
text:
Level 2 - Cache mechanics

Why naive decoding repeats work
Without a cache, generating each new token recomputes attention projections for the full prefix. For a prefix length (L), the next step uses length (L+1), then (L+2), and so on. Earlier tokens are repeatedly projected even though their keys and values do not change in a causal decoder.
A key-value cache stores the key and value tensors produced at each layer for earlier positions. At the next step, the new query attends to stored keys and values plus the new token’s key and value. The cache does not make generation parallel, but it avoids repeatedly rebuilding the earlier prefix.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.5)); ax.axis("off")
for layer in range(3):
    y=2.65-layer*.8; ax.text(.15,y+.2,f"layer {layer+1}",color=grey)
    for i in range(5):
        x=1.35+i*.92; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,y),.72,.38,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.36,y+.19,f"K{i+1}",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,y-.4),.72,.38,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.36,y-.21,f"V{i+1}",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((6.25,1.45),(7.45,1.45),arrowstyle="-|>",color=orange,mutation_scale=14)); ax.text(8.05,1.45,"append K,V\nfor new token",va="center",color=orange)
ax.set_xlim(0,9.5); ax.set_ylim(.1,3.35); plt.show()



Figure 28.3





Cache shape and memory
For batch size (B), layers (n_l), key-value heads (n_{kv}), head width (d_h), and cached length (L), keys and values require approximately
[ 2B n_l n_{kv} L d_h ]
stored numbers. Multiply by bytes per number to obtain a rough memory estimate. Multi-query and grouped-query attention reduce (n_{kv}) relative to the number of query heads, lowering cache memory without changing the causal sequence rule.


Code
B,layers,kv_heads,length,head_dim,bytes_per=1,32,8,8192,128,2
cache_bytes=2*B*layers*kv_heads*length*head_dim*bytes_per
print(f"KV cache: {cache_bytes/2**30:.2f} GiB")


The estimate excludes model weights, activations required by the serving system, allocator overhead, metadata, and temporary attention buffers. It is useful for identifying linear growth with context length, not for replacing a measured memory profile.


Cache correctness is a model test
Cached decoding should agree with full-prefix decoding for the same model, tokens, position treatment, masks, and numerical precision within an explicit tolerance. Disagreement can arise from wrong cache positions, stale entries, incorrect padding handling, rotary-position implementation, or an inconsistency between prefill and decode code paths.


Code
full_prefix_logits=np.array([.1,.2,.7])
cached_logits=np.array([.1,.2,.7])
assert np.allclose(full_prefix_logits,cached_logits,atol=1e-6)
print("cached and full-prefix reference outputs agree")
crumbs: 28  Context Windows and Model Inference

title: Context Windows and Model Inference
text:
Level 3 - Long-context use

Cost grows before the cache is available
The cache improves repeated decoding but does not remove the cost of processing a long initial prompt. Standard dense self-attention forms score relations among positions during prefill, so the attention component grows quadratically with sequence length. Chapter 20 derived this relation. Implementation methods can reduce memory traffic and avoid materialising the full score matrix, but they do not make every long prompt free.




Code
lengths=np.arange(256,8193,256)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5,4)); ax.plot(lengths,(lengths/256)**2,color=purple,label="relative dense score relations"); ax.plot(lengths,lengths/256,color=teal,label="relative cache length"); ax.set_xlabel("prompt length"); ax.set_ylabel("relative quantity"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Prefill and cached state scale differently"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 28.4



Long-context systems may modify the architecture, position method, attention pattern, cache representation, or retrieval pipeline. These choices create different failure modes. A sparse attention pattern restricts which positions can interact directly. A position method may be trained or extrapolated over a limited range. Retrieval can select a subset of external documents, but it does not prove that omitted text was irrelevant. Each mechanism needs evaluation at the position, length, and document structure for which it will be used.


Retrieval is not identical to longer context
Retrieval can reduce the prompt to passages selected from a larger collection. It changes the inference problem from attending over all supplied text to selecting and using evidence. A large window may contain an entire document; it still must locate and apply the relevant information. Chapter 33 will examine retrieval-augmented generation as a complete system, including indexing and evaluation.


Code
document_tokens=20_000; retrieved_tokens=1_500; window=4_096
print("full document fits window:",document_tokens<=window)
print("retrieved subset fits window:",retrieved_tokens<=window)




Context extension needs an explicit comparison
A model may be trained at one maximum length and served at another. Position representations, training examples, attention kernels, and optimisation all affect whether behaviour transfers beyond the length distribution seen during training. A larger configured limit therefore requires a comparison with a stated baseline: the same task at the original and extended lengths, evidence placed across positions, and a record of any change to position handling or continued training.
Long inputs can also conceal a simpler problem: the relevant evidence may be absent from the retained prefix. Sliding-window policies remove older tokens; fixed prompt templates may reserve too little output; and document conversion can add headings, markup, or duplicated material that consumes capacity. The input trace should retain token counts before and after formatting, the truncation decision, and the final token positions supplied to the model.




Code
sequence=list(range(1,10)); limit=5
fig,axes=plt.subplots(3,1,figsize=(8.5,3.8))
for ax,end in zip(axes,[5,7,9]):
    window_tokens=sequence[max(0,end-limit):end]
    ax.axis("off"); ax.text(.02,.5,f"step {end}",weight="bold",color=grey,transform=ax.transAxes)
    for i,t in enumerate(window_tokens):
        x=.18+i*.13; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,.22),.105,.56,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.052,.5,str(t),ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 28.5



The policy should distinguish discarded context from an intentional summary or retrieved representation. A summary is new model-generated text that may omit or distort facts. Retrieval is selected external evidence. Cached tokens are exact retained activations for previous IDs. These mechanisms can be combined, but their information properties differ and they should not be described by one generic claim of “memory”.


Serving constraints change the available context per request
At deployment, many requests may share accelerator memory. Each active sequence has a cache length, and a serving scheduler chooses batching, admission, eviction, and output limits. A context limit that fits one request can reduce concurrency or exceed memory under a busy workload. Conversely, aggressively capping prompts can improve latency while discarding evidence needed for a task. These are operating choices that should be measured against the task and service requirement.


Code
cache_per_request_gib=1.0
available_gib=24
for active in [1,8,16,24]:
    print(active,"active requests require",active*cache_per_request_gib,"GiB of cache")


The calculation is deliberately incomplete because weights, temporary buffers, and allocator behaviour also occupy memory. It makes one relationship visible: higher concurrency, longer retained prefixes, and larger cache representations compete for the same hardware capacity. A serving result should specify whether its reported throughput is for isolated or concurrent requests, along with the prompt-length distribution.


Long-context errors require traces, not only accuracy totals
When a model misses evidence in a long prompt, a useful diagnostic records the original document, tokenised length, retained window, evidence span, retrieval or packing decision, generated tokens, and scoring rule. This can separate an error caused by truncation from one caused by poor retrieval, position sensitivity, or an incorrect answer despite available evidence. Aggregate accuracy remains useful, but it cannot make these failure modes distinguishable.


Code
trace={"document_tokens":9100,"retained_tokens":8192,"evidence_position":7800,"truncated":False,"answer_correct":False}
print(trace)


Position and distraction controls should vary one feature at a time. For example, hold the question and answer constant while moving evidence from early to middle and late positions; then add unrelated material while keeping the evidence position fixed. These comparisons reveal whether a score changes with length, location, or competing content. They provide stronger evidence than a single long document with a single successful answer.

title: Context Windows and Model Inference
text:
Level 4 - Audit and reporting

Length claims need tests that control position and distraction
A useful long-context evaluation places known evidence at several positions, asks a defined question, and compares performance across lengths and numbers of distractors. It should distinguish exact retrieval of a stated item from multi-step use of several items. Repeating a short fact many times, testing only the beginning of a prompt, or scoring a single favourable example cannot establish broad long-context use.
The evaluation should also record tokeniser, actual valid lengths, truncation and packing policy, prompt template, generation limit, sampling rule, and whether the answer was checked automatically or by people. Changing any of these can change the test. An answer that fails may reflect missing evidence, truncation, retrieval failure, cache error, decoding variation, or the model’s conditional distribution; the trace should make those possibilities distinguishable.


Code
positions=[128,1024,4096,7168]
results={p:None for p in positions}
print("record evidence position and outcome:",results)




An inference record separates capacity from service quality
An inference report should include model and tokenizer version, context limit, maximum output length, prompt and output token distributions, prefill latency, decode latency or tokens per second, cache precision and layout, batch policy, hardware, concurrency, truncation behaviour, and failure policy. At least one cache-equivalence test and one boundary test at the configured maximum length should be retained.
The record supports operational decisions. It can show whether a system is limited by long-prompt prefill, by per-token decode latency, by memory available for concurrent caches, or by a context policy that discards needed evidence. A model card that says only “long context” cannot answer those questions.


Code
inference_record={"context_limit":8192,"prompt_tokens":6200,"max_new_tokens":512,"prefill_ms":740,"decode_tokens_per_second":55,"cache_dtype":"float16"}
assert inference_record["prompt_tokens"]+inference_record["max_new_tokens"]<=inference_record["context_limit"]
print("length-budget check passed")

title: Context Windows and Model Inference
text:
Common misconceptions

A context limit is a guarantee of long-document reasoning. It specifies input capacity, not measured use of every position.
Caching makes generation parallel. It removes repeated prefix computation but each selected token still conditions the next step.
The cache stores the whole model state at no cost. It grows with layers, batch size, key-value heads, head width, and length.
A document fits in context, so no truncation policy is needed. Prompt templates and reserved output also consume the total budget.
Retrieval and a longer window solve the same problem. Retrieval selects evidence; a window determines available token capacity.
