title: Context Windows and Model Inference
text:
Summary
Context windows define a finite token-level information boundary. Long prompts create prefill cost, and sequential generation requires one conditional decision after another. Key-value caches avoid repeated projection of earlier tokens but grow linearly with retained sequence length and must be tested against full-prefix decoding.
Capacity, retrieval, and demonstrated long-context use are distinct claims. Chapter 28 compares the policies that select tokens from a next-token distribution; Chapter 33 examines retrieval-augmented generation as a complete pipeline.

title: Decoding and Generation
text: Chapter orientation

title: Decoding and Generation
text:
Why this chapter matters
Chapter 25 defined a language model’s next-token probability distribution. A generated response requires an additional policy that selects or samples from that distribution, repeats the process, and decides when to stop. Greedy decoding, temperature, top-k sampling, nucleus sampling, repetition controls, and output constraints can produce different text from the same model and prompt.
Decoding is therefore part of the deployed system. It changes reproducibility, diversity, latency, output length, and the types of errors a user sees. It does not repair missing evidence, change the model’s training data, or establish truth. This chapter defines the common policies and their evaluation.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish a probability distribution from a decoding policy and a generated sequence;
implement greedy, temperature, top-k, and top-p selection on a toy distribution;
explain why sampling is stochastic and how seeds affect reproducibility;
identify stopping, length, repetition, and constraint policies as generation choices;
evaluate decoding settings against a stated task rather than a generic quality claim; and
record the configuration needed to reproduce a generation.



Running distribution
For one prefix, suppose a vocabulary has probabilities for the, a, cat, slept, and <eos>. The model distribution is fixed in the first examples; only the selection rule changes.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
tokens=np.array(["the","a","cat","slept","<eos>"])
probs=np.array([.42,.25,.17,.10,.06])
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.7)); ax.bar(tokens,probs,color=blue); ax.set_ylim(0,.5); ax.set_ylabel("next-token probability")
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((4.2,.3),(5.45,.3),arrowstyle="-|>",color=orange,mutation_scale=14)); ax.add_patch(Rectangle((5.6,.12),1.3,.36,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(6.25,.3,"decoder",ha="center",va="center",color="white"); ax.text(7.55,.3,"selected\ntoken",ha="center",va="center",color=purple); ax.set_title("Distribution and decision are separate objects"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 29.1

title: Decoding and Generation
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

The model supplies options; decoding makes a choice
Greedy decoding selects the highest-probability token at every step. It is deterministic when model computation is deterministic and the prompt is unchanged. It can be appropriate when a task has a narrow expected continuation, but it can also create repetitive or generic sequences because it always commits to the local maximum.
Sampling selects a token according to the probability distribution, so lower-probability options can appear. Two runs can differ even when the model and prompt are identical. This is not evidence that the model changed; it is a property of the generation policy. A seed can make pseudorandom sampling reproducible for a declared implementation, but it does not make the output uniquely implied by the model.


Code
np.random.seed(7)
print("greedy:",tokens[probs.argmax()])
print("samples:",np.random.choice(tokens,size=8,p=probs))


Generated text is a sequence of such decisions. A locally likely first token can move the prefix into a different region of the model distribution. This is why a loss measured under teacher forcing does not fully describe the behaviour of an autoregressive system that conditions on its own selected tokens.


Stopping is also a decoding decision
Many systems stop when an end-of-sequence token is selected, when a maximum new-token length is reached, or when a configured string or token sequence occurs. Each rule can truncate an answer or permit unnecessary continuation. A maximum length is not merely a user-interface setting: it changes which complete sequences can be emitted and may interact with the context budget in Chapter 27.


Code
generated=["the","cat","slept","<eos>"]
for step,token in enumerate(generated,1):
    print(step,token)
    if token=="<eos>":
        print("stop on end token"); break

title: Decoding and Generation
text:
Level 2 - Distribution transformations

Temperature changes relative concentration
Temperature divides logits before softmax. For logits (z) and temperature (>0), the transformed distribution is ((z/)). Values below one sharpen differences between logits; values above one flatten the distribution. Temperature does not add information or identify an appropriate answer. It changes how sharply the decoder follows the model’s existing ranking.


Code
logits=np.log(probs)
def softmax(x):
    x=x-x.max(); e=np.exp(x); return e/e.sum()
for temperature in [.5,1.0,1.5]:
    print(temperature,np.round(softmax(logits/temperature),3))






Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4))
for temperature,c in [(.5,orange),(1.0,teal),(1.5,purple)]: ax.plot(tokens,softmax(logits/temperature),marker="o",label=f"T={temperature}",color=c)
ax.set_ylabel("sampling probability"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Temperature transforms the distribution"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 29.2



Very low temperature approaches greedy selection but remains a distribution. Very high temperature can allocate substantial mass to tokens that were unlikely under the original model. The useful setting depends on the task, prompt, model, and other controls; one numerical value should not be treated as a universal quality setting.


Top-k and top-p restrict the candidate set
Top-k keeps the (k) highest-probability entries, sets the rest to zero, and renormalises. Nucleus or top-p sampling keeps the smallest high-probability set whose cumulative mass reaches a threshold (p), then renormalises. Top-k has a fixed candidate count; top-p adapts its count to the distribution’s concentration (Holtzman et al. 2020).


Code
def top_k_distribution(p,k):
    keep=np.argsort(p)[-k:]; q=np.zeros_like(p); q[keep]=p[keep]; return q/q.sum()
def top_p_distribution(p,threshold):
    order=np.argsort(p)[::-1]; cumulative=np.cumsum(p[order]); keep=order[cumulative<=threshold]
    if len(keep)==0: keep=order[:1]
    q=np.zeros_like(p); q[keep]=p[keep]; return q/q.sum()
print("top-k=3:",np.round(top_k_distribution(probs,3),3))
print("top-p=.8:",np.round(top_p_distribution(probs,.8),3))


The exact top-p boundary convention must be stated: implementations often include the first token that crosses the threshold, while the toy function above retains entries up to the threshold. Small implementation details can change generated output, especially near a boundary.




Code
order=np.argsort(probs)[::-1]; ranked=probs[order]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); ax.bar(np.arange(len(tokens)),ranked,color=[teal,teal,teal,grey,grey]); ax.plot(np.arange(len(tokens)),np.cumsum(ranked),color=orange,marker="o",label="cumulative mass"); ax.axhline(.8,color=purple,ls="--",label="top-p threshold"); ax.set_xticks(np.arange(len(tokens)),tokens[order]); ax.set_ylabel("probability / cumulative mass"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Candidate restrictions depend on distribution rank"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 29.3

title: Decoding and Generation
text:
Level 3 - Sequence controls

Repetition controls change the sequence distribution
Systems sometimes penalise tokens that appeared in the prefix, block repeated n-grams, or alter logits after selected patterns. These controls can reduce some visible loops, but they also can suppress legitimate repetition: names, quotations, structured lists, and code may require the same token or phrase. A repetition setting should therefore be evaluated on examples where repetition is both undesirable and necessary.


Code
seen={"the","cat"}; adjusted=logits.copy()
for i,t in enumerate(tokens):
    if t in seen: adjusted[i]-=.8
print("original:",np.round(softmax(logits),3))
print("penalised:",np.round(softmax(adjusted),3))


Constraints can be hard rather than soft. A JSON grammar, allowed vocabulary, stop sequence, or tool-call schema can make invalid outputs impossible under the decoder, while leaving questions about the correctness of valid content. Constraints operate on form; they do not verify claims unless they are connected to an external validation process.


Code
allowed=np.array([False,False,True,True,True])
constrained=np.where(allowed,logits,-np.inf)
print("allowed sampling distribution:",np.round(softmax(constrained),3))




Beam search is a search policy, not a probability objective
Beam search retains several partial sequences and expands them, often ranking by accumulated log probability with an optional length adjustment. It can find a higher-probability complete sequence than greedy decoding under its search width, but it is more costly and can favour short or repetitive text without a declared length policy. It is useful to distinguish its search score from a user-facing quality measure.


Code
beams=[(["the"],np.log(.42)),(["a"],np.log(.25))]
extensions={"the":[("cat",.6),("dog",.3)],"a":[("cat",.5),("dog",.4)]}
candidates=[]
for prefix,score in beams:
    for token,p in extensions[prefix[-1]]: candidates.append((prefix+[token],score+np.log(p)))
print(sorted(candidates,key=lambda x:x[1],reverse=True))




Length preferences need to be made visible
Sequence probability multiplies conditional probabilities, so longer sequences usually accumulate more negative log probability than shorter ones. A decoder that ranks complete sequences therefore needs an explicit policy for length, end tokens, and incomplete outputs. Beam search implementations commonly use a length-normalised score or penalty for this reason. The formula and stopping rule matter: a change can favour concise answers, unfinished fragments, or unnecessarily extended text.
The right policy depends on the task. Extracting one span, producing valid code, writing a bounded abstract, and continuing open-ended prose have different length requirements. A generic statement that a setting “improves quality” is not enough. The evaluation must identify the desired completion boundary and assess whether outputs stop too early, too late, or at an inappropriate structural point.




Code
labels=["short candidate","long candidate"]
raw_scores=np.array([-2.0,-2.7]); normalised=np.array([-1.0,-.9]); x=np.arange(2); w=.35
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,3.8)); ax.bar(x-w/2,raw_scores,w,label="raw log score",color=blue); ax.bar(x+w/2,normalised,w,label="illustrative length-normalised score",color=teal); ax.set_xticks(x,labels); ax.axhline(0,color=grey,lw=.7); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Ranking depends on an explicit length policy"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 29.4





Output diversity is not an unconditional good
Sampling several continuations can be useful when a task permits alternatives, such as brainstorming, creative writing, or producing candidate solutions for a later verifier. Diversity can be harmful when an answer must be stable, precisely formatted, or grounded in a supplied record. Increasing temperature or candidate support changes the distribution of output strings; it does not distinguish useful variation from unsupported variation.
An evaluation should therefore state whether it values one reproducible best answer, multiple candidates with a selection stage, or variation subject to a constraint. When several samples are generated, report the number of draws and aggregation rule. Selecting the most attractive sample after inspection without recording that selection produces a result that cannot be reproduced or fairly compared with one deterministic output.


Code
np.random.seed(3)
draws=[np.random.choice(tokens,p=softmax(logits/.9)) for _ in range(20)]
counts={token:draws.count(token) for token in tokens}
print("sample counts:",counts)




Token-level controls interact across steps
Temperature, top-p, penalties, and constraints are recalculated at every generated position. A setting that appears mild for the first token can have a larger effect after the prefix changes or after a penalty has accumulated. Stop sequences can be split into several token IDs, so checking visible strings after decoding is not always equivalent to checking token sequences during decoding. The tokenizer and exact control stage should be recorded.
This interaction is a reason to test full sequences rather than only the first next-token distribution. A policy evaluation can retain traces of logits or candidate sets for a small reference prompt, then compare the selected IDs and stop reason across implementations. The trace is especially useful when a library upgrade changes a boundary convention or numerical path.


Decoding must match the consequence of an error
For a structured extraction task, a system can favour deterministic decoding, an exact schema, and a validator because variation has little value and an incorrect field can cause a downstream error. For exploratory drafting, several sampled candidates may be useful if a reviewer or verifier selects among them. For a question that requires external evidence, sampling cannot compensate for missing or irrelevant context. The selection policy should follow the task’s decision rule and cost of failure.
This is also why output quality and model probability should not be conflated. A highly probable continuation can be generic, outdated, or unsupported. A low-probability continuation may be correct but should be checked against evidence or a task verifier. Decoding controls the way a model distribution is exposed; it is not an independent source of knowledge.


Code
tasks={"extraction":{"temperature":0,"validator":"schema and source match"},"drafting":{"temperature":.8,"validator":"human selection"},"calculation":{"temperature":0,"validator":"exact check"}}
for task,policy in tasks.items(): print(task,policy)

title: Decoding and Generation
text:
Level 4 - Auditing generation

A decoding evaluation varies policies deliberately
An evaluation should hold model version, prompt construction, context policy, and scoring rule fixed while varying one decoding decision at a time. It should report output length, stop reason, random seed where applicable, temperature, candidate restriction, penalties, constraints, and number of samples or beams. Comparing two outputs generated under hiddenly different settings does not identify whether a change came from the model or the decoder.
For deterministic tasks, assess exact validity, extraction accuracy, code execution, or another declared criterion. For open-ended tasks, collect multiple samples and evaluate properties such as factual support, adherence to required format, diversity, and harmful or irrelevant content under a defined protocol. A single appealing sample is not an estimate of a stochastic policy’s expected behaviour.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.3,"model +\nprompt",blue),(2.5,"decoding\npolicy",teal),(4.7,"generated\nsamples",orange),(6.9,"declared\nevaluation",purple)]:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.15),1.5,.62,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.75,1.46,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
    if x<6: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x+1.53,1.46),(x+2.12,1.46),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=12))
ax.text(4.5,.55,"Record the settings that turn a probability distribution into an observable output.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,8.7); ax.set_ylim(.25,2.2); plt.show()



Figure 29.5





A generation record supports reproduction and diagnosis
At minimum, retain the checkpoint and tokenizer versions, prompt template and final token IDs, system messages or tool constraints, context and truncation policy, maximum new tokens, temperature, top-k or top-p convention, seed, repetition controls, stop sequences, beam settings, hardware or numerical settings where determinism matters, output IDs, and stop reason. This record makes it possible to reproduce a result or identify why a boundary case changed after a system update.


Code
generation_record={"temperature":.8,"top_p":.9,"max_new_tokens":256,"seed":17,"stop_reason":"eos","tokenizer":"versioned"}
assert {"temperature","max_new_tokens","tokenizer"} <= set(generation_record)
print(generation_record)

title: Decoding and Generation
text:
Common misconceptions

Greedy output is the model’s only answer. It is one selection rule applied repeatedly.
Temperature improves factuality. It changes the concentration of sampling probabilities.
Top-p always retains the same number of tokens. Candidate count changes with distribution shape.
A fixed seed makes all generation environments identical. Implementations, precision, and sampling conventions can still differ.
Repetition penalties solve hallucination. They alter token preferences without adding evidence.
A valid constrained format proves correct content. Structural validity and factual correctness are separate checks.

title: Decoding and Generation
text:
Summary
Decoding turns next-token distributions into generated sequences through a sequence of explicit decisions. Temperature, candidate restrictions, search, penalties, constraints, and stopping rules all change the output policy. They should be selected and evaluated against a stated task, not presented as generic quality improvements.
Generation records must retain the model, input, tokenisation, and decoding configuration. Chapter 29 examines supervised adaptation from base next-token prediction to instruction-following behaviour.

title: Instruction Tuning
text: Chapter orientation

title: Instruction Tuning
text:
Why this chapter matters
A base language model predicts continuations of token sequences. It may complete an instruction, continue it, imitate an answer, or produce an unrelated pattern depending on the prompt and its pretraining distribution. Instruction tuning adapts the model on examples formatted as requests and preferred responses so that a defined interface more reliably produces the intended response style.
The optimisation remains token prediction, but the training examples, target mask, conversation template, and evaluation task change. This chapter explains that change without claiming that supervised demonstrations establish factuality, safety, or preference alignment. Chapter 30 examines preference optimisation; Chapter 31 examines full and parameter-efficient task adaptation.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish base pretraining from supervised instruction tuning;
define instruction, context, response, template, and target tokens;
explain why loss is normally applied to response tokens rather than the user’s request;
identify data quality, diversity, and split risks in demonstration datasets;
implement a target mask for a toy chat example;
describe catastrophic forgetting and regression evaluation; and
specify the metadata needed to reproduce an instruction-tuning run.



Running conversation
The running example has a system instruction, a user request, and an assistant response. The entire formatted conversation is input to a causal model, but only selected assistant tokens contribute to the supervised loss.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
parts=[("system",blue,False),("user request",teal,False),("assistant response",orange,True)]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3)); ax.axis("off"); x=.35
for label,c,target in parts:
    w=2.55; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.25),w,.58,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+w/2,1.54,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
    ax.text(x+w/2,.87,"loss target" if target else "context only",ha="center",color=orange if target else grey,fontsize=9); x+=w+.25
ax.text(4.6,.35,"Role markers and template tokens are part of the model input contract.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(.1,2.2); plt.show()



Figure 30.1

title: Instruction Tuning
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Demonstrations define a response convention
An instruction-tuning dataset contains demonstrations of an input and a target response. They may include a system message, a user request, documents or tool outputs, and one or more assistant turns. During fine-tuning, the model sees the context and is trained to assign high probability to the demonstrated assistant tokens. Repeated examples establish a convention about when to answer, how to structure an answer, and how to handle specified formats.
This does not convert a model into a database of verified answers. If demonstrations are wrong, incomplete, inconsistent, or narrowly distributed, the model can learn those patterns. A training run can improve compliance with a template while reducing performance on unrelated base-model behaviours. The desired change and the possible regression must both be evaluated.


Code
conversation=["<system>","Be concise.","<user>","Name a mammal.","<assistant>","A whale is a mammal."]
print("\n".join(conversation))




The template is not decoration
Role markers tell the model which span is an instruction, which span is user-provided context, and where an assistant response should begin. A checkpoint trained with one template may respond poorly when served with another, even if the visible wording is unchanged. The tokenizer, special tokens, whitespace rules, and tool-call fields are all part of this interface.




Code
fig,axes=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(9,3.2))
rows=[("template A",["<user>","request","<assistant>","response"]),("template B",["User:","request","Assistant:","response"])]
for ax,(name,pieces) in zip(axes,rows):
    ax.axis("off"); ax.text(.02,.5,name,weight="bold",color=grey,transform=ax.transAxes)
    for i,p in enumerate(pieces):
        c=teal if i<2 else orange; x=.2+i*.18; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,.23),.15,.54,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.075,.5,p,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 30.2

title: Instruction Tuning
text:
Level 2 - Supervised mechanics

Context tokens and target tokens have different roles
The user request must be visible so the model can condition on it. It is usually not a target to reproduce. A common loss mask sets labels for system, user, padding, and structural tokens to an ignore value, while keeping labels for assistant response tokens. The causal model still predicts a distribution at every position, but optimisation averages loss only over supervised positions.


Code
ids=np.array([2,10,11,3,20,21,4,30,31,32,5])
assistant_start=7; pad_label=-100
labels=np.full_like(ids,pad_label)
labels[assistant_start:]=ids[assistant_start:]
print("IDs:   ",ids)
print("labels:",labels)


An off-by-one target mask can train the model to reproduce user text, omit the first assistant token, or include an end marker inconsistently. The model can still show a decreasing scalar loss, so small examples should print formatted tokens and labels before a large run.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3)); ax.axis("off")
for row,(name,values) in enumerate([("token ID",ids),("label",labels)]):
    ax.text(.05,1.8-row*.8,name,weight="bold",color=grey)
    for i,v in enumerate(values):
        x=1+i*.66; c=orange if row==1 and v!=pad_label else (blue if row==0 else grey)
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.53-row*.8),.52,.42,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.26,1.74-row*.8,str(v),ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlim(0,8.7); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.25); plt.show()



Figure 30.3





Demonstration quality determines what is reinforced
Instruction data may be written by people, collected from existing tasks, generated by another model, or revised through review. Each source can be useful, but each has distinct error and provenance risks. A dataset should record authorship or generation process, licensing and consent conditions, task categories, languages, response length, quality-control rules, and the version of any model used to synthesize examples.
Data diversity is not a count of surface prompts. It concerns the distribution of tasks, ambiguity, formats, languages, safety-sensitive requests, and response behaviours. A dataset containing many paraphrases of one answer style can produce a narrow model interface. Evaluation splits should prevent template duplicates, source leakage, and near-identical instructions from inflating reported generalisation.


Code
examples={"extraction":1200,"summarisation":850,"coding":400,"multilingual":150}
print("task counts:",examples)
print("counts describe coverage only when task definitions and selection rules are documented")

title: Instruction Tuning
text:
Level 3 - Adaptation and regression

Fine-tuning changes shared parameters
Full supervised fine-tuning updates model parameters using gradients from the demonstration loss. The new gradients can improve target behaviours while changing probabilities needed for earlier behaviours. This is often called catastrophic forgetting when adaptation materially degrades retained capabilities. The term does not imply that any change is harmful: the question is whether a regression occurs on a predeclared retained-task set.


Code
before={"instruction":.42,"base_completion":.31,"code":.38}
after={"instruction":.61,"base_completion":.27,"code":.33}
for task in before: print(task,"change",round(after[task]-before[task],2))


The trade-off depends on data size and composition, learning rate, update count, sequence length, parameter scope, regularisation, and the mismatch between pretraining and adaptation tasks. A training report should retain intermediate checkpoints and evaluate both target and retained behaviours. A final checkpoint selected only on instruction loss can conceal a broader regression.


Multi-turn and tool examples create additional boundaries
In a multi-turn conversation, later assistant targets can condition on earlier assistant text. A training pipeline must specify whether it applies loss to every assistant turn, how it masks user and tool spans, and whether it truncates from the beginning or end. Tool-call examples also require a schema and a decision about whether tool results are trusted context, target text, or both.


Code
roles=["system","user","assistant","tool","assistant"]
supervise=np.array([False,False,True,False,True])
print(list(zip(roles,supervise)))




Dataset mixtures can create instruction conflicts
Instruction datasets often combine short question-answer examples, summarisation, extraction, coding, safety responses, tool use, and multi-turn conversations. The same visible request can be paired with incompatible target styles across sources: one example may answer directly, another may ask a clarifying question, and a third may refuse. A model cannot infer an unstated hierarchy among such demonstrations. The dataset builder must define source weights, conflict rules, and the intended role of system messages or policy examples.
This is also why response length and formatting deserve an audit. A corpus dominated by terse answers can make longer explanations less probable even when they are appropriate. A corpus dominated by verbose templates can produce unnecessary prefacing. These are not properties of “instruction following” in general; they are patterns in the supervised target distribution.




Code
types=["extraction","explanation","coding","policy"]
shares=np.array([.25,.35,.2,.2])
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,2.9)); left=0
for name,share,c in zip(types,shares,[blue,teal,orange,purple]):
    ax.barh([0],[share],left=[left],color=c,label=name); ax.text(left+share/2,0,f"{int(share*100)}%",ha="center",va="center",color="white"); left+=share
ax.set_xlim(0,1); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel("illustrative supervised-token share"); ax.legend(ncol=4,loc="upper center"); ax.set_title("Mixture choices define the reinforced response distribution"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 30.4





Training loss is an incomplete selection criterion
Response-token cross-entropy measures agreement with held-out demonstration continuations. It can identify overfitting to a declared validation set, but it cannot by itself show that an answer is helpful for a different user, factually supported, secure in a tool environment, or stable under prompt variation. Model selection should combine the validation loss with task-specific target and regression evaluations that were chosen before inspecting the final checkpoint.
The evaluation must also preserve the serving interface. Comparing a base model under a raw completion prompt with a tuned model under a carefully engineered chat template mixes model adaptation and prompting. A fair comparison can report both interfaces, but it should label them separately and make visible any system messages, retrieval context, decoding constraints, or answer extraction rules.


Code
checkpoints={"step_100":(1.42,.52,.41),"step_500":(1.28,.61,.37),"step_900":(1.22,.60,.31)}
for step,(loss,target,retained) in checkpoints.items():
    print(step,"validation loss",loss,"target score",target,"retained score",retained)




Errors often originate before the response span
An incorrect instruction-tuned output can arise from an ambiguous request, an incompatible template, truncated context, unsupported content in the demonstration data, a target-mask error, decoding choices, or a model distribution that fails despite correct inputs. An audit should retain the formatted token sequence, role boundaries, masked labels, selected output IDs, and evaluation rationale for representative failures. This makes it possible to repair the relevant component rather than adding examples blindly.
For a system that uses tools or retrieved documents, source availability should be part of the error record. An answer can be stylistically compliant while failing to use a supplied source, or it can cite a source that was never available in the context. Instruction tuning alone does not establish grounding behaviour; the task interface and evaluation need to test it.


The supervised objective has a length and balance policy
Assistant-only masking is not sufficient to define a dataset loss. Long responses contribute more supervised tokens than short responses when loss is averaged over valid target tokens. A corpus with a few long explanations can therefore exert more gradient influence than a larger number of brief extraction examples. Sampling weights, example packing, maximum length, truncation, and the loss denominator should be chosen together and recorded.
Truncation is particularly important in multi-turn data. Removing the beginning of a conversation can discard system instructions or the question that makes an assistant answer meaningful. Removing the end can cut the supervised answer and produce incomplete targets. A pipeline needs a declared rule and tests on representative long conversations, including tool results and retrieved context.


Code
examples={"short extraction":12,"long explanation":180,"tool conversation":95}
total=sum(examples.values())
for name,tokens in examples.items(): print(name,"supervised-token share",round(tokens/total,2))

title: Instruction Tuning
text:
Level 4 - Audit and interpretation

Evaluate behaviour, not only response overlap
Exact match is useful for extraction and tightly specified outputs. It is insufficient for many instruction tasks where several answers are valid. Evaluations should define the task, input availability, output criterion, scoring procedure, and any human-review protocol. They should compare the base and tuned checkpoints under the same template and decoding policy, then report both improvements and regressions.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.4)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.35,"base\ncheckpoint",blue),(2.55,"tuned\ncheckpoint",orange),(5.05,"target-task\nevaluation",teal),(7.2,"retained-task\nevaluation",purple)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.3),1.55,.58,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.775,1.59,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.text(4.5,.55,"Report target gains and retained-task changes separately.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.25); plt.show()



Figure 30.5





The run record must recover the exact interface
An instruction-tuning record needs base checkpoint and tokenizer, template version, role and special-token rules, source and target masks, training examples and provenance, split policy, maximum length and truncation rule, optimiser settings, parameter scope, checkpoints, target and retained evaluations, decoding settings, and known failure cases. This is the minimum needed to distinguish a model change from a prompt-template or evaluation change.


Code
record={"base":"versioned checkpoint","template":"v3","target_mask":"assistant only","max_length":2048,"evaluation":"target and retained sets"}
assert {"base","template","target_mask","evaluation"} <= set(record)
print("instruction-tuning record complete")

title: Instruction Tuning
text:
Common misconceptions

Instruction tuning replaces the language-model objective. It usually applies the same token loss to a different, masked demonstration distribution.
Every token in a chat transcript should be supervised. User and system text are commonly conditioning context, not desired output.
A chat template can be changed without retraining. Its role markers and separators alter the input token sequence.
More demonstrations automatically give broader instruction following. Coverage, quality, duplication, and task mix determine what is reinforced.
Improved instruction scores prove no retained capability declined. Regression tests are required.
A compliant response is necessarily a correct response. Format following and factual validity require separate evidence.

title: Instruction Tuning
text:
Summary
Instruction tuning adapts a base model to role-formatted demonstrations by applying supervised token loss to declared response spans. The template, tokenizer, target mask, data provenance, and loss denominator define the actual adaptation task. A tuned model must be evaluated for both target behaviour and retained capabilities.
Chapter 30 examines how preference data and related objectives compare candidate responses rather than simply reproducing one demonstration.

Looking ahead

title: Preference Optimisation
text: Chapter orientation

title: Preference Optimisation
text:
Why this chapter matters
Instruction tuning learns to reproduce a demonstrated response. Preference optimisation uses comparisons: for a shared prompt, one candidate response is marked preferred to another. The data therefore express a relative judgement, not a single token-level target. Training methods use those comparisons to change the probability assigned to preferred and rejected responses.
The comparison is only as broad as the judging procedure and prompt distribution. A preferred response can still be false, incomplete, biased, unsafe in another setting, or preferred for a reason that is not documented. This chapter explains reward-model pipelines and direct preference methods, their data requirements, and their failure modes. Chapter 31 turns to parameter-efficient adaptation.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish demonstrations, scalar ratings, and pairwise preferences;
define prompt, chosen response, rejected response, judge, and comparison policy;
explain the Bradley-Terry reward-model likelihood;
distinguish reward-model-plus-RL pipelines from direct preference optimisation;
calculate a toy pairwise preference probability;
identify preference-data quality, ambiguity, and reward-hacking risks; and
specify an evaluation and audit record for a preference-optimised model.



Running pair
The same prompt receives two candidate answers. A judge prefers the chosen answer according to a stated criterion. The dataset should retain both candidates, the prompt, the criterion, and how the judgement was obtained.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.5)); ax.axis("off")
items=[(.3,1.45,1.7,.58,"prompt",blue),(3.1,2.3,2.1,.58,"chosen response",teal),(3.1,.7,2.1,.58,"rejected response",orange),(6.4,1.45,1.8,.58,"preference\nrecord",purple)]
for x,y,w,h,label,c in items: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,y),w,h,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+w/2,y+h/2,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
for a,b in [((2.05,1.74),(3.05,2.55)),((2.05,1.74),(3.05,.95)),((5.25,2.55),(6.35,1.74)),((5.25,.95),(6.35,1.74))]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(a,b,arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.set_xlim(0,8.6); ax.set_ylim(.2,3.2); plt.show()



Figure 31.1

title: Preference Optimisation
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Comparisons add a different kind of supervision
For an instruction such as “summarise this report”, two responses can both be grammatical and relevant while one is judged clearer, more complete, or better supported. A pairwise label records that relative judgement. It does not require the preferred response to be perfect, and it does not state how large the difference is unless the data include that information.
Preference datasets can be created by people, expert judges, rule-based procedures, or model-based judges. The source matters because it defines what the label represents. A preference for a concise answer differs from a preference for a medically accurate answer; an aggregate label can conceal disagreement among judges or a criterion that favours stylistic features over evidence.


Code
pair={"prompt":"Summarise the record","chosen":"States the evidence and limit","rejected":"Adds unsupported detail","criterion":"support and relevance"}
for key,value in pair.items(): print(key+":",value)




Preference learning does not replace evaluation
Optimising against comparisons can make a model more likely to produce responses similar to those preferred in training. It cannot show that the judging distribution matches future users, that the preferred response is factually correct, or that a system is safe under tool use. A model can learn to exploit regularities in a reward signal: polished wording, disclaimers, or length may receive positive labels even when the answer is not useful.
The relevant question is therefore specific: preferred by whom, for which prompts, under which instructions, using what information, and compared with what alternatives? Without this record, “aligned with preferences” has no operational meaning.

title: Preference Optimisation
text:
Level 2 - Pairwise models

A reward model turns responses into scores
A reward model assigns a scalar (r(x,y)) to a prompt (x) and response (y). Under a Bradley-Terry model, the probability that chosen response (y^+) is preferred to rejected response (y^-) is
[ P(y^+ y-x)=(r(x,y+)-r(x,y^-)). ]
Training raises this probability for observed comparisons. Only score differences matter: adding the same constant to both rewards leaves the pairwise probability unchanged.


Code
def sigmoid(x): return 1/(1+np.exp(-x))
chosen_reward,rejected_reward=1.4,.3
print("preference probability:",round(sigmoid(chosen_reward-rejected_reward),3))






Code
differences=np.linspace(-4,4,200)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5,4)); ax.plot(differences,sigmoid(differences),color=teal,lw=2.5); ax.axvline(0,color=grey,lw=.8); ax.set_xlabel("chosen reward minus rejected reward"); ax.set_ylabel("preference probability"); ax.set_title("Pairwise preference model"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 31.2



Reward scores are not calibrated measures of truth or social value. They are learned predictors of the comparison labels under the model and data used. A high reward can be useful for selecting among candidates, but it requires independent tests for reward hacking, distribution shift, and disagreement with the intended criterion.


Two main training routes
One route trains a reward model, then uses reinforcement learning to optimise a policy while constraining it to remain near a reference model. The reference constraint limits uncontrolled changes, but it does not make the learned reward correct. Another route directly optimises the policy with chosen-rejected pairs and a reference policy, avoiding an explicit separate reward-model optimisation. Direct preference optimisation (DPO) is one such formulation (Rafailov et al. 2023).




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3.2)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.25,"preference\npairs",blue),(2.2,"reward\nmodel",teal),(4.15,"RL policy\nupdate",orange),(6.65,"reference +\npairs",purple),(8.55,"direct policy\nobjective",teal)]:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.25),1.35,.62,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.675,1.56,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for x in [1.62,3.58,8.05]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,1.56),(x+.5,1.56),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.text(4.0,.55,"reward-model route",ha="center",color=orange); ax.text(8.1,.55,"direct-preference route",ha="center",color=purple); ax.set_xlim(0,10); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 31.3

title: Preference Optimisation
text:
Level 3 - Objective and data boundaries

Direct preference objectives compare log probabilities
For each pair, DPO encourages the tuned policy to increase the relative log probability of the chosen response over the rejected response, compared with a reference policy. The reference is commonly the supervised model before preference training. The exact objective includes a temperature-like coefficient that sets the strength of the change. It is a policy objective built from pairwise labels, not a claim that the chosen sequence is the only correct continuation.


Code
logp_chosen,logp_rejected=-2.0,-3.1
logref_chosen,logref_rejected=-2.2,-2.8
relative=(logp_chosen-logp_rejected)-(logref_chosen-logref_rejected)
print("relative chosen advantage over reference:",round(relative,3))


Preference data must define response boundaries. If responses have very different lengths, raw sequence log probability can depend strongly on token count. If one response is truncated or contains hidden template text, the pair no longer represents the intended comparison. The dataset should store tokenised lengths, stop reasons, template version, candidate-generation method, and whether judges saw sources or tool outputs.


Judge disagreement is evidence, not noise to hide
When several judges compare a pair, disagreement can reveal ambiguous prompts, competing criteria, poor candidate quality, or a population difference that an aggregate majority label conceals. A pipeline may aggregate labels, retain ties, collect rationales, or route sensitive cases to experts. The choice affects the supervised signal and should be reported.


Code
votes=np.array([1,1,0,1,0]) # 1 means candidate A preferred
print("A share:",votes.mean(),"disagreement rate:",min(votes.mean(),1-votes.mean()))




Candidate generation sets the comparison problem
Preference labels are collected over candidates that a pipeline has made available. If all candidates are poor, the chosen response may still be unsuitable. If candidates differ mainly in length or formatting, judges can learn a superficial comparison rule. If candidates come from one model and decoding policy, a reward model can be poorly calibrated for candidates produced after the policy changes. The pair generator, temperature, length limit, constraints, and filtering rules therefore belong in the dataset record.
Candidate diversity can be useful when it exposes meaningful trade-offs, such as a concise answer versus a detailed answer grounded in different evidence. It can be unhelpful when it creates near-duplicate pairs that add labels without expanding the decision boundary. Sampling pairs should be audited for prompt overlap, candidate similarity, response length, source availability, and the reasons judges were asked to compare them.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.2)); ax.axis("off")
for x,y,label,c in [(.25,1.35,"prompt",blue),(2.0,2.2,"policy A\ncandidates",teal),(2.0,.5,"policy B\ncandidates",orange),(5.0,1.35,"judge\ncriterion",purple),(7.1,1.35,"recorded\npair",teal)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,y),1.45,.58,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.725,y+.29,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
for a,b in [((1.7,1.64),(1.95,2.48)),((1.7,1.64),(1.95,.78)),((3.45,2.48),(4.95,1.64)),((3.45,.78),(4.95,1.64)),((6.45,1.64),(7.05,1.64))]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(a,b,arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.set_xlim(0,8.8); ax.set_ylim(.15,3); plt.show()



Figure 31.4





Preference optimisation needs regression checks
A preferred-response objective can change refusal behaviour, verbosity, calibration language, code style, and the probability of answers outside the labelled prompt categories. Model selection should include a fixed suite of target preferences and retained tasks, with the same template and decoding policy for the reference and tuned checkpoints. The comparison should state whether the evaluation judges are independent from the preference-data judges and whether test prompts were held out before candidate generation.
Reward scores should not be used as the only selection metric because the policy has been optimised against them. A reward model can rank its own training distribution well while disagreeing with a new judge population or task-grounded evaluator. The separation between training signal and independent evaluation is a basic protection against selecting the checkpoint that best exploits the available proxy.


Preference labels need a population and a decision rule
Judges do not supply preferences in the abstract. They evaluate candidates under instructions, time constraints, information access, and a particular population of prompts. Expert review can be needed when an answer requires domain knowledge; general raters can still be appropriate for readability or instruction compliance if that is the criterion. The report should name the criterion rather than treating all labels as one measure of helpfulness.
Pair construction also determines whether a preference is informative. Pairs that differ in only punctuation can estimate a narrow formatting preference. Pairs with one malformed candidate can make the task trivial. Difficult pairs near a decision boundary can reveal disagreement and evaluator limitations, but they also require a policy for ties and uncertainty. Keeping the unaggregated labels supports later analysis of those differences.


Code
pair_types={"trivial malformed alternative":40,"format trade-off":35,"evidence trade-off":25}
print(pair_types)
print("A preference dataset should report how its pair types were sampled and judged.")

title: Preference Optimisation
text:
Level 4 - Audit and failure modes

Reward hacking is an empirical failure mode
Optimising a learned reward can produce outputs that score well under the reward model while failing the intended task. A response may use confident language, repeat a judging rubric, become excessively long, or exploit a blind spot in labelled comparisons. This is not a hypothetical concern that can be dismissed by a high mean reward; it is a reason to evaluate on fresh prompts, new candidate sources, adversarial cases, and human or task-grounded criteria independent of the training reward.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8.7,3.4)); ax.axis("off")
for x,y,label,c in [(.3,1.45,"policy\nupdate",blue),(2.45,1.45,"learned\nreward",orange),(5.0,2.35,"task\nevaluation",teal),(5.0,.55,"independent\nreview",purple)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,y),1.45,.58,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.725,y+.29,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
for a,b in [((1.78,1.74),(2.4,1.74)),((3.9,1.74),(4.95,2.64)),((3.9,1.74),(4.95,.84))]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(a,b,arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.set_xlim(0,7); ax.set_ylim(.2,3.2); plt.show()



Figure 31.5





A preference record supports interpretation
An audit should retain base and reference checkpoints; prompt and template versions; candidate-generation policy and decoding settings; chosen and rejected token sequences; judge population, instructions, information access, and aggregation rule; reward-model architecture and validation where used; objective parameters; training schedule; target and regression evaluations; and representative disagreements or failures. This record allows a reviewer to identify whether a change came from candidates, judges, the objective, or the serving interface.


Code
record={"reference":"instruction checkpoint","pairs":"versioned","judges":"documented instructions","objective":"DPO-like","evaluation":"independent"}
assert {"reference","pairs","judges","objective","evaluation"} <= set(record)
print("preference audit record complete")

title: Preference Optimisation
text:
Common misconceptions

A preference label says the chosen answer is correct. It records a relative judgement under a particular procedure.
Reward scores are calibrated truth scores. They estimate comparison labels under a trained reward model.
Direct preference optimisation needs no reference behaviour. Standard direct objectives define change relative to a reference policy.
More pairwise labels remove ambiguity. They can reproduce a narrow judge distribution or unresolved disagreement.
A higher learned reward proves the model is safer. Independent safety and task tests are required.
Preference optimisation replaces instruction tuning. It usually starts from an instruction-following reference model.

title: Preference Optimisation
text:
Summary
Preference optimisation learns from comparisons between responses for a shared prompt. Reward-model pipelines and direct objectives both depend on the candidate distribution, judging procedure, response boundaries, reference policy, and independent evaluation. A learned reward or preference score is evidence about that comparison process, not a general certificate of truth, safety, or usefulness.
Chapter 31 compares full updates with parameter-efficient adaptation methods such as LoRA.

title: Full and Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning
text: Chapter orientation

title: Full and Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning
text:
Why this chapter matters
Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained checkpoint to a declared task or response distribution. Full fine-tuning updates all trainable model parameters. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) freezes most base weights and trains a smaller set of added or selected parameters. The choice affects optimiser memory, checkpoint storage, deployment, multi-task serving, and the kinds of changes a run can represent.
Neither method removes the need for data documentation or evaluation. A small adapter can overfit, encode an unsafe behaviour, or fail outside its tuning distribution. A full update can improve a target task while degrading retained behaviours. This chapter gives the comparison and the implementation contracts required to make it interpretable.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish full fine-tuning, frozen-base adaptation, and inference-only prompting;
derive the parameter count of a low-rank update;
explain LoRA’s update and merge operation;
compare weight, gradient, optimiser-state, and activation memory;
identify adapter/checkpoint compatibility requirements;
evaluate target gains and retained-task regressions; and
record an adaptation run so that it can be reproduced or served safely.



Running layer
For a linear layer with base weight (W), LoRA learns a low-rank update (W = BA). The base weight remains frozen during training, and the update can be applied separately or merged into a copy of the base weight for inference.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(9,3.5))
for ax,title,mode in zip(axes,["full fine-tuning","frozen base + PEFT"],["full","peft"]):
    ax.axis("off"); ax.set_title(title)
    for i in range(4):
        y=.15+i*.2; c=orange if mode=="full" else blue
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.22,y),.56,.12,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(.5,y+.06,"base layer",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
        if mode=="peft": ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.81,y),.13,.12,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(.875,y+.06,"A",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=7)
    ax.text(.5,.94,"orange: updated" if mode=="full" else "blue: frozen; teal: updated",ha="center",color=grey,transform=ax.transAxes,fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 32.1

title: Full and Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Adaptation changes a checkpoint under a task distribution
Full fine-tuning applies gradients to all selected model weights. It can represent broad changes, but it requires storing gradients and optimiser state for those weights and usually produces a full new checkpoint. Parameter-efficient methods retain the base checkpoint and train a smaller module, such as low-rank matrices, adapters, prompts, or selected bias terms. This makes it possible to store task-specific changes separately and load different adaptations over one base model.
The methods are not ordered by quality in the abstract. The relevant comparison depends on task complexity, data size, available hardware, update frequency, latency constraints, compatibility requirements, and the cost of keeping several adapted versions. A smaller update reduces trainable parameters; it does not make the task specification or evaluation smaller.


Code
base_parameters=7_000_000_000
adapter_parameters=8_000_000
print("trainable fraction:",adapter_parameters/base_parameters)




Frozen weights are still part of the function
A PEFT adapter is not a standalone model. It assumes a particular base checkpoint, architecture, tokenizer, layer naming convention, target modules, rank, scaling rule, and often quantisation configuration. Loading an adapter onto a related model with the same visible size can change or break its function. The serving record must bind the adapter to its compatible base.


Code
adapter_metadata={"base":"checkpoint-v1","target_modules":["q_proj","v_proj"],"rank":8,"scale":16}
print(adapter_metadata)

title: Full and Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning
text:
Level 2 - LoRA mechanics

Low-rank updates reduce trainable parameter count
For a layer (W^{d_{out}d_{in}}), a full update contains (d_{out}d_{in}) parameters. A rank-(r) LoRA update uses (A^{rd_{in}}) and (B^{d_{out}r}), for (r(d_{in}+d_{out})) trainable parameters. The update is commonly scaled by a factor such as (/r) (Hu et al. 2022).


Code
d_in,d_out,r=4096,4096,8
full=d_in*d_out; lora=r*(d_in+d_out)
print("full parameters:",full,"LoRA parameters:",lora,"fraction:",lora/full)






Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.3)); ax.axis("off")
for x,w,label,c in [(.25,1.6,"frozen W\n[dout × din]",blue),(2.45,1.25,"A\n[r × din]",teal),(4.0,1.25,"B\n[dout × r]",teal),(5.65,1.6,"ΔW = BA",orange),(7.35,1.6,"W + ΔW",purple)]:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.25),w,.62,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+w/2,1.56,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.text(4.4,.55,"The update is low rank; the effective layer still maps din to dout.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 32.2



The reduction is largest when rank is much smaller than layer widths. Targeting only some projections reduces it further. These decisions restrict the trainable update family. They can be sufficient for a task, but sufficiency should be demonstrated on target and retained evaluations, not inferred from a low training loss.


Merge and unmerge are numerical operations
At inference, an adapter can be applied as a separate branch or merged by forming (W’ = W + sBA). Merging can reduce runtime overhead, but it creates a new effective weight tensor. Repeated merging, wrong scaling, mismatched dtype, or merging into the wrong base can produce irreversible errors unless the original base and adapter are retained.


Code
np.random.seed(2)
W=np.random.randn(3,4); A=np.random.randn(2,4); B=np.random.randn(3,2); scale=.5
x=np.random.randn(4)
separate=W@x+scale*(B@(A@x))
merged=(W+scale*B@A)@x
assert np.allclose(separate,merged)
print("separate and merged adapter outputs agree")

title: Full and Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning
text:
Level 3 - Resource and deployment accounting

Trainable parameters are not the whole memory account
Training memory includes base weights, trainable weights, gradients, optimiser states, activations, temporary buffers, and communication state. Freezing a base model can remove its gradient and optimiser-state requirements, but the base weights and many forward activations remain. Quantising frozen weights can lower storage further, while introducing a new numerical configuration that must be evaluated. QLoRA combines quantised base weights with low-rank adapters (Dettmers et al. 2023).


Code
params=7_000_000_000; bytes_per_weight=2; bytes_per_adam_state=8
full_weight_gib=params*bytes_per_weight/2**30
full_adam_gib=params*bytes_per_adam_state/2**30
print("base weights GiB:",round(full_weight_gib,1),"Adam moments GiB:",round(full_adam_gib,1))






Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); categories=["base weights","gradients","optimiser","activations"]; full=np.array([4,4,8,3]); peft=np.array([4,.2,.4,3]); bottom=np.zeros(2)
for vals,name,c in zip([np.array([full[i],peft[i]]) for i in range(4)],categories,[blue,orange,purple,teal]): ax.bar(["full","PEFT"],vals,bottom=bottom,label=name,color=c); bottom+=vals
ax.set_ylabel("relative memory components"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Conceptual training-memory account"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 32.3





Multi-adapter serving creates routing decisions
Separate adapters can make several task variants cheaper to store than several full checkpoints. Serving still needs a policy for selecting the adapter, ensuring it is compatible with the request, batching requests that use different adapters, and preventing an adapter intended for one task or policy from being silently applied to another. An adapter identifier is part of the request and audit trace.


Code
routes={"legal-summary":"adapter-legal-v2","code-review":"adapter-code-v1"}
request_task="code-review"
print("selected adapter:",routes[request_task])




Parameter scope is a substantive design choice
PEFT is a family of methods rather than one fixed architecture. An implementation may target attention projections, feed-forward layers, output heads, selected biases, or inserted adapter blocks. Each scope changes which transformations can adapt and how many new parameters are trained. The scope should be reported at the level of module names and layer coverage, not only as a total trainable-parameter count.
Targeting all layers can permit a more distributed adaptation than targeting only a final projection. Targeting a small subset can reduce storage and training time while concentrating the burden of adaptation in fewer locations. The appropriate choice is empirical: test candidate scopes on the declared task and retained suite under the same data and optimisation budget.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5,4)); ax.axis("off")
for i in range(4):
    y=3.15-i*.72; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.8,y),2.0,.45,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(1.8,y+.225,f"Transformer block {i+1}",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((3.05,y),.8,.45,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(3.45,y+.225,"attn",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((4.1,y),.8,.45,facecolor=orange,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(4.5,y+.225,"FFN",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
ax.text(3.95,.25,"Highlighted target modules define where adapter updates are attached.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,6); ax.set_ylim(.05,3.8); plt.show()



Figure 32.4





Checkpoint organisation determines recoverability
An adaptation run should preserve the immutable base identifier, adapter weights, configuration, tokenizer and template versions, training state where resumption is required, and evaluation records. A merged weight file alone can make a task variant convenient to serve, but it loses the clean separation between base and update unless both original artefacts are retained. A safe workflow treats merging as a reproducible build step with an output hash and an equivalence test.


Code
checkpoint={"base_hash":"abc","adapter_hash":"def","merge_scale":16/8,"merged":False,"template":"v3"}
assert checkpoint["base_hash"] and checkpoint["adapter_hash"]
print("recoverable adapter checkpoint metadata present")




Data volume and update scope interact
An adapter with few trainable parameters does not imply that many examples are required, nor does a full update imply that a small dataset is necessarily unsuitable. The relevant risk depends on how far the target distribution differs from the base model, how repetitive the data are, how many update tokens and epochs are used, and which evaluation tasks must remain stable. A small, tightly specified adaptation can overfit through either method when the validation split duplicates templates or sources.
Checkpoint selection should inspect learning curves and held-out behaviour across more than one update count. A model that reaches its best target score early may degrade after additional passes over narrow data. Retaining base and intermediate checkpoints makes it possible to compare the adaptation trajectory rather than selecting only the final artifact.


Code
history={"step_100":{"target":.58,"retained":.71},"step_500":{"target":.66,"retained":.69},"step_900":{"target":.65,"retained":.62}}
for step,metrics in history.items(): print(step,metrics)

title: Full and Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning
text:
Level 4 - Audit and selection

Choose an adaptation method against a declared constraint
An adaptation plan should specify the base checkpoint, task, data provenance, target modules or full parameter scope, rank and scaling where relevant, quantisation and precision, maximum length, optimiser settings, token budget, checkpoint policy, merge status, and serving route. It should report target-task results and a retained-task suite under the same prompt template and decoding policy.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.5)); ax.axis("off")
rows=["target evaluation","retained evaluation","memory account","checkpoint and merge","serving route"]
for i,row in enumerate(rows):
    y=2.7-i*.48; ax.text(.2,y,row,va="center",color=grey); ax.add_patch(Rectangle((3.0,y-.17),2,.34,facecolor=orange,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(4,y,"full",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8); ax.add_patch(Rectangle((5.25,y-.17),2,.34,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(6.25,y,"PEFT",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0,8); ax.set_ylim(.1,3.2); plt.show()



Figure 32.5



The method should not be selected solely because it is cheaper or because it reaches the lowest training loss. A full update may be necessary for a target distribution; a low-rank update may be sufficient and operationally preferable. Both conclusions require evidence under the specified task and deployment conditions.


Regression tests should include the base interface
Adaptation can change outputs for prompts outside the fine-tuning corpus. Retained tests should include general instruction responses, domain tasks that must remain available, formatting or tool contracts, and safety-sensitive inputs where relevant. Tests must specify whether the adapter is active and which system template is used. Comparing a base checkpoint without its standard template to an adapter checkpoint with a richer interface would not isolate the update.


Code
results={"target":{"base":.48,"adapter":.67},"retained":{"base":.72,"adapter":.70}}
for suite,scores in results.items(): print(suite,scores)

title: Full and Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning
text:
Common misconceptions

PEFT changes only a few values, so it cannot cause a large behavioural change. Small modules can substantially change the effective function.
An adapter can be used with any model of the same size. It requires the compatible base and architecture contract.
Freezing the base eliminates training memory demands. Base weights and activations remain.
Merged and separate adapters always give the same result without qualification. Scaling, dtype, and correct base identity are required.
A lower training loss identifies the best adaptation method. Target, retained, and systems constraints require separate evidence.
