title: Full and Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning
text:
Summary
Full fine-tuning updates selected base parameters, while parameter-efficient methods train smaller updates over a frozen checkpoint. LoRA represents one such update as a low-rank matrix product. The choice changes trainable parameter count, optimiser state, checkpoint storage, and serving design, but it does not remove the need for task data, compatibility metadata, or regression evaluation.
Chapter 32 examines lower-precision weights and activations as a separate efficiency and accuracy trade-off.

title: Full and Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning
text:
Looking ahead
Adaptation changes the model or an attached update. Chapter 32 examines how the resulting tensors can be represented and executed under tighter memory and latency constraints.

title: Full and Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning
text:
Further reading
LoRA is introduced by Hu et al. (2022). QLoRA studies low-rank adaptation with quantised base models (Dettmers et al. 2023).






Dettmers, Tim, Artidoro Pagnoni, Ari Holtzman, and Luke Zettlemoyer. 2023. “QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36: 10088–115. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314.


Hu, Edward J., Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, and Weizhu Chen. 2022. “LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models.” International Conference on Learning Representations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685.

title: Quantisation and Efficient Inference
text: Chapter orientation

title: Quantisation and Efficient Inference
text:
Why this chapter matters
Inference requires model weights, temporary computation, and often a key-value cache to fit in available hardware memory. Quantisation represents selected tensors with fewer bits than a higher-precision baseline. It can reduce storage, memory traffic, and sometimes latency, but it introduces approximation error and depends on hardware kernels, tensor formats, calibration choices, and serving configuration.
Quantisation is not a single setting called “4-bit” or “8-bit”. A valid description states which tensors are converted, group sizes and scales, activation and cache formats, compute precision, conversion method, and the evaluation used to detect degradation. This chapter develops that account before Chapter 33 turns to retrieval-augmented generation.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish storage precision, compute precision, and quantised tensor values;
calculate approximate weight-memory savings from bit width;
implement a toy affine quantiser and reconstruction error check;
explain per-tensor, per-channel, and groupwise scaling;
identify weights, activations, and key-value cache as separate quantisation targets;
state why hardware and kernels affect measured speed; and
specify a conversion and evaluation record for an efficient inference deployment.



Running vector
The running vector is represented in floating point, mapped to a small integer range, and reconstructed using a scale. The reconstructed values are close to, but not equal to, the original values.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.25,"float weights\n[-0.8, 0.2, 1.1]",blue),(3.35,"integer codes\n[-3, 1, 4]",orange),(6.45,"reconstructed\n[-0.75, 0.25, 1.0]",teal)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.2),2.0,.65,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+1,1.525,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
for x,label in [(2.3,"quantise"),(5.4,"dequantise")]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,1.525),(x+.95,1.525),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=12)); ax.text(x+.47,.95,label,ha="center",color=grey,fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0,8.8); ax.set_ylim(.4,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 33.1

title: Quantisation and Efficient Inference
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Fewer bits trade representation detail for resource use
A floating-point tensor stores values with a wide numerical range and finite precision. A quantised tensor stores codes from a smaller set, plus scales and sometimes zero points that map codes back to approximate values. Fewer bits reduce the raw weight footprint. They can also reduce data movement, which is frequently a practical bottleneck in generation. The conversion discards detail, so task behaviour must be checked after conversion.
For a model with (P) weights, a simple storage estimate is (Pb/8) bytes for (b)-bit values, before scales, metadata, packing overhead, and non-quantised tensors. This calculation is useful for capacity planning but is not a measured memory requirement.


Code
parameters=7_000_000_000
for bits in [16,8,4]: print(bits,"bit raw weight GiB:",round(parameters*bits/8/2**30,2))






Code
bits=np.array([16,8,4]); gib=parameters*bits/8/2**30
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.bar(["16-bit","8-bit","4-bit"],gib,color=[blue,teal,orange]); ax.set_ylabel("raw weight storage (GiB)"); ax.set_title("Raw storage estimate before quantisation overhead"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 33.2





Precision names do not specify an inference system
“4-bit model” may mean weights stored in four-bit codes while matrix multiplication accumulates in higher precision. It may leave embeddings, output layers, activations, or the key-value cache at another precision. Two deployments with the same advertised weight bit width can therefore have different memory use, latency, and output behaviour.
Quantisation also does not automatically improve latency. A device and runtime need efficient kernels for the format and batch shape. Dequantisation, memory alignment, small batches, long context caches, and unsupported operations can eliminate an expected speed gain. Measure the target workload rather than inferring throughput from a format label.

title: Quantisation and Efficient Inference
text:
Level 2 - Quantisation mechanics

A simple affine quantiser
For symmetric signed quantisation, a scale can map a maximum magnitude to the largest available integer code. Values are divided by the scale, rounded, clipped to the integer range, and reconstructed by multiplying the code by the scale. Real systems add choices about group size, outliers, zero points, packing, and kernel layout.


Code
x=np.array([-.83,-.31,.18,.62,1.04])
qmax=7
scale=np.max(np.abs(x))/qmax
codes=np.clip(np.round(x/scale),-qmax,qmax).astype(int)
reconstructed=codes*scale
print("scale:",round(scale,3),"codes:",codes)
print("reconstructed:",np.round(reconstructed,3))
print("max absolute error:",round(np.max(np.abs(x-reconstructed)),3))






Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5,4.5)); ax.scatter(x,reconstructed,color=teal,s=65); ax.plot([-1.1,1.1],[-1.1,1.1],color=grey,ls="--"); ax.set_xlabel("original"); ax.set_ylabel("reconstructed"); ax.set_title("Toy quantisation reconstruction"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 33.3





Scales determine where error falls
One scale for a whole tensor is simple but can represent small values poorly when a few outliers determine the range. Per-channel or groupwise scaling uses more scale values and metadata while allowing each channel or group a more suitable range. The group definition must be recorded because it changes the representation and can change accuracy.


Code
weights=np.array([[.02,.04,.08,1.1],[.01,.03,.06,.09]])
global_scale=np.max(np.abs(weights))/7
row_scales=np.max(np.abs(weights),axis=1)/7
print("global scale:",round(global_scale,3),"row scales:",np.round(row_scales,3))

title: Quantisation and Efficient Inference
text:
Level 3 - System-level effects

Weights, activations, and caches have different roles
Weight quantisation changes static model storage. Activation quantisation changes intermediate computation and may require calibration data or quantisation-aware training. Key-value cache quantisation changes the growing state of autoregressive serving described in Chapter 27. These choices have different numerical and memory consequences and should not be conflated.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); components=np.array([10,2,5]); ax.bar(["inference request"],components[0],color=blue,label="weights"); ax.bar(["inference request"],components[1],bottom=components[0],color=orange,label="temporary activations"); ax.bar(["inference request"],components[2],bottom=components[:2].sum(),color=teal,label="KV cache"); ax.legend(); ax.set_ylabel("relative memory"); ax.set_title("Quantisation targets have distinct memory roles"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 33.4



The relevant memory budget changes with prompt length, output length, concurrency, batch policy, and cache layout. A conversion that permits a checkpoint to load may still fail under long concurrent requests because the cache becomes dominant. Conversely, reducing cache precision can affect long-context outputs even when the weight-only conversion was accurate on short prompts.


Calibration and validation must follow conversion
Post-training quantisation may use representative activations to choose scales or protect outlier channels. The calibration set should resemble the declared workload in language, length, formatting, and task type. Calibrating only short generic prompts then claiming a result for long code or multilingual documents leaves an untested gap.


Code
baseline=np.array([.62,.58,.71])
quantised=np.array([.61,.57,.68])
print("task deltas:",np.round(quantised-baseline,3))




Numerical error accumulates through a generation loop
Quantisation does not perturb one isolated matrix multiplication. A generated token changes the next prefix, which changes attention keys, values, and later logits. Small differences can leave a short deterministic output unchanged or lead to a different token after a close decision, after which the two generations follow different prefixes. Output disagreement is therefore expected to be task- and decoding-dependent, not proof by itself that conversion failed.
The useful comparison separates numerical equivalence tests from behaviour tests. On a small fixed reference input, compare intermediate or next-token logits within a stated tolerance. On a task suite, compare outcome scores and error categories. On a serving workload, compare memory and latency at the prompt lengths and concurrency that matter. Each test identifies a different conversion property.


Code
baseline_logits=np.array([2.001,1.200,.302])
quantised_logits=np.array([1.996,1.205,.297])
print("max logit difference:",np.max(np.abs(baseline_logits-quantised_logits)))
print("same greedy token:",baseline_logits.argmax()==quantised_logits.argmax())




Quantisation policy should include fallback behaviour
Some deployments keep selected modules in higher precision because they are sensitive to a conversion method or because a runtime lacks a suitable kernel. Others route long-context or high-stakes requests to a higher-precision model. A fallback is not a defect, but it changes cost and comparability. The policy should state when it is triggered and report how often it occurs in the intended workload.


Code
request={"prompt_tokens":12000,"task":"source-grounded answer"}
route="higher precision" if request["prompt_tokens"]>8192 else "quantised"
print("route:",route)

title: Quantisation and Efficient Inference
text:
Level 4 - Audit and deployment

A quantised checkpoint requires a conversion record
The record should state base checkpoint hash, tokenizer, source dtype, weight and activation formats, group size, scales and zero-point method, exempt modules, calibration data and procedure, compute accumulation dtype, cache format, runtime and kernel version, hardware, merge status for adapters, and output artifact hashes. A conversion cannot be audited from a filename such as model-4bit.


Code
conversion={"base_hash":"abc","weight_format":"int4 groupwise","group_size":128,"compute_dtype":"float16","kv_cache":"float16","runtime":"versioned"}
assert {"base_hash","weight_format","compute_dtype","runtime"} <= set(conversion)
print("conversion record complete")




Validate both task behaviour and service behaviour
Compare the baseline and converted model under the same tokenizer, prompt template, decoding policy, maximum lengths, and hardware workload where possible. Report target-task scores, retained tasks, output agreement on a fixed reference set, error categories, peak memory, prefill and decode latency, throughput at declared concurrency, and failure behaviour near the context limit. A lower memory number without a matching accuracy and workload record is incomplete evidence.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8.8,3.2)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.3,"baseline\ncheckpoint",blue),(2.45,"quantised\ncheckpoint",orange),(5.0,"fixed task\nand output tests",teal),(7.2,"serving\nbenchmark",purple)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.25),1.5,.6,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.75,1.55,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
ax.text(4.5,.55,"Hold input, tokenizer, and policy fixed for the accuracy comparison.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 33.5

title: Quantisation and Efficient Inference
text:
Common misconceptions

A 4-bit label fully specifies quantisation. Tensor targets, scales, groups, compute dtype, and runtime remain necessary.
Lower bit width always gives proportional speed gains. Kernel support and workload shape determine observed latency.
Weight quantisation solves all inference memory limits. Activations and KV caches can dominate.
Quantisation error is only a scalar reconstruction error. Task and sequence behaviour can change unevenly.
A model that loads successfully is validated. It needs accuracy, boundary, and service tests.

title: Quantisation and Efficient Inference
text:
Exercises

Calculate raw storage for a parameter count at 16, 8, and 4 bits.
Implement a symmetric affine quantiser for a supplied vector.
Calculate reconstruction error and identify an outlier effect.
Compare global and per-channel scales.
List weight, activation, and cache precision separately for a deployment.
Explain why a KV cache can dominate long-context memory.
Design a representative calibration set for a declared application.
Specify a fixed-output comparison between baseline and quantised models.
List fields needed in a conversion record.
Explain why hardware kernels affect a latency claim.
Compare storage precision and accumulation precision.
Design a context-boundary test after cache quantisation.
Identify an adapter merge field needed before quantisation.
State why a generic short-prompt evaluation is insufficient.
Propose a serving benchmark with stated concurrency.
Identify the next chapter’s retrieval pipeline topic.

title: Quantisation and Efficient Inference
text:
Summary
Quantisation represents selected model tensors with lower-precision codes and associated scaling information. It can reduce weight storage and memory traffic, but its accuracy and latency effects depend on tensor scope, scaling method, activation and cache formats, runtime kernels, workload, and hardware. Conversion must be evaluated as a changed inference system.
Chapter 33 examines a different route to improving responses: retrieving external evidence and constructing the model context from it.

title: Quantisation and Efficient Inference
text:
Looking ahead
Quantisation changes the representation and execution of a fixed model. Chapter 33 examines a different route to extending a system: constructing model context from an external, versioned collection.

title: Quantisation and Efficient Inference
text:
Further reading
QLoRA combines low-rank adaptation with a quantised base model (Dettmers et al. 2023). GPTQ provides one post-training quantisation approach for generative models (Frantar et al. 2023).






Dettmers, Tim, Artidoro Pagnoni, Ari Holtzman, and Luke Zettlemoyer. 2023. “QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36: 10088–115. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314.


Frantar, Elias, Saleh Ashkboos, Torsten Hoefler, and Dan Alistarh. 2023. “GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-Trained Transformers.” International Conference on Learning Representations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323.

title: Retrieval-augmented Generation
text: Chapter orientation

title: Retrieval-augmented Generation
text:
Why this chapter matters
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies a language model with selected external material at inference time. It can make current, private, or domain-specific information available without placing all of it in model weights. It also introduces a pipeline: documents are collected and versioned, split into chunks, indexed, retrieved for a query, placed in a prompt, and used by a generator.
An answer can fail at any stage. Relevant evidence may be absent from the corpus, split across chunks, missed by retrieval, removed by reranking or truncation, ignored by the model, or cited inaccurately. Evaluating only final answer quality cannot diagnose these causes. This chapter treats RAG as a system with explicit information boundaries.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish a corpus, document, chunk, embedding, index, retriever, reranker, and generator;
explain dense and lexical retrieval at a conceptual level;
calculate simple retrieval recall for a labelled query set;
identify chunking, metadata, and context-budget choices as system decisions;
distinguish retrieval relevance, evidence use, citation accuracy, and final-answer correctness;
design a failure trace for a RAG answer; and
specify a versioned RAG evaluation record.



Running collection
The running collection has three short chunks. A query is embedded or represented for retrieval; selected chunks are placed into a context template before answer generation.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(11,3.3)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.2,"versioned\ndocuments",blue),(2.15,"chunks +\nmetadata",teal),(4.1,"index",purple),(6.0,"retrieve +\nrerank",orange),(7.95,"bounded\ncontext",teal),(9.9,"answer",blue)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.25),1.35,.62,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.675,1.56,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for x in [1.58,3.53,5.43,7.33,9.28]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,1.56),(x+.52,1.56),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.text(5.5,.55,"The generator sees constructed context, not the complete indexed collection.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,11.4); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 34.1

title: Retrieval-augmented Generation
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Retrieval changes which evidence is available at inference
A base model answers from its parameters and the prompt. RAG adds a selected subset of an external collection to the prompt. This can support answers about documents added after pretraining, organisation-specific records, or source-backed claims. It does not guarantee that the retrieved text is relevant, current, authoritative, or used faithfully in the output.
The indexed collection is therefore part of the system’s knowledge boundary. A document outside it cannot be retrieved. A document inside it may still be unavailable because access control, filters, metadata, chunking, or index version exclude it. An answer should not imply that a collection was searched unless the trace shows the retrieval operation and corpus scope.


Code
chunks=[
    {"id":"A", "text":"The programme began in 2022.","source":"report-v1"},
    {"id":"B", "text":"Eligibility requires residence in the district.","source":"rules-v2"},
    {"id":"C", "text":"Applications close on 30 June.","source":"rules-v2"},
]
for chunk in chunks: print(chunk["id"],chunk["text"])




A chunk is a retrieval unit, not necessarily a meaningful document
Indexes usually retrieve chunks rather than whole documents so that prompts fit a finite context window and search can identify a local passage. Chunk boundaries can split a table from its heading, separate a definition from an exception, or duplicate text across overlapping windows. Chunking policy therefore affects retrieval recall and what the generator can infer from the supplied evidence.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3)); ax.axis("off")
ax.plot([.4,8.6],[1.6,1.6],color=grey,lw=3)
for x,w,label,c in [(.6,2.8,"chunk 1",blue),(2.7,2.8,"chunk 2",teal),(4.8,2.8,"chunk 3",orange)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.25),w,.7,facecolor=c,alpha=.88,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+w/2,1.6,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.text(4.5,.55,"Overlap can preserve context across boundaries while increasing index size and repeated retrieval.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 34.2

title: Retrieval-augmented Generation
text:
Level 2 - Retrieval mechanics

Lexical and dense retrieval use different matching signals
Lexical retrieval scores overlap among query and document terms, often using weighted term statistics. It can be strong for exact names, identifiers, and rare terms. Dense retrieval maps queries and chunks to vectors and retrieves near neighbours under a similarity measure; it can retrieve semantically related wording even without exact overlap (Karpukhin et al. 2020). Hybrid systems combine these signals, then may apply a reranker to a smaller candidate set.


Code
query=np.array([.8,.2])
chunk_vectors=np.array([[.9,.1],[.3,.7],[.7,.25]])
scores=chunk_vectors@query/(np.linalg.norm(chunk_vectors,axis=1)*np.linalg.norm(query))
print("dense similarity scores:",np.round(scores,3))
print("ranked chunks:",np.argsort(scores)[::-1])


Similarity is a retrieval score, not evidence that a chunk answers the query. A high-scoring passage can share topic words while missing the required fact. A reranker can improve ordering, but it adds another model, version, and failure point. Each score should be stored with the query and retrieved IDs to make the pipeline inspectable.




Code
names=["A","B","C"]; scores=np.array([.91,.76,.68]); relevant=np.array([False,True,False])
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,3.8)); ax.bar(names,scores,color=[grey,teal,grey]); ax.set_ylim(0,1); ax.set_ylabel("retrieval score"); ax.set_title("Ranking and evidence relevance are distinct"); ax.text(1,.82,"labelled evidence",ha="center",color=teal); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 34.3





Context construction is a budget allocation
Retrieved chunks compete with system instructions, the user query, conversation history, formatting, and output reserve for the context window. A top-k setting is not enough to describe what the model sees: chunks may be truncated, deduplicated, reordered, filtered by permissions, or omitted when their combined length exceeds the budget. The final rendered prompt and token IDs should be available for an evaluated request.


Code
budget=1000; system=80; query_tokens=40; output_reserve=200
chunk_lengths=np.array([320,280,260,240])
available=budget-system-query_tokens-output_reserve
selected=[]; used=0
for length in chunk_lengths:
    if used+length<=available: selected.append(length); used+=length
print("chunk budget:",available,"selected lengths:",selected,"unused:",available-used)

title: Retrieval-augmented Generation
text:
Level 3 - Grounded generation

Retrieval relevance is not answer grounding
A response can be correct even when retrieval missed the evidence, because the base model already knew the fact. It can also be wrong after retrieving a relevant passage because the generator ignores, misreads, or combines it with unsupported content. A grounded-answer evaluation therefore separates at least four questions: was relevant evidence in the corpus; did retrieval return it; did the final prompt retain it; and is the claim supported by that retained evidence?


Code
trace={"evidence_in_corpus":True,"retrieved":True,"retained_in_prompt":True,"claim_supported":False}
print(trace)


This separation prevents a final-answer score from being attributed automatically to one component. Retrieval recall can be low while generation remains plausible on familiar questions. High retrieval recall can coexist with poor answer faithfulness. The pipeline should report stage-specific metrics and a joined trace for the same labelled queries.


Citations need a defined link to evidence
Adding source labels to a prompt does not ensure that an answer’s citation supports its claim. A citation system needs a policy for attaching claim spans to retrieved chunks, resolving document versions and locations, and handling claims without sufficient support. It should distinguish a citation to a retrieved source from a verified entailment relation. The latter requires additional annotation, checking, or constrained generation.


Code
answer_claim="Applications close on 30 June."
supporting_chunk="C"
print({"claim":answer_claim,"citation":supporting_chunk,"source":"rules-v2"})




Query rewriting and reranking alter the evidence path
Some systems rewrite a user query before retrieval, expand it into several searches, or decompose a question into subquestions. These steps can improve retrieval when the original query is short or ambiguous, but they create another model-mediated transformation between the user request and the evidence. The audit should retain the original query, every rewritten query, retrieved candidates, reranker scores, and the policy that selected the final context.
Reranking can promote passages that better match a query after a more expensive comparison. It can also remove a passage needed for a multi-document answer if the score is applied independently to each chunk. A pipeline should evaluate the final retained set, not only the first-stage retrieval list. The relevant evidence may require two chunks that each look incomplete alone.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3.3)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.25,"user\nquery",blue),(2.0,"rewritten\nquery",teal),(3.85,"four retrieved\ncandidates",orange),(5.95,"reranked\nlist",purple),(7.8,"two retained\nchunks",teal)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.25),1.4,.62,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.7,1.56,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for x in [1.67,3.52,5.62,7.47]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,1.56),(x+.28,1.56),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.text(5,.55,"Record transformations and candidate IDs, not only the final answer.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,9.5); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 34.4





Corpus quality and permission are upstream conditions
Retrieval cannot correct a source that is out of date, internally inconsistent, wrongly parsed, or unavailable to the relevant user. Metadata should include provenance, update time, document type, ownership, access policy, and where possible an authoritative status. A retrieval score has no authority dimension unless the index and ranking policy encode and evaluate one.
Permissions should be applied before generation context is constructed. Filtering a citation after an unrestricted chunk has entered the prompt does not remove its influence on the generated answer. Access-control tests should include direct queries, paraphrases, metadata-only probes, and queries that combine permitted with restricted documents. The result should state the identity and policy condition used in the test.


Code
candidate_ids=["A","B","C"]
permitted={"A":True,"B":False,"C":True}
retained=[chunk_id for chunk_id in candidate_ids if permitted[chunk_id]]
print("permitted context chunks:",retained)




Retrieval metrics require relevance judgements
Recall@k depends on a judgement of which chunks are relevant for each query. Those judgements can be incomplete when several documents support an answer or when a passage is relevant only with another passage. Evaluation design should say whether relevance means answer-containing, sufficient evidence, useful context, or an authoritative source. The label definition determines what a retrieval score means.
For multi-hop questions, report whether every required evidence item was retrieved, not only whether one related chunk appeared. For time-sensitive questions, check the source version and update date. For private corpora, use held-out documents and queries that were not used to tune chunking, retriever, or prompt templates. These boundaries limit accidental optimisation to an evaluation set.


Abstention is part of a grounded-answer policy
When retrieval finds no sufficient evidence, a system can abstain, ask for clarification, state that the corpus does not establish an answer, or generate an unsupported response. The desired behaviour depends on the application, but it must be defined and evaluated. A retrieval score alone cannot decide whether evidence is sufficient for a claim.
An abstention evaluation should include queries whose answer is absent, outdated, contradictory, or inaccessible under the requester’s permissions. It should measure both unwarranted answers and unnecessary abstentions. This turns “do not hallucinate” into a measurable decision policy over known evidence conditions.


Code
cases=[{"evidence":"sufficient","action":"answer"},{"evidence":"absent","action":"abstain"},{"evidence":"restricted","action":"refuse access"}]
for case in cases: print(case)

title: Retrieval-augmented Generation
text:
Level 4 - Evaluation and operations

Evaluate the pipeline at its component boundaries
For a labelled query set, retrieval recall at (k) asks whether at least one relevant chunk appears among the top (k). It does not measure whether the selected text was sufficient, whether it fitted in the context, or whether the answer used it correctly. Generation evaluation should add answer correctness, support or faithfulness, citation precision, abstention when evidence is missing, latency, and access-control compliance.


Code
relevant={"q1":{"B"},"q2":{"C"},"q3":{"A"}}
retrieved={"q1":["A","B"],"q2":["B","C"],"q3":["C","B"]}
hits=[bool(relevant[q].intersection(retrieved[q])) for q in relevant]
print("recall@2:",sum(hits)/len(hits))






Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3.5)); ax.axis("off")
stages=[("corpus\ncoverage",blue),("retrieval\nrecall",teal),("context\nretention",orange),("claim\nsupport",purple),("latency and\naccess control",blue)]
for i,(label,c) in enumerate(stages):
    x=.25+i*1.95; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.35),1.45,.62,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.725,1.66,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
ax.text(4.9,.55,"Each stage needs a metric and trace; final answer accuracy alone cannot locate failures.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,10); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 34.5





Index updates and access policies are model inputs
An operational RAG system must version source documents, chunks, embeddings, index build, retriever, reranker, prompt template, generator checkpoint, and access policy. Index updates can change answers without a model-weight update. Permissions should be enforced before a chunk enters the constructed prompt, and evaluation must test that restricted material cannot be retrieved or inferred from metadata.


Code
record={"corpus_version":"2026-08-20","chunker":"v4","index":"v12","retriever":"dense-v3","template":"v5","access_policy":"role-filter"}
assert {"corpus_version","index","retriever","access_policy"} <= set(record)
print("RAG run record complete")

title: Retrieval-augmented Generation
text:
Common misconceptions

RAG gives the model access to every indexed document. It supplies only the chunks retained in one constructed context.
A high retrieval score proves answer support. Ranking and claim-level evidence are different objects.
Chunking is only a performance detail. It determines what can be retrieved and read together.
A citation proves grounding. It must be linked to a specific supporting claim and source version.
Updating an index changes no model behaviour. It changes the evidence that can enter inference prompts.
Final answer accuracy diagnoses retrieval. The failure may occur in corpus, retrieval, prompt construction, or generation.

title: Retrieval-augmented Generation
text:
Exercises

Distinguish documents, chunks, embeddings, and index entries.
Explain one consequence of chunk overlap.
Calculate cosine similarity for a supplied query and chunks.
Calculate recall@k for a labelled retrieval set.
Compare lexical and dense retrieval for an identifier-heavy query.
Design a context budget including system text and output reserve.
Identify a case where relevant evidence is retrieved but unused.
Specify a claim-to-citation linking policy.
List RAG components that require version identifiers.
Design an access-control retrieval test.
Explain why index updates require regression evaluation.
Separate corpus coverage from retrieval recall.
Design a failure trace for an unsupported answer.
State why a source label is not an entailment test.
Propose a latency measurement across retrieval and generation.
Identify the chapter that evaluates LLM reliability more broadly.

title: Retrieval-augmented Generation
text:
Summary
RAG constructs a bounded model context from retrieved external chunks. Corpus scope, chunking, indexing, retrieval, reranking, context construction, generation, citations, and access controls form one system. Evaluation must separate evidence coverage, retrieval, prompt retention, claim support, and operational behaviour.
Chapter 34 brings these distinctions together in a broader treatment of capability measurement, reliability, contamination, and the limits of benchmark scores.

title: Retrieval-augmented Generation
text:
Looking ahead
Retrieval-augmented generation combines a model with a corpus, retriever, and context-construction policy. Chapter 34 examines how to evaluate that complete system, alongside the model-only and adaptation systems introduced in this part.

text: Chapter orientation

title: Evaluating LLMs
text:
Why this chapter matters
An LLM evaluation produces evidence about a defined model or system under a defined input distribution, interface, scoring rule, and time. It does not produce a general scalar measure of intelligence, truthfulness, or fitness for every deployment. The same model can score differently after a template change, a decoding change, an index update, a tool change, or a contaminated test item.
This chapter closes Part IV by treating evaluation as a design and measurement problem. It connects the earlier distinctions among token loss, instruction tuning, preference optimisation, inference, and RAG. Part V then turns to reasoning models and the additional question of how to evaluate multi-step computation.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish a capability benchmark, a reliability test, a safety evaluation, and a system evaluation;
define the population, unit, interface, and scoring rule for an LLM evaluation;
calculate an accuracy estimate and a simple confidence interval;
explain contamination, prompt sensitivity, and benchmark overfitting;
separate model, retrieval, tool, and decoding failures in a system trace;
identify when aggregate scores conceal subgroup or task differences; and
specify an evaluation report that can be audited and reproduced.



Running evaluation
The running test has labelled inputs, a fixed template, a checkpoint, a decoding policy, and an exact-match criterion. Changing any of these can change the reported score.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3.4)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.25,"checkpoint +\ninterface",blue),(2.25,"test items\n+ labels",teal),(4.25,"decoding +\ntools",orange),(6.25,"scoring\nrule",purple),(8.2,"metric +\nuncertainty",blue)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.3),1.4,.62,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.7,1.61,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for x in [1.68,3.68,5.68,7.68]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,1.61),(x+.5,1.61),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.text(5,.55,"A score is conditional on the complete evaluation contract.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,9.8); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 35.1

title: Evaluating LLMs
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Scores answer bounded questions
Exact accuracy on multiple-choice questions measures success on those items under the supplied prompt and answer extraction rule. A factuality evaluation measures a different property. A safety red-team, long-context retrieval test, code execution task, and human preference study each answer other questions. A broad evaluation programme may combine them, but their scores should not be collapsed into one claim without explaining the aggregation and the uses it represents.
Benchmark choice defines which errors are visible. A test with short English questions can miss multilingual performance, tool failures, source use, refusal behaviour, latency, and long-document reliability. A test with a fixed answer key can be appropriate for a narrow capability while being unsuitable for an open-ended assistant response.


Code
items=[True,True,False,True,False,True,True,False,True,True]
accuracy=np.mean(items)
print("accuracy:",accuracy,"n:",len(items))




Reliability requires repeated and varied evidence
One successful answer does not estimate how often a system will succeed. Reliability concerns the distribution of outcomes across relevant inputs, including rare but consequential failures. For stochastic generation, the same input can yield different outputs. For tools and retrieval, external state can change. Evaluation should therefore record repetitions, seeds or sampling settings, versions, and the time at which an external collection was queried.




Code
names=["overall","extraction","multilingual","long-context"]
scores=[.72,.86,.61,.49]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); ax.bar(names,scores,color=[grey,teal,orange,purple]); ax.set_ylim(0,1); ax.set_ylabel("score"); ax.set_title("Aggregate performance can hide task differences"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 35.2

title: Evaluating LLMs
text:
Level 2 - Measurement mechanics

The unit and denominator determine a metric
An accuracy denominator can be questions, examples, claims, generated tokens, tool calls, or complete episodes. These choices are not interchangeable. A system that answers one question with five claims may be correct on some claims and not others. A RAG system may retrieve a relevant document but fail the final answer. The report should state the unit, inclusion rule, missing-data rule, and whether an item can receive partial credit.
For binary accuracy over (n) independent labelled units, a simple standard-error approximation is (). It is not sufficient for clustered, repeated, or adaptively sampled data, but it shows why a score from a small test set has substantial uncertainty.


Code
p=.72; n=100
se=np.sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
print("approximate 95% interval:",(round(p-1.96*se,3),round(p+1.96*se,3)))






Code
sizes=np.array([25,100,400]); estimates=np.repeat(.72,3); errors=1.96*np.sqrt(estimates*(1-estimates)/sizes)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5,4)); ax.errorbar(["25","100","400"],estimates,yerr=errors,fmt="o",color=teal,capsize=5); ax.set_ylim(.35,1); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy"); ax.set_xlabel("number of labelled items"); ax.set_title("Illustrative sampling uncertainty"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 35.3





Prompt and scorer choices are part of the treatment
Few-shot examples, system messages, answer options, retrieval context, tool permissions, temperature, and output parsing can all change a score. The evaluation should freeze or systematically vary these choices rather than treating them as invisible plumbing. Automatic scorers should be validated on a labelled subset, particularly when judging open-ended answers, code, citations, or safety properties.


Code
predictions=["A","B","C","A"]
labels=["A","B","B","A"]
exact=[p==y for p,y in zip(predictions,labels)]
print("exact-match score:",np.mean(exact),"errors:",[i for i,x in enumerate(exact) if not x])

title: Evaluating LLMs
text:
Level 3 - Contamination and system boundaries

Contamination changes the interpretation of benchmark performance
If test items, answers, or close variants entered pretraining, fine-tuning, preference data, or prompt examples, benchmark performance can reflect prior exposure as well as generalisation. Exact-string searches are useful but insufficient because paraphrases, translated items, templates, and solutions can differ visibly while preserving the test content. A contamination policy should state search methods, source coverage, match thresholds, exclusions, and what score is reported when exposure is suspected.


Code
test_item="What is the eligibility rule?"
training_texts=["Eligibility requires residence in the district.","What is the eligibility rule?","Other text"]
matches=[text for text in training_texts if test_item.lower() in text.lower()]
print("exact matches:",matches)


Contamination does not always make an evaluation useless, but it narrows the claim. A score may still measure retrieval from memorised material or performance under known exposure. It should not be presented as evidence of behaviour on unseen instances without a defensible boundary.


Evaluate complete systems at component boundaries
An LLM application can include a model, prompt template, decoder, retriever, index, tools, output validator, and user interface. A final failure may originate in any of these. The evaluation trace should retain input tokens, retrieved IDs, tool calls and outputs, generated IDs, validator decisions, and the final displayed answer. This supports component-level measurements and repair.


Code
trace={"retrieval":"relevant chunk missed","tool":"not called","generation":"unsupported answer","validator":"passed"}
print(trace)






Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3.3)); ax.axis("off")
for i,(label,c) in enumerate([("input",blue),("retrieve / tools",teal),("context",orange),("generate",purple),("validate",teal),("display",blue)]):
    x=.15+i*1.62; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.35),1.2,.55,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.6,1.625,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
ax.text(4.9,.55,"Record stage outputs to locate failures rather than treating every error as a model error.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,10); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 35.4

title: Evaluating LLMs
text:
Level 4 - Evaluation design and reporting

Build an evaluation around a decision
The intended decision should determine the test: whether to deploy a model version, select an adaptation, allow a tool action, use a retrieval corpus, or claim performance for a population. Define the target inputs, harm or cost of errors, baseline, required confidence, and stopping rule before inspecting the result. This prevents a convenient benchmark from becoming a proxy for a different deployment decision.


Code
evaluation_plan={"decision":"deploy retrieval update","population":"current policy queries","baseline":"index-v11","primary":"supported-answer rate","guardrail":"no access-control failures"}
print(evaluation_plan)




Report disaggregated evidence and limits
An audit report should state model, tokenizer, prompt, decoding, tools and index versions; test construction and dates; item counts and strata; scoring and adjudication; uncertainty; contamination checks; excluded cases; failures; cost and latency; and known limits. Where human judgements are used, report judge instructions, information access, agreement, and aggregation. Where benchmarks are public, report whether they may have influenced development.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.5)); ax.axis("off")
fields=["claim","population","interface","metric","uncertainty","contamination","failures"]
for i,field in enumerate(fields):
    x=.25+(i%4)*2.15; y=2.45-(i//4)*.85; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,y),1.8,.48,facecolor=[blue,teal,orange,purple][i%4],edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.9,y+.24,field,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.text(4.5,.45,"The report should make the scope of every performance claim inspectable.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(.15,3.2); plt.show()



Figure 35.5





Reliability includes calibration and failure concentration
An evaluation can ask whether a model’s expressed confidence or probability is related to correctness. Calibration is not solved by a single overall accuracy: a system may be reliable on routine examples and confidently wrong on one task slice. When a system does not expose calibrated probabilities, a proxy such as self-reported confidence, verifier score, or retrieval support should be treated as a separate predictor and evaluated against outcomes.
Failure concentration also matters. Ten errors distributed across low-stakes formatting tasks have different implications from ten errors concentrated in access-control, medical, or financial cases. An evaluation report should preserve error categories and severity rules, rather than allowing a broad average to conceal the decision consequences of a rare failure.


Code
outcomes=[{"slice":"routine","correct":1,"confidence":.8},{"slice":"high-stakes","correct":0,"confidence":.95},{"slice":"routine","correct":1,"confidence":.7}]
for row in outcomes: print(row)




Benchmark development is itself an intervention
Once a benchmark is public and used repeatedly for model selection, prompt design, data filtering, or reward design, its score can become a target. This can improve performance on the benchmark while narrowing the evidence it provides about unseen work. Held-out sets, refreshed item pools, task variants, and preregistered evaluation protocols can reduce this risk, but none removes the need to describe the development history.


Code
development={"public_benchmark_used_for_tuning":True,"hidden_holdout":True,"prompt_fixed_before_holdout":True}
print(development)

title: Evaluating LLMs
text:
Common misconceptions

A high benchmark score establishes general intelligence. It measures performance under a specific evaluation contract.
A single accuracy is enough for deployment. Slice performance, uncertainty, reliability, cost, and failure consequences may differ.
Public benchmarks are necessarily uncontaminated. Development and training exposure require explicit assessment.
A final wrong answer is always a model failure. Retrieval, tools, prompts, validators, and interfaces can fail first.
Automatic judging removes evaluation subjectivity. It introduces a scorer model and its own validation requirements.
More benchmarks automatically improve evidence. They can duplicate a narrow distribution or encourage benchmark-specific optimisation.

text:

title: Evaluating LLMs
text:
Summary
LLM evaluation measures defined systems on defined tasks under defined interfaces. Capability scores, reliability studies, safety tests, retrieval evaluation, and service benchmarks provide different evidence. Strong reports retain the population, denominator, uncertainty, contamination policy, component trace, and known limits rather than reducing the system to one aggregate number.

title: What Makes a Reasoning Model?
text: Chapter orientation
crumbs: 36  What Makes a Reasoning Model?

title: What Makes a Reasoning Model?
text:
Why this chapter matters
Language models can produce answers in one continuation, generate several candidate solutions, write intermediate steps, call a verifier, revise a proposal, or allocate more inference-time computation to difficult inputs. These behaviours are often grouped under “reasoning”, but they are not equivalent. A longer visible answer can be stylistic. A correct answer can result from retrieval or pattern completion. A system can perform substantial computation without exposing a faithful natural-language trace.
This chapter uses an operational definition. A reasoning system uses multi-step computation, decomposition, search, verification, or extended inference in a way that can be evaluated against a task. The definition does not assume that a model has human-like reasoning or that its displayed steps reveal its causal internal process. Chapter 36 develops the evaluation problem; Chapters 37–40 develop inference-time scaling and training methods.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish a base model, an instruction-tuned model, and a reasoning-tuned system;
distinguish visible rationale text, latent internal computation, and answer correctness;
identify generation, search, verification, decomposition, and tool use as separate mechanisms;
explain why longer outputs alone do not establish reasoning;
describe an inference-time computation budget and its cost; and
design a minimal trace that records candidates, checks, and answer selection.



Running problem
The running problem asks for an answer with a checkable result. The system can produce one response, sample several candidates, verify them, and select an answer. Each added step consumes tokens, model calls, or tool computation.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3.4)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.3,"problem",blue),(2.05,"candidate\ngeneration",teal),(4.2,"verifier or\nselection",orange),(6.4,"selected\nanswer",purple)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.3),1.45,.62,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.725,1.61,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for x in [1.78,3.78,5.98]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,1.61),(x+.25,1.61),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.text(4.8,.55,"Tokens, samples, verifier calls, and latency are part of the reasoning-system budget.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,8.4); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 36.1
crumbs: 36  What Makes a Reasoning Model?

title: What Makes a Reasoning Model?
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Reasoning is a system property under a task definition
A base model predicts a continuation from its prompt. Instruction tuning changes the response convention. A reasoning-tuned system may additionally be trained to produce intermediate work, reward verifiable outcomes, sample alternative solutions, or use more time before selecting an answer. The label should describe an observed mechanism and task result, not a marketing category.
For an arithmetic expression, a model can answer immediately, write a calculation, generate several calculations and vote, or use a calculator tool. These may have different accuracy, token cost, and failure patterns. A system that calls a calculator can be reliable on arithmetic without demonstrating a general internal ability to reason about every task. A system that writes a long explanation can be incorrect despite a fluent trace.


Code
strategies={"direct":"one answer","rationale":"answer with steps","sample-and-select":"several candidates plus selection","tool-assisted":"external calculation"}
for name,description in strategies.items(): print(name+":",description)


The operational claim needs a comparison condition. For the same prompt set, hold the base checkpoint, prompt template, tools, and answer format fixed, then vary the proposed reasoning mechanism. If a system samples eight candidates, the relevant baseline is not an unrelated model with a shorter answer. It is the same system with one candidate, or with the selector removed, measured under the same task distribution. This comparison can show whether the additional computation improves the outcome and whether the gain survives the cost it introduces.
The task definition must also specify what counts as a correct answer. Arithmetic often has an exact target. A coding task may require tests, resource limits, and a declared execution environment. A factual answer can require source attribution and a date boundary. Open-ended advice has no general exact verifier. Calling all of these settings “reasoning” hides the fact that the available checks, the likely errors, and the appropriate resource budget differ.


Visible reasoning is not automatically faithful reasoning
Chain-of-thought prompting asks a model to generate intermediate natural-language tokens before an answer. It can improve performance on some tasks (Wei et al. 2022). The emitted text is still model output. It may be incomplete, post-hoc, strategically shaped by training, or unrelated to the internal features that caused the final answer. It should not be treated as a transparent record of all computation without a separate faithfulness test.
The distinction matters in evaluation and deployment. A displayed rationale can help a person inspect arithmetic or source use. It can also create unwarranted confidence when the conclusion is unsupported. Some systems may use hidden or compressed intermediate computation and expose only an answer or summary. The appropriate evidence is task correctness, testable intermediate claims where relevant, and a documented system trace.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.axis("off")
for x,y,label,c in [(2.6,2.3,"visible\ntrace",blue),(4.3,2.3,"internal\ncomputation",teal),(3.45,1.25,"correct\nanswer",orange)]:
    circle=plt.Circle((x,y),1.15,color=c,alpha=.35); ax.add_patch(circle); ax.text(x,y,label,ha="center",va="center",weight="bold")
ax.set_xlim(1,6); ax.set_ylim(.1,3.8); plt.show()



Figure 36.2
crumbs: 36  What Makes a Reasoning Model?

title: What Makes a Reasoning Model?
text:
Level 2 - Mechanisms

Candidate generation and selection form a basic search loop
Sampling several completions creates a candidate set. A selection rule can choose the highest model score, a majority answer, a verifier-approved candidate, or an externally checked result. The improvement, if any, comes from the combination of candidate diversity and a selection signal that distinguishes better from worse candidates. More samples without a useful selector can simply add cost and inconsistent answers.


Code
candidates=[{"answer":12,"valid":True},{"answer":13,"valid":False},{"answer":12,"valid":True}]
valid=[c["answer"] for c in candidates if c["valid"]]
print("selected answer:",max(set(valid),key=valid.count))


Decomposition divides a task into subproblems. Verification checks an answer, a step, or a constraint. Search chooses which partial solution to extend. Tool use delegates a defined operation to an external system. These mechanisms can be combined, but they should be named separately because they make different assumptions. A verifier that checks arithmetic cannot verify a legal interpretation; a decomposition can propagate an early mistaken subgoal.


A verifier has a domain, an error rate, and a decision role
An exact verifier can compare a submitted expression with a known answer or run a program against a defined test suite. A learned verifier assigns a score from examples and can make the same systematic mistakes as the generator. A process verifier scores intermediate steps, while an outcome verifier scores a final result. These are different measurement instruments. Work on training verifiers for mathematical problems illustrates why candidate quality and verifier quality must be reported separately: a selector can only improve the candidate set when it can distinguish the better candidates in that set (Cobbe et al. 2021).
The decision rule matters as much as the score. A system may reject every candidate below a threshold, choose the highest-scoring candidate, request another sample, or defer to a person. A threshold selected on an easy development set can accept errors on a changed task distribution. A verifier that marks a valid answer as invalid produces a false rejection; one that approves an invalid answer produces a false acceptance. These errors have different consequences in a system that answers automatically and a system that uses verification only to route uncertain cases for review.
The record should therefore identify the object checked, the verifier type, the threshold or selection rule, and the cases on which verification is unavailable. A claim that a model “checks its work” is not informative until those choices are visible.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.8)); ax.axis("off")
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((3.7,1.55),1.5,.58,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(4.45,1.84,"problem",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
for x,y,label,c in [(.3,2.8,"decompose",teal),(2.2,.45,"generate",orange),(5.6,.45,"search",purple),(7.3,2.8,"verify",teal),(7.3,1.3,"tools",orange)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,y),1.25,.5,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.625,y+.25,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(.1,3.6); plt.show()



Figure 36.3





A budget makes the trade-off observable
Inference-time compute can be counted as generated tokens, model forward passes, samples, verifier calls, tool calls, wall-clock time, energy, or monetary cost. These measures are related but not identical. A system may generate fewer tokens but make more expensive verifier calls, or use a long hidden trace with no user-visible explanation. An evaluation should report the resource definition alongside accuracy.


Code
budget={"samples":8,"tokens_per_sample":250,"verifier_calls":8,"latency_seconds":4.2}
print("generated tokens:",budget["samples"]*budget["tokens_per_sample"])
print(budget)


Budget reporting should be per request and across a workload. The mean number of sampled tokens can conceal a small set of difficult inputs that trigger repeated generation or expensive tools. A deployment record can report median and tail latency, the fraction of requests that use search or tools, failed verifier calls, and the policy for exhausting a budget. These fields allow a reader to distinguish a system that uses extra computation routinely from one that reserves it for a defined slice of requests.
crumbs: 36  What Makes a Reasoning Model?

title: What Makes a Reasoning Model?
text:
Level 3 - Training and inference boundaries

Reasoning tuning changes a policy under selected signals
Reasoning-oriented training may use demonstrations with intermediate steps, outcomes checked by a verifier, preference comparisons among solutions, or reinforcement learning over multi-step trajectories. The system learns from the data and reward signals available; it does not receive a general proof procedure. A reward based only on final answer can favour lucky or opaque trajectories. A process reward can favour steps that look plausible to its judge without guaranteeing they caused the result.


Code
trajectories=[{"steps":4,"answer_correct":1,"process_score":.7},{"steps":8,"answer_correct":0,"process_score":.9}]
for t in trajectories: print(t)


The training objective, rollout policy, stopping rule, verifier, and selection procedure form the reasoning system. They must be separated from the base checkpoint identity. Two systems built on the same model can differ materially if one samples one answer and the other samples twenty candidates with a testable verifier.


Latent computation has an observability limit
Internal activations and any hidden intermediate tokens can influence an answer without being available to the user. This can protect proprietary methods or avoid exposing unsafe detailed work, but it limits direct inspection. A system should not substitute an invented visible rationale for an unavailable trace. It can instead report answer confidence limits, tool outputs, verified constraints, and the inference budget used.


Code
audit={"model":"versioned","samples":4,"selector":"exact verifier","visible_rationale":False,"verified_constraint":"answer parses"}
print(audit)




Training and inference mechanisms should not be conflated
Some systems are trained on step-by-step demonstrations or verified outcomes and then answer in one pass. Others use an ordinary base or instruction model but add sampling, tools, or selection only at inference. A third class combines training changes with a multi-step inference loop. These routes can produce similar visible answers while making different resource, data, and evaluation claims.
The distinction is useful because a claimed gain may come from additional test-time sampling rather than a changed base policy, or from a verifier rather than a better generator. Controlled comparisons should hold one component fixed at a time: compare one-pass and multi-sample inference for the same checkpoint; compare a learned selector and an exact verifier over the same candidate set; compare tuned and untuned checkpoints under the same budget.
This separation also limits what a visible rationale can establish. A policy trained on worked solutions may produce orderly steps in one pass, while a search procedure may return a concise answer after evaluating many hidden candidates. The first system exposes more text; the second may use more inference-time computation. Neither observation identifies the cause of correctness without an intervention or a controlled comparison. Process-supervision research makes the distinction operational by scoring intermediate steps, but those scores still require validation against the task and the intended use (Lightman et al. 2023).




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.7)); ax.axis("off")
paths=[("training change\n→ one-pass answer",orange,2.7),("base model\n→ search + verifier",teal,1.8),("training change\n→ search + verifier",purple,.9)]
for label,c,y in paths:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.45,y),2.0,.5,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(1.45,y+.25,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8); ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((2.5,y+.25),(4.25,y+.25),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11)); ax.add_patch(Rectangle((4.35,y),1.4,.5,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(5.05,y+.25,"answer",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.text(3.2,.25,"Hold routes fixed or compare them explicitly.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,6.2); ax.set_ylim(.1,3.5); plt.show()



Figure 36.4

title: What Makes a Reasoning Model?
text:
Level 4 - Audit and scope

Evaluate the mechanism claimed
A system claiming search should show how candidates are expanded and selected. A system claiming verification should test verifier accuracy and failure modes. A system claiming improved reasoning from longer inference should compare accuracy against the same task under controlled compute budgets. A system claiming faithful traces needs evidence that changes in the trace correspond to changes in the computation or answer under an explicit intervention design.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.5)); ax.axis("off")
rows=[("search","candidate coverage and selection"),("verification","verifier errors and calibration"),("extra inference","accuracy versus cost"),("visible trace","faithfulness intervention")]
for i,(claim,test) in enumerate(rows):
    y=2.8-i*.62; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.45,y),2.1,.4,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(1.5,y+.2,claim,ha="center",va="center",color="white"); ax.add_patch(Rectangle((3.0,y),4.8,.4,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(5.4,y+.2,test,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(0,8.5); ax.set_ylim(.15,3.4); plt.show()



Figure 36.5





Scope claims should remain narrow
Reasoning benchmarks can reward answer formats, familiar problem templates, or verifier-compatible outputs. A gain on one set of mathematical problems does not establish general reasoning across science, law, planning, or open-ended advice. Contamination and benchmark-specific optimisation remain concerns from Chapter 34. The module will therefore report task distributions, inference cost, selected mechanisms, and failure cases rather than treating one score or one trace style as a global capability measure.
An adequate report begins with the base model and task distribution, then states the generator, candidate budget, tools, verifier, selection rule, stopping rule, and answer interface. It reports the outcome measure and resource measures together, followed by examples of false acceptance, false rejection, exhausted budgets, and cases that the system could not verify. That record does not settle whether a system has a general reasoning capability. It does make the narrower claim inspectable and provides the inputs Chapter 36 needs for a valid evaluation.


Code
record={"task":"verifiable arithmetic","base":"checkpoint-v2","samples":8,"verifier":"exact answer","cost":"tokens and latency","evaluation":"held-out problems"}
assert {"task","samples","verifier","evaluation"} <= set(record)
print("reasoning-system record complete")

title: What Makes a Reasoning Model?
text:
Common misconceptions

A long explanation proves the model reasoned correctly. It is visible text that requires separate correctness and faithfulness checks.
Reasoning models are a distinct architecture class. They can share an architecture with base models while changing training or inference procedures.
More inference tokens always improve answers. Additional computation needs useful candidate diversity and selection or verification.
A correct final answer validates every intermediate step. Some trajectories are lucky, incomplete, or inconsistent.
A verifier establishes general reasoning. It validates only the property it is designed and tested to check.
Hidden computation makes evaluation impossible. It limits direct trace inspection but system-level outcomes and resource use remain evaluable.

title: What Makes a Reasoning Model?
text:
Summary
A reasoning model is best defined operationally: it uses additional multi-step computation, search, decomposition, verification, or extended inference that can be evaluated on a task. Visible rationales, internal computation, and answer correctness are distinct objects. The relevant evidence includes task outcomes, mechanism-specific tests, inference cost, and failure traces.
Chapter 36 develops evaluation for answer accuracy, process evidence, verifiers, contamination, robustness, and the cost of additional computation.
