title: Evaluating Reasoning
text: Chapter orientation

title: Evaluating Reasoning
text:
Why this chapter matters
Chapter 35 defined reasoning systems through additional computation, search, decomposition, and verification. An evaluation must now determine whether those mechanisms improve the intended task and at what cost. A correct final answer is useful evidence, but it cannot show whether a visible trace was faithful, whether a verifier was valid, whether the gain survives prompt variation, or whether more inference-time compute is worth its latency and expense.
Reasoning evaluation should therefore retain outcome, process, and systems measures. The relevant criterion depends on the task. Exact arithmetic permits an exact verifier; open-ended planning requires another source of evidence. Chapter 37 will compare accuracy against inference-time computation, using the measurement contract established here.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish outcome, process, verifier, robustness, and systems evaluation;
define an exact verifier and state its scope;
calculate outcome accuracy and verifier precision or recall on a toy set;
explain why a plausible trace is not evidence of faithfulness;
design prompt- and problem-variant robustness tests;
report accuracy together with samples, tokens, calls, latency, and cost; and
build a trace that separates candidate, verifier, selection, and final-answer errors.



Running task
The running task has a checkable answer. The system generates candidate solutions, applies a verifier, and selects one result. This permits separate measurements of candidate coverage, verifier behaviour, and final accuracy.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3.5)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.25,"task",blue),(1.8,"candidates",teal),(3.55,"verifier",orange),(5.3,"selection",purple),(7.05,"outcome\nscore",blue)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.35),1.3,.58,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.65,1.64,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for x in [1.58,3.33,5.08,6.83]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,1.64),(x+.2,1.64),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.text(4.8,.55,"Record tokens, samples, calls, latency, and cost alongside task outcomes.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 37.1

title: Evaluating Reasoning
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

A final answer is necessary but incomplete evidence
For a task with one exact answer, outcome accuracy asks whether the selected result is correct. This is often the primary metric. It does not show whether the system used a valid method, whether a visible rationale was accurate, whether a tool call succeeded, or whether the same result would survive a modest change in wording.
A reasoning system may produce a correct answer through a lucky candidate, a memorised pattern, an external tool, or a verified search process. These mechanisms have different implications for generalisation and cost. Evaluation should not claim more than the measure supports.


Code
outcomes=np.array([1,1,0,1,1,0,1,1])
print("outcome accuracy:",outcomes.mean(),"items:",len(outcomes))




Outcome measures need a denominator and an error record
Accuracy is the proportion of scored items for which the selected answer meets the stated criterion. It is only interpretable with its denominator: the task version, number of items, inclusion and exclusion rules, answer normalisation, and treatment of abstentions, timeouts, and tool failures. A system that abstains on unverified cases can appear more accurate if those cases are removed from the denominator. Report coverage alongside accuracy, and state whether an abstention is counted as incorrect, deferred, or outside the task.
Aggregate accuracy also compresses different errors. A candidate generator may never produce a valid answer; a verifier may reject the valid candidate; a selector may choose an inferior accepted candidate; an answer parser may score a correct response as wrong. Retaining these boundaries identifies which component changed after a revision. It also prevents a later chapter from interpreting an accuracy gain as evidence that the generator improved when the gain came from a more permissive answer parser.


Process text and process evidence are different
A visible chain of steps can be checked for local arithmetic or logical consistency. It may still omit the operation that determined the answer, contain a post-hoc explanation, or lead to a different answer after a small intervention. Process evaluation is useful when steps are observable and a task supplies criteria for them. It should not be treated as a general window into latent computation.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5,3.4)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c,test in [(.3,"correct\nanswer",blue,"outcome scorer"),(3.0,"valid visible\nsteps",teal,"step checks"),(5.7,"faithful\ntrace",orange,"intervention test")]:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.45),1.9,.62,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.95,1.76,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white"); ax.text(x+.95,.9,test,ha="center",color=grey,fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(0,8); ax.set_ylim(.4,2.5); plt.show()



Figure 37.2

title: Evaluating Reasoning
text:
Level 2 - Verifiers and metrics

A verifier has a defined acceptance condition
An exact verifier can check a numeric answer, proof syntax, executable code output, a formal constraint, or a known solution. Its value comes from a clearly specified condition. A verifier can be wrong, incomplete, vulnerable to formatting, or unable to assess the property that matters. A code test suite may accept an implementation that fails an untested case; a symbolic checker may reject a correct answer in an unsupported form.


Code
def exact_verifier(candidate,answer):
    return candidate==answer
print([exact_verifier(x,12) for x in [12,11,12,13]])


Verifier evaluation itself needs labelled cases. Precision asks how often accepted candidates are actually correct; recall asks how often correct candidates are accepted. A selector built on a low-precision verifier can choose attractive errors. A low-recall verifier can discard valid solutions and flatten the gain from candidate generation.


Code
accepted=np.array([1,1,1,0]); actually_correct=np.array([1,0,1,1])
precision=(accepted & actually_correct).sum()/accepted.sum()
recall=(accepted & actually_correct).sum()/actually_correct.sum()
print("verifier precision:",round(precision,2),"recall:",round(recall,2))






Code
matrix=np.array([[18,3],[4,25]])
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5,4)); im=ax.imshow(matrix,cmap="Blues"); ax.set_xticks([0,1],["actually correct","actually incorrect"]); ax.set_yticks([0,1],["accepted","rejected"])
for i in range(2):
    for j in range(2): ax.text(j,i,str(matrix[i,j]),ha="center",va="center",fontsize=14)
ax.set_title("Verifier confusion matrix (illustrative)"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 37.3





Candidate coverage, verifier quality, and selection quality are separate quantities
For a multi-candidate system, candidate coverage asks whether at least one generated candidate is correct. Verifier precision and recall ask whether the verifier classifies individual candidates accurately. Selection accuracy asks whether the final policy chooses a correct candidate from the candidates available. These measures identify different ceilings. Sampling cannot rescue a task when coverage remains low; a highly accurate verifier cannot help if no valid candidate is generated; a selector can still fail when several accepted candidates disagree.
Report the measures on the same items and candidate sets. If a verifier is evaluated only on generated candidates, its score may differ from its score on deliberately constructed hard negatives or different answer formats. The difference is useful: it describes the verifier’s operating distribution. Evaluation work on language models treats performance as conditional on the scenario, metric, and slice being measured, rather than as a single property of a model (Liang et al. 2022).

title: Evaluating Reasoning
text:
Level 3 - Robustness and cost

Robustness tests vary a declared factor
Reasoning claims should be tested under controlled variants: paraphrase the prompt while preserving the answer, alter irrelevant numbers or names, move evidence position, change the order of answer options, or generate new instances from a problem family. The purpose is to identify whether performance depends on surface cues rather than the relation the task is intended to measure.


Code
variants={"original":1,"paraphrase":1,"renamed variables":0,"reordered options":0}
print("variant outcomes:",variants)


Robustness does not mean invariance to every transformation. A wording change can legitimately alter the problem. The evaluation must state which property is preserved and how variants were built. It should also avoid constructing variants after viewing the model’s failures in a way that turns the test into an unreported development set.
The unit of analysis should remain visible. Report the original and each variant as paired outcomes, rather than pooling them immediately into one score. A system that succeeds on the original item and fails whenever variable names change has a different failure pattern from one that fails randomly across variants, even when their pooled accuracy is the same. Paired records also show whether candidate generation, verification, or selection caused the difference.


Contamination is a provenance question
Benchmark exposure can inflate an outcome score without showing that a system solves new instances. The relevant question is not whether an item appears verbatim in a public dataset alone. It is whether the training data, instruction data, demonstrations, retrieval index, prompt template, or evaluation-development process supplied information that makes the test easier. A reasoning benchmark can also become a development target through repeated prompting and manual inspection, even if the model checkpoint was trained earlier.
Record the dataset version, item source, generation procedure, public availability date, benchmark access policy, and any overlap search or decontamination rule. When a task family permits it, use newly generated or held-out instances and keep the generator and answer key separate from the system-development loop. Established broad benchmarks demonstrate the value of specifying task categories and scoring conventions, but their scores remain tied to the particular item collection and answer format (Hendrycks et al. 2021). A contamination check cannot prove absence of all exposure; it can make the remaining uncertainty visible.




Code
variants=["original","paraphrase","renamed\nvariables","reordered\noptions"]
candidate_acc=[.82,.79,.61,.67]; selected_acc=[.88,.83,.64,.70]
x=np.arange(len(variants)); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4,4))
ax.bar(x-.18,candidate_acc,.36,label="candidate coverage",color=teal)
ax.bar(x+.18,selected_acc,.36,label="selected-answer accuracy",color=purple)
ax.set_xticks(x,variants); ax.set_ylim(0,1); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy")
ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Illustrative paired robustness slices")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 37.4





Accuracy must be paired with computation
If a reasoning system samples ten candidates and calls a verifier ten times, its accuracy cannot be compared fairly with a one-pass answer without reporting the additional tokens, calls, latency, and cost. The relationship may be nonlinear: one extra sample can help substantially, while later samples add little. Chapter 37 will estimate such curves; this chapter establishes the shared denominator.
Cost records also need a decision rule. Mean latency can conceal a long tail caused by retries, tool calls, or a search budget reached only for difficult prompts. State whether calls were parallel, whether failed calls count, the hardware or service configuration, and whether cost includes verification. These choices determine what a reported token or latency budget means in deployment.
Comparisons also need uncertainty appropriate to the evaluation unit. When two systems answer the same items, retain their paired outcomes and report how many items changed from wrong to correct and from correct to wrong. A small average difference can be driven by a few cases, especially on a short benchmark or a rare but costly slice. Confidence intervals or resampling summaries can describe sampling uncertainty, but they do not repair an unrepresentative task set or an undeclared change in prompt policy.


Code
records=[{"n":1,"accuracy":.54,"tokens":180,"latency":.4},{"n":4,"accuracy":.68,"tokens":720,"latency":1.7},{"n":8,"accuracy":.72,"tokens":1440,"latency":3.3}]
for row in records: print(row)






Code
tokens=np.array([180,720,1440]); accuracy=np.array([.54,.68,.72])
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.plot(tokens,accuracy,marker="o",color=purple); ax.set_xlabel("generated-token budget"); ax.set_ylabel("task accuracy"); ax.set_ylim(.4,.8); ax.set_title("Illustrative accuracy-cost curve"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 37.5





Open-ended tasks require a scoring protocol, not an implied exact answer
Some reasoning applications produce plans, explanations, or recommendations for which there is no single reference string. Evaluation then needs a rubric that states the required facts, constraints, source use, prohibited content, and treatment of uncertainty. Human assessment can judge properties that an exact verifier cannot, but it introduces assessor training, disagreement, order effects, and cost. Model-based judging adds another model with its own prompt, calibration, and failure modes.
The protocol should specify who scores which outputs, whether assessors are blinded to system identity, how disagreements are resolved, and which cases require expert review. A rubric score should be reported by criterion and, where possible, alongside concrete error categories. This does not make an open-ended task exact. It permits claims about the property that was actually assessed and leaves the unassessed properties outside the conclusion.

title: Evaluating Reasoning
text:
Level 4 - Audit and interpretation

Faithfulness requires an intervention claim
To claim that a visible trace explains an answer, an evaluation needs more than a correlation between plausible steps and correct answers. Interventions can alter, remove, reorder, or replace parts of the trace and test whether the answer changes in the predicted way. These tests are difficult because a model may regenerate a different trace, rely on hidden state, or answer from a shortcut. A negative result should be reported as a limit rather than repaired with a more persuasive explanation.


Code
trace_test={"original_answer":12,"altered_trace_answer":12,"expected_change":True}
print("trace intervention supports claim:",trace_test["altered_trace_answer"]!=trace_test["original_answer"])




A reasoning evaluation record joins components
The audit should retain task generator or dataset version, answer key or verifier, prompt and template, checkpoint, candidate-generation policy, samples, selection rule, tool and verifier versions, visible-trace policy, token and call counts, latency, outcome scoring, robustness variants, contamination checks, and error categories. It should record whether an item was solved directly, through a verifier, or through a tool. This is the minimum needed to interpret an apparent reasoning gain.
Evaluation should also distinguish a planned test from a diagnostic added after observing errors. Diagnostic slices are often useful, especially when a failure points to a specific parser, tool, or prompt condition. They should not be folded silently into a confirmatory headline score. Keep a development record, freeze the evaluation policy for the final comparison, and state which analyses were exploratory. The resulting account is less tidy than one number, but it permits another evaluator to reproduce the decision boundary.


Code
record={"task":"verifiable problems","generator":"v2","samples":8,"verifier":"exact-v1","selector":"first accepted","tokens":1440,"robustness":"paraphrase set"}
assert {"task","samples","verifier","selector","tokens"} <= set(record)
print("reasoning evaluation record complete")

title: Evaluating Reasoning
text:
Common misconceptions

A correct answer proves a correct reasoning process. It does not identify the route that produced the answer.
A verifier is objective by definition. It has coverage, parsing, and implementation limits.
A plausible rationale is a faithful explanation. Faithfulness requires an intervention or another causal test.
More samples can be compared without reporting cost. Candidate count, tokens, calls, and latency change the system.
Prompt robustness means invariant outputs under every rewording. Variants need a declared preserved property.
A reasoning benchmark rules out contamination. Development and training exposure still require checks.

title: Evaluating Reasoning
text:
Summary
Reasoning evaluation needs outcome metrics, verifier diagnostics, robustness tests, faithfulness limits, and inference-time resource records. No single metric establishes all of these properties. A system should be evaluated at its candidate, verifier, selection, and final-answer boundaries under a declared task distribution.
Chapter 37 uses this measurement framework to test when sampling, voting, and verification improve accuracy enough to justify their additional computation.

title: Inference-time Scaling
text: Chapter orientation

title: Inference-time Scaling
text:
Why this chapter matters
Inference-time scaling allocates more computation to a problem after a model has been trained. A system can sample several solutions, vote over answers, use a verifier to select a candidate, search a tree of partial solutions, or spend additional tokens refining a response. Performance can improve when the extra computation produces useful candidate diversity and a selection signal can identify better candidates. It can also plateau, amplify a shared error, or cost more than the task warrants.
This chapter develops controlled comparisons between compute budgets. It does not assume that best-of-N sampling, self-consistency, or verification helps every problem. Chapter 38 studies refinement and search loops; Chapter 39 turns to training policies with reasoning rewards.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

define inference-time scaling and a compute budget;
implement best-of-N and majority-vote selection on toy candidates;
calculate the probability that at least one of several independent samples is correct;
explain why sample independence and selection quality limit scaling gains;
plot accuracy against tokens, calls, latency, or monetary cost; and
design a controlled scaling experiment with fixed model, task, and selection rule.



Running candidates
For a checkable problem, a system samples several candidate answers. A vote or verifier selects one. Increasing the number of samples increases cost and can increase the chance that at least one candidate is correct.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3.5)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.3,"problem",blue),(2.0,"N candidates\nN=1,4,8",teal),(4.25,"vote or\nverifier",orange),(6.5,"answer",purple)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.3),1.45,.62,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.725,1.61,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for x in [1.78,3.78,6.03]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,1.61),(x+.2,1.61),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.text(4.8,.55,"Report candidate count together with tokens, calls, latency, and selection rule.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,8.5); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 38.1

title: Inference-time Scaling
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

More attempts can raise coverage
If a single sampled solution has probability (p) of being correct and samples are independent, the probability that at least one among (N) is correct is (1-(1-p)^N). This is an upper-bound intuition for best-of-N: the system still needs to recognise or select the correct candidate. Correlated mistakes, narrow decoding, and weak selectors reduce the practical gain.


Code
p=.35
for n in [1,2,4,8]: print(n,"independent coverage",round(1-(1-p)**n,3))


Sampling does not create new evidence. It produces several continuations of the same model under the same context. If all candidates repeat a common misconception, a majority vote can reinforce it. If a verifier checks the relevant property, it can select a rare correct candidate. The mechanism must be evaluated on the task rather than inferred from candidate count.


Code
candidates=[12,13,12,11,12]
print("majority answer:",max(set(candidates),key=candidates.count))




Independence is an assumption, not a decoding setting
The coverage expression assumes that each draw succeeds independently with the same probability. Model samples rarely meet that condition. The same prompt, context, model weights, and high-probability tokens can produce near-duplicate continuations. Lowering temperature can make repetition more likely; raising it can produce candidates that are different but less likely to satisfy the task. Changing the prompt between samples may increase diversity, but then the scaling comparison includes a prompt ensemble rather than a fixed prompting policy.
Measure dependence from the candidates produced, not from the requested sample count. Useful diagnostics include duplicate-answer rate, answer entropy after normalisation, pairwise agreement, and the proportion of items for which every candidate gives the same wrong answer. These records identify whether a larger budget added coverage or simply repeated the same trajectory. They also establish the conditions under which the independent-coverage calculation is a teaching approximation rather than an empirical prediction.

title: Inference-time Scaling
text:
Level 2 - Selection methods

Best-of-N needs a score with useful ranking power
Best-of-N generates (N) candidates and chooses the highest-scoring one. The score can be an exact verifier, a learned reward, a self-evaluation, or a task-specific heuristic. An oracle score that knows the answer provides a useful educational upper bound but is not a deployable selection rule. A learned scorer requires its own precision, recall, and distribution-shift evaluation from Chapter 36.


Code
candidates=[{"answer":12,"score":.91},{"answer":13,"score":.63},{"answer":11,"score":.42}]
selected=max(candidates,key=lambda row:row["score"])
print("selected:",selected)




The oracle gap bounds a selection claim
For each candidate set, an oracle selector chooses a correct candidate whenever one exists. It therefore measures coverage, not deployable performance. The difference between oracle-selected accuracy and the system’s actual selected accuracy is the selection gap. A large gap indicates that more candidate generation may still be useful if the system can obtain a better verifier or ranking signal. A small gap with low oracle accuracy indicates that the main limitation is candidate generation under the current budget.
This decomposition prevents two opposite errors. An oracle result should not be reported as an achievable system result, because the oracle has access to the answer that deployment lacks. Conversely, a weak learned selector should not be used to conclude that sampling itself has no value when correct candidates were present but discarded. Verifier-guided reasoning makes this distinction practical: the value of a verifier depends on how it ranks the candidate set it actually receives (Cobbe et al. 2021).




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.2)); ax.axis("off")
for i,(label,c) in enumerate([("wrong",grey),("correct",teal),("wrong",grey)]): ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.4+i*1.2,1.4),1,.48,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(.9+i*1.2,1.64,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((4.1,1.64),(5.1,1.64),arrowstyle="-|>",color=orange,mutation_scale=12)); ax.add_patch(Rectangle((5.25,1.35),1.35,.58,facecolor=orange,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(5.93,1.64,"selector",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((6.65,1.64),(7.6,1.64),arrowstyle="-|>",color=orange,mutation_scale=12)); ax.add_patch(Rectangle((7.75,1.4),.9,.48,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(8.2,1.64,"answer",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(.4,2.4); plt.show()



Figure 38.2





Self-consistency votes over answers
Self-consistency samples several reasoning paths and selects the most common final answer. It can help when correct paths converge on a shared answer while errors are diverse (Wang et al. 2023). It fails when candidates share a systematic error, when answer extraction is ambiguous, or when an answer requires evidence rather than a stable vote. The grouping rule for equivalent answers must be explicit.


Code
answers=["12","12","twelve","13","12"]
normalised=[a.lower().replace("twelve","12") for a in answers]
print("vote:",max(set(normalised),key=normalised.count))




Votes need an equivalence rule and a policy for disagreement
Voting operates on grouped answers, not raw strings. The grouping may parse integers, canonicalise algebraic expressions, compare executable outputs, or apply a task-specific normaliser. A loose normaliser can merge distinct answers; a strict one can split equivalent answers and discard the vote’s intended signal. Store the raw candidate, normalised answer, and any parse failure so that the grouping can be inspected.
A vote can tie, distribute its mass across many answers, or return an answer supported by only a small share of candidates. The system needs a predeclared response: choose a tie-breaker, generate more candidates up to a budget, invoke a verifier, abstain, or return the answer with an uncertainty flag. The result should report the frequency of these conditions. Selecting the first answer that wins after an undeclared manual inspection converts a scaling experiment into an untracked selection procedure.

title: Inference-time Scaling
text:
Level 3 - Curves and controls

A scaling curve needs matched conditions
Hold the checkpoint, tokenizer, prompt template, task set, maximum candidate length, decoding distribution, and evaluator fixed while changing the compute budget. Then report mean outcome, uncertainty, total generated tokens, model calls, verifier calls, latency, and cost. If a larger budget also uses a different prompt or a stronger verifier, the result does not isolate inference-time scaling.
Sampling adds randomness, so one run at each budget is a weak basis for a curve. Use repeated draws or record seeds and report variation across them when feasible. The purpose is not to manufacture a precise estimate from a small benchmark; it is to show whether the apparent ordering of budgets persists under the stated sampling policy.


Code
budgets=np.array([1,2,4,8]); accuracy=np.array([.51,.59,.66,.69]); tokens=budgets*220
for n,a,t in zip(budgets,accuracy,tokens): print({"samples":int(n),"accuracy":a,"tokens":int(t)})






Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5,4)); ax.plot(budgets,accuracy,marker="o",color=purple); ax.set_xscale("log",base=2); ax.set_xticks(budgets,[str(x) for x in budgets]); ax.set_xlabel("candidate count"); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy"); ax.set_ylim(.4,.8); ax.set_title("Illustrative inference-time scaling curve"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 38.3





Candidate count is not a complete compute budget
Two systems that each sample eight candidates can use very different resources. Candidate length, context length, decoding parameters, model size, precision, tool calls, verifier cost, batching, and parallel execution all change latency and cost. Generated tokens are a useful common unit for some comparisons, but they omit input processing, cache reuse, external computation, and hardware utilisation. Wall-clock latency is the relevant constraint for an interactive service, while total accelerator time can matter more for capacity planning.
Choose the primary budget measure before inspecting the curve, then retain the other measures as supporting records. For example, an interactive mathematical assistant may set a p95 latency ceiling and report tokens and verifier calls under that ceiling. An offline data-cleaning system may instead set a total compute or monetary budget. The choice is a deployment decision, not a property of the model; Chapter 48 will treat the broader serving consequences.
The curve can flatten because candidate quality is low, errors are correlated, the verifier is weak, or the task already saturates at one pass. A negative result is informative: it identifies a budget that adds cost without improving the measured outcome.
Scaling curves should also be reported by task slice. Arithmetic with an exact verifier, multi-step questions with ambiguous answer extraction, and long-context tasks with substantial input cost can have different frontiers even when their pooled accuracy is similar. A budget chosen from an aggregate curve may spend most of its additional computation on items that already saturate while leaving the relevant failures unchanged. The item-level record from Chapter 36 allows the curve to be decomposed without changing the evaluation after results are known.




Code
gains=np.diff(accuracy); labels=["1→2","2→4","4→8"]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8,3.7)); ax.bar(labels,gains,color=[teal,orange,purple]); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy gain"); ax.set_title("Illustrative diminishing marginal gains"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 38.4





A scaling policy needs a stopping rule
Sampling can stop at a fixed candidate count, after an exact verifier accepts a result, when a vote margin reaches a threshold, or when a cost or latency limit is reached. Each rule changes the distribution of computation across inputs. Stopping after the first accepted candidate may be efficient when the verifier is reliable, but it can introduce order effects when early candidates are systematically easier to accept. A fixed budget is easier to compare; an adaptive stopping rule can be more efficient if it is evaluated as a policy rather than reported as a single average.
Record the stopping event for each item. The rate of verification acceptance, timeout, tie, exhausted budget, and abstention shows how the policy behaved. If an evaluation silently retries only the items that fail at a small budget, its reported large-budget accuracy no longer describes the policy that would run in deployment.

title: Inference-time Scaling
text:
Level 4 - Audit and limits

Budgets should be adaptive only under a declared rule
An adaptive system can allocate more samples to uncertain or difficult inputs. It then needs a routing rule and an evaluation that reports performance by route. Sending only failed cases to a large budget after viewing their answers would overstate an online system’s performance. The trigger must use information available before the final answer is known.


Code
uncertainty=np.array([.12,.66,.31])
budgets=np.where(uncertainty>.5,8,2)
print("allocated sample budgets:",budgets)






Code
labels=["low uncertainty","high uncertainty","medium uncertainty"]; assigned=[2,8,2]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2,3.7)); ax.bar(labels,assigned,color=[teal,purple,teal]); ax.set_ylabel("candidate budget"); ax.set_title("Illustrative adaptive budget routing"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 38.5





Adaptive allocation needs route-specific evaluation
An adaptive policy should be compared with fixed budgets using the same incoming items and the same total resource accounting. Report the fraction assigned to each route, route-specific accuracy and cost, and the performance of the routing signal itself. An uncertainty score may route many easy but unfamiliar prompts to a high budget, or it may fail to identify a category of confidently wrong answers. Aggregate accuracy can conceal either pattern.
The routing signal must be available at the point where the policy acts. It may use prompt features, a preliminary model score, or an inexpensive first-pass answer; it cannot use the gold answer or a later human judgment. Preserve the route assignment in the trace so that an evaluator can test whether a change in accuracy came from better allocation, a change in the mix of routed inputs, or extra computation spent everywhere.


The audit record identifies the actual source of gain
Record task and item version, model and template, candidate-generation settings and seeds, candidate IDs, selector or verifier version, answer-normalisation rule, budget, tokens, calls, latency, cost, and outcome. Compare direct generation, generation plus selection, and any tool-assisted route. This makes clear whether an improvement came from sampling, a better selector, a tool, or a changed task interface.
The audit should include unsuccessful scale points. A curve with no gain, a drop after larger budgets, or a high-cost route with little coverage identifies a practical boundary. Removing those points and presenting only the best budget makes it impossible to assess the policy’s trade-off. The result of an inference-time experiment is therefore a measured frontier under a task and system configuration, not a general statement that additional computation improves reasoning.


Code
record={"samples":8,"temperature":.7,"selector":"exact verifier","answer_normalisation":"integer","tokens":1760,"latency":3.3}
assert {"samples","selector","tokens","latency"} <= set(record)
print("scaling record complete")

title: Inference-time Scaling
text:
Common misconceptions

More samples guarantee a better answer. Gains require candidate diversity and a useful selector.
Best-of-N measures model capability alone. It measures a model-plus-selection system under a budget.
Majority vote verifies an answer. It aggregates candidate frequency, not external correctness.
Independent-sample coverage describes real model samples exactly. Samples can be strongly correlated.
A larger budget can be compared without cost. Tokens, calls, latency, and deployment capacity change.
Adaptive allocation is unbiased by default. Its routing rule and route distribution require evaluation.

text:
Exercises

Calculate independent coverage for a stated per-sample success probability and N.
Implement best-of-N selection with a toy exact verifier.
Implement answer normalisation before majority voting.
Give an example of correlated candidate errors.
Design a controlled accuracy–token-budget experiment.
List fields needed to reproduce a scaling curve.
Explain why oracle selection is not a deployable result.
Compare a verifier and a vote as selectors.
Identify a curve that should lead to a smaller production budget.
Design an adaptive routing rule using only pre-answer information.
State why a candidate count does not fully measure cost.
Separate generator and selector improvements in an ablation.
Explain why a larger sample budget can worsen latency.
State how to evaluate a long-context scaling task.
Propose an error taxonomy for failed selection.
Identify the next chapter’s refinement and search focus.

title: Inference-time Scaling
text:
Summary
Inference-time scaling allocates a larger candidate, verification, or search budget to a fixed model and task. More computation can improve results through coverage and selection, but it can also add correlated errors and cost. Credible comparisons report matched conditions, selection quality, outcome uncertainty, and the complete resource budget.
Chapter 38 examines critique, revision, and search procedures that use the available computation across several dependent steps.

title: Inference-time Scaling
text:
Looking ahead
Inference-time scaling defines a budget and a selection rule. Chapter 38 examines two ways to use that budget across dependent steps: revising a candidate and retaining alternatives through search.

title: Inference-time Scaling

Further reading
Self-consistency is developed by Wang et al. (2023). Chain-of-thought prompting provides the related setting in which sampled traces can yield alternative answer paths (Wei et al. 2022).

title: Self-refinement and Search
text: Chapter orientation

title: Self-refinement and Search
text:
Why this chapter matters
Inference-time scaling can sample independent candidates. Self-refinement and search use computation across dependent steps: a model proposes a solution, evaluates or critiques it, revises it, or expands several partial solutions before selecting one. These procedures can correct a detectable error, but they can also repeat the same unsupported claim in more polished language.
The relevant question is whether each step adds information, tests a constraint, or changes a candidate set under a declared rule. This chapter distinguishes revision loops from search, explains verifier-guided branching, and records the failure trace needed to assess them. Chapter 39 turns to reinforcement learning for reasoning trajectories.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish drafting, critique, revision, search, and verification;
implement a bounded critique-and-revision loop;
represent a search tree with nodes, scores, and expansion rules;
explain why a self-critique may repeat a shared model error;
identify stopping and pruning rules as part of the system; and
evaluate whether refinement improved correctness rather than style alone.



Running loop
The running system produces a draft, applies a check, and either accepts or revises within a fixed budget. A checkable failure is needed for the loop to know what to change.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.6)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.3,"draft",blue),(2.2,"critique or\nverifier",orange),(4.3,"revise",teal),(6.3,"accept or\nstop",purple)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.35),1.4,.6,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.7,1.65,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for x in [1.73,3.73,5.73]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,1.65),(x+.42,1.65),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((5.0,1.3),(2.9,.8),connectionstyle="arc3,rad=.3",arrowstyle="-|>",color=teal,mutation_scale=11)); ax.text(4.1,.55,"repeat only while budget remains and a failure is identified",ha="center",color=grey,fontsize=8); ax.set_xlim(0,8); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.6); plt.show()



Figure 39.1

title: Self-refinement and Search
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Revision is useful when it can target an error
A revision loop can improve a calculation when a verifier identifies an incorrect result, a compiler reports an error, or retrieved evidence contradicts a draft claim. A generic prompt to “check your work” can help on some tasks, but it gives the same model an opportunity to restate its initial error. The critique must be evaluated as a signal, not assumed to be independent evidence.


Code
draft={"answer":13,"check":"expected 12","passes":False}
revised={"answer":12,"check":"expected 12","passes":True}
print(draft); print(revised)




A critique is useful only when it changes the available evidence
A critique can identify a failed test, a violated constraint, a missing source, an inconsistent intermediate result, or a mismatch between a response and the requested format. Each signal has a different provenance. A compiler error or exact arithmetic check supplies an external condition; retrieved evidence can contradict a factual claim; a self-critique is another model completion conditioned on the same draft and prompt. Treating these signals as equivalent obscures why one revision may correct an error while another only changes its wording.
The revision prompt should state the signal and the permitted action. If a verifier reports an invalid equation, the system can recompute the equation. If retrieval supplies a conflicting source, it can compare claims against the source and record the citation boundary. If the critic only says that an answer is unclear, the system may improve presentation without changing task correctness. Self-refinement methods demonstrate how generated feedback can be used to revise outputs, but the resulting gain must still be tested against an independent task measure (Madaan et al. 2023).
Refinement differs from search. A single revision follows one trajectory. Search retains several candidates or partial states and allocates further work among them. It can recover from an early bad branch when the expansion and selection rules preserve alternatives. It also consumes more state, tokens, and verifier calls.
Branching is warranted when a task has materially different partial solutions and early commitment creates a known risk: alternative decompositions of a proof, several query plans, competing retrieval paths, or different tool arguments. It is not warranted merely because a response can be rewritten many ways. For stylistic or single-answer tasks, retaining branches may add cost without adding independent evidence. The system should state why an alternative is being preserved and what later check could distinguish it from the other branches.




Code
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(9,3.5))
axes[0].axis("off"); axes[0].set_title("revision")
for i in range(3): axes[0].add_patch(Rectangle((.15+i*.28,.4),.2,.22,facecolor=[blue,orange,teal][i],edgecolor="white")); axes[0].text(.25+i*.28,.51,f"v{i}",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
axes[1].axis("off"); axes[1].set_title("search")
for x,y,c in [(.1,.5,blue),(.4,.75,teal),(.4,.25,orange),(.72,.75,purple),(.72,.25,teal)]: axes[1].add_patch(plt.Circle((x,y),.07,color=c));
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 39.2

title: Self-refinement and Search
text:
Level 2 - Mechanics

A revision state needs an invariant
Each revision should retain the task, constraints, evidence, and the previous candidate rather than silently rewriting the problem. An invariant is a property that must remain true across steps: an answer may need to address the same question, preserve quoted source material, stay within a word limit, or satisfy a tool’s input schema. Without such a record, a loop can appear to improve by dropping a difficult requirement or by replacing the original task with an easier one.
Revision also needs a change criterion. A loop can accept a candidate only when a declared verifier passes, a score improves by a stated margin, or a newly available source resolves a prior gap. Repeating a near-identical candidate should count as a stalled step, not as independent progress. Store the difference between candidate versions and the signal that authorised the change. This makes it possible to identify loops that consume a budget while cycling around the same error.


A loop needs a stopping rule
Stop when a verifier accepts, a maximum number of revisions is reached, a score fails to improve, a time budget expires, or no valid action remains. Each rule has a failure mode. Stopping on self-reported confidence can preserve an error; stopping only on a verifier can loop when the verifier is incomplete; unlimited revision can increase latency without adding information.
A stop reason should be an output of the procedure, not an after-the-fact explanation. Distinguish accepted solutions from exhausted budgets, repeated states, unavailable tools, parser failures, and empty frontiers. These conditions require different treatment in deployment: an accepted answer may be returned, while an exhausted or unverifiable trajectory may need an abstention, a fallback, or a request for more information.


Code
answer=13
for step in range(3):
    if answer==12: break
    answer=12 if step==0 else answer
print("answer",answer,"steps used",step+1)






Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,3.2)); ax.axis("off")
for i,(label,c) in enumerate([("verifier accepts",teal),("maximum steps",orange),("no improvement",purple),("time budget",blue)]): ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.35+(i%2)*3.35,2.2-(i//2)*1.0),2.7,.48,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(1.7+(i%2)*3.35,2.44-(i//2)*1.0,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 39.3





Search requires node and score semantics
A search node can contain a partial solution, accumulated cost, verifier state, and a score used for expansion or pruning. A score may represent probability, a learned value, a constraint count, or an exact check. These are not interchangeable. A high language-model probability can favour fluent partial text while an exact verifier favours a narrow feasible state.


Code
frontier=[{"state":"2+2=", "score":.6},{"state":"2+3=", "score":.5}]
expanded=[{"state":"2+2=4","score":.95},{"state":"2+3=5","score":.94}]
print(max(expanded,key=lambda node:node["score"]))




Search allocates a finite expansion budget
Search needs a policy for choosing which frontier node to expand next. Breadth-first expansion spreads work across shallow alternatives; depth-first expansion follows one path before returning; a beam keeps the best-scoring fixed number of nodes; best-first expansion prioritises the current score. These policies have different coverage and memory profiles. They should be named in the system record rather than described loosely as exploration.
The expansion action also needs semantics. A node may add one calculation step, retrieve one document, call one tool, propose one subgoal, or append a token block. The cost and meaning of a depth limit depend on this action. Tree-of-Thoughts makes branching prompts explicit, but a branching prompt alone does not establish a useful search procedure without a score, retention rule, and evaluation of the paths it discards (Yao et al. 2023).

title: Self-refinement and Search
text:
Level 3 - Search and failure propagation

Pruning can discard the correct path
Beam width, score threshold, depth limit, and branching factor determine which partial states survive. Narrow pruning reduces cost but can remove a low-scoring path that would later become correct. Broad search retains alternatives but can make a weak verifier or heuristic dominate the total cost. Evaluation should report candidate coverage at each depth and where correct paths were discarded.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,3.8)); ax.axis("off")
for x,y,label,c in [(1,1.9,"root",blue),(3,2.7,"high",teal),(3,1.1,"low",orange),(5,2.7,"leaf",purple)]: ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((x,y),.22,color=c)); ax.text(x,y,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
ax.plot([1.2,2.8],[2,2.6],color=grey); ax.plot([1.2,2.8],[1.8,1.2],color=grey); ax.plot([3.2,4.8],[2.7,2.7],color=grey); ax.text(3.5,.55,"crossed branch: pruned before later evidence",color=orange); ax.set_xlim(0,6); ax.set_ylim(.2,3.4); plt.show()



Figure 39.4





Scores must be comparable across the nodes they rank
A score can rank candidates only if the compared nodes represent the same decision stage or if the score accounts for their different states and costs. Comparing a short partial derivation with a complete answer using a raw language-model probability can favour brevity. Comparing nodes evaluated with different retrieved evidence can favour the node that received an easier source. A value estimate may guide expansion, but it is not proof that a node is correct.
Record when a score was produced, what inputs and tools were available, and whether it was used for pruning, ordering, or final selection. Test whether correct continuations were systematically assigned lower scores before they were pruned. This diagnostic distinguishes a search limit imposed by the budget from a selection failure imposed by the scoring rule.


Critique can propagate an early framing error
If a draft assumes a false premise, a critic generated from the same context may assess internal consistency rather than external validity. Adding retrieval, tools, independent candidate generators, or exact constraints can provide a different signal, but each also has coverage limits. The trace should identify which information was available at each revision, not only the final revised prose.


Code
trace=[{"step":0,"draft":"unsupported claim","signal":"self-critique"},{"step":1,"draft":"rephrased unsupported claim","signal":"self-critique"}]
for row in trace: print(row)




Verification can occur before, during, or after search
An early verifier can reject an infeasible partial state before the system spends resources extending it. A later verifier may have more context and be able to check a complete result, but it leaves more weak branches alive. Some tasks need both: cheap checks for syntax or known constraints during expansion and a stronger final check for the selected answer. The checks should be logged separately because their coverage and errors differ.
Verification can also distort the search when it rewards a proxy. A format checker may cause the system to optimise well-formed output while leaving the substantive task unsolved. A learned critic can rank familiar styles of explanation above an unusual but valid path. Compare a verifier-guided procedure with a matched procedure that exposes the verifier’s acceptances and rejections; otherwise an apparent search gain may be a change in answer formatting or evaluation rather than a gain in task solution.

title: Self-refinement and Search
text:
Level 4 - Audit and evaluation

Compare refinement with matched baselines
Compare a one-pass answer, a one-pass answer plus verifier, a fixed-budget refinement loop, and a search procedure under the same task and model. Report outcome correctness, accepted-candidate rate, revision count, candidates expanded and pruned, tokens, tool calls, latency, and failure types. A more fluent final response is not evidence of improved reasoning unless the task criterion improves.


Code
systems={"one-pass":(.55,180),"revise":(.61,520),"search":(.68,1100)}
for name,(accuracy,tokens) in systems.items(): print(name,accuracy,tokens)






Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8,3.8)); ax.scatter([180,520,1100],[.55,.61,.68],s=95,color=[blue,teal,purple]);
for x,y,label in zip([180,520,1100],[.55,.61,.68],["one-pass","revision","search"]): ax.text(x,y+.012,label,ha="center")
ax.set_xlabel("tokens"); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy"); ax.set_ylim(.5,.72); ax.set_title("Illustrative refinement and search trade-off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 39.5





Evaluate trajectories as well as final answers
Final-answer accuracy cannot show whether a revision fixed an error, a search retained a useful alternative, or a verifier happened to accept a lucky candidate. For each item, classify the initial candidate, each critique or check, each revision or expansion, each pruning event, and the final selection. A trajectory can then show a generation failure, a false critique, an unnecessary revision, premature pruning, verifier false acceptance, or budget exhaustion.
Counterfactual comparisons make these categories useful. Run the same initial candidates with and without a critique, vary the beam width while holding the score fixed, or replace a learned verifier with an exact check where the task permits. The objective is not to attribute every successful answer to one token or step. It is to establish which component changes the measured task outcome under the declared budget.


The audit record must retain the trajectory
Store prompt, model and template, initial draft, critiques or verifier outputs, revision prompts, node states, expansion and pruning rules, stop reason, selected output, evaluation result, and resource use. This record makes a repeated failure identifiable: a wrong candidate may have been generated, a correct candidate may have been pruned, or a verifier may have accepted an error.
The record should preserve failures even when the final answer is correct. A correct answer reached after repeated invalid tool calls, unstable critiques, or an exhausted branch budget has different deployment implications from a direct verified solution. Report trajectory length and resource distributions, not only the best final path. The next chapter changes the policy through reinforcement learning; it will require the same distinction between an observed trajectory and the signal used to reward it.


Code
record={"max_depth":3,"beam_width":2,"verifier":"exact-v1","stop":"accepted","tokens":840,"selected_node":"n7"}
assert {"beam_width","verifier","stop","tokens"} <= set(record)
print("search audit record complete")

title: Self-refinement and Search
text:
Common misconceptions

Revision automatically corrects an answer. It needs a signal that identifies an error or supplies new evidence.
A critique is independent verification. It can share the generator’s assumptions and errors.
Search is just a longer chain of thought. It retains, expands, and prunes alternative states under explicit rules.
Pruning only removes bad candidates. A heuristic can discard a path that would later be correct.
More iterations always help. Loops can plateau or amplify a mistaken premise.

title: Self-refinement and Search
text:
Exercises

Log a trace that identifies a pruned correct candidate.

Identify the next chapter’s reinforcement-learning focus.

title: Self-refinement and Search
text:
Summary
Self-refinement and search allocate inference-time computation across dependent steps. Revision can correct a detected error; search can preserve alternatives when early choices are uncertain. Both require explicit signals, budgets, stopping rules, and trajectory traces. Their value is established by task outcomes and cost, not by the apparent sophistication of revised prose.
Chapter 39 introduces rewards, trajectories, and policy updates for training reasoning behaviour rather than only allocating more inference-time computation.

title: Self-refinement and Search

Looking ahead
Refinement and search alter inference-time computation around a fixed policy. Chapter 39 turns to changing that policy through rewards assigned to sampled trajectories.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning
text: Chapter orientation

title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning
text:
Why this chapter matters
Chapters 37 and 38 allocated additional computation after training. Reinforcement learning for reasoning changes the policy so that it is more likely to generate trajectories associated with a reward. A rollout is a sampled sequence of actions or tokens; a reward evaluates an outcome, a process, or both; a policy update changes probabilities in response to those signals.
The reward does not become the task merely because it is optimised. A verifiable final answer can provide a strong outcome signal for some tasks. A process reward can identify local errors or encourage useful steps, while also rewarding a style that looks correct to its judge. This chapter establishes the objects needed for Chapter 40’s group-relative methods.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

define policy, rollout, trajectory, reward, and return;
distinguish outcome and process rewards;
calculate a toy expected reward and policy-gradient weight;
identify reward-model, verifier, and exploration limitations;
explain credit assignment across a multi-step trajectory; and
specify an RL-for-reasoning run record.



Running rollout
A policy samples a multi-step solution. An exact answer checker supplies an outcome reward; a separate process scorer may assign values to individual steps.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.5)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.3,"policy",blue),(2.0,"rollout\ntrajectory",teal),(3.95,"reward or\nverifier",orange),(5.9,"update\nsignal",purple)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.3),1.4,.62,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.7,1.61,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for x in [1.73,3.73,5.68]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,1.61),(x+.22,1.61),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((6.6,1.28),(.95,.92),connectionstyle="arc3,rad=.25",arrowstyle="-|>",color=purple,mutation_scale=11)); ax.text(4.4,.45,"new rollouts are sampled from the updated policy",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,7.8); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 40.1

title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Rewards select among sampled behaviours
If a task has an exact answer, a verifier can reward a rollout that reaches it and reject one that does not. The policy update increases probability for rewarded trajectories relative to alternatives under the chosen algorithm. For open-ended tasks, a reward may be learned from preferences or process annotations, which introduces the limits of the judge described in Chapter 30.


Code
rollouts=[{"steps":3,"correct":1,"reward":1.0},{"steps":5,"correct":0,"reward":0.0},{"steps":4,"correct":1,"reward":1.0}]
print("mean outcome reward:",np.mean([r["reward"] for r in rollouts]))




The reward interface defines which trajectories are eligible to learn from
Before optimisation, specify the task input, the permitted actions, the end condition, the reward source, and what happens when a rollout is malformed, incomplete, unsafe, or impossible to verify. An exact checker may return a binary reward only for answers that parse; a tool-based task may need to distinguish a failed call from an incorrect result; a human or model judge may return a score with uncertainty. These cases are part of the training data distribution, not implementation noise to discard without a rule.
The interface also determines which shortcuts the policy can use. If a reward checks only a final number, a trajectory may contain irrelevant or invalid intermediate statements and still receive reward. If a process scorer rewards a preferred format, the policy may learn the format without improving the task. A useful reward specification names the intended property, the observed proxy, the cases the proxy cannot evaluate, and the fallback for those cases.
Outcome rewards evaluate the final state. They can tolerate unusual valid solution paths, but provide little information about where a failed trajectory went wrong. Process rewards score intermediate steps. They can give denser feedback, but require a process evaluator whose judgements are valid for the task.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,3.2)); ax.axis("off")
for i in range(3): ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.45+i*2.1,1.5),1.5,.48,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(1.2+i*2.1,1.74,f"step {i+1}",ha="center",va="center",color="white"); ax.text(1.2+i*2.1,1.15,"process score",ha="center",color=orange,fontsize=8)
ax.text(6.7,1.74,"final answer",ha="center",color=purple); ax.text(6.7,1.15,"outcome reward",ha="center",color=purple,fontsize=8); ax.set_xlim(0,8); ax.set_ylim(.6,2.4); plt.show()



Figure 40.2





Outcome and process signals need a disagreement analysis
When outcome and process scores disagree, the disagreement is evidence about the evaluators as well as the trajectory. A correct final answer with a low process score may reflect an unusual valid route, incomplete annotations, or a weak process judge. A high process score with an incorrect answer may reveal a plausible-looking but invalid step that the evaluator rewarded. Record these cases by task type and inspect a bounded sample before treating either signal as the authoritative account of quality.
Process supervision can provide more frequent feedback, but its advantage depends on the validity and coverage of the step evaluator. Research comparing process and outcome supervision therefore concerns a defined task and judging procedure, not a universal guarantee that visible intermediate steps represent the policy’s causal computation (Lightman et al. 2023).

title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning
text:
Level 2 - Objective mechanics

Policy gradients weight sampled actions by return
For a trajectory () sampled from policy (), a basic policy-gradient estimator increases log probability in proportion to return (R()): (R()_()). In practice a baseline or advantage reduces variance by comparing the return with an expected value. The update does not copy a rewarded sequence exactly; it changes the distribution from which future trajectories are sampled.


Code
rewards=np.array([1.,0.,1.,0.]); baseline=rewards.mean(); advantages=rewards-baseline
print("baseline:",baseline,"advantages:",advantages)




Returns require scale and reference choices
The numerical scale of a reward changes the magnitude and variance of an update. A sparse binary reward, a graded verifier score, and a sum of process scores create different learning signals even when they refer to the same task. Clipping, normalising, discounting, or subtracting a baseline can stabilise estimation, but each transformation changes which trajectory differences the update emphasises. Report the transformation and its unit alongside the raw reward distribution.
The policy also needs a reference point. Without a constraint, repeated updates can shift the model away from useful instruction-following, formatting, or safety behaviour that the reward does not measure. A KL penalty or another reference-policy control makes that trade-off explicit. The relevant question is not whether the policy changed, but whether the measured reasoning gain remains after accounting for changes in the behaviours that the reward left unscored. Standard reinforcement-learning accounts distinguish the return signal, variance-reduction estimate, and policy update for this reason (Sutton and Barto 2018).
Credit assignment asks which earlier decisions contributed to a final reward. Assigning one outcome reward to every token can reinforce accidental or irrelevant steps. Process labels can localise credit, but only where the process scorer can distinguish a valid from invalid step. This is a measurement problem, not merely an optimisation detail.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,3.4)); ax.axis("off")
for i in range(4): ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.35+i*1.35,1.6),.9,.42,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(.8+i*1.35,1.81,f"a{i+1}",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((5.9,1.6),1.1,.42,facecolor=orange,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(6.45,1.81,"reward",ha="center",va="center",color="white"); ax.text(3.6,.75,"Which actions deserve credit is an estimator and evaluator question.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,7.5); ax.set_ylim(.3,2.5); plt.show()



Figure 40.3





Credit assignment should not rewrite the trajectory record
An update may attach the same return to every action, assign different weights to time steps, or use process labels for selected states. Keep the original trajectory separate from the credit signal derived from it. Otherwise a later analysis cannot tell whether a step was observed, judged, or inferred by the advantage estimator. This matters when a correct answer follows an invalid intermediate claim: outcome reward confirms the final result, while a process label may identify the earlier error.
Credit assignment also has an eligibility boundary. A trajectory generated under one prompt template, tool version, or answer parser may not be comparable with a trajectory generated under another. Mixing them without a record changes the reward distribution and can make an apparent training gain reflect a changed interface. The rollout log should therefore bind each action sequence to its prompt, tools, reward version, and termination reason before an update is calculated.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning
text:
Level 3 - Exploration and reward limits

A reward can be exploited
Optimisation searches for trajectories that obtain high reward, including behaviours that satisfy a proxy without meeting the intended task. A verifier may accept a formatting loophole; a learned reward may prefer confident language or a familiar process style. Fresh tasks, adversarial cases, reward-model diagnostics, and independent outcome checks are needed throughout training.


Code
cases=[{"trajectory":"correct solution","reward":1,"task_success":1},{"trajectory":"format exploit","reward":1,"task_success":0}]
for case in cases: print(case)


Exploration determines which trajectories the reward can evaluate. A policy that rarely samples a correct long solution cannot learn from its reward without a curriculum, a stronger starting policy, broader sampling, or another source of demonstrations. More exploration raises rollout cost and can generate unsafe or low-quality candidates, so its policy must be bounded and logged.
Exploration should be diagnosed before it is credited with learning. Separate the share of rollouts that are novel, verifier-accepted, duplicate a previous answer, malformed, or stopped by a budget. A rise in average reward can come from repeatedly sampling one already common trajectory. Conversely, a policy may explore widely but supply no usable reward signal if the verifier rejects nearly every candidate.


Rollout collection is a data-generation process
Rollouts are generated data, not a neutral sample from a fixed corpus. Their distribution depends on the current policy, prompt mix, decoding settings, tool availability, filters, and retry policy. If a training run keeps only accepted trajectories, the retained set can conceal how many candidates were invalid, duplicated, or rejected by a narrow verifier. Retaining only successful samples may be appropriate for a defined objective, but it must be recorded as a selection rule.
Separate the policy that generated a rollout from the policy being updated. A stale rollout pool can improve throughput, but it may no longer represent the current policy’s behaviour; an on-policy pool is more current but requires repeated generation. This chapter does not require one choice. It requires naming the choice, recording the policy version and sampling conditions, and evaluating the resulting policy on held-out tasks rather than on the filtered rollout pool.




Code
labels=["lower\ntemperature","higher\ntemperature"]
parts=np.array([[48,35,14,3],[37,42,13,8]])
colours=[teal,orange,purple,grey]; names=["accepted","incorrect","duplicate","malformed"]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); bottom=np.zeros(2)
for values,colour,name in zip(parts.T,colours,names):
    ax.bar(labels,values,bottom=bottom,label=name,color=colour); bottom+=values
ax.set_ylabel("share of rollouts (%)"); ax.set_ylim(0,100); ax.legend(ncol=2)
ax.set_title("Illustrative rollout composition")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 40.4





Reward failures need a response policy during training
Training should specify how it handles a verifier outage, contradictory tool output, a suspected exploit, a high rate of malformed trajectories, or a sudden increase in reward without an independent outcome gain. Possible responses include pausing updates, excluding a versioned batch, reducing exploration, routing cases for review, or reverting to an earlier checkpoint. These are governance decisions around a training signal, not evidence that the policy has learned less.
The response record should identify the triggering measurement and the affected trajectories. Quietly changing a reward threshold or deleting inconvenient rollouts destroys the comparison across checkpoints. A bounded, versioned intervention preserves the possibility of diagnosing whether later behaviour changed because of the policy update or because the training signal changed.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning
text:
Level 4 - Audit and reporting

Compare the policy to its reward and its task
An RL evaluation should report reward during training, independent task outcome, selected trajectory length, token and rollout budgets, verifier or judge version, reward-hacking cases, and retained capability tests. A rising training reward with flat task accuracy is a diagnostic signal, not a success criterion. The comparison should include the pre-RL reference policy under the same inference procedure.
The evaluation set and verifier version must remain fixed across checkpoints. Otherwise a policy may seem to improve because a reward implementation, prompt template, decoding temperature, or test composition changed. Report checkpoint-level uncertainty or task slices where sample sizes permit. The purpose is to identify the source of the observed change, not to turn a training curve into a broad capability claim.


Checkpoint selection needs an independent criterion
Selecting the checkpoint with the highest training reward selects for the training signal by construction. Select on a held-out task metric, a predeclared composite of task and resource measures, or a fixed training budget, then report the alternative checkpoints and their outcomes. If the task requires safeguards or retained capabilities, include those tests in the selection rule or state explicitly that they are constraints rather than optimisation targets.
Compare the selected policy with the reference policy under matched inference conditions. A post-training policy that receives more samples, a stronger tool, or a different prompt at evaluation cannot be attributed to reinforcement learning alone. The evaluation record should allow a reader to reproduce both the checkpoint decision and the policy comparison.




Code
checkpoints=np.arange(1,6); reward=[.42,.55,.66,.74,.79]; task=[.51,.52,.54,.53,.55]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.plot(checkpoints,reward,marker="o",label="training reward",color=orange)
ax.plot(checkpoints,task,marker="o",label="held-out task accuracy",color=blue)
ax.set_xlabel("checkpoint"); ax.set_ylabel("score"); ax.set_ylim(.35,.85); ax.legend()
ax.set_title("Illustrative reward-outcome divergence")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 40.5





Code
history={"before":{"reward":.42,"task":.51},"after":{"reward":.78,"task":.55}}
print(history)




The run record defines the policy change
Store base policy, rollout prompt and template, sampling settings, reward or verifier implementation, outcome and process labels, baseline or advantage method, update schedule, KL or reference constraint where used, checkpoints, independent evaluations, and cost. This allows a reviewer to distinguish a model improvement from a changed reward, a changed sampler, or a changed benchmark.
Include the rejected and interrupted portions of the run: rollout counts before filtering, reward and parser failures, policy and tool versions, aborted updates, and the reason for each intervention. This establishes the training distribution actually used by the optimiser and makes later reward-hacking or regression findings traceable to a specific run condition.


Code
record={"base":"instruction-v1","rollouts":8,"reward":"exact verifier","advantage":"baseline-subtracted","evaluation":"held-out outcome"}
assert {"base","reward","advantage","evaluation"} <= set(record)
print("RL reasoning record complete")

title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning
text:
Common misconceptions

A reward is the task definition. It is a signal that can be incomplete or exploited.
Outcome rewards show a good process. Correct answers can arise through poor or lucky trajectories.
Process rewards are automatically more faithful. Their quality depends on the process evaluator.
More rollouts always improve a policy update. They change cost and can repeat a weak exploration distribution.
A rising reward proves general reasoning improvement. Independent task and robustness tests remain necessary.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning
text:
Summary
Reinforcement learning for reasoning changes a policy through rewards assigned to sampled trajectories. Outcome and process supervision offer different feedback and different failure modes. The quality of the resulting system depends on exploration, reward validity, credit assignment, reference constraints, and independent task evaluation.
Chapter 40 develops group-relative advantages and related policy-update choices for reasoning rollouts.
