title: GRPO and Related Training Methods
text: Chapter orientation
crumbs: 41  GRPO and Related Training Methods

title: GRPO and Related Training Methods
text:
Why this chapter matters
Reinforcement learning for reasoning requires a policy update signal for sampled rollouts. Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) samples several completions for the same prompt, compares their rewards within that group, and uses the relative results to increase or decrease policy probability. The group provides a local baseline, avoiding a separately learned value model in the basic formulation.
This chapter gives the mechanism and its limits. It does not reproduce frontier training data, infrastructure, or confidential procedures. The educational implementation uses small arrays to make the group-relative calculation inspectable.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

define rollout group, reward, group mean, group standard deviation, and advantage;
calculate normalised group-relative advantages;
explain the role of a reference policy and clipping constraint;
identify zero-variance groups and reward-hacking limits; and
specify a small GRPO experiment and audit record.



Running group
One prompt produces four rollouts. An exact verifier assigns rewards. Each rollout is compared with others from the same prompt rather than against a global reward scale.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5,3.5)); ax.axis("off")
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.3,1.4),1.3,.55,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(.95,1.67,"prompt",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
for i,r in enumerate([1,0,1,0]):
    x=2.1+i*1.15; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.4),.9,.55,facecolor=teal if r else orange,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.45,1.67,f"r={r}",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((6.85,1.67),(7.65,1.67),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11)); ax.add_patch(Rectangle((7.75,1.4),1.3,.55,facecolor=purple,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(8.4,1.67,"advantages",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.text(4.7,.55,"Each rollout's reward is interpreted relative to its prompt-specific group.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,9.5); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.4); plt.show()



Figure 41.1
crumbs: 41  GRPO and Related Training Methods

title: GRPO and Related Training Methods
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Relative rewards provide a local comparison
For a prompt with several rollouts, GRPO gives positive advantage to rewards above the group average and negative advantage to rewards below it. If one candidate is verifier-correct and others are not, the update favours the successful candidate. The signal is prompt-specific: a reward of one can be excellent in a difficult group and uninformative in a group where every rollout succeeds.


Code
rewards=np.array([1.,0.,1.,0.])
mean=rewards.mean(); std=rewards.std()
advantages=(rewards-mean)/(std+1e-8)
print("mean",mean,"advantages",np.round(advantages,3))




A group is a prompt-level experimental unit
All rollouts in a GRPO group must answer the same task instance under a declared prompt and tool state. Grouping completions from different prompts would make the local baseline reflect task difficulty, answer format, or verifier coverage as well as policy variation. The prompt identifier, prompt template, retrieval context, tool versions, and sampling policy should therefore be fixed within the group and retained in the rollout record.
The grouping decision also defines what counts as a comparison. A system may group independently sampled completions, completions with different random seeds, or completions produced from several permitted prompt variants. The latter can be useful for a defined robustness objective, but it no longer estimates variation under one fixed prompt. State the grouping unit before training and preserve it when reporting group statistics or comparing an update with another method.
crumbs: 41  GRPO and Related Training Methods

title: GRPO and Related Training Methods
text:
Level 2 - Mechanics

The group-relative advantage
For rewards (r_1,,r_G), a common educational form is (A_i=(r_i-r)/(s_r+)). The normalisation reduces sensitivity to reward scale within a group. It does not make the reward correct, independent, or comparable across different prompt distributions.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,3.8)); ax.bar(np.arange(4)-.18,rewards,.35,label="reward",color=teal); ax.bar(np.arange(4)+.18,advantages,.35,label="advantage",color=purple); ax.axhline(0,color=grey,lw=.8); ax.set_xticks(range(4),["rollout 1","2","3","4"]); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Group-relative rewards"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 41.2



When every reward is identical, the standard deviation is zero and the group contains no relative learning signal. Adding a small epsilon prevents numerical failure but does not create information. The data pipeline should record such groups and the policy used for skipping or handling them.


Code
flat=np.array([1.,1.,1.,1.])
print("flat-group advantages:",(flat-flat.mean())/(flat.std()+1e-8))




Group size changes coverage and the stability of the local baseline
Larger groups can increase the chance of observing both successful and unsuccessful rollouts, which creates a relative signal on sparse-reward tasks. They also consume more generation and verifier budget per prompt. A large group of near-duplicate completions may still have little effective diversity, while a small group can produce a highly variable mean and standard deviation. Report group size together with duplicate rate, answer diversity, completion length, and the fraction of groups with mixed rewards.
The appropriate group size depends on the reward and task. With an exact verifier and a difficult problem, a small group may be uniformly rejected; with an easy task, a large group may be uniformly accepted. Neither case identifies an update direction. Changing group size after inspecting training outcomes changes the learning signal and should be treated as an experimental change rather than a minor throughput adjustment.
The comparison is deliberately within prompt. A raw reward can vary because one problem is easier than another, because a verifier is stricter for one answer form, or because a reward model has different scale across topics. Group-relative advantages remove part of that prompt-level variation. They do not establish that two prompts contribute equally useful training information. Inspect group means, standard deviations, acceptance rates, and repeated candidates before aggregating an update.




Code
groups=[np.array([1,0,1,0]),np.array([1,1,1,1]),np.array([0,0,0,0])]
titles=["mixed rewards","all accepted","all rejected"]
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(9,3),sharey=True)
for ax,g,title in zip(axes,groups,titles):
    ax.bar(range(1,5),g,color=[teal if r else orange for r in g]); ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xticks(range(1,5)); ax.set_ylim(0,1.15)
axes[0].set_ylabel("verifier reward"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 41.3





Reward transformation and ties need an explicit policy
The raw reward may be binary, graded, clipped, length-adjusted, or combined with a penalty for an invalid tool call. GRPO normalisation acts on the value that enters the group calculation, so reward transformations determine the relative ordering that the policy learns from. A length penalty can discourage excessive traces but may also punish a valid longer solution; a format penalty can prevent parser failures but may dominate a weak outcome score. Report each component separately before presenting the transformed reward.
Ties are common with binary rewards. A mixed group can contain several equally rewarded completions with different quality under an unmeasured property, while a flat group has no relative advantage at all. The training policy may skip flat groups, retain them for another objective, or collect additional rollouts up to a fixed limit. Whichever policy is used, it should be applied before outcome evaluation and not adjusted selectively for prompts that later appear difficult.
crumbs: 41  GRPO and Related Training Methods

title: GRPO and Related Training Methods
text:
Level 3 - Policy constraints

Updates are constrained relative to a reference
The policy probability ratio compares the updated policy with the rollout or reference policy. Clipping or a KL-style penalty limits large changes that could exploit finite rewards or destabilise training. These controls do not validate the reward; they limit the size of a policy move under a chosen measure.


Code
old_prob=np.array([.25,.25,.25,.25]); new_prob=np.array([.35,.15,.35,.15])
ratio=new_prob/old_prob
clipped=np.clip(ratio,.8,1.2)
print("ratio",ratio,"clipped",clipped)




Sampling, old, and reference policies answer different questions
The sampling or old policy generated the rollout and supplies the probability in the importance ratio. A reference policy supplies a behavioural anchor through a KL-style term or related constraint. They may be the same at the start of an iteration, but they need not remain the same across updates. Confusing them makes it unclear whether a ratio measures change from the data-generating policy or distance from a fixed instruction-following reference.
The log-probability record must use the exact generated tokens, including termination and any tool-call representation that the policy models. A mismatch between the stored rollout and the tokens scored by the updated policy changes the ratio without representing a learning effect. Clipping methods provide an example of why this bookkeeping matters: the constraint depends on the comparison policy and the likelihood of the observed action sequence (Schulman et al. 2017).




Code
x=np.linspace(.4,1.8,100); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8,3.7)); ax.plot(x,x,label="raw ratio",color=blue); ax.plot(x,np.clip(x,.8,1.2),label="clipped",color=orange); ax.legend(); ax.set_xlabel("raw probability ratio"); ax.set_ylabel("update ratio"); ax.set_title("Illustrative clipping constraint"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 41.4





A small calculation exposes the update direction
Suppose a group contains two accepted and two rejected rollouts. The accepted rollouts receive positive advantages and, within the clipping range, their token probabilities are increased; rejected rollouts receive negative advantages. This description remains conditional on the reward. If the verifier accepts a loophole, the same calculation strengthens the loophole. Reward design decides what counts as success; group normalisation supplies a relative signal; and the constrained update determines how far the policy moves.
For one update, the operational order is straightforward. Fix a prompt batch and the policy used to sample from it. Generate a declared number of completions per prompt, preserving their token log probabilities. Apply the reward or verifier to every completion. Compute group-relative advantages only from the matching prompt group, record groups with no variation, and combine each completion’s advantage with its log-probability ratio. Apply the clipping or reference constraint, update the policy, then evaluate a saved checkpoint with an independent task scorer. The update must not use the held-out evaluation outcome as a reward. This order makes clear where a result can change: generation, reward calculation, normalisation, optimisation control, or evaluation.




Code
advantages=np.array([1.,-1.,1.,-1.]); ratios=np.array([1.15,.88,1.12,.90])
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4,3.8)); ax.axhspan(.8,1.2,color="#e7edf1",label="clipping region")
ax.scatter(range(1,5),ratios,s=120,c=[teal if a>0 else orange for a in advantages])
for i,(a,r) in enumerate(zip(advantages,ratios),1): ax.annotate("increase" if a>0 else "decrease",(i,r),xytext=(0,10 if a>0 else -15),textcoords="offset points",ha="center")
ax.set_xticks(range(1,5),["rollout 1","2","3","4"]); ax.set_ylabel("new / old probability ratio"); ax.set_ylim(.7,1.3); ax.legend(loc="upper right")
ax.set_title("Illustrative constrained update directions"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 41.5





Sequence length can change the update weight
A rollout probability is the product of token probabilities, usually handled as a sum of token log probabilities. Longer completions therefore contribute more token-level terms unless the objective uses a stated length normalisation or masking rule. This is not a purely numerical choice. It determines whether a positive advantage reinforces every token in a long trace more strongly than the same advantage in a short trace, and how padding, end tokens, or tool output are treated.
Record the token span receiving the update, the handling of prompt tokens, and any maximum-length truncation. If an exact reward accepts short and long answers equally, a length-sensitive update can still shift the policy towards one form. Check outcome, completion length, and invalid-termination rates together before interpreting a reward gain as an improvement in reasoning quality.


Optimisation settings remain part of the method
GRPO specifies a relative advantage construction; it does not remove ordinary optimisation choices. Learning rate, batch composition, number of update epochs over a rollout batch, gradient clipping, precision, and checkpoint frequency affect how a group signal changes the policy. A large learning rate or repeated updates over the same small rollout pool can cause a policy move that the reference constraint does not fully contain. A very small update can leave a useful group signal with no measurable effect.
Report these settings with the group construction and evaluate checkpoints over the same held-out task. If one experiment changes group size and learning rate together, it cannot attribute an outcome difference to the group-relative baseline. This is the same control principle used earlier in the book: hold the mechanism under test fixed while varying one declared component.

title: GRPO and Related Training Methods
text:
Level 4 - Audit and limits

Group quality determines the learning signal
Groups need candidate diversity, a valid reward, and a documented rollout policy. If all completions share one error, relative normalisation cannot recover a correct answer. If a verifier has a loophole, the policy can learn to exploit it. If groups differ greatly in difficulty, aggregate reward may conceal where updates are useful or harmful.
An audit should retain prompt identifiers or reproducible generators, the complete group before filtering, completion lengths, sampling settings, raw and transformed rewards, flat-group handling, old-policy log probabilities, reference-policy choice, clipping or KL coefficient, and the checkpoint used for independent evaluation. Report group statistics by task slice. A mean reward across all rollouts is insufficient because it hides whether signal came from a small set of prompts or from a change in group composition.
The evaluation should include component ablations. Hold prompts, rollout counts, reward, and independent task scorer fixed while removing group normalisation, changing group size, or varying the reference constraint one at a time. Compare the resulting policy checkpoints under the same inference budget. These comparisons do not prove that one method is universally preferable; they show which component explains the measured change in the declared training setting.
Report the checkpoint-selection rule before comparing ablations. Selecting the highest result from each run on the same small development set can turn optimisation noise into a method claim.
For any sample-efficiency claim, report total rollouts, accepted groups, discarded groups, update steps, and the complete evaluation budget alongside the final outcome.


Code
record={"group_size":4,"reward":"exact verifier","epsilon":1e-8,"ratio_clip":.2,"reference":"policy-v1","flat_groups":"skip"}
assert {"group_size","reward","reference"} <= set(record)
print("GRPO record complete")




An educational implementation is not a frontier reproduction
Small demonstrations can show group normalisation, clipped ratios, and verifier-dependent learning signals. They do not reproduce the data mixtures, distributed rollout systems, model scale, reward engineering, or training stability of large reasoning runs. Report this boundary directly and evaluate a toy method on held-out checkable tasks before interpreting a training curve.

title: GRPO and Related Training Methods
text:
Common misconceptions

GRPO makes rewards objective. It normalises rewards within a group; reward validity remains separate.
A group baseline guarantees learning. Flat or correlated groups can contain little useful signal.
Clipping prevents reward hacking. It limits update size but does not repair a flawed reward.
A toy implementation reproduces frontier reasoning training. It demonstrates the update logic only.
More rollouts always improve the update. They add cost and can repeat the same error.

text:
Summary
GRPO uses relative rewards among several rollouts from the same prompt to construct local advantages for a constrained policy update. Its behaviour depends on rollout diversity, reward validity, group handling, and reference-policy controls. Educational implementations clarify the calculation but do not reproduce frontier-scale systems.
Chapter 41 examines how slower reasoning systems can train or guide smaller and cheaper students.

title: Distillation and Efficient Reasoning
text: Chapter orientation

title: Distillation and Efficient Reasoning
text:
Why this chapter matters
A reasoning system can improve accuracy by sampling, searching, verifying, or using a larger model, but these procedures can be too slow or costly for every request. Distillation trains a student to imitate selected teacher outputs or distributions. In reasoning settings, the teacher may provide answers, checked solution traces, candidate rankings, or a routing policy that decides when extra computation is warranted.
Distillation transfers observed behaviour under a data and interface distribution. It does not prove that the student has acquired the teacher’s internal computation, and it can transfer errors, style, or reward-hacking patterns. This chapter treats teacher generation, selection, student training, and efficiency evaluation as one pipeline.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish teacher, student, distillation dataset, and deployment policy;
explain answer, trace, and logit distillation;
identify teacher-selection and trace-quality risks;
compare teacher and student on accuracy, latency, tokens, and cost;
describe adaptive routing between a student and teacher; and
specify a distillation audit record.



Running system
The teacher uses a larger inference budget to generate and verify candidates. Accepted outputs become a dataset for a smaller student, which is then evaluated without assuming that imitation loss measures reasoning quality.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3.4)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.2,"prompts",blue),(1.85,"teacher\nrollouts",purple),(3.65,"verify /\nselect",orange),(5.45,"distillation\ndata",teal),(7.35,"student",blue)]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.3),1.3,.62,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.65,1.61,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for x in [1.53,3.33,5.13,7.03]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,1.61),(x+.25,1.61),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=11))
ax.text(4.8,.55,"The selected teacher output is a training target, not a certificate of faithful reasoning.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,8.9); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 42.1

title: Distillation and Efficient Reasoning
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

A teacher can spend more computation than a student
The teacher may be larger, use more samples, call a verifier, or search longer trajectories. The student is trained to produce a useful answer with fewer parameters, shorter outputs, or one pass. The intended gain is a better accuracy–latency–cost frontier, not necessarily identical outputs.


Code
systems={"teacher":{"accuracy":.78,"tokens":1800,"latency":4.1},"student":{"accuracy":.69,"tokens":260,"latency":.5}}
for name,metrics in systems.items(): print(name,metrics)




Distillation targets can have different information
Answer distillation trains on a final selected answer. Trace distillation includes intermediate text. Logit distillation matches a teacher distribution over tokens. Each target changes what the student can imitate. A long teacher trace can contain useful decomposition, unnecessary prose, or an error that happened not to affect the final answer. Selection and filtering are therefore part of the dataset construction.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5,3.2)); ax.axis("off")
for i,(label,c) in enumerate([("answer",blue),("trace",orange),("logits",teal)]): ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.5+i*2.65,1.35),1.8,.6,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(1.4+i*2.65,1.65,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.text(4.3,.55,"Choose targets according to the student task and evaluation, not because a trace appears explanatory.",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(0,8.5); ax.set_ylim(.2,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 42.2





A target needs provenance as well as content
For every retained target, record which teacher version generated it, the prompt and context supplied to the teacher, generation settings, tools or retrieval sources used, selection rule, verification result, and date. A student trained on an answer produced with a private retrieval index or an unavailable tool may learn a response pattern that cannot be supported at deployment. A student trained on public sources may still need a record of the source boundary when the task asks for citations or time-sensitive facts.
Provenance also separates teacher quality from data leakage. If a teacher response was generated after exposure to an evaluation item or with access to its answer key, it should not become a target for a student evaluated on that item family. Classical distillation transfers a teacher signal through a defined training objective; the signal is only interpretable when its source distribution and interface are known (Hinton, Vinyals, and Dean 2015).

title: Distillation and Efficient Reasoning
text:
Level 2 - Data and training mechanics

Teacher filtering determines what is learned
Teacher outputs can be retained only when an exact verifier accepts, when several samples agree, when a human reviewer approves, or when a learned score crosses a threshold. Each policy changes coverage. Filtering only easy verified examples can create a clean but narrow student dataset; retaining unverified traces can transfer errors and unsupported claims.


Code
teacher_outputs=[{"answer":12,"verified":True},{"answer":13,"verified":False},{"answer":12,"verified":True}]
targets=[row for row in teacher_outputs if row["verified"]]
print("retained targets:",targets)


The student loss can be ordinary next-token cross-entropy over selected targets, a divergence from teacher logits, or a mixture with original data. The data mixture, target mask, template, tokenizer, and maximum length remain the training contract from Chapters 25 and 29.
Target selection is a substantive modelling choice. A verified final answer may be appropriate when the deployment task only needs a final answer. A trace may be retained when intermediate steps are needed for checking or user-facing explanation, but it should be filtered separately from the answer. A teacher can produce a correct answer with an unsupported trace, or a useful trace that is too long for the student’s context and serving budget. Store answer and trace acceptance decisions separately so that later evaluation can identify what the student was trained to imitate.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9.2,3.7)); ax.axis("off")
steps=[("teacher\noutputs",purple),("answer\ncheck",orange),("trace\nreview",teal),("length and\ndeduplication",blue),("targets",purple)]
for i,(label,c) in enumerate(steps):
    x=.2+i*1.8; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.45),1.25,.58,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.625,1.74,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=8)
    if i<len(steps)-1: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x+1.28,1.74),(x+1.72,1.74),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=10))
ax.text(4.6,.65,"Keep rejection reasons: incorrect answer, unsupported trace, excess length, or duplicate target.",ha="center",color=grey,fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(0,9.1); ax.set_ylim(.25,2.5); plt.show()



Figure 42.3





Filtering changes coverage and the student task distribution
Filtering is often described as quality control, but it also changes which problems the student sees. Exact verification can concentrate targets in tasks with easy-to-check answers. A length limit can remove the multi-step cases that motivated the teacher. Deduplication can reduce repeated templates while also removing an important high-frequency deployment pattern. Report retention rates by task type, difficulty proxy, target length, verifier result, and rejection reason.
The student dataset may combine teacher targets with original instruction data, human-written examples, or tasks designed to preserve general capabilities. The mixture weights define a trade-off between imitation of the teacher and retention of behaviours outside the teacher-target distribution. Changing that mixture changes the effective objective. Hold the evaluation suite fixed and report student outcomes by the sources of the training mixture rather than treating a single loss value as evidence of general transfer.
Target diversity needs its own review. Multiple teacher answers can encode alternative valid strategies, but a dataset dominated by one preferred trace style can narrow the student’s outputs and make it brittle when a task requires another route. Group targets by task, answer form, length, tool use, and verifier outcome; then inspect whether the retained distribution reflects deployment demand or only the teacher’s easiest successes. Diversity is not a goal in itself. It is evidence about the range of behaviour the student has an opportunity to learn.
Evaluate the student both on target-like held-out tasks and on tasks that deliberately require a different valid answer form. The first tests transfer fidelity; the second tests whether filtering produced an unnecessarily narrow response policy.
Report both results before choosing a target-filtering policy for deployment.

title: Distillation and Efficient Reasoning
text:
Level 3 - Efficiency and routing

Efficiency needs a matched comparison
Compare teacher and student under the same task set, prompt template, decoding rule, context policy, and scoring criterion. Report accuracy, calibration or abstention where relevant, generated tokens, model calls, peak memory, latency distribution, throughput, and cost. A student that copies short answers may appear efficient while failing tasks that need a longer explanation or tool call.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8,4)); x=[4.1,.5,1.0]; y=[.78,.69,.74]; labels=["teacher","student","routed"]
ax.scatter(x,y,s=100,color=[purple,blue,teal]);
for a,b,l in zip(x,y,labels): ax.text(a,b+.01,l,ha="center")
ax.set_xlabel("latency"); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy"); ax.set_ylim(.6,.82); ax.set_title("Illustrative accuracy-latency trade-off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 42.4





Efficiency claims need a break-even boundary
Teacher generation is an upfront cost that can be amortised only over a stated number of student-served requests. Let teacher-data generation cost be (C_T), student training cost be (C_S), teacher serving cost per request be (c_T), and student serving cost be (c_S). The student becomes cheaper than teacher-only serving after enough requests that the saved per-request cost exceeds (C_T+C_S), subject to the quality constraint that motivated distillation. The calculation changes when a routed system still sends some requests to the teacher.
Memory footprint and throughput can matter separately from single-request latency. A smaller student may permit larger batches or a cheaper device, but a long student trace can erase the expected token saving. Report the serving configuration, batch policy, precision, context length, caching policy, and quality threshold used for the comparison. Chapter 32 explains some execution mechanisms; this chapter uses them only to define a matched teacher–student efficiency claim.


Routing can reserve the teacher for difficult inputs
A deployment can use a student for routine requests and route uncertain, high-stakes, or verifier-failing requests to a slower teacher. The routing signal must be available before the final answer and evaluated by route. A student confidence score can be miscalibrated; a failed verifier may be a verifier limitation rather than evidence of a difficult problem.
Routing has false positives and false negatives. An unnecessary teacher escalation consumes the budget without improving the answer. A missed escalation leaves a difficult input with the student. Evaluate routing on a held-out set by reporting the fraction routed, student-only accuracy, teacher-routed accuracy, and the counterfactual performance of the alternative route where it can be obtained. The threshold is a deployment decision that trades expected error against latency and cost.




Code
matrix=np.array([[62,8],[12,18]])
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5,4)); ax.imshow(matrix,cmap="Purples")
ax.set_xticks([0,1],["student sufficient","teacher needed"]); ax.set_yticks([0,1],["student route","teacher route"])
for i in range(2):
    for j in range(2): ax.text(j,i,str(matrix[i,j]),ha="center",va="center",fontsize=14)
ax.set_title("Illustrative routing confusion matrix"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 42.5





Code
uncertainty=np.array([.1,.7,.3]); routes=np.where(uncertainty>.5,"teacher","student")
print(routes)




Routing needs abstention, fallback, and drift rules
The routing policy should specify what happens when its uncertainty signal is unavailable, the student output cannot be parsed, the teacher is unavailable, or the request falls outside the routing model’s intended domain. A system can abstain, use a conservative teacher route, return a bounded student answer, or request clarification. These choices change both error and cost and should be evaluated as policy branches rather than handled silently.
Routing also changes over time when the request distribution, student version, teacher version, or verifier changes. Monitor the routed fraction, escalation reasons, teacher benefit on a sampled counterfactual set, and route-specific failure categories. A rising escalation rate may indicate that the student no longer covers the workload; a falling rate may reflect a threshold change rather than a better student. Keep the threshold and routing model version in the deployment record.

title: Distillation and Efficient Reasoning
text:
Level 4 - Audit and limits

Distillation can transmit errors and incentives
The teacher may be wrong, exploit a reward, cite unavailable sources, or produce a plausible trace that is not faithful. A verified answer target can still hide an invalid process; a trace target can teach stylistic reasoning without improved outcomes. Audit teacher error categories, filtering exclusions, data overlap with evaluations, and student regressions on inputs unlike the teacher dataset.
Efficiency claims need the whole pipeline boundary. Teacher-data generation can be expensive even if the student is cheap at serving time. Report whether the claimed saving is per request, after amortising teacher generation over a stated number of requests, or at a fixed quality threshold. A routed system also needs a route-level error record: which inputs were escalated, why, and whether the teacher actually improved the result.


Teacher–student disagreement identifies what was and was not transferred
Evaluate cases where teacher and student disagree, including teacher-correct/student-wrong, student-correct/teacher-wrong, both-wrong, and answers that differ only in format or trace. This is more informative than an average imitation loss. A student may improve on a narrow deployment slice by avoiding an expensive teacher habit, while losing performance on tasks that require the teacher’s search or tool use. These outcomes need task scoring, not a presumption that the teacher is always the gold standard.
Regression tests should cover inputs outside the teacher-target distribution: different lengths, formats, domains, languages where relevant, tool availability, and adversarial or malformed requests. The objective is to identify the scope of transfer and the system conditions under which the student should defer, not to claim that a student contains a compressed copy of all teacher capabilities.


Code
record={"teacher":"search-v2","selection":"exact verifier","target":"answer only","student":"small-v1","routing":"uncertainty threshold","evaluation":"held-out"}
assert {"teacher","selection","target","student","evaluation"} <= set(record)
print("distillation record complete")


The audit record should include the cost of target generation and filtering, data retention by reason, student training configuration, route policy and threshold, and the model versions used for every comparison. If the teacher is updated, regenerate or version the target set rather than treating new teacher outputs as interchangeable with the old dataset. These fields permit a later evaluator to separate a student-model change from a new teacher, a changed filter, or a change in the request mix.

title: Distillation and Efficient Reasoning
text:
Common misconceptions

A distilled student contains the teacher’s reasoning procedure. It learns from selected outputs under a limited distribution.
Verified targets make student evaluation unnecessary. The student can fail to generalise or change formatting and stopping behaviour.
Shorter traces always mean efficient reasoning. They can omit needed computation or explanation.
Routing removes the need to evaluate the student. Each route and routing error requires measurement.
A student matching teacher loss has matched task capability. Outcome and systems evaluation remain necessary.

title: Distillation and Efficient Reasoning
text:
Summary
Distillation transfers selected teacher behaviour to a student that can be cheaper to deploy. Its result depends on teacher generation, target type, filtering, student training, and routing policy. Evaluate the student and complete system on task outcome, reliability, latency, and cost rather than treating imitation as proof of transferred reasoning.
Chapter 42 closes Part V with reward hacking, trace faithfulness, verification gaps, benchmark overfitting, and unresolved questions about reasoning evaluation.

title: Distillation and Efficient Reasoning
text:
Looking ahead
Distillation changes the cost and observability of a reasoning system without removing the need to evaluate its resulting behaviour. Chapter 42 brings together the limits of proxy rewards, verifiers, search, evidence, and deployment claims.

text:
Further reading
Classical knowledge distillation is introduced by Hinton, Vinyals, and Dean (2015). Reasoning-model distillation should be assessed with the outcome and process distinctions developed in Chapters 35–40.






Hinton, Geoffrey, Oriol Vinyals, and Jeff Dean. 2015. “Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1503.02531. https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531.

title: Limits and Open Questions
text: Chapter orientation

title: Limits and Open Questions
Limits and Open Questions
section: Level 1 - Limits follow from the training signal
text:
Level 1 - Limits follow from the training signal

A proxy can be optimised without solving the intended task
Rewards, learned judges, automatic verifiers, and benchmark metrics are signals. They simplify a broader task into a measurable condition. A policy can improve the signal while exploiting a loophole, selecting an easy subset, or producing an answer that looks appropriate to the evaluator. The more aggressively a system is optimised against a proxy, the more independent evaluation matters.
The relevant question is always which task property the proxy actually observes. An exact arithmetic checker observes a narrow but useful property. A learned judge may observe style, answer format, or agreement with its own training labels in addition to the intended property. A benchmark score observes performance on its item set and interface. The audit should name this measurement boundary before interpreting an optimisation gain.


Proxy audits need deliberate abuse cases
A reward audit should construct cases that satisfy the observable condition while failing the intended task, then test whether the system receives reward or selection preference. For a parser, vary equivalent answer forms, malformed delimiters, and extraneous text. For a source-based response, test irrelevant citations, outdated sources, and claims that cite a source without being entailed by it. For a learned judge, include confident but false answers and unusual but valid answer forms. The purpose is to map the proxy’s known blind spots before a policy is trained aggressively against it.
Record the exploit family, the expected task judgement, the proxy result, and the mitigation or residual risk. A mitigation can close one loophole while opening another or changing the distribution of accepted outputs. The independent test must remain outside the optimisation loop; otherwise the policy can learn the revised test rather than the intended task. This is the same distinction between a verifier’s score and the outcome it is supposed to indicate that motivates verifier-guided evaluation (Cobbe et al. 2021).


Code
cases=[{"reward":1,"task_success":1,"description":"valid solution"},{"reward":1,"task_success":0,"description":"verifier loophole"}]
for case in cases: print(case)






Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,3)); ax.axis("off")
for x,label,c in [(.4,"policy\nupdate","#24527a"),(2.7,"proxy score","#d97745"),(5.2,"task\noutcome","#3a9188")]: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.2),1.5,.6,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.75,1.5,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((1.95,1.5),(2.65,1.5),arrowstyle="-|>")); ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((4.25,1.5),(5.15,1.5),arrowstyle="-|>")); ax.text(4.3,.55,"Measure both; do not infer one from the other.",ha="center"); plt.show()



Figure 43.1







Code
rows=[["numeric answer","exact parser","unsupported answer form","alternative parser"],
      ["useful plan","learned judge","confident wording","expert review"],
      ["grounded response","citation check","irrelevant citation","source entailment"]]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,2.8)); ax.axis("off")
table=ax.table(cellText=rows,colLabels=["intended property","observed proxy","possible loophole","independent check"],loc="center",cellLoc="left")
table.auto_set_font_size(False); table.set_fontsize(8); table.scale(1,1.55)
ax.set_title("Illustrative proxy-audit record",pad=12); plt.show()

title: Limits and Open Questions
text:
Level 2 - Trace and verification limits

Visible steps are not a complete account of computation
A natural-language rationale may be useful for checking an arithmetic step or communicating an answer. It can also be incomplete, post-hoc, or selected for readability. Hidden computation cannot be inspected directly by a user. Neither condition justifies an invented explanation. Faithfulness remains an intervention question: does changing the proposed explanatory element change the relevant computation or outcome in the predicted way?


Code
trace_test={"trace_plausible":True,"answer_correct":False,"faithfulness_established":False}
print(trace_test)


Verification has a parallel limit. Exact verifiers are strong where the specification is complete. Many real tasks have incomplete rules, ambiguous objectives, or evidence that changes over time. A system should state which condition it checked and which it did not.
Verification should therefore be treated as a component with coverage. A program test can establish that a submitted program passes listed cases, not that it satisfies every unstated requirement. A source checker can establish that a citation is present, not that it supports the claim. When the specification is partial, an accepted result should be described as accepted under the stated test, and independent cases should target the most plausible omissions.


A verifier also has false acceptance, false rejection, and abstention behaviour
Coverage is not enough to describe a verifier. A verifier can accept an invalid candidate, reject a valid one, fail to parse an answer, time out, or abstain because the property cannot be checked. These outcomes affect both training and deployment. False acceptance can teach or return an error; false rejection can remove a rare correct candidate from search or distillation; an unrecorded abstention can make an accepted-only accuracy statistic appear stronger than the actual system outcome.
Evaluate the verifier on labelled cases that include its expected operating distribution and likely adversarial or out-of-format cases. Report error rates by task slice and state the policy for unverified candidates: reject, defer, request another candidate, route to review, or return a bounded response. Process-supervision work highlights a related limitation: adding intermediate evaluation creates another judge whose validity requires separate evidence (Lightman et al. 2023).




Code
from matplotlib.patches import Circle
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5,4)); ax.axis("off")
ax.add_patch(Circle((3.0,2.0),1.45,facecolor="#dce9f2",edgecolor=blue,alpha=.9)); ax.text(3.0,2.8,"intended task",ha="center",color=blue)
ax.add_patch(Circle((2.45,1.75),.85,facecolor="#f4d9c9",edgecolor=orange,alpha=.9)); ax.text(2.45,1.75,"checked\ncondition",ha="center",fontsize=9)
ax.text(4.15,1.3,"uncovered\nproperties",ha="center",color=grey); ax.set_xlim(1,5.2); ax.set_ylim(.3,3.6); plt.show()



Figure 43.3

title: Limits and Open Questions
text:
Level 3 - Evaluation and generalisation

Benchmark performance is conditional evidence
Reasoning benchmarks can be contaminated, public, narrow, or susceptible to prompt and reward optimisation. A high score may establish performance on a well-defined test distribution while leaving open whether the system transfers to new variants, other languages, longer contexts, or tasks without an exact verifier. Refreshing item pools and retaining hidden holdouts help, but they do not replace task-specific deployment evaluation.
Generalisation evidence has layers. A held-out split from the same generator tests one form of interpolation. Paraphrases, changed values, and new templates test declared surface invariances. A new task generator or deployment workflow tests a stronger transfer claim. These designs answer different questions and should not be reported as if they supplied the same evidence. Contamination checks likewise need a documented search procedure, data cutoff, and a decision about items with uncertain exposure.


Benchmark provenance and deployment evidence answer different questions
A benchmark record should identify its item source, generator or collection process, publication date, answer interface, scoring rule, access conditions, and the model-development activities that could have exposed the system to it. These fields do not prove that contamination is absent. They make the exposure claim inspectable and identify which items need replacement or separate reporting. Broad language-model evaluations illustrate why a single aggregate score must be read through its scenarios and measurement choices (Liang et al. 2022).
Deployment evidence begins where the benchmark ends. It records the incoming task distribution, tool availability, user-facing constraints, route or abstention policy, resource budget, and observed failures after release. A model can score well on a static test and still fail because its inputs arrive in a different format, its sources are stale, or a downstream decision requires a property the benchmark did not score. These are not exceptions to evaluation; they define the scope of the system claim.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,3.2)); ax.axis("off")
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.5,1.35),2.1,.6,facecolor="#7655a6",edgecolor="white")); ax.text(1.55,1.65,"benchmark result",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((3.4,1.35),1.9,.6,facecolor="#3a9188",edgecolor="white")); ax.text(4.35,1.65,"tested claim",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((5.9,1.35),1.6,.6,facecolor="#d97745",edgecolor="white")); ax.text(6.7,1.65,"new domain",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.text(6.7,.8,"new evaluation required",ha="center",color="#d97745"); plt.show()



Figure 43.4







Code
levels=["held-out\nitems","controlled\nvariants","new task\ngenerator","deployment\nevaluation"]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,3.7)); ax.axis("off")
for i,label in enumerate(levels):
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.4+i*1.85,.55+i*.42),1.45,.55,facecolor=[blue,teal,purple,orange][i],edgecolor="white")); ax.text(1.125+i*1.85,.825+i*.42,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
ax.text(4.0,2.75,"Broader claims require evidence beyond the fixed benchmark interface.",ha="center",color=grey)
ax.set_xlim(0,8); ax.set_ylim(.2,3.2); plt.show()



Figure 43.5





Generalisation estimates have uncertainty and failure concentration
An observed difference across a benchmark or a controlled variant is an estimate from a finite set of items. Report the number of items, paired outcomes where systems are compared on the same cases, and uncertainty appropriate to the score. More importantly, inspect whether the difference is concentrated in one template, one answer format, one verifier condition, or a small number of high-cost errors. A stable aggregate can conceal a deployment-relevant slice that fails consistently.
New task generators and deployment tests also need versioning. If an evaluation set is refreshed after a model failure, retain the earlier version and mark the change; otherwise later comparisons cannot distinguish a model improvement from an easier or differently composed test. The objective is not an immutable benchmark. It is a record of which evidence supported each system decision at the time it was made.

title: Limits and Open Questions
section: Level 4 - Open questions and responsible claims
text:
Level 4 - Open questions and responsible claims

The unresolved questions are empirical
Open questions include how to measure whether a trace is faithful; how to train process supervision without rewarding a style; how to verify open-ended reasoning; how inference-time compute generalises across tasks; how to detect reward hacking before deployment; and how to compare systems with different hidden computation and costs. These questions require experiments with defined interventions and held-out tasks, not labels attached to outputs.
An appropriate concluding claim names the task distribution, the mechanism, the comparison, the resource change, and the remaining uncertainty. For example, a result may show that a fixed candidate-and-verifier procedure improves exact accuracy on held-out problems from one generator at a stated token cost. It does not establish faithful visible reasoning, broad transfer, or a property of hidden computation unless those claims received separate evidence. This is a restriction on interpretation, not a reason to discard a measured result.


Hidden computation changes the evidence available to users and auditors
A system may use internal activations, private tools, hidden tokens, or proprietary retrieval and still be evaluated on observable task outcomes, resources, and interfaces. What cannot be concluded is that a concise visible explanation faithfully reports the inaccessible computation. An organisation that withholds traces should state what record is retained for debugging, what an external evaluator can inspect, which failures can be reconstructed, and which claims remain untestable because the relevant state is unavailable.
This is an accountability boundary. It does not require exposing every intermediate representation or confidential prompt. It does require that the system not substitute a polished rationale for an unavailable audit trail. Task outcomes, verifier decisions, tool-call status, budget exhaustion, and versioned policy changes can be recorded without claiming that they reveal the model’s entire internal process.


Limits require a deployment decision, not only a disclosure
An identified limit should change a system policy where the consequence warrants it. A verifier with poor coverage can trigger abstention or review for the uncovered class. A suspected reward exploit can pause a training update or remove the affected reward version. A trace that is useful for communication but not faithful should be labelled as an explanation or summary rather than evidence of the causal process. A benchmark that no longer reflects the workload should lose its role as the main release criterion.
The decision record should identify the limit, the affected task slice, the monitoring signal, the action threshold, the owner, and the review date. This makes uncertainty operational. It also prevents a general warning about limitations from becoming a reason to leave known high-consequence failures without a response policy.
Version the decision record with the model, verifier, tool, prompt, and deployment configuration it governs. A response policy that was adequate for one system can become invalid when any of those components changes.
Review changes before they reach users, not only after incidents occur.


Open questions require a stated evidential path
Each unresolved question should be converted into an experiment or monitoring obligation. Trace faithfulness requires a defined intervention and predicted outcome. Process supervision requires labelled step data, judge-error analysis, and a comparison with outcome-only feedback. Reward-hacking detection requires held-out abuse cases and independent outcomes. Claims about inference-time scaling require matched budgets, candidate dependence records, and task slices. Claims about general transfer require a new generator or deployment evaluation rather than another score on the same public item pool.
The remaining uncertainty should be recorded when a system is deployed, not deferred to a final caveat. Name the unmeasured property, the evidence that would be needed, the consequence if the property fails, and the decision owner responsible for updating or limiting the system. That record connects the reasoning module to the deployment and safety questions developed in Part VI.

ax.add_patch(Rectangle((3.0,1.65),2.0,.62,facecolor=purple,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(4.0,1.96,"measured result",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
for x,y,label,c in [(0.6,2.7,"task",blue),(5.8,2.7,"mechanism",teal),(.6,.65,"comparison",orange),(5.8,.65,"resources",blue),(3.0,.35,"limits",orange)]:

ax.set_xlim(0,8); ax.set_ylim(0,3.5); plt.show()

title: Limits and Open Questions
text:
Common misconceptions

A reasoning trace is a proof of reasoning. It is output that needs its own evaluation.
A verifier closes the evaluation problem. It covers only its declared acceptance condition.
Reward optimisation solves alignment. It can optimise an incomplete proxy.
A benchmark gain is a general capability claim. It is evidence under a measured distribution.
Hidden computation removes accountability. Outcomes, resources, and system traces remain evaluable.

title: Limits and Open Questions
text:
Summary
Reasoning systems can improve defined outcomes through search, verification, reward learning, and distillation. Their limits arise from proxy optimisation, incomplete verifiers, unreliable traces, narrow benchmarks, and unobserved computation. Claims should remain tied to the task, mechanism, evaluation, cost, and known gaps.
Part VI turns to modern AI systems: mixture-of-experts models, vision and diffusion architectures, multimodality, scaling, deployment, and safety.

title: Mixture-of-experts Models
text: Chapter orientation

title: Mixture-of-experts Models
text:
Why this chapter matters
A dense Transformer applies the same feed-forward parameters to every token. Increasing its capacity therefore increases the computation and memory required for every token. A mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer replaces one feed-forward subnetwork with several experts and a router that activates only a small subset for each token. The model can contain many more parameters than a comparably priced dense layer, while its active computation remains bounded by the selected experts.
That arithmetic is incomplete. A useful MoE layer must decide which experts receive which tokens, prevent a few experts from receiving most of the work, and move token representations to the devices that hold the selected experts. Routing and communication are therefore part of the model, not implementation detail. This chapter establishes those mechanisms before the later chapters on serving, monitoring, and safety.


Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish total parameters from active parameters per token;
describe router scores, top- k selection, expert outputs, and weighted combination;
calculate a toy expert-capacity limit and identify dropped or rerouted tokens;
explain why load balancing changes both training and systems behaviour;
compare dense and MoE cost under a stated routing policy; and
specify an MoE evaluation and deployment record.



Running layer
The running example has four feed-forward experts and a router that selects two per token. The numbers are deliberately small so that routing, capacity, and aggregation can be inspected directly.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")

fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,4)); ax.axis("off")
for i in range(3):
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.3,.7+i*.8),1.1,.38,facecolor=blue,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(.85,.89+i*.8,f"token {i+1}",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((2.2,1.35),1.2,.6,facecolor=purple,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(2.8,1.65,"router",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
for i in range(4):
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((4.4,2.75-i*.8),1.25,.42,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(5.03,2.96-i*.8,f"expert {i+1}",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((7.0,1.35),1.55,.6,facecolor=orange,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(7.78,1.65,"weighted output",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
for y in [1.09,1.89,2.69]: ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((1.45,y),(2.15,1.65),arrowstyle="-|>",color=grey,mutation_scale=9))

ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(.2,3.5); plt.show()



Figure 44.1

title: Mixture-of-experts Models
text:
Level 1 - Intuition

Capacity can grow without activating every parameter
The dense layer asks one feed-forward network to process every token. An MoE layer gives the router several such networks and lets it select specialists conditionally. A token associated with code-like text may be routed differently from a token in another language or a mathematical expression. The system does not need a semantic story about each expert for this to be useful; the operational claim is that different tokens activate different parameter subsets.
Sparse activation changes the comparison. A model with eight experts may store roughly eight feed-forward parameter sets, but a top-2 router only executes two for one token. Parameter count therefore measures stored capacity, while active parameters and communication determine per-token cost. The sparsely gated MoE layer formalised this conditional-computation approach, and subsequent work made routing simple enough to support large Transformer training (Shazeer et al. 2017; Fedus, Zoph, and Shazeer 2022).


Code
dense_parameters=100
experts,active=8,2
print({"dense_active":dense_parameters,"moe_total":experts*dense_parameters,"moe_active":active*dense_parameters})






Code
labels=["dense\nactive","MoE\ntotal","MoE\nactive"]; values=[100,800,200]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5,4)); ax.bar(labels,values,color=[blue,purple,teal]); ax.set_ylabel("illustrative parameter units")
ax.set_title("Stored and active parameter counts"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 44.2





Routing is conditional on a token and its batch context
The router score is computed from a token representation, but the realised dispatch can depend on the surrounding batch. Capacity limits, token order, expert-parallel layout, and tie handling determine which selected assignments are actually processed when several tokens request the same expert. Two copies of the same token can therefore receive different fallback treatment in different batches even when their router scores are unchanged. A routing claim should distinguish the score produced by the router from the assignment that reached an expert.
This distinction matters for reproducibility. Record the batching and packing policy, sequence lengths, top-k rule, capacity factor, token ordering where relevant, and whether assignment is deterministic under a fixed seed. An average routing histogram can conceal a capacity conflict that occurs only in long sequences or one language slice. The relevant unit for systems evaluation is the realised assignment and its outcome, not only the router’s preferred expert.

title: Mixture-of-experts Models
text:
Level 2 - Routing and capacity mechanics

Router scores become a sparse dispatch decision
For token representation (x), a router produces one score per expert. A softmax can turn the scores into non-negative weights. Top- k routing retains only the k largest weights, renormalises them, sends the token to those experts, and combines their outputs. If experts are functions (f_e), the layer output is the weighted sum of the selected (f_e(x)). This is conditional computation: routing determines which parameters participate in this token’s forward and backward pass.


Code
scores=np.array([1.8,.4,1.2,-.3])
weights=np.exp(scores-scores.max()); weights=weights/weights.sum()
chosen=np.argsort(weights)[-2:]; selected=weights[chosen]/weights[chosen].sum()
print("router weights:",np.round(weights,3),"experts:",chosen,"renormalised:",np.round(selected,3))






Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); colours=[orange if i in chosen else grey for i in range(4)]
ax.bar(range(4),weights,color=colours); ax.set_xticks(range(4),["expert 1","2","3","4"]); ax.set_ylabel("router weight")
ax.set_title("Illustrative top-two router decision"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 44.3





Top-k selection has ties, normalisation, and gradient consequences
Top-k creates a discontinuous membership decision: an expert just below the cutoff receives no expert computation for that token, while one just above it receives a renormalised weight. Ties and near-ties therefore require a deterministic or recorded tie rule. The selected weights should sum to one if the implementation defines a weighted combination, but the unselected router scores can still matter for the router’s learning signal and auxiliary objectives.
The router and experts also receive different gradients. Selected experts receive token-specific gradients; unselected experts do not receive that token’s expert-path gradient. Router updates depend on the routing formulation and losses used to encourage balance or exploration. These are reasons to report router settings separately from the feed-forward expert architecture. A change in top-k or normalisation affects both the active computation and the data each expert sees during training.
Report these choices with the checkpoint, training batch policy, and evaluator version.


Capacity limits make dispatch observable
Experts cannot process an unlimited number of token assignments in one batch. A capacity factor sets a per-expert quota relative to the average expected load. When an expert is full, the implementation may drop an assignment, send it to a backup expert, or preserve a residual path. Each choice changes the layer output and must be reported. A low capacity limit raises the chance of discarded routes; a high limit reserves memory and can leave accelerator work uneven.


Code
assignments=np.array([0,0,0,1,1,2,3,3]); capacity=2
counts=np.bincount(assignments,minlength=4); overflow=np.maximum(counts-capacity,0)
print("expert loads:",counts,"overflow:",overflow)






Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.bar(range(4),counts,color=[orange if c>capacity else teal for c in counts])
ax.axhline(capacity,color=purple,linestyle="--",label="capacity"); ax.set_xticks(range(4),["expert 1","2","3","4"]); ax.set_ylabel("token assignments"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title("Illustrative capacity overflow"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 44.4





Overflow handling defines an output contract
Dropping an assignment, rerouting it to a lower-ranked expert, or using a residual dense path are different model behaviours. Dropping can reduce computation but may remove information from a token’s update. Rerouting can retain an expert computation while changing the router’s intended choice. A residual path can preserve a dense fallback but changes the active-parameter and cost comparison. There is no neutral overflow policy.
The overflow record should therefore include the selected experts, successful assignments, fallback type, and the final path used for each affected token. Measure overflow separately from router entropy or load balance: a router can look balanced on average while still producing concentrated conflicts at the capacity boundary. Evaluate overflow on held-out batches and changed sequence-length distributions, because a capacity factor chosen on one workload may fail on another.

title: Mixture-of-experts Models
text:
Level 3 - Training and systems constraints

Load balancing supplies a training signal and a hardware constraint
If a router repeatedly selects one expert, that expert becomes a bottleneck while other experts receive little data or gradient signal. MoE training commonly adds an auxiliary load-balancing objective based on routing probabilities and realised assignments. The objective encourages use of the available experts; it does not prove that expert specialisation is meaningful or that all experts should receive identical traffic.
The systems consequence is immediate. Tokens assigned to experts on other devices must be exchanged, processed, and returned. The slowest or most overloaded expert can determine the layer’s step time. GShard treated conditional computation and sharding together because large MoE training requires both a routing rule and an execution plan (Lepikhin et al. 2020).


Code
loads=np.array([47,26,17,10]); uniform=np.repeat(25,4)
print("absolute deviation from equal load:",np.abs(loads-uniform).sum())






Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.bar(range(4),loads,color=[orange,teal,teal,teal]); ax.axhline(25,color=purple,linestyle="--",label="equal share")
ax.set_xticks(range(4),["expert 1","2","3","4"]); ax.set_ylabel("share of assignments (%)"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Illustrative routing imbalance")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 44.5





Load balancing has probability, assignment, and quality diagnostics
The router’s average probability mass and the realised token assignments are related but not identical. A load-balancing loss can encourage probability mass to spread across experts while top-k selection and capacity constraints still produce uneven realised loads. Report both quantities, together with overflow, expert utilisation, duplicate selections, and the coefficient of variation or another stated imbalance measure. A single auxiliary-loss value is not evidence that the dispatch is balanced.
Balance also has a quality boundary. Equal traffic can be undesirable if a subset of tasks genuinely needs a particular expert and the balance penalty forces it elsewhere. Conversely, concentrated traffic may expose an expert to a narrow data slice and leave other experts poorly trained. Compare task outcome and routing diagnostics as the balance coefficient changes, keeping the rest of the training contract fixed. Sparse-routing systems such as GShard and Switch Transformers make these routing and capacity choices part of the training design, not a post-training serving adjustment (Lepikhin et al. 2020; Fedus, Zoph, and Shazeer 2022).


A dense comparison requires an end-to-end cost record
MoE can reduce active feed-forward computation for a given stored capacity, but it can also add router work, dispatch overhead, all-to-all communication, padding to expert capacity, and latency variation across requests. Compare dense and sparse models under the same sequence lengths, batch policy, precision, hardware, and quality metric. A parameter count alone cannot establish a serving advantage.


Code
systems={"dense":{"compute":100,"communication":0,"latency":12},"moe":{"compute":35,"communication":18,"latency":14}}
for name,record in systems.items(): print(name,record)




Dispatch has a topology and a synchronisation cost
In an expert-parallel layout, a token may need to leave the device that computed its shared attention representation, be grouped with tokens for its selected expert, and return before the next shared layer. The cost depends on the device placement of experts, communication links, token imbalance, message sizes, and the slowest participating device. All-to-all exchange can make the latency of a layer depend on a small overloaded expert even when the average active computation is low.
Measure dispatch separately from expert matrix multiplication. A useful systems record includes expert-to-device placement, number of devices, communication volume, padding induced by capacity, collective-operation timing, and tail rather than only mean latency. Distributed training and model-parallel work supplies the relevant distinction between local computation and communication or synchronisation cost (Li et al. 2020; Narayanan et al. 2021). The same distinction applies when comparing a sparse layer with a dense layer on a declared hardware topology.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.bar(["dense","MoE"],[100,35],color=[blue,teal],label="expert computation")
ax.bar(["dense","MoE"],[0,8],bottom=[100,35],color=purple,label="routing")
ax.bar(["dense","MoE"],[0,18],bottom=[100,43],color=orange,label="communication")
ax.set_ylabel("illustrative cost units"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("End-to-end cost decomposition"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 44.6

title: Mixture-of-experts Models
text:
Level 4 - Evaluation, deployment, and limits

Evaluate routing as well as task output
An MoE report should include task quality, total and active parameters, experts and top-k, routing distribution, capacity factor, overflow or fallback rate, auxiliary-loss weight, sequence length, batch size, precision, hardware topology, communication volume, throughput, and latency distribution. Report these by input slice where routing differs across languages, lengths, or domains. Aggregate accuracy can conceal an expert that is overloaded only for a small but important set of inputs.
Expert labels should also be interpreted cautiously. Similar token clusters in one expert can be a useful diagnostic; they do not establish a stable semantic role, causal explanation, or fairness property. Rerouting, changing capacity, or changing the batch can alter the traffic observed by an expert. The appropriate claim concerns the measured routing policy and workload.


Evaluate routing changes with matched quality and workload slices
An MoE intervention can change top-k, capacity factor, balance coefficient, overflow fallback, expert count, or device placement. Evaluate one such change at a time under the same checkpoint where possible, input distribution, sequence lengths, batch policy, precision, and quality scorer. Report task outcome together with overflow, routed fraction, per-expert load, communication, p50 and p95 latency, and memory. A throughput gain that relies on dropping more assignments or a quality gain that relies on a larger batch is not a routing result alone.
Slice the record by properties that plausibly change routing: language, input length, token class, domain, tool-call format, or a declared sensitive workload category. The purpose is not to assign an expert a human-readable identity. It is to discover whether the routing policy creates concentrated overflow, latency, or quality loss for a subset that aggregate results hide. A deployment decision can then adjust capacity, routing, or fallback for the affected workload rather than treating a global average as sufficient evidence.


Code
record={"experts":8,"top_k":2,"capacity_factor":1.25,"overflow_rate":.03,"load_cv":.31,"p95_latency_ms":28,"quality":"held-out exact match"}
assert {"experts","top_k","overflow_rate","p95_latency_ms","quality"} <= set(record)
print("MoE evaluation record complete")

title: Mixture-of-experts Models
text:
Common misconceptions

An MoE uses all of its parameters for every token. Routing activates only the selected experts.
More total parameters imply proportionally more per-token computation. Active experts, routing, and communication determine the relevant cost.
Load balancing makes experts interchangeable. It changes traffic incentives; it does not establish what each expert represents.
A router is a minor pre-processing step. It determines computation, gradients, overflow, and communication.
Sparse activation guarantees lower serving latency. Dispatch and cross-device communication can dominate the gain.

title: Mixture-of-experts Models
text:
Summary
Mixture-of-experts layers increase stored capacity through conditional expert activation. Their behaviour depends on router selection, capacity limits, load balance, dispatch, and hardware communication. Evaluate task quality together with the full routing and systems record; sparse parameters alone do not establish an efficiency claim.

title: Mixture-of-experts Models
text:
Looking ahead
Sparse routing changes where computation occurs, but it does not change the token interface that the Transformer processes. Chapter 44 examines what happens when that interface is built from image patches rather than text tokens, including the positional and data requirements that follow.
