title: Vision Transformers
text: Chapter orientation

title: Vision Transformers
Vision Transformers
text:
Level 1 - Images become token sequences

Patchification determines the visual interface
For an image of height (H) and width (W), square patches of side (P) produce (N=(H/P)(W/P)) tokens when the dimensions divide exactly. Each flattened patch is projected into the model dimension. The projection does not preserve every pixel relationship explicitly; it supplies a learned representation from which later layers must recover useful visual structure.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
blue,teal,orange,purple,grey="#24527a","#3a9188","#d97745","#7655a6","#5f6b76"
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3.8)); ax.axis("off")
for i in range(4):
 for j in range(4): ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.4+i*.28,1.3+j*.28),.27,.27,facecolor=blue if (i+j)%2 else teal,edgecolor="white"))
ax.text(.95,.75,"image patches",ha="center")
for i in range(5): ax.add_patch(Rectangle((2.2+i*.52,1.55),.42,.42,facecolor=purple,edgecolor="white"))
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((1.7,1.8),(2.1,1.8),arrowstyle="-|>")); ax.text(3.45,1.2,"patch + position embeddings",ha="center",fontsize=9)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((4.9,1.8),(5.5,1.8),arrowstyle="-|>")); ax.add_patch(Rectangle((5.6,1.48),1.4,.64,facecolor=orange,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(6.3,1.8,"Transformer",ha="center",va="center",color="white")
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((7.1,1.8),(7.7,1.8),arrowstyle="-|>")); ax.text(8.3,1.8,"class",ha="center"); ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(.4,2.7); plt.show()



Figure 45.1





Code
H=W=224; P=16; N=(H//P)*(W//P)
print({"patches":N,"tokens_with_class":N+1})




Patch projection fixes channels, scale, and patch boundaries
Patchification begins with a specific image representation: colour channels, value range, orientation, resizing policy, and crop. Flattening a 16-by-16 RGB patch produces a vector with 768 scalar values before projection; a grayscale image or a multispectral image has a different input dimension and cannot use the same projection without an explicit adaptation. The patch projection is therefore an interface between image acquisition and the Transformer, not a generic conversion from pixels to tokens.
Patch boundaries also matter. An object or edge can fall across two patches, a crop can remove a small object, and resampling can blur the feature that a downstream label depends on. Smaller patches expose more local detail but do not guarantee that the model will use it; larger patches can be sufficient when the visual signal is coarse. Store the resize, crop, channel, and patch policy with the checkpoint and evaluate the same policy on the held-out images.


Resolution and patch size are model choices
Smaller patches retain finer detail but create more tokens. Since full self-attention compares token pairs, the attention-score matrix grows approximately with (N^2). A 224-by-224 image with 16-by-16 patches gives 196 patch tokens; halving patch side length gives 784. The later model may have more visual detail available, but it also has a much larger attention computation and memory requirement.




Code
sizes=np.array([32,16,8]); tokens=(224//sizes)**2
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8,4)); ax.plot(sizes,tokens**2,marker="o",color=purple); ax.invert_xaxis(); ax.set_xlabel("patch side length (pixels)"); ax.set_ylabel("token-pair count"); ax.set_title("Attention cost from patch resolution"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 45.2





Resolution changes both evidence and computation
Increasing resolution can reveal a small object, text, or boundary that was absent from a lower-resolution input. It also changes the number of positions the model must process and the memory needed for attention. A comparison between two resolutions is therefore not a pure systems benchmark: it changes the information available to the classifier as well as the cost. Report the acquisition resolution, resize rule, crop selection, patch size, token count, and evaluation distribution together.
Position representations need a declared treatment when image grids change. A learned position table trained for one patch grid may be interpolated, resized, replaced, or used only at its original resolution. Each choice changes the input contract. Test performance at the intended resolution and, if resolution transfer is claimed, on a separately reported set rather than assuming that a position representation will generalise without loss.

title: Vision Transformers
text:
Level 2 - Position and attention

Patches require an explicit spatial contract
Flattening patches produces a sequence but does not itself specify where each patch came from. Learned or fixed positional embeddings add location information before the Transformer blocks. Without them, permuting patch order leaves the attention mechanism equivariant to that permutation, as in Chapter 21. Position tells the model that a patch came from the upper left rather than the lower right; it does not by itself supply translation invariance or local edge detectors.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,3.3)); ax.axis("off")
for x,pos in [(1.0,"row 1, col 1"),(4.3,"row 4, col 4")]:
 ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.5),1.4,.55,facecolor=teal,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.7,1.78,"patch content",ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9); ax.text(x+.7,1.1,pos,ha="center",color=purple)
ax.set_xlim(0,7); ax.set_ylim(.6,2.5); plt.show()



Figure 45.3





Spatial position and visual invariance are different requirements
Position embeddings identify where a patch occurs in the processed image grid. They do not specify whether a class should remain unchanged after translation, crop, rotation, scale change, illumination shift, or a new camera. Some transformations should leave a label stable; others should not. A medical image label may depend on a small position change, while an object-class label may not. The appropriate invariance is a property of the task and data-generating process, not of the word Transformer.
Specify which transformations are represented in training augmentation, which are held out for evaluation, and which make an image no longer comparable. An augmented crop that removes the labelled object changes the target rather than testing invariance. This distinction prevents an apparent robustness result from mixing valid visual variation with a changed task definition.


Global attention and local inductive bias differ
Convolution applies shared local filters and builds larger receptive fields across layers. ViT attention can connect distant patches directly within a layer. Neither property settles which model is preferable: the answer depends on data scale, augmentation, pretraining, resolution, compute, and the intended transfer task. A fair comparison fixes those conditions and reports them rather than treating architecture labels as results.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
for i in range(5):
 for j in range(5): ax.add_patch(Rectangle((i,j),1,1,facecolor="#e7edf1",edgecolor="white"))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((1,1),3,3,fill=False,edgecolor=orange,lw=3)); ax.annotate("attention",xy=(4.5,4.5),xytext=(.5,.5),arrowprops={"arrowstyle":"-|>","color":purple}); ax.set_xlim(0,5); ax.set_ylim(0,5); ax.set_title("Local window and distant token access"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 45.4





Architecture comparisons require matched visual evidence
Global attention and convolutional locality are architectural properties, but a reported image result also depends on the images and training policy available to each model. Match preprocessing, augmentation, label set, pretraining data boundary, optimiser, schedule, parameter or compute budget, resolution, and checkpoint-selection rule before attributing a difference to the architecture. The original ViT and data-efficient DeiT results illustrate how pretraining scale, augmentation, and distillation change the setting in which a visual Transformer is assessed (Dosovitskiy et al. 2021; Touvron et al. 2021).
The comparison should also define the prediction interface. A class token, average pooling, multi-scale feature aggregation, or a dense prediction head uses the final patch representations differently. A classification result does not establish object detection, segmentation, or localisation behaviour without a head, labels, and metrics for those tasks. Keep the claim at the task interface actually evaluated.

title: Vision Transformers
text:
Level 3 - Training and representation checks

The classification representation is a declared interface
A classification ViT can prepend a learned class token and use its final representation for a classifier, or pool patch representations. These are different interfaces and should be reported. Training also inherits the earlier contracts: image normalisation, crop policy, augmentation, label mapping, optimiser, schedule, checkpoint selection, and the split used for final evaluation.


Code
patches=np.array([[.2,.1],[.7,.3],[.1,.8]])
class_token=np.array([.5,.5]); sequence=np.vstack([class_token,patches])
print("sequence shape including class token:",sequence.shape)




Pretraining data and labels define the visual task
Pretraining can provide visual features that a small labelled dataset alone would not learn reliably. It can also introduce label definitions, geographic concentration, image-source conventions, or licensing and privacy constraints that differ from the deployment setting. Record the pretraining objective and data boundary separately from the fine-tuning dataset. A claim about transfer should identify which visual condition changed and which remained shared between pretraining and evaluation.
Label quality needs the same attention as architecture. A label may describe the whole image, a central object, a scene, a temporal state, or an annotator judgment. Crop and resize policies can change whether the labelled feature is visible. Inspect disagreement, class imbalance, missing labels, and the treatment of multi-label or ambiguous images before interpreting an apparent model error as a representation failure. The data and label contract determines the error that accuracy measures.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3)); ax.axis("off")
for i,(label,c) in enumerate([("image",blue),("preprocess",teal),("patches",purple),("train",orange),("held-out\nevaluation",blue)]):
 x=.2+i*1.75; ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1.25),1.25,.55,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white")); ax.text(x+.63,1.53,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(0,9); ax.set_ylim(.6,2.3); plt.show()



Figure 45.5





Training comparisons need checkpoint and augmentation controls
Augmentation may include random crops, flips, colour changes, masking, or mixing images and labels. These transformations can improve a model’s fit to a declared visual distribution, but they can also create examples that no longer support the original label. State the augmentation probability and order, the normalisation statistics, the optimisation schedule, and the criterion used to select the final checkpoint. Do not compare a ViT chosen from a large hyperparameter search with a baseline chosen from one run without recording the search policy.
Evaluate training stability as well as the selected checkpoint. Report variation across seeds or repeated runs where feasible, learning curves, and the relation between validation and held-out performance. A visual model can appear to improve because a crop policy matches one validation source unusually well. Preserving the split definition and checkpoint-selection record makes that possibility testable.

title: Vision Transformers
text:
Level 4 - Evaluation and limits

Image accuracy is conditional on the visual distribution
Image-classification results should report resolution, patch size, crop and normalisation policy, augmentation, pretraining data, class definitions, label quality, and test distribution. Evaluate slices where the visual task changes: viewpoint, lighting, background, object size, camera type, or geographic source. A high score on a fixed benchmark does not establish that the model recognises the same object under a changed acquisition process.
Attention maps can support an inspection of which patch relations received high weight. They do not on their own establish a causal explanation for the class prediction. Test an interpretation with interventions on patches, positional information, or the relevant visual feature, and report when the result is sensitive to preprocessing or patch boundaries.


Visual explanations need a prediction-changing intervention
An attention map, saliency map, or selected patch can be a useful hypothesis about which visual region matters. Test that hypothesis by masking, replacing, moving, or perturbing the specified region while preserving the task as far as possible, then measure the resulting prediction change. A patch that receives high attention but can be altered without affecting the result is not established as causally necessary. A prediction that changes after a broad blur or crop may reflect a preprocessing shift rather than the importance of one semantic object.
Record the intervention, the images selected for inspection, the baseline prediction, the transformed prediction, and any change in the model’s confidence or abstention decision. Visual explanations should be evaluated by image and slice; a convincing example can coexist with a procedure that fails on another acquisition condition. These records establish the limited claim that the intervention supports, not a general account of what the model sees.


Slice evaluation should distinguish acquisition, label, and representation failures
When performance falls on a visual slice, the source can be acquisition quality, a shifted class definition, label error, preprocessing mismatch, insufficient resolution, or a representation failure. Record the slice construction and inspect a bounded sample of errors before assigning cause. Low-light images may be darker because of a camera pipeline; small objects may be lost at the resize stage; a new geographic source may use another background or label convention. These are different interventions and need different responses.
For high-consequence image tasks, report abstentions, confidence calibration, review routes, and the consequences of false positives and false negatives by slice. A high aggregate accuracy cannot determine an appropriate decision threshold when the cost of errors differs across visual conditions. The evaluation record should make clear whether the model was assessed as a classifier, a triage aid, or a component that can defer to a human or another measurement process.




Code
slices=["standard","low light","small object","new camera"]; acc=[.88,.74,.67,.70]
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.bar(slices,acc,color=[blue,teal,orange,purple]); ax.set_ylim(0,1); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy"); ax.set_title("Illustrative visual-distribution slices"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



Figure 45.6

title: Vision Transformers
text:
Common misconceptions

Image patches are semantic objects. They are fixed spatial blocks projected into vectors.
Position embeddings create visual invariance. They identify location; invariance must be learned or evaluated.
Smaller patches are always better. They trade visual detail for token and attention cost.
An attention map is a causal explanation. It is a weight pattern that needs an intervention test.
ViT and convolutional models can be compared by architecture alone. Data, augmentation, resolution, pretraining, and compute affect the result.

title: Vision Transformers
text:
Summary
Vision transformers turn images into patch-token sequences and use position-aware Transformer blocks to combine visual information. Patch size, position, training data, and evaluation distribution are part of the modelling contract. The architecture offers global token interactions, but its visual claims require evidence across the relevant image conditions.

title: Vision Transformers
text:
Looking ahead
Patch-based Transformers describe how an image can be represented as a sequence; they do not specify how a new image is generated. Chapter 45 addresses that generative problem by treating image synthesis as a sequence of noise-removal decisions under a declared sampling procedure.

title: Vision Transformers
text:
Further reading
Vision Transformer is introduced by Dosovitskiy et al. (2021). Data-efficient image Transformer training and distillation are studied by Touvron et al. (2021).






Dosovitskiy, Alexey, Lucas Beyer, Alexander Kolesnikov, Dirk Weissenborn, Xiaohua Zhai, Thomas Unterthiner, Mostafa Dehghani, et al. 2021. “An Image Is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale.” In International Conference on Learning Representations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929.


Touvron, Hugo, Matthieu Cord, Matthijs Douze, Francisco Massa, Alexandre Sablayrolles, and Hervé Jégou. 2021. “Training Data-Efficient Image Transformers and Distillation Through Attention.” In International Conference on Machine Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.12877.

title: Diffusion Models
text:
Chapter orientation
Diffusion models generate an image by learning to reverse a controlled corruption process. Training starts from a data image, adds noise at a randomly chosen time step, and trains a network to predict the noise or a related denoising target. Sampling starts from noise and applies the learned reverse process repeatedly. This makes the number of denoising steps, the noise schedule, and conditioning interface part of the model’s behaviour (Ho, Jain, and Abbeel 2020).

title: Diffusion Models
section: Level 1 - From noise to an image
text:
Level 1 - From noise to an image
The forward process gradually destroys image structure. The reverse model receives a noisy image and its time step, then predicts how to remove some of that noise. One prediction does not usually recover a complete image; generation is an iterative sequence of denoising decisions.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
rng=np.random.default_rng(4); x0=np.outer(np.linspace(0,1,24),np.linspace(0,1,24))
fig,axs=plt.subplots(1,4,figsize=(9,2.5))
for ax,a,title in zip(axs,[0,.25,.6,1],["data","early","late","noise"]):
 ax.imshow(np.sqrt(1-a)*x0+np.sqrt(a)*rng.normal(size=x0.shape),cmap="viridis");ax.set_title(title);ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout();plt.show()



Figure 46.1





Code
x_t=np.array([.3,-.1,.7]); predicted_noise=np.array([.1,-.2,.2]); print(x_t-predicted_noise)

title: Diffusion Models
text:
Level 2 - Schedule, denoiser, and sampling

The schedule defines what the denoiser sees
At time (t), a schedule determines the mixture of original signal and Gaussian noise. A common representation is (x_t=x_0+). The denoiser must therefore use both (x_t) and (t): the same noisy value can require different corrections at different noise levels. A schedule that adds noise too quickly can remove useful training signal; a schedule that changes slowly can require more steps.




Code
t=np.linspace(0,1,100); signal=np.exp(-3*t); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5,3.6));ax.plot(t,signal,label="signal share");ax.plot(t,1-signal,label="noise share");ax.legend();ax.set_xlabel("diffusion time");plt.tight_layout();plt.show()



Figure 46.2





Sampling is a compute-quality trade-off
The reverse chain is expensive because it calls the denoiser repeatedly. Faster samplers can use fewer steps but must be evaluated at a matched conditioning, resolution, seed policy, and quality measure. DDIM retains the training objective while permitting faster deterministic or partially stochastic sampling trajectories (Song, Meng, and Ermon 2020).
The training target and the sampling rule must be kept distinct. Training commonly selects one time step per image and minimises error in a predicted noise term; sampling applies a sequence of model calls whose errors can accumulate. A model can have a low average training loss while producing poor samples at a particular guidance scale, resolution, or condition. Report the time-step distribution, target parameterisation, schedule, sampler, step count, and randomisation policy together.
The basic training calculation makes this distinction concrete. Draw a clean training image (x_0), a noise vector (epsilon), and a time step (t). Use the schedule to form (x_t), then provide (x_t) and a representation of (t) to the denoiser. If the model predicts (_(x_t,t)), a common loss is the mean squared difference between () and the sampled (). The target is known because the training procedure created the corruption. The model is not shown a target clean image at every reverse sampling step; it must generalise its learned correction from many noisy examples.
The reverse update uses the predicted noise together with coefficients implied by the schedule. Its purpose is to move the current state toward a less noisy distribution while retaining an appropriate amount of uncertainty. An implementation therefore has at least four linked contracts: the forward schedule used to create training inputs, the time representation, the denoiser target, and the reverse solver. Changing one while retaining the others can make a checkpoint or a reported sample comparison invalid.


Code
# A toy single-step noise-prediction loss: real image models use tensors and many time steps.
rng=np.random.default_rng(7)
x0=np.array([.2,.7,-.1]); epsilon=rng.normal(size=3); alpha_bar=.64
x_t=np.sqrt(alpha_bar)*x0+np.sqrt(1-alpha_bar)*epsilon
predicted=np.array([.1,-.2,.3])
print("noise loss:",np.mean((predicted-epsilon)**2))


Classifier-free guidance illustrates the trade-off. It combines conditional and unconditional denoising predictions to increase the influence of a condition. Raising its scale can improve apparent prompt adherence while producing artefacts or reducing diversity. It is therefore a generation control to evaluate, not a free improvement to attach to a model result.


Reverse solvers define the sampling trajectory
The schedule supplies a family of noisy distributions; the solver determines how the model traverses them at generation time. A stochastic solver introduces fresh random variation at reverse steps. A deterministic solver can map a fixed initial noise and condition to a repeatable trajectory. Reduced-step solvers select a subset of training-time noise levels or approximate a longer trajectory. These alternatives may have the same denoiser checkpoint but different latency, diversity, failure rate, and sensitivity to guidance.
Compare solvers under a fixed image resolution, condition set, seed policy, and hardware configuration. Record wall-clock latency as well as step count: a nominally short trajectory can be slower if it increases memory pressure or uses a less efficient kernel. For interactive systems, inspect cancellation, partial preview, timeout, and retry behaviour. A sample is produced by a service, not an isolated reverse equation.


Code
solvers={"stochastic":{"steps":50,"latency_ms":620,"seed_repeatable":False},"deterministic":{"steps":25,"latency_ms":340,"seed_repeatable":True}}
for name,settings in solvers.items(): print(name,settings)




Conditioning has an information boundary
Text, masks, reference images, depth maps, and class labels constrain different parts of the generation problem. A mask may identify where to edit without specifying what should be drawn. A prompt can specify an object while leaving count, viewpoint, style, or background uncertain. A reference image can preserve identity cues while also introducing unwanted detail. State the condition type, encoding, preprocessing, and allowed transformation before judging adherence.
For image editing, retain the unedited source, mask, prompt, seed, solver, and output. Evaluate preservation outside the mask separately from success inside it. This distinguishes an edit that follows the request but damages unrelated content from one that preserves the image but ignores the requested change.


Latent spaces change the unit of generation
Pixel-space diffusion applies the forward and reverse process directly to image arrays. This retains a direct relationship between model state and pixels, but high-resolution arrays make denoising expensive. Latent diffusion first encodes the image into a lower-dimensional continuous representation, performs diffusion in that representation, and decodes the resulting latent state back to an image. The computational saving can be substantial, but it introduces a second component whose reconstruction errors, training distribution, and conditioning interface affect the final image.
The latent representation is not a neutral compression. Fine text, small objects, local texture, and image boundaries can be weakened before the denoiser begins. Evaluation therefore needs to separate encoder-decoder reconstruction quality from the behaviour of the diffusion model. A visually plausible output may fail because the denoiser did not follow the condition, because the latent decoder discarded relevant information, or because the evaluation prompt did not identify the intended property. These are different errors and require different changes.


Code
# A toy representation contract: the generator works in a compressed latent space,
# then a decoder maps the latent result back to image coordinates.
image_shape=(512,512,3); latent_shape=(64,64,4)
print({"pixel_values":np.prod(image_shape),"latent_values":np.prod(latent_shape)})

title: Diffusion Models
section: Level 3 - Training, conditioning, and generation controls
text:
Level 3 - Training, conditioning, and generation controls

A training run contains more than a loss curve
The training record should state where images came from, how they were filtered and deduplicated, the image resolution and aspect-ratio policy, encoder and decoder configuration, noise schedule, target parameterisation, denoiser architecture, optimiser and learning-rate schedule, precision, batch policy, checkpoint-selection rule, and validation data. For a conditional model, it must additionally retain the text or other condition encoder, prompt preprocessing, dropped-condition rate, and any classifier-free guidance training procedure.
Checkpoint selection deserves particular care. A validation noise-prediction loss may be useful for detecting optimisation failure, yet the chosen deployment checkpoint may depend on a separate set of condition-adherence, image-quality, diversity, and safety evaluations. Selecting a checkpoint after inspecting a public benchmark converts that benchmark into a development resource. The report should identify the development evaluations, the final held-out evaluation, and the decision rule used to choose the checkpoint.


Diversity, fidelity, and adherence are separate outcomes
For a fixed condition, a generator can produce many near-identical images, highly varied images that ignore the condition, or a narrow set of images that score well on an automated metric. Diversity is meaningful only relative to a task and a condition. A product-image generator may be expected to preserve identity and vary background; an editing system may be expected to preserve most of the image and change one selected region. Define the allowed variation before counting it as a benefit.
Evaluation should use repeated seeds per condition and repeated conditions per requested concept. Retain a sample table that records the prompt or condition, seed, model and sampler versions, steps, guidance, output, reviewer decision where used, and failure category. This permits a reviewer to inspect whether an apparent quality gain came from a few favourable seeds, a changed prompt set, or a more general change in generation behaviour.


Code
generation_record={"condition":"red cube left of blue sphere","seed":17,"steps":30,
                   "guidance":5.0,"sampler":"deterministic","resolution":"512x512",
                   "adherence":"relation correct","failure":"none"}
print(generation_record)




Safety and misuse need a generation-specific boundary
An image model can be used to create deceptive media, expose private attributes, reproduce unwanted material, or generate content that is unsuitable for a particular audience or workflow. These are not all properties of the denoising objective. The service layer determines what conditions are accepted, which reference images can be supplied, what watermarking or provenance information is retained, what outputs are blocked or reviewed, and how users can report a harmful result.
Controls should be evaluated under the actual generation interface. A filter that blocks one text phrase may not block an equivalent paraphrase, an image condition, or an editing request. A provenance marker may be removed by cropping or re-encoding. The relevant audit records the threat path, the control, the tested variants, the residual risk, and the action if the control fails. This carries the discussion forward to Chapter 49 without treating diffusion architecture as a complete safety solution.


Parameterisation changes numerical behaviour
The denoiser can be trained to predict several related quantities. Noise prediction asks for the Gaussian noise used in the forward process. Other formulations predict the clean image, a velocity-like combination of clean image and noise, or a score related to the gradient of the noisy distribution. These formulations describe related reverse-process information, but they can weight time steps differently and behave differently under a chosen schedule. The training objective must name the parameterisation; a reported “diffusion loss” does not identify the target on its own.
The choice has a practical interpretation. At early time steps, the input retains much of the original image; at late steps, the signal is weak. A target that is numerically convenient at one part of the trajectory may be poorly conditioned elsewhere. Inspect loss and generation failures by noise interval. If a model produces plausible broad shapes but fails on detailed conditioning, the evidence may point to a high-noise schedule, a latent bottleneck, the conditioning interface, or the reverse solver. A single aggregate loss cannot locate the cause.


Code
# Record per-noise-bin error rather than relying on the run-wide mean.
noise_bins={"low noise":.09,"middle":.16,"high noise":.28}
for noise_level,error in noise_bins.items(): print(noise_level,error)




Guidance is an intervention on the conditional signal
Classifier-free guidance is often described as strengthening the prompt. More precisely, it changes the denoising direction by combining a prediction with condition information and one without it. The scale determines the relative contribution. This can make a requested concept more visible, but it can also amplify common associations in the training data, over-saturate an image, reduce variation across seeds, or make an editing result depart from the source image.
Treat guidance as a controlled factor. Select a grid of scales before reviewing samples, generate multiple seeds for every condition, and score both condition adherence and unwanted change. For an image-editing workflow, use region-preservation checks; for text-to-image, use relation and count checks; for a product workflow, use identity and brand constraints. A guidance value selected after browsing outputs needs to be reported as a development decision rather than an unbiased quality result.


Sampling budgets are a product policy
A denoising budget determines how long a user waits, how many accelerators are required, and how many outputs can be produced under a cost limit. It also determines the distribution of failure: a low step count may preserve broad category while losing fine relations; a high step count may improve some conditions and merely consume more time on others. Measure marginal gains by task slice and establish a stopping or fallback rule. For example, an interactive preview may use a low budget, while a final export receives more steps after a user confirms the condition.
The policy should make this distinction visible. A preview is not evidence that the final output will satisfy a condition; a final output should identify its generation settings where reproducibility matters. Cancellation, timeout, and retry rules need the same care as the sampler itself. A repeated request with a new seed may be a legitimate diversity control, while an automatic retry after a failed edit can overwrite a user decision if it is not bounded.

title: Diffusion Models
text:
Level 4 - Evaluation, deployment, and limits

Evaluation protocols should resist selective sampling
Generated images are easy to curate after the fact. A credible protocol fixes prompts or source images, seeds or seed-selection policy, output count, sampler settings, and evaluation criteria before generation. If human reviewers compare outputs, randomise presentation order and hide model identity where feasible. Report reviewer instructions, disagreement, exclusions, and whether reviewers saw the original condition. Automated measures should be accompanied by the feature extractor, preprocessing, sample count, and confidence interval.
Failure categories should be defined before inspection but refined transparently if new failures appear. Useful categories include condition omission, relation error, object-count error, unreadable text, identity drift, unwanted edit outside a mask, unsafe content, and corrupted output. Count categories by condition slice rather than selecting memorable failures. A system that performs well on common prompts but fails on low-light inputs, unusual languages, or small objects has a bounded capability that should be stated directly.


Reproducibility and change control
Diffusion results depend on many coupled software components. Updating a text encoder, latent decoder, scheduler library, precision kernel, safety filter, or prompt template can change output without a new denoiser checkpoint. Preserve versions and hashes where the environment permits, and retain a small fixed regression suite of conditions, seeds, and source images. Run it whenever a component changes. Visual inspection is useful, but a change log and predefined checks provide stronger evidence that a new release has not silently altered expected behaviour.
The regression suite should include both desired and undesired requests. It can test that a permitted edit preserves an unmasked region, that a condition is followed within a stated tolerance, that an unsupported request is handled according to policy, and that latency remains within a budget. This is the link between a generative model chapter and the operational material in Chapter 48: the deployed system includes model, sampler, interface, controls, and monitoring.


Research claims need an appropriate comparison
Diffusion papers and systems often compare architecture, schedule, sampler, guidance, latent representation, or conditioning method at the same time. A reader should ask what is actually held fixed. If one model is trained at higher resolution, uses a different encoder, has more sampling steps, or receives a more favourable prompt protocol, a difference in displayed samples cannot be assigned to one architectural component. Ablations are useful when they preserve the relevant data, training budget, evaluation set, and output protocol.
Comparisons with autoregressive or adversarial generators require the same discipline. Diffusion offers an iterative denoising route; it does not make quality, diversity, controllability, or cost automatically superior for every task. State the resolution, quality and adherence criterion, hardware, latency percentile, sample count, and condition distribution. A system decision can then weigh the observed trade-off rather than rely on a category label.


Questions that remain open in a deployment
Several limits are empirical. It is difficult to know whether an apparent visual relation was learned from a condition or produced through a frequent association. It is difficult to measure memorisation over a large and partly undocumented training corpus. It is difficult to compare quality across prompts that have many valid outputs, and to distinguish an unsafe request from an allowed creative transformation without a task-specific policy. These uncertainties should lead to narrower claims and continued monitoring, not to a generic disclaimer.
For a deployed generator, the accountable organisation must decide which evidence is sufficient for a particular use, which failures require human review, what data and outputs are retained, and how users can contest or report a result. The denoising mechanism explains how samples are produced. It does not decide whether a sample is appropriate, lawful, or reliable in a given workflow.
The practical lesson is to keep generation decisions inspectable. A request should be traceable to a condition, model version, sampler, budget, output policy, and evaluation boundary. An evaluation should identify the task property it measures and the populations or requests it leaves uncertain. With those records, a diffusion model can be compared, revised, or withdrawn on evidence. Without them, impressive samples can conceal an unmeasured system.
Those records also make later replication possible when hardware, libraries, interfaces, and policies inevitably change after the original experiment or release.
They support audit, comparison, and accountable correction.




Code
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,2.5));ax.axis("off")
for i,label in enumerate(["noise","step T","step T/2","step 1","sample"]):
 ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.2+i*1.55,1),1.1,.48,facecolor=["#7655a6","#d97745","#3a9188","#24527a","#3a9188"][i],edgecolor="white"));ax.text(.75+i*1.55,1.24,label,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(0,8);ax.set_ylim(.5,2);plt.show()



Figure 46.3





Conditional-generation record
Conditioning supplies information that the reverse model should respect: a class label, text representation, masked image region, or another image. The condition is an input to the denoiser, not proof that every sample follows it. Evaluate adherence separately from visual quality, and retain the text encoder, guidance scale, negative condition, scheduler, seed policy, and resolution in the generation record.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5,3));ax.axis("off")
for x,l,c in [(.3,"noisy\nimage","#24527a"),(2.2,"time","#7655a6"),(3.7,"text\ncondition","#d97745"),(5.6,"denoiser","#3a9188")]:ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1),1.1,.55,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white"));ax.text(x+.55,1.28,l,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(0,7);ax.set_ylim(.5,2);plt.show()



Figure 46.4





Output evaluation and data-provenance boundary
Image-quality scores compare generated and reference distributions under a specific feature extractor and sample protocol. They do not establish prompt adherence, representation of rare groups, absence of memorisation, or suitability for a particular user task. Report data provenance, filtering, resolution, conditioning, sampler, steps, guidance, seeds, compute, and failure slices.
Evaluation should retain individual samples and prompts alongside aggregate scores. Inspect failures by requested relation, object count, text rendering, low-frequency visual structure, sensitive attribute, and training-data proximity. For applications with a user-facing claim, the relevant question is whether the stated condition is respected under that workflow, not whether samples look plausible after selective inspection.
Memorisation and provenance require a separate audit. Nearest-neighbour checks against training and evaluation data can detect some suspiciously close outputs, but they cannot demonstrate the absence of training-data reproduction. Record data collection and filtering, opt-out and removal procedures, known copyrighted or sensitive material, and the conditions under which a sample may be retained for review. These are deployment decisions with consequences beyond a feature-based image-quality score.




Code

title: Diffusion Models
text:
Common misconceptions

Diffusion creates an image in one denoising call. Sampling is normally iterative.
A lower noise-prediction loss proves better conditional images. Adherence and visual quality require separate evaluation.
More steps always justify their cost. The quality-latency curve depends on sampler and task.
A conditional prompt guarantees content. Conditions steer a distribution and can be ignored or only partly followed.

title: Diffusion Models
text:
Summary
Diffusion models learn denoising across a declared noise schedule and generate through repeated reverse steps. The sampler, condition, and evaluation protocol define the system’s practical behaviour.

title: Diffusion Models
text:
Looking ahead
Diffusion provides one route from a learned representation to generated images, but applications often require a model to coordinate more than one modality. Chapter 46 examines the interfaces and objectives needed to align text, images, and other inputs without treating cross-modal performance as a single undifferentiated capability.

Further reading

title: Multimodal Models
text:
Chapter orientation
Multimodal models connect representations from images, text, audio, video, or other inputs. The connection can be a shared embedding space, cross-attention between modality-specific encoders, or a generative model conditioned on another modality. The relevant question is not whether two modalities appear in one interface, but what data, objective, and fusion mechanism make one representation usable by another.

title: Multimodal Models
text:
Level 1 - Aligning representations
An image encoder and a text encoder can map their inputs to vectors that should be close for matched image-text pairs and less similar for mismatched pairs. This contrastive interface supports retrieval and zero-shot classification, but it does not by itself establish grounded visual explanation or reliable generation. CLIP is a prominent example of paired image-text contrastive pretraining (Radford et al. 2021).




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6,4));ax.scatter([1,4,2.1,5],[1,3,1.2,3.2],c=["#24527a","#24527a","#d97745","#d97745"],s=90);ax.text(1,1.2,"image A");ax.text(2.1,1.4,"text A");ax.text(4,3.2,"image B");ax.text(5,3.4,"text B");ax.set_title("Illustrative aligned pairs");plt.show()



Figure 47.1

title: Multimodal Models
text:
Level 2 - Encoders and fusion

Shared space and cross-attention answer different questions
A shared space compares whole inputs or regions through similarity. Cross-attention lets tokens from one modality query representations from another. A text token can therefore attend to image patches while a decoder generates a response. Early fusion combines modalities before many layers; late fusion combines separately processed summaries. These alternatives change what information is available at each stage and what failures can be inspected.




Code
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,3));ax.axis("off")
for x,l,c in [(.4,"image\nencoder","#24527a"),(2.1,"text\nencoder","#d97745"),(4,"shared\nspace","#7655a6"),(6.1,"cross-\nattention","#3a9188")]:ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1),1.2,.55,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white"));ax.text(x+.6,1.28,l,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(0,8);ax.set_ylim(.5,2);plt.show()



Figure 47.2





Code
image=np.array([.8,.1]); text=np.array([.7,.2]); print("similarity",image@text/(np.linalg.norm(image)*np.linalg.norm(text)))

title: Multimodal Models
text:
Level 3 - Generation and supervision
Image captioning, visual question answering, and text-to-image generation require more than aligned pairs. A generative decoder receives a condition and produces tokens or a denoising direction. Training data determine which visual relations, languages, and answer formats are represented. Preserve modality encoders, preprocessing, prompt template, fusion locations, decoding or sampling policy, and loss masks in the training record.
Paired data also contain their own errors. A caption can omit an object, describe a photographer’s convention, or be copied from surrounding web text rather than visual evidence. A contrastive objective can reward agreement with these labels without distinguishing a grounded relation from a frequent association. Dataset construction should record pairing source, deduplication, language coverage, caption policy, rights, and the treatment of uncertain or conflicting labels.
Contrastive supervision is usually built from a batch of paired examples. For image (i), its accompanying text is treated as a positive match and the other texts in the batch as negatives; the same comparison can be made from text to images. The loss increases similarity for the stated pair relative to alternatives. This is useful because it permits learning without a class label for every image, but it makes batch composition part of the objective. Repeated captions, near-duplicate images, mislabeled pairs, and systematically missing descriptions change which distinctions the representation can learn.


Code
# A toy image-to-text contrastive probability for one positive pair among a batch.
similarities=np.array([3.1,1.2,.4,-.3])
probabilities=np.exp(similarities)/np.exp(similarities).sum()
print("probability assigned to the matched text:",round(probabilities[0],3))


Cross-attention introduces a different training and inference path. A query token from a decoder or text stream receives scores against image-patch keys, converts the scores to weights, and forms a weighted value combination. If a visual question asks about a particular region, that mechanism makes region information available to the text decoder. It does not require the decoder to use the relevant patches, and high weights do not establish that changing those patches would change the answer. A grounded claim needs an intervention: alter or mask the purported evidence while holding the question and other visible content fixed, then measure the answer change.

Fusion location determines what can be shared
Early fusion permits image and text tokens to interact in many layers. It can model fine cross-modal relations, but requires the joint sequence and therefore increases memory and training cost. Late fusion keeps modality encoders largely separate and combines summaries near the output. It can be efficient for retrieval, while limiting token-level visual-language interaction. Connector modules provide a third option: they compress image features into a smaller set of tokens before a language decoder consumes them.
The design should be matched to the task. Whole-image retrieval may require a global embedding. Counting, reading, spatial reference, and visual question answering need a route that retains relevant local information. State where fusion occurs, how many visual tokens reach the decoder, whether image encoders are frozen, and how image resolution or cropping affects that interface.


Code
architectures={"late fusion":{"visual_tokens_to_decoder":0,"use":"retrieval"},"cross attention":{"visual_tokens_to_decoder":196,"use":"grounded generation"},"connector":{"visual_tokens_to_decoder":32,"use":"compressed multimodal decoding"}}
for name,record in architectures.items(): print(name,record)




Grounded generation needs a claim-level audit
A grounded caption or answer makes several possible claims: object presence, attribute, count, location, relation, text in the image, or an inference about an unseen event. Score these separately. An answer can be correct about a broad category and wrong about the relation that a user actually asked about. Evaluation should include negative questions, ambiguous images, image-text mismatches, and cases in which the appropriate response is uncertainty.
Human review also needs a reference protocol. Reviewers require the source image at adequate resolution, a question, permitted answer options or rubric, and a way to record uncertainty. Agreement is evidence about the review procedure, not proof that the system is grounded. Compare model and reviewer errors by claim type before using a single aggregate score.
For generation, condition adherence is not one quantity. An output may preserve broad scene category while missing count, spatial relation, negation, or named entity. Build evaluation sets that isolate these claims and distinguish an encoder failure, fusion failure, and decoder failure where possible.




Code
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,3));ax.axis("off")
for x,l,c in [(.3,"image","#24527a"),(1.8,"text","#d97745"),(3.5,"fusion","#7655a6"),(5.3,"decoder","#3a9188"),(6.7,"output","#24527a")]:ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x,1),1,.5,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white"));ax.text(x+.5,1.25,l,ha="center",va="center",color="white",fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(0,8);ax.set_ylim(.5,2);plt.show()



Figure 47.3





Evaluation conditions must follow the intended action
Evaluate each link in the chain: image retrieval, text retrieval, condition adherence, factual grounding, output quality, and latency. A plausible answer can name objects absent from an image; a visually good generated image can fail a stated relation. Report source data, preprocessing, modality availability, language, image resolution, prompts, output policy, and slice results for rare or shifted combinations.
Multimodal systems also need an abstention and escalation policy. If an image is unreadable, missing, outside the supported modality, or paired with an ambiguous question, the application should describe what it can and cannot infer. Returning a fluent answer in those conditions may conceal a missing input or a weak visual signal.
Evaluation should be matched to the intended action. A retrieval system can be measured by whether a relevant paired item appears among the top results. A clinical or administrative image assistant requires a more demanding record: image acquisition conditions, intended and excluded uses, annotator and reference standard, error consequences, disagreement handling, and a human decision boundary. The model should not be credited with a capability because it answers a descriptive benchmark when the proposed deployment asks it to make a consequential judgement.


Modality encoders define what information reaches fusion
An image encoder can produce one global vector, a grid of patch vectors, a hierarchy of visual features, or a compressed set of learned query tokens. An audio encoder can retain frames at different temporal resolutions. A text encoder can produce token states or one pooled representation. These choices determine the information that the fusion mechanism can access. A decoder cannot recover a small visual object if the encoder discarded it, and a global embedding may support retrieval while being inadequate for a question about the relative position of two objects.
The encoder is therefore part of the task contract. Record the image resolution, crop and resize policy, colour space, normalisation values, patch or feature stride, number of visual tokens, and whether the encoder was pretrained, frozen, or updated during multimodal training. For audio or video, record sampling rate, frame rate, windowing, and any temporal pooling. A change in one of these choices can alter both accuracy and the population of inputs on which the system can make a claim.


Code
encoder_records={
    "global retrieval":{"image_tokens":1,"resolution":224,"local_questions":"limited"},
    "patch cross-attention":{"image_tokens":196,"resolution":224,"local_questions":"supported"},
    "compressed connector":{"image_tokens":32,"resolution":336,"local_questions":"depends on compression"},
}
for design,record in encoder_records.items(): print(design,record)




Alignment objectives create useful and misleading shortcuts
Contrastive learning rewards a paired image and text description for being more similar than alternatives in a batch. This can produce representations that are useful for search, classification with text labels, or selecting candidate captions. It can also exploit correlations that are easier than the intended relation: a caption may be predicted from a watermark, a common background, a language convention, or repeated web template rather than from the object the evaluator expects the model to recognise.
Evaluate these shortcuts through controlled counterexamples. Keep the target object fixed while changing background; keep the question fixed while replacing an irrelevant caption phrase; pair an image with a plausible but mismatched text; and compare examples from a new source or camera. A model that loses performance under a change that preserves the intended visual property may be relying on a shortcut. The result should be reported by comparison type, not hidden in an aggregate retrieval score.


Instruction tuning changes the output contract
Many multimodal assistants are trained after alignment using demonstrations of questions, answers, tool calls, or dialogue. This stage teaches a response format and can make the model appear more helpful, but it also creates risks of unsupported confidence and answer-style imitation. The target mask must state which tokens are supervised, especially where a prompt includes image placeholders, tool output, or quoted source material. The data mixture should distinguish captioning, question answering, OCR, reasoning, refusal, and uncertainty examples.
An instruction-following result needs tests for the response policy as well as visual accuracy. Ask whether the system abstains when the evidence is missing, cites the supplied image or source when required, follows an output schema, and avoids inventing measurements or text that are not visible. These are behavioural claims produced by the training interface, not automatic consequences of image-text alignment.


Multi-image and temporal inputs add binding problems
An application may provide several images, a document with figures, or a video. The model then needs to identify which image supports which part of a question, preserve ordering, and avoid mixing evidence across inputs. A global pooled representation can make these bindings difficult to inspect. The input protocol should label image order, page, timestamp, and source, and the evaluation should include deliberately confusable examples in which only one input contains the answer.
Temporal tasks need another distinction: a frame can show an object, while an action or change requires evidence across frames. Sampling a few frames may miss the decisive event. Record frame-selection policy and test changes in speed, camera movement, occlusion, and event duration. A model that performs on static representative frames has not established video understanding.


Code
multi_image_record={"images":["page-1","page-2"],"question":"Which panel contains the red marker?",
                    "expected_evidence":"page-2 panel B","ordering":"preserved","answer_policy":"cite page and panel"}
print(multi_image_record)

title: Multimodal Models
text:
Level 4 - Evaluation and limits

Output evaluation must retain uncertainty and source boundaries
For visual question answering, compare an answer against evidence in the image and the reference answer. Mark whether disagreement comes from visual perception, ambiguous wording, an unsupported inference, or a reference-label problem. For retrieval, measure both whether a relevant item was found and whether irrelevant items were presented in positions where a user may rely on them. For image generation, measure condition adherence and unintended content separately. These tasks cannot be collapsed into a single general “multimodal score”.
Where a system makes claims about documents, photographs, or people, distinguish description from inference. “The chart has a downward line” can be assessed from visible pixels. “The programme failed” introduces a causal or evaluative claim that may require information outside the image. Interface wording and evaluation rubrics should make that boundary visible. If the relevant source is absent, unreadable, or inconsistent, the appropriate output may be uncertainty or a request for another input.


Privacy, consent, and access controls are multimodal design choices
Images, audio, and video can contain faces, locations, documents, identifiers, and incidental third parties. A multimodal deployment needs rules for collection, storage, access, retention, redaction, and deletion that match those input types. Storing derived embeddings does not necessarily remove the need for a privacy assessment; embeddings can preserve information useful for linkage or retrieval. A user should know what material is sent to the model and whether it will be retained for training, debugging, or review.
Access controls also need to apply to evidence sources. A retrieval assistant should not expose an image or document merely because a user can ask about its topic. Bind the retrieval permission to the account and context before the representation reaches the model. Test cross-user, cross-tenant, and shared-device cases. These controls connect the chapter’s representation mechanisms to the systems and safety material later in Part VI.


Dataset curation is part of the multimodal model
Multimodal corpora are often assembled from heterogeneous sources. One collection may contain carefully written captions; another may use filenames, alt text, surrounding page text, or automatically generated descriptions. These sources have different reliability, language coverage, ownership, and association structure. A dataset card should distinguish them rather than report one aggregate number of pairs. It should also state how near-duplicates were detected across images and text, how train and evaluation sources were separated, and how broken links, corrupted files, or conflicting captions were handled.
Filtering decisions require an explicit purpose. Removing material may reduce exposure to unwanted content, but it can also remove a language, cultural setting, or visual style from the data. Filtering faces or documents may protect privacy while weakening a task that legitimately requires authorised document understanding. Report the criterion, the affected share, the affected slices, and the unresolved risk. A data-cleaning claim without these fields says little about the distribution that reaches the model.
Annotation is another source of uncertainty. Different reviewers can disagree about what is visible, whether a relation holds, whether text is readable, or whether a question is answerable from an image. Preserve the reference protocol and disagreement rather than collapsing all labels into one apparent truth. Where the deployment allows abstention, annotation should include unanswerable and ambiguous cases so that the model is not trained to answer every request confidently.


Routing and fallback should respect modality limits
A multimodal application may decide whether to use a lightweight retrieval model, a more expensive cross-attention model, OCR, a document parser, a human reviewer, or no automated response. The routing signal can use file type, resolution, detected text, image count, confidence, or stated consequence. It should be evaluated as a policy: unnecessary escalation consumes resources, while missed escalation can leave a difficult request with an inadequate model.
For low-quality images, a useful fallback may ask for a clearer scan or a different crop. For a document with complex tables, it may route to a layout-aware extraction tool. For a high-consequence image interpretation, it may provide a descriptive summary and require an authorised reviewer to make the decision. Each outcome should be distinguishable in logs and user-facing language. A generic answer from an unsupported modality can hide an information failure.


Code
routing_cases=[
    {"input":"clear product image","route":"visual retrieval","reason":"global match sufficient"},
    {"input":"blurred invoice","route":"request clearer scan","reason":"text evidence unavailable"},
    {"input":"high-consequence document","route":"human review","reason":"decision boundary"},
]
for case in routing_cases: print(case)




System comparisons need matched interfaces
Comparing a multimodal model with a text-only baseline, a separate OCR pipeline, or a retrieval system requires a matched task interface. If one system receives a high-resolution original image and another receives a compressed crop, the result measures both model and input differences. If one system may call a tool or see multiple pages while another cannot, report that as part of the system comparison. A capability benchmark should identify whether answers can be derived from pixels alone, from external knowledge, or from the combination.
Resource reporting is similarly specific. Measure encoder time, fusion or decoder time, visual-token count, image memory, request queue time, tool calls, and output-token cost. A connector that reduces visual tokens may reduce latency while losing small-object evidence. An end-to-end result should show that trade-off by task slice rather than infer it from the number of model parameters.


Open questions and bounded claims
There remains no general test that proves a multimodal model’s explanation is faithful to its image evidence. Attention weights, retrieved regions, and generated rationales can be useful diagnostic artefacts, but they require interventions and alternative explanations. There is also no single score for multimodal reliability across languages, camera types, document layouts, and consequences. These are empirical limitations of the evidence available for a deployment claim.
A bounded claim might state that a specified model, given authorised 336-pixel images and a fixed prompt template, improves retrieval of matched product records on a held-out source at a stated latency. It should not become a claim that the model reliably understands every image, provides causal explanations, or can make an unreviewed decision in a different workflow. The terms of the claim identify what must be re-evaluated when data, modality, user population, or system interface changes.


Change control preserves the meaning of an evaluation
Multimodal systems are particularly sensitive to component changes. Replacing an image encoder, changing a resize library, altering an OCR model, updating a text tokenizer, or changing the visual-token connector can change outputs even when the language decoder has not moved. Maintain a fixed regression set containing matched and mismatched pairs, low-quality inputs, multiple-image questions, authorised document examples, unanswerable prompts, and selected safety cases. Run it after any material change and record which component changed.
The regression set should support both numerical and qualitative review. Numerical checks can test retrieval rank, schema validity, abstention rate, and latency. Expert review can inspect a small predeclared sample for relation, count, text, and uncertainty failures. Where a regression is found, determine whether the model, preprocessing, data access, routing, or interface caused it before changing the system. This preserves the evidence boundary established by the chapter rather than treating every visible error as an undifferentiated model failure.


Summary of the deployment record
For every evaluated system version, retain the modality encoders, preprocessing, fusion architecture, token budget, training data and instruction mixture, routing policy, prompts, output policy, permission context, evaluation protocol, error slices, resource record, and change history. The record is necessarily longer than a model name because the same model behaves differently when these components change. It is the basis for comparing a multimodal system with another system or with a later version of itself.

for i,(l,c) in enumerate([("encode","#24527a"),("fuse","#7655a6"),("ground","#d97745"),("generate","#3a9188")]):ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.4+i*1.8,1),1.2,.5,facecolor=c,edgecolor="white"));ax.text(1+i*1.8,1.25,l,ha="center",va="center",color="white")

Common misconceptions

A shared embedding proves visual understanding. It establishes similarity under a trained objective.
Cross-attention guarantees grounding. It provides an access path, not a verified attribution.
A multimodal benchmark is one task. Retrieval, grounding, and generation need distinct measures.
Missing modalities are ordinary inputs. The training and deployment policy must specify their handling.

title: Scaling Laws and Compute
text:
Chapter orientation
Scaling laws summarise empirical relations between model size, training data, compute, and a measured loss. They are fitted regularities over stated model families and ranges, not guarantees that every capability or deployment outcome changes by the same rule. This chapter treats a scaling curve as an evaluative object: specify the data, objective, architecture, compute accounting, and held-out measure before extrapolating it.

title: Scaling Laws and Compute
section: Level 1 - More resources can change a measured loss
text:
Level 1 - More resources can change a measured loss
Holding a training recipe broadly comparable, larger models or more data often reduce held-out loss with diminishing returns. The practical question is allocation: whether another unit of compute should be spent on parameters, tokens, optimisation, or inference. A curve can inform that decision only for the distribution and training family from which it was estimated.




Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
compute=np.logspace(2,6,30); loss=2.3*compute**-.13+.7
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5,3.7));ax.loglog(compute,loss,color="#24527a");ax.set_xlabel("training compute");ax.set_ylabel("held-out loss");plt.tight_layout();plt.show()



Figure 48.1

title: Scaling Laws and Compute
section: Level 2 - The fitted relation has a contract
text:
Level 2 - The fitted relation has a contract
A simple form is (L(C)=aC^{-b}+c), where (L) is a chosen loss and (C) is a declared compute measure. The exponent is estimated from observations; it is not supplied by the equation. Changing tokenisation, data quality, architecture, optimiser, or evaluation distribution can change the fitted curve. Kaplan and colleagues reported such empirical relationships for language models (Kaplan et al. 2020), while later compute-optimal analysis changed the recommended balance between parameters and training tokens (Hoffmann et al. 2022).
Fitting starts with repeated runs at deliberately varied budgets. For every run, retain the model family, parameter count, FLOP convention, training tokens, batch and sequence length, optimiser and schedule, checkpoint rule, and held-out evaluation. Plot the observed points before fitting a line. A regular-looking curve can be driven by one failed run, a changed data source, or an excluded small model. Residuals and uncertainty intervals are evidence about the fitted relation, not decorative additions.


Code
log_compute=np.log(np.array([1e3,3e3,1e4,3e4])); log_loss=np.log(np.array([1.90,1.63,1.43,1.31]))
slope,intercept=np.polyfit(log_compute,log_loss,1)
print("estimated exponent:",round(slope,3),"residuals:",np.round(log_loss-(slope*log_compute+intercept),3))

fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5,4));im=ax.imshow(z,cmap="viridis");ax.set_xticks(range(4),t);ax.set_yticks(range(4),p);ax.set_xlabel("token allocation");ax.set_ylabel("parameter allocation");fig.colorbar(im,label="illustrative loss");plt.tight_layout();plt.show()

title: Scaling Laws and Compute
section: Level 3 - Compute accounting and capability tests
text:
Level 3 - Compute accounting and capability tests
Training compute should distinguish model FLOPs, data-processing cost, failed runs, communication, and evaluation where those affect the claimed comparison. Inference compute belongs in a separate record: Chapters 36-41 show that additional sampling and search can change task performance without changing pretraining. A falling average loss also does not establish a particular capability, calibration property, or safety outcome; test each claim on a held-out task.
Allocation studies require comparable stopping criteria. A larger model trained on too few tokens and a smaller model trained longer may have the same nominal compute but different optimisation states. State the token count, number of updates, sequence length, batch policy, learning-rate schedule, and checkpoint-selection rule. Without these fields, a compute-optimal conclusion can instead reflect an unreported training mismatch.
Data is another limiting input. Repeating low-quality or duplicated data changes the effective information available to a model and may contaminate evaluation. A scaling plan should therefore give a data-mixture and deduplication record alongside parameter and FLOP counts.
Compute-optimal does not mean cost-optimal for every organisation. A larger model may have attractive training loss but fail a serving-memory or latency budget. A smaller model may be preferable once fine-tuning, retrieval, distillation, quantisation, or inference-time search are included. The allocation decision should define the target workload and total lifecycle cost, then compare candidate systems under that workload rather than select a parameter count from a pretraining curve alone.

Allocation is a constrained decision
Start with a fixed budget and a declared objective. A research run may prioritise held-out loss; a service may require a maximum latency, a memory limit, a language mix, or an evaluation threshold for a particular task. Generate candidate allocations over parameters, tokens, steps, sequence length, and data cleaning. Train enough points to identify whether the proposed optimum is stable. Then test the selected allocation with the intended adaptation and serving configuration. A pretraining-only comparison cannot settle a deployment allocation.
Token count also has a quality dimension. Tokens from a duplicated, narrow, or poorly documented mixture do not provide the same evidence as tokens from a broader, curated mixture. Report source categories, language and domain proportions, filtering, deduplication method, cutoff dates, and known gaps. This record makes clear whether a scaling gain came from more computation, a changed data distribution, or both.


Code
candidates=[{"parameters":"small","tokens":"high","loss":1.18,"p95_ms":45},{"parameters":"large","tokens":"medium","loss":1.12,"p95_ms":180}]
for candidate in candidates: print(candidate)
