title: Scaling Laws and Compute
text:
Level 4 - Extrapolation and systems limits
Extrapolation is weakest where the model family, data mixture, hardware, objective, or target metric changes. A smooth loss curve can coexist with discontinuous operational constraints: memory capacity, communication topology, data availability, licensing, latency, and evaluation saturation. Report uncertainty around fitted exponents, the range used for fitting, excluded runs, and the decision that the extrapolation is intended to support.
Use extrapolation as a budgeting hypothesis, then test the first system outside the fitted range. A useful report states the predicted value, observed value, error, changed assumptions, and decision consequence. This prevents a fitted line from becoming an unexamined justification for a much larger training or deployment commitment.
Capability claims need an additional design. Define the task population before scaling, keep evaluation independent of model selection where possible, report uncertainty and slices, and compare observed task change with loss change. If a task score rises sharply, saturates, or falls while loss declines smoothly, that pattern identifies a limit of using aggregate loss as a proxy for the task.

Scaling plans need stopping rules
A scaling programme should state the result that would change its next investment. Examples include a fitted exponent becoming unstable across data mixtures, a held-out capability target failing to improve, a hardware limit increasing cost faster than projected, or an independent evaluation revealing contamination. These are not failures of the curve; they are evidence that the original allocation or extrapolation should be revised.
Keep a decision log for each scale transition: predicted loss or task change, observed result, variance across seeds or slices, altered assumptions, total cost, and the next decision. This permits later review of whether a large run followed evidence or simply continued a smooth trend beyond the conditions where it was measured.


What a scaling experiment estimates
A scaling experiment does not observe an abstract relation between intelligence and resources. It observes the outcomes of a particular family of training runs. The family includes an architecture, tokenizer, data pipeline, optimiser, curriculum, sequence length, precision policy, checkpoint criterion, and held-out loss. If several of those components change as compute increases, the fitted relation describes the bundled programme rather than parameter or token scaling alone.
This is why a run table should precede a fitted exponent. For every point, report the random seed, parameter accounting convention, active versus total parameters where sparse models are used, training and validation token counts, source mixture, update count, batch size, learning-rate schedule, precision, hardware, wall-clock time, and any restart or exclusion. If a point failed, record the failure and its cause. Removing divergent or undertrained runs can be appropriate, but a reader needs to see the rule used to remove them.


Code
run_table=[
 {"params_m":120,"tokens_b":3,"updates_k":45,"loss":1.84,"status":"complete"},
 {"params_m":360,"tokens_b":9,"updates_k":90,"loss":1.54,"status":"complete"},
 {"params_m":1000,"tokens_b":18,"updates_k":120,"loss":1.37,"status":"complete"},
 {"params_m":3000,"tokens_b":18,"updates_k":70,"loss":None,"status":"unstable"},
]
for run in run_table: print(run)




Fit uncertainty is part of the allocation decision
A small set of run points can support several plausible fitted relations. The uncertainty is larger when each larger model is also trained on more tokens, uses a revised data mixture, or receives a different optimisation schedule. In that setting, the points do not identify the separate contribution of parameters, data, and training procedure. A reported exponent may still describe the observed programme, but it cannot justify a claim about one input in isolation.
Repeat selected allocations across seeds, retain intermediate checkpoints, and compare fits that differ in the stated assumptions about the loss floor or functional form. The practical output is a range of predicted losses and a ranking of candidate allocations, not a single apparently precise exponent. If two allocations overlap within observed variation, the next decision can depend on serving cost, data coverage, or an independent task result. A larger training run is warranted when the expected decision-relevant difference exceeds that uncertainty, rather than because a fitted line has been extended by one more point.


Loss measurement must remain comparable
Held-out cross-entropy is useful because it evaluates the same predictive objective used in training, but it depends on tokenisation, target masking, context length, and data distribution. A change in vocabulary can change the unit over which loss is averaged. A new validation mixture can change the difficulty of the measured task. A benchmark may also overlap with training data or be used repeatedly for model selection. Report these details before interpreting a lower number as a broad model improvement.
Perplexity is an exponentiated loss and is often easier to describe, but it inherits the same boundaries. Neither measure establishes factuality, calibration, retrieval quality, arithmetic performance, security, or a particular user outcome. Add task-specific tests only after defining the task population and scoring rule. This protects against a common error: interpreting a smooth average loss curve as direct evidence that every capability or risk moves smoothly with compute.


Parameter, token, and optimisation budgets interact
For a given compute budget, increasing model size reduces the number of tokens or updates that can be processed under a fixed schedule. Increasing token count can leave too little capacity for the data’s structure. The useful allocation is an empirical question. Construct candidate grids that span undertrained large models, adequately trained middle models, and smaller models trained on more tokens. Fit only after checking that all candidates receive viable optimisation and that the comparison uses a common stopping rule.
The terms “undertrained” and “overtrained” should be tied to evidence rather than intuition. Inspect training and validation curves, token-to-parameter ratios, learning-rate state, and task regressions. A model that has seen many tokens can still be poorly trained if optimisation was unstable or data quality changed. Conversely, a model that has seen fewer tokens may satisfy the intended deployment trade-off. The run record permits these distinctions.


Data quality changes the scaling input
Token counts are often reported with a precision that the underlying data record cannot support. Text may be duplicated across sources, translated versions may be near duplicates, documents may be truncated, and source proportions may change over time. Data cleaning can improve a measured loss at the same nominal token count; it can also narrow language or domain coverage. Treat data mixture as an allocation dimension alongside parameters and FLOPs.
Maintain source, licence, language, domain, date, deduplication, and quality-filtering records. Test scaling curves on separate validation slices to see whether the observed gain is concentrated in one source type. If a larger run improves an aggregate loss while degrading a low-resource language or long-context slice, the allocation decision should state that trade-off. It is not enough to report the mean.


Code
slices={"general web":1.21,"technical":1.34,"long context":1.59,"low-resource language":1.72}
for name,loss in slices.items(): print(name,loss)




Compute has a physical and organisational boundary
FLOP estimates abstract away memory limits, communication, failed jobs, data movement, cooling, procurement, and the availability of qualified staff. They remain useful for normalising certain training comparisons, but a project budget should retain those omitted costs. Sparse models may have high total parameter capacity and lower active computation while requiring communication that changes throughput. Long-context models can change activation memory and attention cost. Precision changes both numerical behaviour and hardware performance.
Organisational constraints can be decisive before a theoretical compute optimum is reached. A team may have a fixed cluster reservation, a data-access agreement that expires, an evaluation requirement, or a deployment deadline. Report these boundaries as constraints on the decision, not as unexplained deviations from an ideal scaling curve. This makes a plan auditable and permits another team to apply the evidence under its own constraints.


Extrapolation has a range and an error
Interpolation uses observed points within the range of the experiment. Extrapolation predicts beyond that range. The second claim is usually more valuable for planning and less directly supported by evidence. A power-law fit can appear stable over several orders of magnitude and then change when the data mixture, architecture, optimiser, hardware, or loss floor changes. The uncertainty is not eliminated by reporting more decimal places in the exponent.
An extrapolation report should name the lowest and highest observed budget, the proposed new budget, the prediction interval, and the assumptions that must remain fixed. It should also identify the first evidence that would cause the plan to stop or change: a larger residual than expected, a failure to reach an optimisation threshold, a data shortage, a serving constraint, or an independent capability regression. This turns extrapolation into a testable planning hypothesis.


Code
forecast={"observed_compute_range":"1e18–1e21 FLOPs","proposed":"3e21 FLOPs",
          "predicted_loss":1.18,"acceptable_error":.04,"stop_if":"held-out loss exceeds 1.22"}
print(forecast)




Capability tests have their own scaling curves
Suppose a model family is evaluated on document extraction, code generation, multilingual retrieval, or reasoning with a verifier. Each task has its own population, prompt or interface, scoring rule, and failure cost. Plot task performance against the same training budget, but do not assume the curve follows the loss exponent. A task may show a threshold-like change, saturate early, depend heavily on prompt policy, or be limited by missing context rather than model capacity.
Use fixed and refreshed evaluation sets. Fixed sets permit comparison across checkpoints but can become development resources or be contaminated. Refreshed tasks test transfer but require a documented generator or sampling frame. Record both where possible. Analyse errors by task slice and inspect the cases that change between scale levels. The aim is to identify what additional compute changed in the model’s observed behaviour, not to attach a broad capability label to one score.


Code
capability_curve=[
 {"compute":1,"loss":1.72,"structured_extraction":.51,"multilingual_retrieval":.42},
 {"compute":3,"loss":1.49,"structured_extraction":.62,"multilingual_retrieval":.44},
 {"compute":10,"loss":1.32,"structured_extraction":.71,"multilingual_retrieval":.50},
]
for point in capability_curve: print(point)




Training compute and inference compute are complementary budgets
Part V established that candidate sampling, search, verification, and refinement can improve a system’s task outcome after training. A scaling decision should therefore compare at least two routes: spend more on pretraining to change the base policy, or retain a smaller base model and spend more computation per request. The relevant comparison depends on request volume, latency, task distribution, verifier availability, and the cost of a wrong answer.
For example, a high-volume routine classification service may benefit from an efficient model with low per-request cost. A low-volume, verifiable reasoning task may justify several candidates and an exact checker. Report training cost separately from average serving cost, and state the assumed request volume used to amortise training. A training scaling law alone cannot choose between these system designs.


Scale programmes require governance and reproducibility
Large runs consume shared resources and may change the risks of data exposure, environmental impact, supplier dependency, and deployment concentration. A scale programme should assign an owner for the budget, data access, evaluation protocol, incident response, and go/no-go decision. The owner needs predeclared decision criteria, not only a dashboard of training loss.
Reproducibility does not require another team to own identical hardware. It requires enough information to understand what was done and test the material claims: code version, configuration, random seeds where feasible, data description and access restrictions, compute accounting, checkpoint-selection rule, evaluation suite, and known deviations from plan. If a result cannot be reproduced because data or hardware are unavailable, say which parts are independently checkable and which are not.


A bounded conclusion from a scaling study
A defensible conclusion may state that, for a named architecture and data mixture, increasing training tokens and parameters within the observed range reduced a specified held-out loss and improved a named task slice at a measured cost. It should separately state whether the selected allocation met serving constraints and whether an extrapolation beyond the observed range remains untested. This is sufficient to inform a real decision without claiming a universal law.
The next chapter uses this same discipline at serving time. Throughput, latency, cache pressure, and monitoring signals are empirical properties of a declared deployment configuration. They cannot be derived from parameter count or training FLOPs alone.


Designing a small scaling study
An educational scaling study can use a modest model family and a controlled corpus. Choose two or three parameter sizes, two token budgets, and a common optimiser policy. Hold tokenisation, validation data, sequence length, and evaluation code fixed. Train enough seeds to show whether differences exceed run-to-run variation. Plot training and validation loss, then report a task score only for a predeclared held-out task. The point is not to recover a frontier exponent; it is to learn how many assumptions sit behind a curve.
The study should include a deliberately mismatched allocation. A large model trained on too little data or stopped too early illustrates why parameter count alone is not a result. A smaller model trained longer can illustrate the opposite trade-off. Record the actual tokens and updates rather than describing one run as “larger” and the other as “smaller”. Readers should be able to identify the allocation, not infer it from a graph legend.


Code
study_design={"sizes_m":[30,90,270],"tokens_m":[60,180],"seeds":[1,2],
              "held_fixed":["tokenizer","validation set","sequence length","optimizer family"],
              "outcome":"validation loss plus predeclared task score"}
print(study_design)




Interpreting an apparent break in a curve
An apparent break can be an important finding, but first check mundane causes. Confirm that the tokenizer and loss implementation did not change, that the validation set was identical, that token counts use the same convention, and that the larger run reached a comparable optimisation state. Inspect hardware errors, loss scaling, gradient norms, checkpoint recovery, and data-pipeline logs. If the break remains after these checks, compare error slices and component changes before attributing it to a capability transition.
The same caution applies to a sudden task improvement. A benchmark may have a formatting shortcut, a few easy items, or a score that is sensitive to one decoding setting. Repeat with alternative prompts, seeds, and independently generated variants. If the improvement survives, describe the conditions under which it was observed and the mechanisms that remain uncertain. A careful conditional claim is stronger than a dramatic inference from one curve.


Reporting a scaling decision
The final report should answer five questions. What was varied? What was held fixed? How was compute and data counted? What changed on independent outcomes? What decision follows under a stated budget? A compact table can answer these questions more clearly than a single plotted exponent. Include the observed range, uncertainty, exclusions, resource cost, deployment assumptions, and the next test required before further scale.
This reporting standard also permits negative results. If a larger run did not improve the task that motivated it, report the loss, task, data, and systems evidence together. The outcome may indicate that the task needs better retrieval, a different training objective, more representative data, or an inference-time procedure rather than another increase in model scale. The relevant response follows from the diagnosed constraint.


Limits of a scaling-law account
Scaling evidence is useful when it narrows a decision under conditions that can be described and revisited. It becomes misleading when an exponent is detached from its data, objective, evaluation, and systems boundary. Models are trained and served through coupled technical and organisational systems. A measured curve can guide the next experiment, but it cannot relieve the team of testing the next configuration, inspecting distributional consequences, or deciding whether the resulting system is appropriate for its intended users.
For that reason, retain the configuration, outcome, and decision record for every material scale transition. The record makes later correction possible when evidence, costs, or user needs change.
It also prevents retrospective stories in which every scale increase is described as inevitable. A documented alternative allocation, a negative result, and a stated stopping rule are evidence of a disciplined programme rather than signs that the programme failed to scale.
They preserve the conditions under which later teams can reassess the decision honestly.




Code
x=np.arange(1,7);y=np.array([2,1.7,1.5,1.38,1.3,1.24]);fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5,3.5));ax.plot(x[:4],y[:4],marker="o",color="#24527a",label="observed");ax.plot(x[3:],y[3:],"--",color="#d97745",label="extrapolated");ax.legend();ax.set_xlabel("log compute level");ax.set_ylabel("loss");plt.tight_layout();plt.show()

title: Scaling Laws and Compute
text:
Summary
Scaling laws describe measured relations under a training contract. They can inform compute allocation, but they do not replace capability evaluation or systems accounting.

title: Scaling Laws and Compute
text:
Looking ahead
Training curves do not determine whether a model can serve users within a latency, throughput, reliability, or cost target. Chapter 48 treats deployment as an operational system whose behaviour must be measured after the model leaves training.

title: Scaling Laws and Compute

Empirical language-model scaling laws are reported by Kaplan et al. (2020); compute-optimal token and parameter allocation is reconsidered by Hoffmann et al. (2022).

title: Serving, Deployment, and Monitoring
text:
Chapter orientation
A trained model becomes a service only when requests can be admitted, processed, observed, and recovered under a declared reliability and cost budget. Model quality measured offline is one component of that system. Prompt length, batching, queueing, decoding, cache policy, hardware, fallbacks, and user traffic determine what a deployment delivers. The dependence of model behaviour on surrounding technical systems is a central source of accumulated machine-learning technical debt (Sculley et al. 2015).

title: Serving, Deployment, and Monitoring
section: Level 1 - A request has a lifecycle
text:
Level 1 - A request has a lifecycle
A request is validated, queued, prefixed through the model, decoded token by token, checked against policy or tool constraints where relevant, and returned with a record. Latency includes waiting as well as model execution. Throughput is the number of completed requests over time. Improving one can worsen the other: larger batches often raise throughput while delaying individual requests.




Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,3));ax.axis("off")

title: Serving, Deployment, and Monitoring
section: Level 2 - Batching and caching change the cost model
text:
Level 2 - Batching and caching change the cost model
Prefill processes the prompt context; decoding produces later tokens sequentially. Continuous batching can combine requests at different stages, raising hardware utilisation while making queue policy part of latency. A key-value cache retains attention keys and values for prior tokens, avoiding repeated work during decoding. It consumes memory proportional to active sequences, layers, hidden dimensions, and context length. Cache eviction or truncation changes what the model can condition on.
Admission control decides which requests enter the system when capacity is scarce. A service may limit prompt length, generated tokens, concurrent tool calls, or per-user rate; it may prioritise one workflow over another. These are policy decisions with quality consequences. A rejected request, a truncated context, and a degraded fallback response should be counted separately in service reporting.
Caching also has correctness boundaries. Reusing a prefix cache is appropriate only when the model version, tokenizer, system prompt, and cached tokens match the current request. Reuse across users or security contexts can expose data. Record cache key design, isolation rules, hit rate, eviction cause, and the effect of cache pressure on latency.
Token budgets are another admission decision. A system can truncate a long prompt, reserve space for output, summarise earlier context, reject the request, or route it to a larger-context model. These responses are not equivalent: truncation can remove evidence, summarisation can introduce an unverified representation, and a rejection can be the safest result. Log the selected policy and the fraction of requests affected so that an apparent quality or latency change is not attributed solely to the model.
Capacity planning should use arrival patterns rather than average traffic alone. Short bursts can create a queue even when mean utilisation appears moderate. A production record needs concurrency, request-length distribution, batch policy, accelerator allocation, timeout rate, and tail latency. These fields identify whether a regression came from model decoding, long prompts, a traffic change, or insufficient capacity.

Queue policy distributes a scarce resource
Requests may be processed in arrival order, grouped by length, prioritised by workflow, or limited by user and tenant quotas. Each policy changes who waits and whose context is truncated or rejected under load. A short-request preference can improve aggregate latency while delaying long-document work; a priority lane can protect a high-consequence workflow while reducing capacity for others. State these choices and measure their effects by request class.
Retries require the same care. Retrying a failed generation can improve completion rates, but retries also increase load and can duplicate a consequential tool action. Use idempotency keys for actions, cap retry budgets, distinguish transient infrastructure failures from policy refusals, and record whether the retry changed prompt, model, tool state, or user-visible result.

requests=[{"class":"interactive","queue_ms":18,"completed":True},{"class":"long-context","queue_ms":140,"completed":True},{"class":"tool-action","queue_ms":31,"completed":False}]
for request in requests: print(request)

section: Level 3 - Deployment is an experiment with safeguards
text:
Level 3 - Deployment is an experiment with safeguards
Release policies should define model and prompt versions, traffic allocation, fallback model, timeout, rate limit, tool permissions, and rollback criteria. An offline evaluation set cannot represent every live request. Staged release can compare a candidate against a baseline under matched traffic, while protecting users from known failure modes. Logging requires a retention, access, and redaction policy; observability is not authorisation to retain raw user data.
A comparison requires a denominator. Report the eligible traffic population, assignment rule, exclusions, sample size, time window, and whether users can retry into another arm. Compare quality, safety, cost, and latency jointly; a candidate that reduces average latency by refusing more requests or routing difficult inputs to a baseline has not established a general operational improvement. For consequential workflows, define a human-review route before exposure rather than after an incident.

title: Serving, Deployment, and Monitoring
section: Level 4 - Monitor system and outcome signals
text:
Level 4 - Monitor system and outcome signals
Monitor availability, errors, queue time, prefill and decoding latency, token counts, cache pressure, cost, refusals, tool failures, and fallback rates. These describe service behaviour. Monitor outcome quality separately through sampled review, user feedback with known selection bias, task-specific checks, and recurring held-out tests. Drift can arise from a changed request population, new documents in retrieval, altered tool behaviour, policy changes, or a model update.
An alert should name an owner and a response. A p95-latency increase may require capacity adjustment; a rise in tool failures may require disabling a connector; a measured quality regression may require rollback or a narrower eligibility rule. Monitoring without a threshold, decision authority, and incident record produces dashboards without operational control.
Separate product metrics from validity evidence. A fall in abandonment may reflect faster answers, but it may also reflect a misleading interface or users who cannot identify an error. Retain independent checks for the task property the service is meant to support.
Drift investigation should begin with a traceable change. Compare model and prompt versions, retrieval index and tool versions, request-length distribution, language and task slices, and any policy or interface change. The response may be to correct a data source, adjust an eligibility rule, disable a tool, retrain a component, or roll back. A dashboard cannot decide among these actions without the record that connects an alert to the deployment configuration.
Incident exercises should test the recovery path. Simulate a dependency outage, runaway queue, cache exhaustion, malformed tool output, and a measured quality regression. Confirm who receives the alert, who can change traffic, what user communication is required, and how the regression test prevents recurrence. These are properties of the operated system, not of the model checkpoint alone.

State and versioning determine reproducibility
A deployed answer depends on more than model weights. Preserve the model and tokenizer version, system and user prompt templates, retrieval index and corpus version, tool schemas, policy configuration, decoding settings, cache and batching policy, and deployment region or hardware class where it materially affects behaviour. When an incident occurs, this record permits replay or bounded reconstruction without retaining more user data than the retention policy allows.
Recovery should also be tested for partial failure. A tool may finish after the model times out; a client may disconnect after an action was submitted; a new deployment may receive traffic while an old cache remains warm. Define the authoritative state, the reconciliation procedure, and the user-facing status in each case. These details prevent a service from turning an infrastructure fault into an untraceable model error.


Measure latency as a distribution, not one number
An average response time can be compatible with an unacceptable experience for a minority of requests. Long prompts may take longer to prefill; long outputs may occupy a decoder slot; tool calls may pause a response; and requests arriving during a burst may wait in a queue. Report median, p95, p99, timeout, and cancellation rates, together with the prompt-length, output-length, and request-class distributions. A service that looks fast on short prompts can be unusable for the document workflow it was intended to support.
Break the end-to-end trace into admission, queueing, prefill, decoding, retrieval, tool execution, safety checks, network transfer, and client rendering where the boundary is observable. The purpose is diagnosis. A rising p95 may originate in a new model, cache pressure, an index rebuild, a connector, or traffic composition. Without component traces, a team can make a costly model change to solve a queueing problem.


Code
latency_trace={"admission_ms":2,"queue_ms":47,"prefill_ms":210,"decode_ms":380,
               "tool_ms":0,"checks_ms":9,"network_ms":18}
print("end-to-end ms:",sum(latency_trace.values()))




Throughput depends on scheduling and fairness
Throughput is not simply a property of the model. It depends on concurrent requests, batch construction, memory reservation, scheduler policy, hardware topology, cache state, and the output lengths requested by users. Continuous batching can improve utilisation by inserting new work while existing sequences decode, but it can also make the timing of one request depend on others. State the scheduler policy and test it under realistic arrival patterns rather than a uniform synthetic load alone.
Fairness in serving is operational. A length-aware queue can protect short interactive requests while delaying long-context requests. A tenant quota can stop one client from exhausting capacity while making a high-volume legitimate workflow slower. A priority lane can protect an emergency task but requires an eligibility rule and audit record. Report latency, rejection, truncation, and fallback rates by request class so that efficiency improvements do not hide uneven service.


Caches require both a performance and a data policy
The key-value cache is a model-state optimisation during autoregressive decoding. A prefix cache can additionally reuse an identical initial context across requests. Both save work only under strict identity and isolation conditions. The key must bind the correct model and tokenizer versions, system prompt, retrieved context where applicable, and permission context. It must not permit one user’s context to become another user’s starting state.
Cache policies should describe what is stored, where, for how long, who can access it, and what triggers eviction. Memory pressure can cause queueing, an out-of-memory error, truncation, or a lower-concurrency mode. Test these paths. A cache hit rate is not sufficient evidence of a correct design; evaluate cross-user isolation, stale-context risk, and the quality effect of any truncation or summarisation used to preserve capacity.


Code
cache_record={"key_fields":["model","tokenizer","system prompt","authorisation context"],
              "ttl_minutes":15,"shared_across_users":False,"eviction":"least recently used",
              "pressure_action":"admit fewer long contexts"}
print(cache_record)




Release candidates need a matched comparison
Before a release, define the baseline, candidate, eligible request population, allocation method, duration, outcomes, safety checks, and rollback rule. A candidate that receives only easy traffic cannot be compared with a baseline handling the full request distribution. A test in which users retry after a bad response may also contaminate the apparent completion or satisfaction rate. Preserve assignment and retry paths in the analysis.
Compare release candidates on task outcome, refusal and fallback behaviour, latency distribution, token and tool cost, incident rate, and user burden. A lower cost is not a general improvement if it comes from truncating more contexts or sending hard cases to a human without reporting that route. For workflows with material consequences, stage the release under a defined human-review and recovery boundary before broad exposure.


Observability has a data-minimisation boundary
Logs help diagnose failures, evaluate drift, and investigate incidents. They can also retain sensitive prompts, documents, outputs, tool arguments, identifiers, and model-internal metadata. Decide which fields are necessary, which can be aggregated or redacted, how long raw traces are retained, who may query them, and how a user or organisation can request deletion where applicable. The retention policy should be tested against actual incident and debugging needs rather than assumed to be harmless.
Observability records need version links. A quality regression cannot be investigated if the trace lacks model, prompt, retrieval index, tool schema, policy, and deployment identifiers. At the same time, logging every raw input indefinitely creates its own exposure. The design problem is to retain enough information to reconstruct a failure under authorised review while limiting data collection and access.


Drift is a hypothesis about a changed system
Dataset-shift evaluations show that predictive uncertainty can itself become unreliable when the data distribution changes (Ovadia et al. 2019). A deployed AI system has several distributions and components that can change. Users may ask new questions, provide longer documents, switch languages, adopt a new interface, or retry differently. A retrieval corpus can be updated. A tool endpoint can alter its schema or availability. A safety policy can change what is refused. The model may remain fixed while the system outcome changes materially.
Start a drift investigation with a baseline window and a defined comparison window. Compare request characteristics, routing, model and prompt versions, retrieval and tool versions, latency components, output or outcome samples, and failure categories. Slice by task, language, user role, context length, and consequence where those dimensions are relevant. An aggregate metric can remain stable while one important workflow deteriorates.
When a change is observed, state competing explanations before selecting a remedy. A rise in hallucination reports may reflect a new knowledge domain, weaker retrieval, changed user expectations, or a reporting-interface change. A rise in latency may reflect traffic, cache pressure, model version, or an external service. The corrective action should follow the diagnosis: change a corpus, adjust routing, modify a prompt, add capacity, disable a tool, or roll back a release. Monitoring cannot decide this without a traceable configuration record.


Code
drift_compare={"baseline":{"long_context_share":.14,"p95_ms":820,"grounding_score":.76},
               "current":{"long_context_share":.31,"p95_ms":1260,"grounding_score":.68},
               "first_checks":["request length","retrieval index version","cache pressure","prompt version"]}
print(drift_compare)




Service-level objectives specify an acceptable operating region
A service-level objective (SLO) translates a user or organisational need into a measurable target. It may specify availability, p95 latency for an eligible request class, successful completion rate, tool-action correctness, or a rate of independently checked grounded answers. The target must name its denominator and exclusions. “99% available” is incomplete unless it states which requests, regions, dependencies, and time window count.
SLOs involve trade-offs. A strict latency objective can require shorter contexts, lower output budgets, more hardware, a simpler model, or a fallback. A strict quality objective can reduce throughput or increase human review. Define an error budget and the action when it is exhausted: pause a feature release, add capacity, narrow eligibility, or roll back. This makes reliability a decision rule rather than a retrospective dashboard.


Incidents require containment and learning
An incident can involve availability, data exposure, harmful output, unauthorised tool action, severe quality regression, or a combination. The immediate priority is containment: stop traffic, disable a tool, revoke a credential, isolate a corpus, or route requests to a safe fallback. The response should preserve authorised evidence, identify affected users or assets, and communicate status according to the consequence and policy.
Investigation then reconstructs the path. Which request or input class triggered the failure? Which model, prompt, policy, retrieval index, cache state, and tool version were active? Did a safeguard fail, or was the pathway outside its declared coverage? Corrective work should add a regression test that reproduces the failure under safe conditions. Closing an incident because a visible symptom disappeared does not demonstrate that the underlying pathway is controlled.


Code
incident={"signal":"unexpected tool calls","containment":"disable write scope","owner":"on-call lead",
          "evidence":"authorisation and request traces","correction":"validate structured arguments",
          "regression":"hostile retrieved-content test"}
print(incident)




Cost accounting must follow the served request
Cost is influenced by prompt and output length, batch utilisation, cache hits, model routing, hardware reservation, tool calls, retries, monitoring, human review, and incident work. Report a distribution or request-class table rather than one average. A cheap average can hide a small group of requests that consumes most compute or a fallback path that moves cost to staff.
For a change proposal, estimate both marginal and total cost. Adding a larger model for difficult requests may have a modest marginal cost at low volume and a large capacity cost at high volume. Adding a cache can reduce compute while adding memory and data-governance obligations. The decision record should state the assumed traffic volume, quality requirement, and resource constraint so that another team can revisit it when the workload changes.


The operational record connects the chapter’s mechanisms
For each production version, retain a concise record of the model and tokenizer, prompt and policy configuration, routing and batching rules, cache policy, hardware and region, retrieval and tool versions, eligible traffic, SLOs, monitoring fields, incident contacts, rollback procedure, data-retention policy, and evaluation evidence. This extends the reporting discipline proposed for model documentation (Mitchell et al. 2019) to the configuration that actually serves users. It is the minimum information required to interpret a latency number, a quality metric, or an incident report.
The record also establishes the boundary for Chapter 49. Safe and responsible use depends on service permissions, data handling, monitoring, and recovery as well as model behaviour. A model can be well evaluated offline and still be deployed through an unsafe operational configuration.


Test the service before and after deployment
Offline load tests should include the request-length and concurrency distributions expected in use, not only a batch of identical short prompts. Test cold starts, cache warm-up, long outputs, cancelled requests, dependency delays, retrieval failures, malformed tool responses, and traffic bursts. Confirm that metrics are emitted when the system degrades; an outage that also disables monitoring cannot be diagnosed from a normal dashboard.
Before broad release, run a staged test with the defined eligible population and fallback. After release, retain a small independent quality sample and compare it with the pre-release baseline. The objective is to detect a regression early, not to declare success because the service remained available. If the system changes a user-facing decision or action, include the human review and remedy path in the exercise.


Bounded claims about a deployed system
A credible serving claim can state that a named configuration achieved a defined p95 latency, completion rate, and independently checked task outcome for an eligible traffic population during a specified period. It should list major exclusions, fallback routes, and the monitoring that would detect a changed condition. It does not establish the same result for a different prompt policy, data source, hardware region, traffic pattern, or consequence level without new evidence.
This bounded account makes operational work cumulative. Later deployments can compare configuration records and investigate changes rather than rebuilding an explanation from anecdote. It also leaves a clear handoff to safety and governance: performance goals do not determine whether a system has appropriate permissions, user protections, or accountability.
The final operational question is therefore practical: when a measured objective conflicts with another requirement, who is authorised to decide, what evidence will they use, and how will the resulting change be tested and communicated? A service that cannot answer those questions has not completed its deployment design.
The answer should be recorded before a crisis, reviewed after each material change, and available to the people who operate, audit, and rely on the service.
It should include the authority to pause traffic, notify affected users, preserve authorised evidence, and require a verified regression test before restoration.

title: Serving, Deployment, and Monitoring
text:
Summary
Serving turns a model into a queueing, caching, and monitoring system with explicit rollout and recovery policies. Performance must be assessed in both service and outcome terms.

title: Serving, Deployment, and Monitoring
text:
Looking ahead
Operational controls can expose failures and limit their spread, but they do not define which threats a system must withstand or who is accountable when controls fail. Chapter 49 addresses those safety, security, data-handling, and governance decisions.

title: Safety, Security, and Responsible Use
text:
Chapter orientation
Safety work begins with a stated system, users, assets, and failure consequences. A general-purpose model can produce harmful content, follow malicious instructions embedded in retrieved material, disclose data supplied in a conversation, or fail in a high-consequence workflow. These are different risks and require different evidence. Model Cards provide a structured way to report intended uses, evaluation, and limitations (Mitchell et al. 2019), but a refusal rate or a model-card statement cannot substitute for threat modelling, controlled evaluation, access controls, and incident response.

title: Safety, Security, and Responsible Use
section: Level 1 - A safeguard addresses a defined failure
text:
Level 1 - A safeguard addresses a defined failure
Misuse concerns what a user may ask the system to do. Security concerns an adversary who manipulates inputs, tools, retrieval content, credentials, or surrounding infrastructure. Responsible use concerns whether the intended task has appropriate human oversight, redress, data handling, and accountability. The same output can be acceptable in one setting and unacceptable in another because the user, action, and consequences differ.

title: Safety, Security, and Responsible Use
section: Level 2 - Threat models identify trust boundaries
text:
Level 2 - Threat models identify trust boundaries
Prompt injection occurs when untrusted content attempts to redirect a model or tool from the application’s intended instructions. Retrieval, web pages, documents, tool outputs, and user text can all be untrusted. Treating retrieved text as if it were a trusted instruction is a design error. The application should separate data from authority, restrict tool permissions, validate arguments, and require confirmation before consequential actions.
The threat model should identify the attacker capability and the asset at risk. A malicious document might try to make a retrieval assistant reveal a secret, send an unauthorised message, or alter a database query. The relevant test is not whether the model notices a particular phrase, but whether the application preserves the permission boundary when hostile content is present. Tool outputs must be parsed as data and validated before reuse as an instruction or action.
Threat modelling should also distinguish accidental and deliberate failure. A user can paste confidential information without malicious intent; a model can misunderstand a policy even when all inputs are benign; an attacker can exploit the same interface deliberately. The response differs across these cases, but each needs a pathway from input to affected asset, consequence, detection method, and control. A broad label such as “unsafe output” obscures the intervention that is actually required.
Data exposure has separate routes: training memorisation, prompt and conversation retention, retrieval access, logs, caches, administrator access, and connected tools. Each route has different controls. A policy that focuses only on model output filtering can leave the more direct access path untouched.
Data governance begins before deployment. Define what data may be collected, why it is needed, which fields are sensitive, who can access raw and derived records, how long each is retained, and how deletion or correction requests are handled. This extends the documentation of collection, composition, and intended use proposed for datasets (Gebru et al. 2021) to records created while a service operates. Test access controls with accounts that have different roles. Redaction should be evaluated for the data formats the service actually receives, including attachments, tool responses, and quoted material, rather than on a narrow set of clean examples.

title: Safety, Security, and Responsible Use
section: Level 3 - Safeguards require tests and records
text:
Level 3 - Safeguards require tests and records
Safeguards can include authentication, least-privilege tool scopes, rate limits, content filters, structured outputs, human confirmation, retrieval provenance, output checks, and incident logging. Each has a coverage boundary and possible bypass. Test them with benign adversarial cases, representative user tasks, and failure scenarios that do not expose real secrets or harm people. Record model, prompt, policy, tool, retrieval, evaluator, and deployment versions.
Safety evaluation should specify a threshold and its consequence. A high block rate may reduce an intended service; a low block rate may leave a dangerous pathway open. Report false refusals, false acceptances, evaluator disagreement, the tested population, and the decision owner. For tool-enabled systems, evaluate the completed action and its authorisation record, not only the model’s textual response before a tool call.

Evaluation should follow the proposed use
An evaluation population is not simply a benchmark name. Define the users, requests, languages, data types, tools, and consequence levels that the deployment will cover. Include cases that the service should decline, route to a human, or handle through a constrained workflow. If a high-consequence decision is proposed, compare the system against the relevant existing process and specify which person or institution remains accountable for the final action.
Safety metrics should be decomposed by harm pathway. A result on harmful-content refusal does not measure unauthorised tool use. A prompt-injection test does not measure whether stored conversations can be accessed by the wrong account. A data-leakage test does not measure discriminatory error in a classification workflow. The assurance case should connect each claim to the test that supports it and name the untested pathways.


Code
assurance={"claim":"tool actions require user authority","evidence":"permission-boundary tests","limit":"unseen connector behaviour","owner":"service lead","review":"quarterly"}
print(assurance)


Red-team exercises are useful when they test an agreed threat model and produce a repairable finding. Preserve the scenario, system version, observed path, safeguard behaviour, severity assessment, corrective action, and regression test. Do not publish operational details that would make a harmful bypass easier, but do retain enough internal evidence to establish that a claimed control was tested.

title: Safety, Security, and Responsible Use
text:
Level 4 - Governance makes decisions reviewable
Governance assigns ownership for approving a use case, defining unacceptable outcomes, reviewing evaluation evidence, managing data retention, responding to incidents, and pausing or withdrawing a system. It should also specify what users can contest, how errors are corrected, and when a human must make the final decision. Aggregate safety scores are insufficient where harms are concentrated in one population or workflow.
A decision record should state the intended use, excluded uses, affected groups, evidence reviewed, residual risks accepted, accountable owner, review date, and trigger for reconsideration. This permits a later reviewer to see whether a system changed beyond its approval boundary. It also distinguishes an organisational decision from a property claimed for the model.
Redress needs an operational path. Users and affected parties should be able to report an error, obtain a correction where possible, and receive a response proportionate to the consequence. Incident analysis should ask whether the failure arose from model behaviour, interface design, data access, tool permission, or inadequate human review; the corrective action follows from that diagnosis.
Governance also needs a review cadence. A model, retrieval corpus, connected tool, policy, or user population can change after the original approval. Set review dates and change triggers, such as a new high-consequence workflow, a material model update, a sustained drift signal, or an incident. Reassessment should revisit the original threat model and decision record, not merely confirm that the service remains available.

Approval has a scope boundary
An approval should cover a named system configuration and use case, not a model in the abstract. Changing a model provider, enabling a new tool, adding a retrieval corpus, extending access to another user group, or changing retention can alter the threat model. Classify these changes before release: some may be routine configuration changes, while others require a new evaluation, privacy review, or decision by the accountable owner.
Document residual risk in language that supports a decision. State the plausible failure, affected asset or person, control in place, evidence of its performance, remaining uncertainty, and the action if the risk materialises. This is more useful than a generic statement that a system is “safe”, because it permits users and reviewers to see what was accepted and why.


User communication is part of the control
Users need to know when an output is generated, what sources or tools were used where this matters, what data will be retained, and when a response should not be relied upon. Interfaces should make escalation and correction possible without forcing users to reveal unnecessary personal information. Where an action is blocked or delayed, a clear explanation can prevent unsafe workarounds and gives the organisation evidence about a safeguard’s practical cost.
Post-incident communication should separate known facts from open investigation. Preserve records needed for accountability, correct the immediate exposure or erroneous action, notify affected parties according to the consequence and applicable policy, and test the corrective change against the pathway that produced the incident. Closing an incident because the visible output has stopped does not establish that the underlying access or governance failure has been repaired.


Map harms to assets, actors, and controls
Safety and security work becomes actionable when a risk statement identifies who can be affected, what asset is at stake, what the system does, and how a failure reaches a consequence. The asset may be a person’s privacy, an organisation’s records, a user’s autonomy, a financial resource, a physical environment, or the integrity of a decision process. The actor may be an ordinary user, an authorised operator acting in error, a malicious outsider, a compromised tool, or a model component responding to an ambiguous instruction.
The same capability can sit in different harm pathways. A summarisation model may omit a material qualification in an internal draft, expose a confidential paragraph through a retrieval error, or produce a persuasive but unsupported public statement. Each pathway has a different control: review and source citation for the first, permission and retrieval isolation for the second, and publication workflow and accountability for the third. A single “safety score” cannot show whether these controls are present or effective.


Code
risk_paths=[
 {"asset":"private document","path":"retrieval permission error","control":"account-bound access check"},
 {"asset":"financial action","path":"injected tool argument","control":"schema validation plus confirmation"},
 {"asset":"user decision","path":"unsupported confident answer","control":"evidence display and human review"},
]
for path in risk_paths: print(path)




Misuse analysis requires a proportionate response
Some requests are clearly outside an application’s intended use. Others are legitimate in one context and harmful in another. A chemistry explanation may support education or facilitate an unsafe action; a document-analysis tool may be appropriate for an authorised employee and inappropriate for an unverified account. The response should reflect the capability, user context, available evidence, and consequence rather than rely on a brittle keyword list.
Define the intended use, excluded use, escalation route, and uncertainty policy before release. A refusal should be evaluated for both false acceptance and false refusal. It should not expose sensitive details, but it can explain the available safe alternative or route the user to an authorised process. For a tool-enabled service, blocking text alone is insufficient if an equivalent tool action remains available through a different prompt or retrieved instruction.


Security controls need adversarial testing
Prompt injection is one way untrusted content can alter a system. Other paths include malicious file attachments, compromised retrieval sources, tool-output manipulation, credential leakage, insecure logging, dependency compromise, and interface confusion that causes a user to approve an action they do not understand. The threat model should state which actors can control each input and which permissions the system holds at that boundary.
Test controls with safe adversarial scenarios. For example, place hostile instructions in a retrieved document and verify that the model can quote or summarise the document without treating it as authority. Provide malformed tool output and verify that parsers reject it. Attempt an action with a token that lacks the required scope. Test a confirmation interface with an ambiguous request. Preserve the outcome, version, and residual weakness for regression testing. These tests assess the application boundary, not only the model’s ability to identify suspicious wording.


Sensitive data requires lifecycle controls
Data protection covers collection, transmission, processing, storage, review, retention, sharing, and deletion. A model may receive sensitive information in a prompt, an image, a retrieved record, a tool response, a cache entry, or a log. Identify the purpose for each field and avoid retaining material merely because it could be useful later. Separate production access from debugging access, and ensure that support or evaluation staff do not receive broader data than their role requires.
Deletion and correction procedures should be tested. A request may require removal from a retrieval index, cache, conversation store, audit log, derived dataset, or access-control list. Some records may need retention for legal, security, or accountability reasons; if so, the policy should state the basis, access restriction, and duration. A generic promise that data are “secure” does not explain how a system handles these distinct stores.


Human oversight must have authority and information
Human review is useful only when the reviewer can understand the decision, has enough evidence to challenge it, and has authority to change the outcome. A reviewer who receives a fluent model answer without source material, uncertainty, tool trace, or time to inspect cannot provide meaningful oversight. Define the review trigger, materials shown, time budget, escalation authority, and record of the final decision.
The human role changes by workflow. In a low-consequence creative application, it may be the user’s choice to regenerate or discard an output. In a high-consequence administrative process, an authorised professional may need to make the final decision and document reasons. Do not describe these different arrangements with one generic “human in the loop” label. The system should be evaluated with the actual oversight procedure it will use.


Fairness and access need task-specific evidence
An AI system can perform differently across language, disability-related access need, geography, device type, image quality, writing style, or institutional role. The relevant groups and fairness criteria depend on the task; Model Cards similarly require evaluation to state its population, factors, and limitations (Mitchell et al. 2019). Start by asking whose inputs, outcomes, burdens, and remedies could differ. Then collect or construct evaluation slices that make those differences measurable, while avoiding claims about groups that the available data cannot support.
Assess not only error rates but also access to the service, refusal patterns, latency, escalation, and the quality of redress. A system that has similar average accuracy but consistently routes one language group to a slower fallback has an operational disparity. A system that blocks legitimate requests from a group at a high rate has a different problem from one that produces more incorrect answers. Report the mechanism and consequence rather than applying a generic fairness label.


An assurance case links a decision to evidence
An assurance case is a structured account of why a system is considered acceptable for a stated use. It does not assert that risk is absent. It identifies a claim, the evidence that supports it, the assumptions that limit it, the controls that reduce a failure path, the residual risk, and the accountable decision maker. The format is useful because it exposes gaps: a claim about tool safety may have evidence from permission tests but no evidence about a new connector; a claim about data handling may cover prompts but omit caches or evaluation exports.
Keep the assurance case proportionate to consequence. A small internal drafting tool may need a concise use boundary, access rule, and incident contact. A system that affects eligibility, money, health, safety, legal status, or public information needs stronger evidence, independent review where appropriate, and a clear route for correction or appeal. The standard is not one document length; it is whether the evidence matches the harm pathway and decision consequence.


Code
assurance_case={
 "use":"authorised document triage", "claim":"no write action without user authority",
 "evidence":["scope tests","injection tests","confirmation audit"],
 "assumptions":["connector schema unchanged"], "residual_risk":"novel interface confusion",
 "owner":"service manager", "review_trigger":"new tool or high-severity incident"
}
print(assurance_case)




Change management reopens the relevant evidence
An approval cannot be transferred automatically to a changed system. A model update can alter refusal and tool-use behaviour. A new retrieval corpus can introduce confidential, malicious, or low-quality material. A different prompt template can change output format and grounding. A new user population can alter consequence and accessibility needs. Classify changes according to their likely effect, then specify whether the existing evaluation is sufficient, whether a regression suite is required, or whether the use case must be reviewed again.
Preserve a versioned decision record: system components, intended use, excluded use, evaluators, results, residual risk, owners, approvals, and date. Link incidents and user complaints to that record. This allows a reviewer to establish which configuration was authorised at the time of a decision and whether a later change moved the system beyond its evaluated boundary.


Transparency should support contestability
Users do not need every implementation detail, but they need information that changes how they can act. Explain when an output is automated, what input sources it used when relevant, what it cannot determine, whether an action will be taken, what data is retained, and how to seek correction or human review. Avoid notices that merely shift responsibility to users while withholding the evidence required to identify an error.
Contestability is especially important when a system influences another person’s options or access. Provide a route to challenge an output, submit corrected information, understand the review decision, and obtain a response within a stated process. Measure whether this route is accessible across languages, devices, and user roles. A remedy that exists only in policy but cannot be reached in practice is not an effective safeguard.


A responsible-use conclusion is conditional
The evidence in this chapter supports conditional statements. A system may be acceptable for authorised users, a specific data source, limited tool scopes, a defined workflow, and a stated review process. It may be inappropriate when permissions broaden, new data enters retrieval, users need an appeal, or the consequence becomes higher. The conditions should be visible to operators and users, then revisited as the system changes.
This does not make safety analysis an obstacle to technical work. It makes the relevant technical work visible: permission checks, data isolation, evaluation design, logging controls, interface decisions, version records, and recovery procedures. Chapter 48 supplies the operational infrastructure for many of these controls. Together, the two chapters establish that responsible use is maintained through ongoing evidence and decisions, not attached to a model at release.
The final question for every deployment is therefore specific: which risks remain, who has accepted them, what evidence supports that decision, and what event will require the decision to be revisited? Recording and testing that answer is a practical form of accountability.
It also provides a durable basis for independent review, user remedy, and organisational learning after a system changes or an incident occurs.
Responsible use is therefore a claim about an organisation’s choices under stated conditions. It can be audited through records of intended and excluded uses, evaluation evidence, access decisions, residual risk, incident response, and remedies. It should not be presented as a trait automatically supplied by a model architecture or a content filter.

title: Safety, Security, and Responsible Use
text:
Common misconceptions

A refusal solves a security problem. Tool permissions and trust boundaries remain necessary.
Retrieved text is trusted because it came from a database. Its source and authority must be assessed.
A safety benchmark covers deployment risk. Live workflows, users, and integrations add failure paths.
Logging is harmless by default. It can itself create data-exposure risk.

Summary
Responsible AI deployment joins safeguards to explicit threats, evidence, ownership, and response. Security boundaries, data handling, and human accountability cannot be inferred from model quality alone.

title: Safety, Security, and Responsible Use
text:
Closing perspective
The handbook has followed machine-learning systems from prediction and optimisation to representations, reasoning procedures, deployment, and governance. Across those levels, a model claim is only as strong as the task definition, evidence, implementation conditions, and limits attached to it. The same discipline applies when the system changes: state the mechanism, measure the relevant outcome, record the resources and risks, and assign responsibility for decisions that the model cannot make on its own.

title: Appendix A — Concepts and Notation

Foundations
This appendix is generated from the marked concept boxes in the chapters. Definitions remain authored at their first conceptual home.

title: Appendix A — Concepts and Notation
text:
Activation function
Core concept; Chapter 7: activation functions.
Activation function. A fixed, usually coordinate-wise non-linear transformation applied to a layer’s pre-activations. Activations allow stacked layers to represent relationships that a composition of affine transformations cannot. An activation used inside a hidden layer has a different role from an output transformation interpreted as a probability.


Artificial neuron
Core concept; Chapter 5: artificial neuron.
Artificial neuron. A unit that forms a weighted sum of input values, adds a bias, and may pass the result through an activation function. The weighted sum is an affine calculation; non-linearity enters only when an activation is applied. A neuron’s weights are parameters, but not every model parameter is a connection weight.


Backpropagation
Core concept; Chapter 4: backpropagation.
Backpropagation. A method for calculating derivatives of a model’s scalar loss with respect to its parameters by applying the chain rule backwards through the recorded forward computation. It calculates gradients; an optimiser uses those gradients to choose parameter updates.


Gradient descent
Core concept; Chapter 3: gradient descent.
Gradient descent. An optimisation procedure that changes parameters in the direction expected to reduce a stated loss locally. The gradient records how that loss changes with each parameter, and the learning rate sets the size of one update. A lower loss after an update is evidence about the specified objective, not a general guarantee about future performance.


Loss, metric, and objective
Distinction; Chapter 2: models predictions loss.
Loss, metric, and objective. A loss scores one prediction against a target. A metric reports a property relevant to evaluation or use. An objective is the quantity that the training procedure is instructed to optimise, which may combine a loss with penalties or constraints. The same formula can appear in more than one role, but the roles are not interchangeable.


Machine learning
Core concept; Chapter 1: what is machine learning.
Machine learning. A procedure that fits a parameterised mapping from inputs to outputs using examples and a stated objective. Training changes the fitted parameters; inference applies the resulting model to new inputs. A prediction can be useful without establishing that its inputs cause the outcome.


Model, parameters, prediction, target, and loss
Core concept; Chapter 2: models predictions loss.
Model, parameters, prediction, target, and loss. A model maps an input to a prediction through fitted parameters. The target is the observed outcome against which that prediction is assessed. A loss turns their discrepancy into a number that the training procedure can reduce; it does not by itself decide whether the resulting prediction serves the intended use.


Neural-network layer
Core concept; Chapter 6: neural network layers.
Neural-network layer. A shared transformation applied across a batch or sequence of representations. Its weight matrix and bias vector define how input coordinates are combined into output coordinates; broadcasting applies the same bias to each relevant observation. Layer shape determines both the representation interface and the number of trainable parameters.


Training loop
Core concept; Chapter 8: small neural network.
Training loop. The repeated sequence that selects a batch, runs a forward calculation, evaluates a loss, calculates gradients, and updates parameters. Its state includes more than model weights when resuming a run: optimiser state, random-number state, data order, and fitted preprocessing can change later updates or predictions.

title: Appendix A — Concepts and Notation
text:
Training and evaluation

Generalisation and overfitting
Core concept; Chapter 9: generalisation overfitting.
Generalisation and overfitting. Generalisation is performance on observations not used to fit or select the procedure, within a stated target population. Overfitting occurs when an apparent training improvement relies on details that do not transfer. Neither label can be inferred from training loss alone.


Training, validation, and test sets
Distinction; Chapter 9: generalisation overfitting.
Training, validation, and test sets. Training data estimate parameters. Validation data support choices among procedures or checkpoints and therefore belong to development. A test set is reserved for the final assessment after those choices are fixed. A held-out set is excluded from the particular fitting or selection stage under discussion; it is not automatically an untouched final test set.
